Staff Software Engineer · UKG · Development track

Development: Staff Software Engineer

This tab prepares for Staff Software Engineer roles at UKG that focus on building products, not on test platforms. The postings ask for large-scale distributed systems in Java or Python, multi-tenant SaaS, data, messaging, observability, cloud and AI-first engineering. Some also ask for React. The DevOps 1 and DevOps 2 tabs hold the test-platform and architecture-and-leadership material. This tab links to them where they help.

How each question works

Read the interviewer quote. Say the 30-second answer out loud, then stop. Read the full answer only when you need depth. Learn each concept card.

Start with the gap

The postings ask for Java or Python at depth. Your strongest stack is JavaScript and TypeScript. Start with the Java basics lesson, then the Java practice problems, and prepare an honest gap answer (DV12).

Use real stories only

Fill the design portfolio in DV13 with systems you really built. Never claim back-end ownership that you did not have. Say what you owned and what you learned.

Study sessions, in this order

  1. Session 1Read What these roles ask and the Workforce management primer. Then Java basics for a JavaScript developer: type the example and run it. Say DV12 out loud.
  2. Session 2Java lessons on the runtime and concurrency, then Spring Boot and REST, and the data lesson. Write the Java solutions from memory (DV16 to DV18). Say DV7 to DV9.
  3. Session 3Messaging, multi-tenant SaaS and observability lessons. Then do the design prompts DV1 to DV3 on paper, 35 minutes each.
  4. Session 4Cloud, security and quality lessons. Then DV4 to DV6 and DV10 to DV11.
  5. Session 5Front-end architecture lesson (strong ground for you) and DV15. Fill your design portfolio in DV13.
  6. Session 6Read the AI questions in DevOps 2 (AI1 to AI9) and the leadership questions (LD1 to LD20). Pick five questions to ask them.

Chapter 02

Workforce management primer

Many UKG roles are about workforce management (WFM). If you know the words, you can design better examples and ask better questions.

Eight terms to know
TermMeaningWhy it matters
PunchOne clock-in or clock-out event from a device, app or web page.Arrives in bursts at shift start and end.
TimecardThe record of a worker's punches and hours for a pay period.Managers edit and approve it. It must keep an audit trail.
Pay rulesRules that turn hours into pay: overtime, breaks, shift differentials and rounding.Rules differ by country, state, union and customer. Treat them as versioned data.
AccrualTime off that a worker earns, such as vacation or sick leave.Computed from hours and policy. It must be correct and explainable.
ScheduleWho works which shift, where and when.Needs forecasts, skills, availability and labour-law checks.
ForecastA prediction of demand, such as customers per hour.Drives how many workers to schedule.
ComplianceLabour law, fair-workweek and union rules.A wrong result can cause fines. Show the reason for each decision.
Pay period closeThe deadline when hours go to payroll.Creates a predictable load peak and a hard correctness need.

Tip UKG publishes Pro WFM REST domains such as Scheduling, Timekeeping, Timecards, Forecasting, Leave and Attendance. Use these words in your answers.

Chapter 03

Concepts: Java, data, messaging, platform

Twelve lessons. The first one teaches Java from a JavaScript point of view. Do it first. Each lesson has the problem it solves, a table or example, and one line to remember.

Lesson 01

The problem it solvesYou read Java well but have not used it at work. Most Java ideas map to something you already know in TypeScript. Learn the differences, and you can talk about Java with confidence.

IdeaJavaScript or TypeScriptJava
TypesDynamic. TypeScript checks at build time and then erases types.Static and checked by the compiler. Types stay in the bytecode.
Run modelNode or the browser runs the source. One main thread plus an event loop.javac builds bytecode. The JVM runs it. Many threads share memory.
Code layoutModules with import and export.Every class lives in a package. One public class per file. The file name matches the class name.
ClassesClass, prototype, duck typing.Class, interface, abstract class, enum, record. Inheritance is explicit. A class has one parent and many interfaces.
Data shapeObject literal {a: 1}.A class or a record. You cannot add fields at run time.
Nullnull and undefined.Only null. Using null causes NullPointerException. Return Optional for a result that may be missing.
Equality=== compares values for primitives.== compares references for objects. Use equals() to compare content.
CollectionsArray, Map, Set.List, Map, Set interfaces. ArrayList, HashMap, HashSet and others implement them. You choose the implementation.
GenericsTypeScript generics are erased.Generics are erased too, but the compiler enforces them. List<String>.
FunctionsFirst-class functions.Lambdas implement functional interfaces such as Function, Predicate and Runnable.
AsyncPromises and async/await.Threads, executors and CompletableFuture. Virtual threads in Java 21 make blocking code cheap.
Errorsthrow and try/catch. Any value can be thrown.Exceptions are classes. Checked exceptions must be declared or caught. Unchecked ones need not be.
Packagesnpm and package.json.Maven or Gradle. Dependencies in pom.xml or build.gradle. Artefacts are JAR files.
TestsJest, Vitest, Cypress.JUnit 5 and Mockito. Run by Maven or Gradle.
  • Primitives and wrappers: int and double are primitives. Integer and Double are objects. Collections hold objects. Boxing converts between them. Unboxing a null throws.
  • Access modifiers: public, protected, package-private (the default) and private.
  • static means it belongs to the class, not to an object. final means it cannot be reassigned.
  • Strings are immutable. Use StringBuilder in loops. Compare with equals.
  • Interfaces define a contract. Program to the interface: List<String> x = new ArrayList<>();.
  • Enums are a fixed set of constants. They can have fields and methods.
  • Records (Java 16 and later) give an immutable data class with equals, hashCode and toString for free.
  • var (Java 10 and later) lets the compiler infer a local variable type.
Build tool pieceWhat it does
Maven pom.xmlDeclares dependencies, plugins and the build lifecycle: validate, compile, test, package, verify, install, deploy.
Gradle build.gradleThe same job with a script. Faster incremental builds.
Standard layoutsrc/main/java for code. src/test/java for tests. src/main/resources for config.
mvn test or gradle testCompile and run the unit tests.
Spring Boot application.ymlConfiguration for a service. Profiles select the environment.

To practise: type the program above into a file named Demo.java, then run javac Demo.java and java Demo. Change one rule at a time and predict the output before you run it.

RememberJava is statically typed, class-based and runs on the JVM. Learn equals versus ==, null and Optional, collections, interfaces and Maven. Your TypeScript skills transfer.

Lesson 02

The problem it solvesThe postings ask for Java at depth. A Staff interviewer will not test syntax. He will test if you understand the runtime, correctness and trade-offs.

TopicWhat to knowWhy it matters
Memory and GCHeap (objects) and stack (calls). G1 is the default collector. ZGC offers low pauses. Objects that stay referenced cannot be collected.Explains leaks, long pauses and out-of-memory errors.
equals and hashCodeEqual objects must have equal hash codes. Mutable keys break a HashMap.A common source of lost entries.
ImmutabilityFinal fields, no setters, defensive copies. Records give immutable data classes (Java 16 and later).Immutable objects are safe to share between threads.
CollectionsArrayList, LinkedList, HashMap, TreeMap, ConcurrentHashMap. Know the cost of get, add and iterate.Wrong choice means slow code.
Streams and OptionalStreams express transform and filter steps. Do not use a stream for tiny loops or for side effects. Do not return null. Use Optional for a return value that may be empty.Readable code and fewer null errors.
ExceptionsChecked versus unchecked. Use try-with-resources to close resources. Do not swallow exceptions.Resource leaks and hidden failures.
Modern JavaRecords, sealed types, pattern matching for switch and virtual threads are final in Java 21.Shows you keep current.

The JVM runs bytecode. The JIT compiler turns hot code into machine code at run time. A service is slow at the start and faster after warm-up. This matters for cold starts and for autoscaling.

Garbage collection
Idea

The JVM frees objects that nothing can reach.

Example

A cache that holds old requests keeps them alive. Memory grows.

Term

Automatic memory management with generational and region-based collectors.

Happens-before
Idea

A rule that makes one thread's write visible to another.

Example

A volatile write is visible to later reads of that field.

Term

The memory-model ordering guarantee between actions in different threads.

RememberKnow the JVM memory model, equals and hashCode, immutability, collections cost, stream limits and exception handling. Explain trade-offs, not syntax.

Lesson 03

The problem it solvesBack-end services handle many requests at once. Bugs in shared state are rare, hard to find and expensive.

ToolUse it forWatch out for
synchronized and ReentrantLockProtect a short critical section.Deadlock, long holds and lock contention.
volatileVisibility of one flag or reference.It does not make a compound action like count++ atomic.
Atomic classes (AtomicInteger, LongAdder)Lock-free counters.Only single variables.
ConcurrentHashMapA shared map with high concurrency. Use compute and merge for atomic updates.check-then-put is not atomic.
ExecutorServiceA bounded pool of worker threads.An unbounded queue hides overload. Always bound it.
CompletableFutureCompose async steps.Run blocking calls on a separate pool. Handle exceptions.
Virtual threads (Java 21)Many cheap threads for blocking I/O code.They do not speed up CPU-bound work. Avoid pinning with long synchronized blocks.
  • Deadlock needs four things: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no pre-emption and a circular wait. Break one of them. The simplest fix is a fixed lock order.
  • Thread-safe by design beats thread-safe by locks: immutable data, no shared state, and message passing.
  • For a request-per-thread server, the thread pool size is a capacity limit. Size it from the work type: CPU-bound near the core count, I/O-bound larger.

RememberShare less. Prefer immutable data and atomics. Bound every pool. Use virtual threads for blocking I/O on Java 21. Never assume check-then-act is atomic.

Lesson 04

The problem it solvesMost Java SaaS back ends use Spring Boot. You should be able to draw one and name the common failures.

  1. Controller: validates input and maps HTTP to a call
  2. Service: business rules and transaction boundary
  3. Repository: data access with JPA or SQL
  4. Database
  5. Client: calls to other services, with timeouts and retries
TopicWhat to know
Dependency injectionSpring creates and wires beans. Prefer constructor injection. It makes classes easy to test.
@TransactionalWorks through a proxy. A call from inside the same class skips the proxy and the transaction. By default it rolls back on unchecked exceptions only.
N+1 queriesLoading a list and then one query per row. Fix with a join fetch, a batch size or a purpose-built query.
Lazy loadingTouching a lazy field outside a transaction gives an exception. Return DTOs, not entities.
Connection poolA fixed pool of database connections (HikariCP). A slow query holds a connection. A full pool makes every request wait.
REST designNouns for resources, correct status codes, pagination, filtering, versioning and idempotency keys for unsafe retries.
Validation and errorsValidate at the edge. Return one error format with a stable code. Do not leak stack traces.
ResilienceTimeouts on every call. Retries with backoff for safe calls. Circuit breaker for slow dependencies.
TestingJUnit and Mockito for units. Slice tests for the web layer. Testcontainers for real database tests.

RememberController, service, repository. Know where the transaction starts, how the connection pool limits you, and how N+1 and self-invocation hurt.

Lesson 05

The problem it solvesEvery design question ends at the data store. A wrong choice is hard to reverse.

StoreGood atWeak atExample in WFM
Relational (Postgres, SQL Server, MySQL)Transactions, joins, constraints, ad hoc queriesHuge write volume on one node, schema changes at scaleEmployees, pay rules, timecard approvals
Document (MongoDB)Flexible nested documents, fast reads by keyCross-document transactions and joins are weakerA schedule document with nested shifts
Wide-column (Cassandra)Very high write volume, linear scale, multi-regionNo joins. You must design tables for each queryRaw punch events by device and time
Key-value or cache (Redis)Very low latencyNot a system of recordSession data, rate limits
Column store and warehouse (BigQuery, Snowflake)Large analytics scansNot for single-row transactionsLabour cost reports
  • Indexes speed up reads and slow down writes. Index the columns in your filters and sorts. A composite index follows the order of its columns.
  • Isolation: Postgres defaults to read committed. Higher levels stop more anomalies and cost more. Know dirty read, non-repeatable read and phantom read.
  • Optimistic locking uses a version column. A conflicting update fails and the caller retries. It suits low-conflict edits like a timecard change.
  • Cassandra modelling starts from the queries. Choose a partition key that spreads load and keeps one query on one partition. Avoid unbounded partitions.
  • Schema change without downtime: expand, migrate, contract. Add the new column, write both, backfill, switch reads, remove the old one.
  • Partitioning by tenant limits the blast radius and makes per-tenant moves possible. Watch for a very large tenant.

RememberChoose by access pattern and consistency need. Relational by default. Wide-column for extreme write volume. Always say what you give up.

Lesson 06

The problem it solvesThe postings ask for messaging and event-driven design. You need to compare the two tools and know the failure cases.

KafkaRabbitMQ
ModelA distributed log. Consumers track their own offset.A broker with exchanges, queues and bindings. Messages are removed after acknowledgement.
StrengthHigh throughput, replay, many independent readers, stream processing.Flexible routing, per-message acknowledgement, task queues, low latency.
OrderGuaranteed within one partition.Order within one queue, but not once there are several consumers.
Scaling consumersUp to the number of partitions in a group.Add consumers to a queue.
Use forEvent streams: punches, audit trails, change data capture.Work distribution: send an email, run a job.
  • Delivery: assume at-least-once. Make consumers idempotent. Exactly-once is possible inside Kafka with idempotent producers and transactions, but not across your database without extra design.
  • Ordering: choose a message key, such as the employee id, so related events go to one partition.
  • Consumer lag is the gap between the newest offset and the consumer's offset. Alert on it.
  • Poison messages: send them to a dead-letter topic after a few tries.
  • Schema evolution: use a schema registry with compatible changes. Never break old consumers.
  • Outbox pattern: write the event in the same transaction as the data change, then publish it.

The DevOps 2 tab has more on this: AR4 covers queue versus log. AR5 covers one action that updates three services.

RememberKafka is a replayable log. RabbitMQ is a routing queue. Assume duplicates and design idempotent consumers. Key by what must stay in order.

Lesson 07

The problem it solvesEvery UKG posting mentions multi-tenant SaaS. A wrong boundary leaks one customer's data to another.

ModelHowGoodCost
Shared tables with a tenant idOne schema. Every row has tenant_id.Cheapest. Easy to scale out.One missing filter leaks data. Hard to move one tenant.
Schema per tenantOne database, one schema each.Better isolation. Per-tenant backup.Many schemas make migrations slow.
Database per tenantSeparate databases.Strong isolation. Easy to move or delete a tenant.Highest cost and operations load.
HybridShared for small tenants. Dedicated for big ones.Balances cost and risk.Two models to run.
  • Tenant context: resolve the tenant from the token at the edge. Carry it in the request context and in log fields. Never read it from a client-controlled field alone.
  • Enforce in the data layer: use row-level security or a mandatory filter in the repository. Do not rely on every developer to add a WHERE clause.
  • Noisy neighbours: per-tenant rate limits, queues and quotas. Give very large tenants separate capacity.
  • Per-tenant configuration: feature flags, pay rules and branding stored as data, versioned and cached.
  • Peaks: WFM load peaks at shift change and at pay period close. Use queues and autoscale on queue depth.
  • Data residency: some customers need data to stay in a region. Plan a regional deployment model.

RememberPick an isolation level by risk and cost. Resolve the tenant at the edge. Enforce it in the data layer. Limit noisy neighbours. Plan for peaks.

Lesson 08

The problem it solvesThe postings name Grafana, OpenTelemetry, Kibana, Datadog and Splunk. Staff engineers own service health.

SignalAnswersTools
MetricsIs it healthy? Is it getting worse?Prometheus, Grafana, Datadog
LogsWhat happened in this request?Kibana, Splunk, Datadog logs
TracesWhere did the time go across services?OpenTelemetry, Datadog APM, Jaeger
  • Golden signals: latency, traffic, errors and saturation. Start every dashboard there.
  • RED for services: rate, errors, duration. USE for resources: utilisation, saturation, errors.
  • OpenTelemetry is a vendor-neutral standard for traces, metrics and logs. Instrument once and send to any back end.
  • Structured logs with a trace id, tenant id and request id. Never log secrets or personal data.
  • SLOs and burn-rate alerts: see AR7 in DevOps 2.
  • Cardinality: a label with millions of values (such as user id) breaks a metrics store. Put such data in logs or traces.
  • Incident habit: a runbook, an owner, a timeline and a blameless review.

RememberMetrics for health, logs for detail, traces for the path. Use OpenTelemetry to avoid lock-in. Alert on SLO burn, not on every spike.

The problem it solvesThe postings accept any of the three clouds. You know AWS. Map your knowledge to the other two.

NeedAWSGCPAzure

Managed KubernetesEKSGKEAKS

Object storageS3Cloud StorageBlob Storage
Managed relational DBRDS or AuroraCloud SQL or AlloyDBAzure SQL Database
Queue or streamSQS, Kinesis, MSKPub/SubService Bus, Event Hubs
Data warehouseRedshiftBigQuerySynapse
IdentityIAM rolesIAM and service accountsEntra ID and managed identities
  • Managed services first. Run less. Buy reliability. Check lock-in and cost.
  • Infrastructure as Code (Terraform) makes environments repeatable and reviewable. Use modules and remote state.
  • Kubernetes basics are in the DevOps 1 tab, chapter K0.
  • Cost (FinOps): tag everything, right-size, autoscale, use committed use or savings plans for steady load and Spot for fault-tolerant work. See AR11.
  • Reliability: multiple zones by default. Multi-region only when the business needs it and pays for it.

RememberLearn the equivalents. Prefer managed services. Use Terraform. Tag and measure cost.

Lesson 10

The problem it solvesThe full-stack postings ask for expert React and TypeScript. This is your strongest ground. Give clear, structured answers.

AreaWhat a Staff answer covers
Rendering strategyClient-side, server-side, static and streaming. Choose by data freshness, SEO and time to first paint.
PerformanceCore Web Vitals: LCP for loading, INP for responsiveness and CLS for stability. Set a budget. Split bundles. Lazy load. Virtualise long lists.
StateServer state (a query cache) is not client state. Keep global state small. Colocate state near its use.
Data visualisationSVG for hundreds of points. Canvas or WebGL for many thousands. Aggregate on the server for huge sets.
Real-time dataWebSockets or Server-Sent Events. Handle reconnect, back-pressure and out-of-order updates.
Design systemTokens, accessible components, versioning, a migration path and a clear owner. Support theming and white-labelling.
Micro-frontendsIndependent deploys per team. Costs: duplicated dependencies, shared state and testing across parts. Use only when team scale needs it.
AccessibilityWCAG 2.1 AA: keyboard use, focus, contrast, labels and screen reader names. Test with tools and by hand.
SecurityEscape output, use a content security policy, keep tokens out of local storage where you can, and mask personal data in the UI.
API layerREST or GraphQL. A backend-for-frontend shapes data per client. Contract tests keep both sides honest.

Use your real work: the micro-frontend platform and the shared component library. For each, say the scale, the decision, the trade-off and the result.

RememberPick the rendering mode by need, budget performance, separate server state, make accessibility a default and use micro-frontends only for team scale.

Lesson 11

The problem it solvesWorkforce data holds pay, schedules and personal details. The postings stress privacy and compliance.

TopicWhat to know
AuthenticationOIDC on top of OAuth 2.0. Short-lived access tokens and refresh tokens. Validate signature, issuer, audience and expiry.
AuthorisationRBAC for roles. ABAC for rules on attributes such as location or department. Check on the server for every request.
Data protectionTLS in transit. Encryption at rest with managed keys. Mask personal data in logs and UIs. Collect the minimum.
AuditAn append-only log of who changed what and when. Needed for pay disputes and compliance.
Common attacksKnow the OWASP Top 10: broken access control, injection, insecure design, vulnerable components and others.
SecretsA secrets manager. Rotate. Short-lived workload identities. Never in code or images.
Supply chainPin dependencies. Scan them. Review third-party actions and packages.

Broken access control is the most common failure in multi-tenant systems. Test it directly: try to read tenant B's data with tenant A's token.

RememberAuthenticate, authorise on the server, protect data, audit changes and test for broken access control.

Lesson 12

The problem it solvesThe postings ask for the testing pyramid, CI/CD oversight and an AI-first mindset. This is also your background.

LayerShareTools
UnitMost tests. Fast and isolated.JUnit, Mockito
IntegrationReal database and queue in a container.Testcontainers
ContractConsumer and provider agree on the API.Pact or schema checks
End-to-endA few critical paths.Playwright, Selenium, Cypress
  • CI/CD: build once, test in stages, deploy the same artefact through environments, and roll back fast. Details are in the DevOps 1 tab.
  • Technical debt: list it, link it to cost, and reserve a fixed share of time.
  • AI-first engineering (the postings' wording): use AI tools across design, code, tests, docs and troubleshooting, with clear rules. The author owns every change. Humans review. No secrets or customer data in prompts. See the AI chapter in DevOps 2, questions AI4 and AI7.
  • Measure: the four DORA metrics, not lines of code.

RememberMany unit tests, some integration and contract tests, few end-to-end tests. Use AI with rules and measure outcomes.

Chapter 04

System design questions

Design prompts for a Staff Software Engineer. Use the same shape each time: ask about the needs, name the trade-offs, choose, then say how you would check it works.

UKG-DV1

Interviewer

Architect: "Design a platform that collects clock-in and clock-out punches from devices and apps for thousands of customers. Peaks happen at shift change."

What this tests He tests multi-tenant design, burst handling, correctness and the data model for a core WFM feature.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

I would accept punches through a thin, stateless API. It validates the device and the tenant, writes the raw event to a durable log and returns at once. Consumers build timecards from the log, so peaks only grow the queue. Punches are idempotent by a device event id. Raw events are append-only, and timecard views are derived and can be rebuilt. I would shard by tenant and employee and alert on consumer lag.

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. Frame the problem

    Number of customers and punches per second at peak. Offline devices. Latency promise. Audit needs. Accuracy: a lost punch means a pay error.

  2. 2. Accept fast

    API gateway, authentication per device or user, tenant resolved from the token. Validate, write to a durable log (Kafka) and return 202 or 200. Do no heavy work in the request.

  3. 3. Make it idempotent

    Each punch has a client event id. The consumer ignores a duplicate. Devices retry and may send late, so store both the event time and the receive time.

  4. 4. Process

    Consumers group by employee and apply rules to build the timecard. Key the stream by tenant and employee so one employee's punches stay in order.

  5. 5. Store

    Raw punches: append-only, wide-column or partitioned relational tables. Timecards: relational with a version column for edits and approvals. Keep an audit table for every change.

  6. 6. Handle peaks and failure

    The queue absorbs the peak. Autoscale consumers on lag. A dead-letter topic holds bad events. A replay can rebuild timecards after a rule fix.

  7. 7. Operate

    Per-tenant rate limits. Metrics: ingest rate, lag, error rate and time from punch to timecard. Alert on SLO burn.

Concepts you must own 1

Event sourcing (light)
Idea

Keep the raw events. Build current state from them.

Example

Punches are events. A timecard is a view.

Term

Persisting state changes as an immutable sequence of events from which state is derived.

Follow-up questions

  • What if a device is offline for a day?

    The device stores punches locally and sends them later with the original time. The server accepts late events within a policy window and flags large gaps.

  • How do you fix a bug in the rules and recompute?

    Replay the raw events through the new rules into a new version of the timecards. Compare, then switch. This is why the raw log is the source of truth.

Caution
  • Doing all work in the request.
  • Updating a timecard in place with no audit trail.
  • No plan for duplicates and late events.
Staff signal

A Staff answer treats raw events as the source of truth, derives views, and designs for bursts, replay and audit.

UKG-DV2

Interviewer

Architect: "Design a service where managers build and publish weekly schedules. It must respect labour rules and handle thousands of tenants."

What this tests He tests domain modelling, consistency for edits, rules checking and multi-tenant isolation.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

I would model a schedule as shifts that belong to a tenant, a location and a week. Managers edit a draft with optimistic locking. A rules service checks labour rules and returns the reasons. Publishing is a single versioned action that triggers notifications through a queue. Data is partitioned by tenant, and the tenant id is enforced in the data layer.

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. Frame the problem

    Users, edit concurrency, size of a schedule, rules, how fast publishing must be and who gets notified.

  2. 2. Model it

    Tenant, location, employee, shift, assignment, availability and schedule version. A draft and a published version are separate.

  3. 3. Handle edits

    Several managers can edit. Use optimistic locking with a version number. A conflict returns the current state for the user to merge.

  4. 4. Check rules

    A rules engine takes the schedule and the rule set for the jurisdiction and customer. It returns pass or fail with a reason for each shift.

  5. 5. Publish

    One transaction marks the version as published. An outbox event starts notifications, calendar updates and payroll-side updates.

  6. 6. Isolate tenants

    Tenant id from the token in every query. Row-level security in the database. Per-tenant limits for heavy operations such as auto-scheduling.

  7. 7. Scale and operate

    Cache read-mostly data. Run auto-scheduling as an asynchronous job with progress. Measure publish time and rule-check time.

Follow-up questions

  • What if two managers publish at once?

    The version check lets only one win. The other sees the new version and decides what to do.

  • Where does the forecast fit?

    A separate forecasting service produces demand numbers. The scheduler reads them as input. Keep them loosely coupled.

Caution
  • One shared mutable schedule with last-write-wins.
  • Rules checked only in the UI.
  • No tenant enforcement in the data layer.
Staff signal

A Staff answer separates draft and published states, checks rules on the server and enforces tenant isolation.

UKG-DV3

Interviewer

Architect: "Pay and compliance rules differ by country, state, union and customer, and they change often. How do you build the engine?"

What this tests He tests design for change: rules as data, versioning, explainability and testing.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

I would store rules as versioned data with an effective date, not as code branches. The engine evaluates the rules for a worker, jurisdiction and date, and returns the result plus the rule and inputs that produced it. Every change to rules is reviewed and tested against a library of known cases. Old results can be replayed with the rule version that was active.

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. Frame the problem

    How many rules, how often they change, who edits them (engineers or compliance staff) and what a mistake costs.

  2. 2. Model rules as data

    Condition, action, scope (tenant, region), priority and effective dates. A domain-specific format or a table-driven design. Avoid a general scripting language unless you need it.

  3. 3. Version and date

    A result for 3 March must use the rules in force on 3 March. Keep history. Never edit a rule in place.

  4. 4. Explain every result

    Return the rule id, the version and the inputs. A payroll dispute needs a reason that a person can read.

  5. 5. Test heavily

    A large library of golden cases from compliance experts. Run it in CI on every rule change. Add each production bug as a case.

  6. 6. Roll out safely

    Shadow mode: run new rules beside the old ones and compare. Then canary by tenant.

  7. 7. Operate

    Metrics on rule evaluation time and mismatches. A kill switch to go back to the previous version.

Follow-up questions

  • Why not hard-code the rules?

    Code changes need a release, and rules change weekly and differ per customer. Data with tests is faster and safer.

  • How do you handle a retroactive rule change?

    Recompute affected periods with the corrected version. Keep both results and an audit note.

Caution
  • Rules scattered in code.
  • No effective dating.
  • No explanation for results.
Staff signal

A Staff answer treats rules as versioned, tested, explainable data.

UKG-DV4

Interviewer

Architect: "Design an analytics dashboard for managers that shows labour cost, overtime and attendance across many locations. Data is large and some of it is real time."

What this tests He tests full-stack judgement: data shaping, performance, accessibility and privacy. This is your strongest ground.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

On the back end I would pre-aggregate metrics into a warehouse or read models. I would expose a small API (REST or GraphQL) with filters and pagination. On the front end I would use React and TypeScript with a query cache, virtualised tables and charts that match the data size. Real-time numbers come over Server-Sent Events. I would apply role-based access on the server, mask personal data and meet WCAG 2.1 AA.

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. Frame the problem

    Users, data size, freshness needs, device types and which numbers must be exact.

  2. 2. Shape the data

    Pre-aggregate by day, location and tenant. Never scan raw punches for a dashboard. Keep a freshness timestamp on each metric.

  3. 3. Design the API

    Few endpoints shaped to screens. Filters, date ranges and cursor pagination. A backend-for-frontend can combine calls. Cache with a short time-to-live.

  4. 4. Build the front end

    React and TypeScript. Server state in a query cache. Skeleton loading. Virtualise long tables. Charts: SVG for hundreds of points, canvas for thousands.

  5. 5. Add real time

    Server-Sent Events for one-way updates. Reconnect with a last-event id. Show a live badge and a stale warning.

  6. 6. Secure and protect

    Role and location checks on the server. Mask personal data. Audit exports.

  7. 7. Accessibility and performance

    Keyboard use, contrast and chart summaries as tables. A budget for bundle size and Core Web Vitals. Test with real data volumes.

Follow-up questions

  • REST or GraphQL here?

    GraphQL fits varied screens and avoids over-fetching, but needs query cost limits and caching care. REST with purpose-built endpoints is simpler for a fixed set of screens.

  • How do you keep charts accessible?

    Give a text summary and a data table. Do not use colour alone. Support keyboard focus on points.

Caution
  • Querying raw data from the browser.
  • Hiding data only in the UI.
  • Ignoring accessibility.
Staff signal

A Staff answer shapes data on the server, budgets front-end performance and secures access.

UKG-DV5

Interviewer

Architect: "A column used by 2,000 tenants must change type. The service must stay up. How do you do it?"

What this tests He tests migration discipline: backward compatibility, rollout order and rollback.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

I would use expand and contract. Add the new column. Deploy code that writes both and reads the old one. Backfill in small batches. Switch reads to the new column. Then stop writing the old one and drop it later. Each step is reversible. I would run the backfill with rate limits and verify counts before each switch.

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. Expand

    Add the new nullable column. This is a safe, fast change in most databases. Check that it does not lock a large table.

  2. 2. Dual write

    Deploy code that writes both columns. Reads still use the old one.

  3. 3. Backfill

    Copy old data in small batches with a rate limit, per tenant. Monitor load and replication lag.

  4. 4. Verify

    Compare old and new values. Fix mismatches. Do this before any read switch.

  5. 5. Switch reads

    Use a feature flag. Roll out by tenant. Keep the old column as a fallback.

  6. 6. Contract

    Stop writing the old column. After a safe wait, drop it in a later release.

  7. 7. Rollback

    At each step, turn the flag off. The old data is still current until step 6.

Follow-up questions

  • What about code that runs old and new versions at once?

    That is why each version must work with both schemas. Never ship a change that needs an exact lockstep.

  • Which tools help?

    Versioned migrations (Flyway or Liquibase), online schema change tools and a staging copy with realistic data.

Caution
  • One big migration in a release.
  • No verification.
  • Dropping the old column at once.
Staff signal

A Staff answer makes every step backward compatible and reversible.

UKG-DV6

Interviewer

Architect: "Managers open timecards and the page takes 6 seconds. The data comes from five tables and two services. What do you do?"

What this tests He tests diagnosis first, then caching and data-shape trade-offs.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

I would measure first with a trace to find where the 6 seconds go. Then I would fix the largest part: a missing index, an N+1 pattern, or a slow downstream call. If reads still dominate, I would add a read model or a cache with clear invalidation. I would set a latency goal and check it after the change.

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. Measure

    Use a trace for one slow request. Split the time: network, app, database and downstream calls.

  2. 2. Fix the cheap things

    Indexes, N+1 queries, over-fetching, serial calls that can run in parallel, and missing connection reuse.

  3. 3. Choose a cache

    Cache-aside with a time-to-live for data that may be slightly stale. Per-tenant keys. Protect against stampedes.

  4. 4. Consider a read model

    A table or view shaped for this page, updated by events. Reads become one fast query.

  5. 5. Decide on invalidation

    Time-based for low risk. Event-based when freshness matters. Say what a stale read costs.

  6. 6. Verify

    Compare p95 latency before and after under load. Watch the cache hit rate.

Follow-up questions

  • What if the data must be fresh?

    Use event-driven invalidation or update the read model in the same flow. Or skip caching and fix the query.

  • Where do you not cache?

    Data that must be exact at read time, such as an approval check, and data that is rarely read.

Caution
  • Adding a cache before measuring.
  • No invalidation plan.
  • Caching per-user data under a shared key.
Staff signal

A Staff answer measures first, fixes the cause and names the freshness trade-off.

Chapter 05

Debugging and data questions

Concurrency, performance, Kafka, database choice and isolation. Think aloud and name the evidence you would check first.

UKG-DV7

Interviewer

Interviewer: "Two requests approve the same timecard at the same time. Sometimes the approval runs twice and a payroll event is sent twice. How do you find and fix it?"

What this tests He tests whether you understand race conditions at the data layer, not only at the thread level.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

This is a race: both requests read the state as pending and both write approved. I would reproduce it with a test that runs two requests in parallel. The fix is to make the state change atomic: an update with a condition on the current state, or an optimistic version check. Then the second request fails or does nothing. For the event, I would use an idempotency key and an outbox.

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. Reproduce

    Write a test that calls approve twice in parallel. Add a delay in the code to widen the window.

  2. 2. Name the cause

    Check-then-act with no atomic guard. The thread-level lock does not help with several service instances.

  3. 3. Fix the state change

    UPDATE timecard SET status='APPROVED' WHERE id=? AND status='PENDING'. Check the affected row count. Zero rows means someone else won.

  4. 4. Or use a version column

    Optimistic locking: the update includes the version. A conflict raises an error that you handle.

  5. 5. Fix the event

    Write the event to an outbox in the same transaction. A unique key on the event stops duplicates.

  6. 6. Prove the fix

    Run the parallel test many times. Add it to CI.

Code to know

Follow-up questions

  • Why not use synchronized?

    It only protects one JVM. A service runs many instances. You need a database-level guard or a distributed lock.

  • Is a distributed lock a good idea?

    Use it rarely. Conditional updates are simpler and safer.

Caution
  • Using an in-process lock for a multi-instance service.
  • Fixing it in the UI by disabling the button.
  • No test for the race.
Staff signal

A Staff answer fixes the invariant in the data layer and adds a test that proves it.

UKG-DV8

Interviewer

Interviewer: "A Java service gets slow under load. CPU is low. Threads pile up and requests time out. What do you check?"

What this tests He tests diagnosis: pools, blocking calls and downstream dependencies.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

Low CPU with waiting threads usually means blocking. I would take a thread dump. I would look for many threads waiting on the same thing: the connection pool, a slow downstream call or a lock. I would check pool metrics and traces. Fixes include timeouts, a bulkhead per dependency, a right-sized pool, a faster query and backpressure.

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. Look at the symptoms

    Latency, error rate, thread count, pool use and downstream latency. Low CPU points away from compute.

  2. 2. Take thread dumps

    Take two or three, a few seconds apart. Group threads by their top frames. A large group on one frame is the bottleneck.

  3. 3. Check the connection pool

    A full pool with waiting threads means slow queries or too few connections. Do not just raise the pool size: the database may be the limit.

  4. 4. Check downstream calls

    A call with no timeout can hold a thread for minutes. Look at the traces.

  5. 5. Check locks

    Threads blocked on the same monitor point to contention.

  6. 6. Fix and protect

    Set timeouts. Add a circuit breaker and a bulkhead. Fix the slow query. Bound queues and shed load. Consider virtual threads for blocking I/O.

  7. 7. Prevent

    Load test. Alert on pool saturation and thread count.

Follow-up questions

  • What if CPU is high instead?

    Profile the hot methods, check for GC pressure and look for expensive serialisation or regex.

  • What is thread starvation?

    All pool threads are busy waiting, so new work cannot run. A common cause is blocking calls inside a small pool.

Caution
  • Adding more pods first.
  • Raising the pool size blindly.
  • No timeouts.
Staff signal

A Staff answer reads thread dumps and pool metrics, then fixes the bottleneck and adds protection.

UKG-DV9

Interviewer

Interviewer: "Consumers on a punch topic fall behind at shift change. Events for one employee must stay in order. What do you do?"

What this tests He tests Kafka fundamentals: partitions, keys, consumer groups and idempotency.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

Order is guaranteed only within a partition, so I key by employee id. Throughput scales with partitions, so I would add partitions and consumers up to the partition count, and make each handler fast and idempotent. I would check for slow handlers, hot partitions and rebalances. I would alert on lag and keep a dead-letter topic for bad messages.

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. Find the cause

    Is lag growing on all partitions or one? One hot partition means a skewed key. All partitions mean the consumers are too slow.

  2. 2. Speed up the handler

    Batch writes. Avoid a remote call per event. Move slow work to another step.

  3. 3. Scale consumers

    Add consumer instances up to the partition count. More partitions need planning, because the key mapping changes for new events.

  4. 4. Fix a hot key

    If one tenant is huge, key by tenant plus employee. Keep order per employee, not per tenant.

  5. 5. Keep order

    Process one partition at a time per consumer. Do not hand one partition's records to many threads without ordering.

  6. 6. Handle failure

    Retry with a limit. Send poison messages to a dead-letter topic. Commit offsets after the work is done. Expect duplicates.

  7. 7. Monitor

    Lag per partition, processing time, rebalance count and error rate.

Follow-up questions

  • What causes rebalances?

    Consumers joining or leaving, or missing the poll interval because a handler is too slow.

  • Exactly-once?

    Kafka supports it inside Kafka with idempotent producers and transactions. For a database write, use idempotent handlers.

Caution
  • More consumers than partitions.
  • Random keys that break order.
  • No idempotency.
Staff signal

A Staff answer links order, keys, partitions and idempotency, and watches lag per partition.

UKG-DV10

Interviewer

Architect: "For punches, schedules and reports, which databases would you pick, and why?"

What this tests He tests that you choose by access pattern and consistency, not by fashion.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

I would start with Postgres for schedules, timecards and configuration, because they need transactions and joins. For very high-volume raw punches I would consider a wide-column store such as Cassandra, designed for the read patterns. A partitioned Postgres table may do if the volume allows. Reports go to a warehouse. A document store fits nested, flexible documents read by key. I would keep the number of different databases small.

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. List the access patterns

    Writes per second, reads by key or by range, joins, transactions and retention.

  2. 2. Pick for each need

    Relational for transactions and constraints. Wide-column for huge append-only writes with known queries. Document for flexible nested data. Warehouse for analytics.

  3. 3. State the cost

    Each new database adds backups, upgrades, skills, monitoring and security work.

  4. 4. Consider consistency

    Postgres gives strong consistency on one node. Cassandra offers tunable consistency per query and favours availability.

  5. 5. Check scale limits

    Partition large relational tables by time or tenant before moving to a new store.

  6. 6. Decide and set a trigger

    For example: stay on partitioned Postgres until writes exceed a stated limit, then move raw punches to a wide-column store.

Follow-up questions

  • What does Cassandra modelling look like?

    One table per query. A partition key that spreads load and keeps a query on one partition. Clustering columns to sort rows. No joins.

  • When is MongoDB the wrong choice?

    When you need multi-row transactions and many joins across entities.

Caution
  • Picking by popularity.
  • Many databases for a small team.
  • No trigger to revisit.
Staff signal

A Staff answer matches stores to access patterns and limits the number of technologies.

UKG-DV11

Interviewer

Interviewer: "Two users edit the same record. One edit disappears. Why, and how do you stop it?"

What this tests He tests database fundamentals: transactions, isolation and locking.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

This is a lost update: both read the old value, both write, and the last write wins. Higher isolation can help but is not the first tool. I would use optimistic locking with a version column, or a conditional update, or a row lock with SELECT FOR UPDATE for short critical steps. I would choose by conflict rate and by how bad a retry is for the user.

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. Name the anomaly

    Lost update. Related: dirty read, non-repeatable read and phantom read.

  2. 2. State the defaults

    Postgres uses read committed by default. MySQL InnoDB uses repeatable read. Check your database.

  3. 3. Optimistic locking

    Add a version. Update with where id=? and version=?. Zero rows means a conflict. Retry or ask the user.

  4. 4. Pessimistic locking

    SELECT ... FOR UPDATE locks the row until commit. Use it for short, high-conflict steps. Watch for deadlocks.

  5. 5. Choose

    Low conflict and user edits: optimistic. High conflict and money: pessimistic or a queue per key.

Follow-up questions

  • What is a deadlock?

    Two transactions each hold a lock that the other needs. Lock rows in a fixed order and keep transactions short.

  • Serializable isolation?

    It is the strongest and can abort transactions. Use it only for rare, critical logic.

Caution
  • Relying on the UI to prevent it.
  • Long transactions.
  • Not checking the affected row count.
Staff signal

A Staff answer names the anomaly and picks the guard by conflict rate.

Chapter 06

Positioning, portfolio and AI

The honest Java gap answer, your design portfolio, AI-first engineering and learning the domain. Use only true facts. Where you see [fill: ...], write your own fact.

UKG-DV12

Hiring manager

Hiring manager: "Your background is JavaScript, TypeScript and test automation. This role is a Java platform role. How do you close the gap?"

What this tests He tests honesty, learning speed and whether your strengths still serve the role. Do not bluff.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

I would be direct. I have read and reviewed Java and I understand the language and its ecosystem, but I have not owned a Java service in production. What I bring is system design, API design, delivery, observability and leading engineers across teams, and those carry over. I am building Java depth now with practice projects, and I would pair with an owner in my first weeks. [fill: one Java project or exercise you have really done].

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. State the facts

    Say it plainly: you read Java well and have not used it at work. A short, calm answer earns trust.

  2. 2. Show what carries over

    API and contract design, distributed system design, CI/CD, testing strategy, observability, mentoring and cross-team influence. Name one real example for each that you choose.

  3. 3. Show the plan

    Java practice problems, a small Spring Boot service with a database and a queue, JUnit tests and a Kubernetes deploy. Only say what you have really done: [fill: your practice work].

  4. 4. Show how you learn

    Give one example where you learned a new stack fast and delivered. Use a real one: [fill: your example].

  5. 5. Ask for the first-month plan

    Ask who you would pair with and which service you would own first. It shows ownership.

Follow-up questions

  • Will you be effective in the first three months?

    Say what you would deliver: a design review, a reliability or test improvement and one service change with a pair. Be concrete.

  • Why not apply to a front-end Staff role?

    Say that you want to broaden into full-stack and platform work, and that you also fit the full-stack roles. Do not run the other roles down.

Caution
  • Claiming Java experience you do not have.
  • Apologising too much.
  • No plan to learn.
Staff signal

A Staff answer is honest about the gap, shows transferable strengths and a concrete, believable plan.

UKG-DV13

Hiring manager or architect

Hiring manager or architect: "Pick a system you designed or led. Walk me through the architecture and the trade-offs."

What this tests He tests clear structure, real depth and honest ownership. The postings ask for a design portfolio.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

I would use a fixed shape. First the problem and the scale. Then the architecture in one picture. Then the two or three key decisions and the options I rejected. Then what went wrong, and the result with numbers. I would say clearly what I owned and what the team owned. [fill: your system]. I would prepare two or three systems this way.

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. Choose systems you really built

    Candidates from your work: the micro-frontend platform used by 20+ teams. The GraphQL API layer over 14+ AWS-API-compatible services. The end-to-end test framework and CI pipelines. The shared component library. Pick two or three.

  2. 2. Use the same shape

    Problem and scale. Constraints. Architecture picture. Key decisions and rejected options. Failures and fixes. Result: [your number]. What you would change.

  3. 3. Draw it

    Practise a simple box-and-arrow picture. Use C4 level 1 and 2.

  4. 4. Own your part

    Say what you decided, what you built and what others built. Credit the team.

  5. 5. Prepare for probing

    Why not the alternative? What broke? How did you test it? How did it scale? What would you change?

  6. 6. Map it to UKG

    Link each system to the role: multi-tenant, scale, reliability or developer productivity.

Follow-up questions

  • Which system should you lead with?

    The one closest to the role and the one you know best. For a full-stack role, the micro-frontend platform. For a platform role, the API layer or the test platform.

  • What if you do not know the numbers?

    Give honest ranges and say they are estimates. Do not invent figures.

Caution
  • A tour of technologies instead of decisions.
  • No rejected options.
  • Claiming the team's work as your own.
Staff signal

A Staff answer shows decisions, trade-offs and honest ownership with a repeatable structure.

UKG-DV14

Interviewer

Hiring manager: "The role asks for an AI-first mindset and responsible AI practices across the development cycle. What does that mean to you?"

What this tests He tests practical AI use and judgement. You have real experience, so give concrete examples.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

I use AI tools across the cycle: exploring code, drafting designs and tests, reviewing changes and writing docs. The rules are simple. The author owns every change, humans review, tests must prove the change, and no secrets or customer data go into prompts. I measure results with delivery metrics and I build team setups, such as shared instructions, hooks and checks, so good practice is the default. [fill: your real example, such as the LLM test-failure tool].

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. Give a real example

    Describe the LLM-based failure analysis tool you built: the input, the output, the limits and what a person still checked. Use only true details.

  2. 2. Show use across the cycle

    Design, code, tests, review, docs and troubleshooting. Name one example for each that you really did.

  3. 3. State the rules

    Ownership, review, tests, data rules, least privilege for agents and licence policy.

  4. 4. Make it the default

    Shared instructions in the repository, hooks that run checks, approved connections and a short guide.

  5. 5. Measure

    Lead time, change failure rate and review time. Do not count lines of code.

  6. 6. Be honest about limits

    AI can write plausible wrong code. Tests and review catch it.

Follow-up questions

  • How do you test AI-generated code?

    The same way as other code, plus a check that new tests fail without the change.

  • What is your view on responsible AI?

    People stay accountable. Data is protected. Risky actions need approval. Quality is measured.

Caution
  • Hype with no examples.
  • No rules.
  • Claiming AI makes review unnecessary.
Staff signal

A Staff answer gives a real example, clear rules and a measure of results.

UKG-DV15

Interviewer

Hiring manager: "This team builds workforce management software. You have not worked in this domain. How would you get up to speed?"

What this tests He tests curiosity and a plan to learn the domain, because domain mistakes are costly.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

I would learn the vocabulary first: punches, timecards, pay rules, accruals, schedules and forecasts. Then I would read the public API docs and trace one flow end to end, from a punch to a paycheque. I would sit with support and product people and read real incidents. I would write a short glossary and a diagram and ask the team to correct it.

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. Learn the words

    Use the WFM primer in this tab. Add the terms the team uses.

  2. 2. Trace one flow

    Punch to timecard to approval to payroll. Draw it. Mark where rules apply.

  3. 3. Read incidents

    The last ten incidents show where the domain is hard.

  4. 4. Talk to the experts

    Product, support and implementation consultants know the edge cases.

  5. 5. Write and check

    A glossary and a one-page diagram. Ask the team to correct them.

  6. 6. Ship a small change

    A small, safe change teaches the delivery path and the data model.

Follow-up questions

  • Why are WFM systems hard?

    Many rules by place and customer, strict accuracy for pay, predictable load peaks and long data retention.

  • What question would you ask first?

    Which numbers must never be wrong, and how do we know they are right?

Caution
  • Saying that domain does not matter.
  • Pretending to know it.
  • No learning plan.
Staff signal

A Staff answer shows a concrete learning plan and respect for domain risk.

Chapter 07

Java coding practice

Five small problems with tested Java solutions. Type each one from memory. Say the approach and the complexity first.

UKG-DV16

Coding practice

Interviewer: "Given a list of shifts as start and end hours, merge the overlapping ones."

What this tests He tests if you can write clean, correct Java and explain the complexity. This is practice for the coding round.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

Sort by start. Walk the list. If the next shift starts after the last merged end, add it. Otherwise extend the last merged end to the larger end. It runs in O(n log n) time because of the sort.

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. Clarify

    Do touching intervals (end equals the next start) merge? In this code they do. Ask what the interviewer wants.

  2. 2. Plan

    Sort by start. One pass with a result list.

  3. 3. Code

    Use a record for the interval. Use Comparator.comparingInt.

  4. 4. Test

    Empty list, one interval, fully nested intervals and unsorted input.

  5. 5. Complexity

    Time O(n log n). Space O(n).

Code to know

Follow-up questions

  • What if the list is already sorted?

    Skip the sort. The pass is O(n).

  • How would you use this in WFM?

    Combine overlapping punches or availability windows before you count hours.

Caution
  • Silent coding with no explanation.
  • Not asking about edge cases.
  • Overcomplicating a simple problem.
Staff signal

A Staff answer states the approach, writes simple correct code, explains complexity and names edge cases.

UKG-DV17

Coding practice

Interviewer: "Given punches with a worker and hours, return the overtime hours per worker when the weekly total is over 40."

What this tests He tests if you can write clean, correct Java and explain the complexity. This is practice for the coding round.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

Group by worker and sum the hours. For each worker with a total above the limit, put total minus limit in the result. It runs in O(n). In real pay rules the limit and the rounding differ by place, so I would pass the rule in, not hard-code it.

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. Clarify

    Week boundary, time zone, rounding and daily overtime rules. Say these are real-world traps.

  2. 2. Plan

    One stream with groupingBy and summingDouble. Then filter.

  3. 3. Code

    Return a sorted map so output is stable.

  4. 4. Test

    A worker at exactly 40, a worker split across punches and an empty list.

  5. 5. Improve

    Use BigDecimal or minutes as integers for money and time. Doubles can round badly.

Code to know

Follow-up questions

  • Why not use double for pay?

    Binary floating point cannot store many decimal values exactly. Use BigDecimal or integer minutes and cents.

  • How do you handle a week that crosses midnight?

    Convert times to the tenant's time zone and assign each segment to a day before you sum.

Caution
  • Silent coding with no explanation.
  • Not asking about edge cases.
  • Overcomplicating a simple problem.
Staff signal

A Staff answer states the approach, writes simple correct code, explains complexity and names edge cases.

UKG-DV18

Coding practice

Interviewer: "Implement a least-recently-used cache with a fixed capacity."

What this tests He tests if you can write clean, correct Java and explain the complexity. This is practice for the coding round.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

Extend LinkedHashMap with access order set to true and override removeEldestEntry to evict when the size is above the capacity. Get and put are O(1). It is not thread-safe, so I would wrap it or use a library such as Caffeine for production.

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. Clarify

    Capacity, thread safety and eviction order.

  2. 2. Plan

    A hash map for lookup and a linked list for order. LinkedHashMap gives both.

  3. 3. Code

    Pass true as the access-order flag in the constructor.

  4. 4. Test

    Put, get and evict order. Capacity of one.

  5. 5. Discuss

    Add Collections.synchronizedMap or use Caffeine. Add a time-to-live if staleness matters.

Code to know

Follow-up questions

  • How would you build it without LinkedHashMap?

    Use a HashMap from key to a node of a doubly linked list. Move a node to the head on each access and remove the tail on overflow.

  • Is this good for a multi-tenant cache?

    Add the tenant to the key and per-tenant limits, or one cache per tenant, so one tenant cannot evict all others.

Caution
  • Silent coding with no explanation.
  • Not asking about edge cases.
  • Overcomplicating a simple problem.
Staff signal

A Staff answer states the approach, writes simple correct code, explains complexity and names edge cases.

UKG-DV19

Coding practice

Interviewer: "Given a list of error codes, return the K most frequent. Break ties alphabetically."

What this tests He tests if you can write clean, correct Java and explain the complexity. This is practice for the coding round.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

Count with groupingBy and counting. Sort entries by count descending and then by key, and take K. It runs in O(n + m log m) for m distinct codes. For very large m, a min-heap of size K gives O(n + m log K).

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. Clarify

    Ties, case, K larger than the number of codes.

  2. 2. Plan

    Count, sort, limit.

  3. 3. Code

    Use Map.Entry.comparingByValue().reversed().thenComparing(...).

  4. 4. Test

    Ties, K equal to zero, an empty list.

  5. 5. Improve

    A bounded min-heap when m is large.

Code to know

Follow-up questions

  • How would you do this on a stream of events?

    Keep counts in a keyed store and update a bounded heap, or use an approximate structure such as a count-min sketch.

  • Why is the sort key order important?

    A stable and complete order makes the output deterministic, which makes tests reliable.

Caution
  • Silent coding with no explanation.
  • Not asking about edge cases.
  • Overcomplicating a simple problem.
Staff signal

A Staff answer states the approach, writes simple correct code, explains complexity and names edge cases.

UKG-DV20

Coding practice

Interviewer: "Write a token bucket rate limiter that is safe for many threads."

What this tests He tests if you can write clean, correct Java and explain the complexity. This is practice for the coding round.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

Keep the token count and the last refill time. On each call, add tokens for the elapsed time up to the capacity, then take one if available. Make the method synchronized, which is simple and enough for one JVM. I inject the clock so the test is deterministic. For many instances I would keep the state in Redis with an atomic script.

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. Clarify

    Rate, burst size, one JVM or many, and what to do on reject.

  2. 2. Plan

    Two fields: tokens and last time. Refill on demand. No timer thread.

  3. 3. Code

    Inject a LongSupplier as the clock.

  4. 4. Test

    Use a fake clock. Drain the bucket, advance time and check the refill.

  5. 5. Scale

    For many instances use a shared store with an atomic update, and accept a small error for local counters.

Code to know

Follow-up questions

  • Why is refill on demand better than a timer?

    It needs no extra thread and no drift. It is exact at the moment of the call.

  • Would you use a library?

    Yes for production, for example Bucket4j or Resilience4j. Know how it works to choose well.

Caution
  • Silent coding with no explanation.
  • Not asking about edge cases.
  • Overcomplicating a simple problem.

Chapter 08

Quick-fire answers

Short answers for fast questions. Say each one in 20 seconds. Tick Studied when you can say it without notes.

Java: language and runtime

What is the JVM, the JRE and the JDK?

The JVM runs bytecode. The JRE is the JVM plus the standard libraries. The JDK adds tools such as the compiler javac. You install the JDK to develop.

How does Java run a program?

javac compiles source to bytecode. The JVM loads it, interprets it and compiles hot code to machine code with the JIT compiler.

What is the difference between == and equals()?

== compares references for objects. equals() compares content when the class overrides it. Strings and other objects need equals().

What is the equals and hashCode contract?

Equal objects must return the same hash code. If you override one, override both. Use fields that do not change, or hash-based collections lose entries.

Why are Strings immutable?

It makes them safe to share between threads, safe as map keys and cacheable. Use StringBuilder to build text in a loop.

Primitive versus wrapper types?

int is a primitive. Integer is an object that can be null. Collections hold wrappers. Unboxing a null throws a NullPointerException.

What are the access modifiers?

public, protected, package-private (the default) and private.

Interface versus abstract class?

An interface is a contract and a class can implement many. An abstract class can hold state and shared code, and a class extends only one. Prefer interfaces.

What is a record?

A short way to write an immutable data class. Java generates the constructor, accessors, equals, hashCode and toString.

What is an enum?

A fixed set of constants. It can hold fields and methods and works well in a switch.

Checked versus unchecked exceptions?

Checked exceptions must be caught or declared. Unchecked ones, such as RuntimeException, need not be. Do not swallow exceptions.

What is try-with-resources?

A try block that closes resources that implement AutoCloseable, even when an exception occurs. It prevents leaks.

What are generics?

Type parameters such as List<String> that let the compiler check types. The types are erased at run time.

What are lambdas and functional interfaces?

A lambda is a short function. It implements an interface with one abstract method, such as Predicate, Function or Runnable.

When do streams help?

For clear filter, map and collect steps over collections. Avoid them for tiny loops, side effects or when they hide the logic.

What is Optional for?

A return type for a value that may be missing. Do not use it for fields or parameters. Do not call get() without a check.

How does HashMap work?

It hashes the key to a bucket. Collisions form a list that turns into a tree when long. Average get and put are O(1).

ArrayList or LinkedList?

ArrayList for most cases. It has fast index access and a compact layout. LinkedList is rarely better in practice.

What is garbage collection?

The JVM frees objects that nothing refers to. G1 is the default. ZGC gives very short pauses. Leaks happen when you keep references that you no longer need.

What causes OutOfMemoryError?

A heap that is too small, a leak such as a growing cache, too many threads or a native memory problem. Take a heap dump and look at what holds the memory.

What is the classpath and what is a JAR?

The classpath lists where the JVM finds classes. A JAR is an archive of classes and resources. Maven and Gradle build and manage them.

What changed in recent Java versions?

Records, sealed types, pattern matching, text blocks and virtual threads. Java 21 is a long-term support release.

Java: concurrency

What is the difference between a process and a thread?

A process has its own memory. Threads in one process share memory. Sharing is fast and needs care.

What does synchronized do?

It lets one thread at a time run a block on a given lock. It also makes changes visible to the next thread that takes the lock.

What does volatile do?

It makes reads and writes of one variable visible across threads. It does not make count++ atomic.

What is a race condition?

Two threads act on shared state and the result depends on timing. Fix with atomics, locks, immutable data or by not sharing.

What is a deadlock and how do you avoid it?

Threads wait on each other's locks forever. Take locks in a fixed order, keep locks short and use timeouts.

What is a thread pool and why bound it?

A fixed set of workers that run tasks. A bound and a bounded queue stop overload from using all memory.

What is CompletableFuture?

A way to compose async steps with callbacks. Run blocking calls on a separate pool and handle exceptions.

What are virtual threads?

Cheap threads managed by the JVM, final in Java 21. They make blocking I/O code scale. They do not help CPU-bound work.

ConcurrentHashMap versus synchronizedMap?

ConcurrentHashMap allows concurrent reads and fine-grained writes. Use its compute and merge methods for atomic updates.

What is a CountDownLatch or a Semaphore for?

A latch waits for N events. A semaphore limits how many threads use a resource.

Why is thread safety harder with many service instances?

In-process locks only protect one JVM. Use database guards, idempotency and, rarely, distributed locks.

How do you size a thread pool?

CPU-bound work: close to the core count. I/O-bound: larger, based on the wait time. Measure under load.

Spring Boot, REST and JPA

What does Spring Boot give you?

Auto-configuration, an embedded server, starters for dependencies and production features such as health checks and metrics.

What is dependency injection?

Spring creates objects and passes in their dependencies. It decouples classes and makes tests easy. Prefer constructor injection.

How does @Transactional work?

Spring wraps the bean in a proxy that opens and commits a transaction. Calls inside the same class skip the proxy. It rolls back on unchecked exceptions by default.

What is the N+1 query problem?

One query loads a list and then one more query runs per row. Fix with a join fetch, a batch size or a custom query.

Why return DTOs and not entities?

Entities carry lazy loading and database details. DTOs give a stable API and avoid lazy-loading errors and over-exposure.

What is a connection pool?

A fixed set of reusable database connections, such as HikariCP. If the pool is full, requests wait.

How do you make a POST safe to retry?

Use an idempotency key. The server stores the key and the result and returns the same result for a repeat.

Which HTTP status codes matter most?

200, 201, 204, 400, 401, 403, 404, 409, 422, 429, 500 and 503. Use them correctly and keep one error format.

How do you version a REST API?

In the path or a header. Add fields without breaking old clients. Announce a deprecation period.

What do you test in a Spring service?

Unit tests with JUnit and Mockito. Web-layer slice tests. Integration tests with Testcontainers. A few end-to-end checks.

Databases and data

What is an index and what does it cost?

A structure that speeds up reads. It slows writes and uses space. Index the columns that you filter and sort on.

What does ACID mean?

Atomicity, consistency, isolation and durability. These are the guarantees of a transaction.

Name the isolation anomalies.

Dirty read, non-repeatable read, phantom read and lost update. Higher isolation levels prevent more of them.

Optimistic or pessimistic locking?

Optimistic uses a version check and suits low conflict. Pessimistic locks the row and suits high conflict and short steps.

What is normalisation, and when do you denormalise?

Normalisation removes duplicates. Denormalise for read speed in a read model, and keep the source of truth clean.

What is the difference between a clustered and a non-clustered index?

A clustered index defines the physical row order. A non-clustered index is a separate structure that points to the rows.

Why does a query not use my index?

A function on the column, a type mismatch, low selectivity or stale statistics. Read the query plan.

When is Cassandra a good choice?

Very high write volume, linear scale and multi-region needs with known queries. Not for ad hoc queries or joins.

How do you model data in Cassandra?

Design one table per query. Choose a partition key that spreads load, and clustering columns for order.

When is MongoDB a good choice?

Nested, flexible documents read by key. Be careful when you need joins or multi-document transactions.

What is sharding?

Splitting data across databases by a key. It scales writes and complicates joins and resharding. Choose an even key.

How do you change a schema without downtime?

Expand and contract: add, dual write, backfill, switch reads, then remove the old column.

OLTP versus OLAP?

OLTP handles many small transactions. OLAP handles large analytic scans. Use a warehouse for OLAP.

Messaging and events

Kafka in one sentence?

A distributed, replicated log. Producers append, consumers track their own offsets and can replay.

What are partitions and consumer groups?

A topic splits into partitions. In a group, each partition goes to one consumer. This gives scale and order within a partition.

How do you keep order in Kafka?

Use a key so related events go to the same partition. Order is only guaranteed inside a partition.

What is consumer lag?

The gap between the latest offset and the consumer's offset. Alert on it.

What delivery guarantee should you assume?

At-least-once. Make consumers idempotent.

When would you pick RabbitMQ?

For task queues, flexible routing and per-message acknowledgement.

What is a dead-letter queue?

A place for messages that keep failing. A person or a job reviews them.

What is the outbox pattern?

Save the event in the same database transaction as the data change. A relay publishes it. It avoids lost or phantom events.

What is schema evolution?

Changing event formats without breaking readers. Use a schema registry and compatible changes.

Multi-tenancy, security, observability and cloud

Three ways to isolate tenants?

Shared tables with a tenant id, a schema per tenant and a database per tenant. A hybrid is common.

How do you stop a tenant data leak?

Resolve the tenant from the token. Enforce it in the data layer with row-level security or a mandatory filter. Test cross-tenant access.

What is the noisy-neighbour problem?

One tenant uses too many shared resources. Use quotas, rate limits and separate capacity for big tenants.

OAuth 2.0 versus OIDC?

OAuth 2.0 is about authorisation to access resources. OIDC adds identity: who the user is.

RBAC versus ABAC?

RBAC grants by role. ABAC decides by attributes such as location and department.

What is broken access control?

A user can reach data or actions that they should not. It is the top OWASP risk. Check on the server for every request.

What are the three pillars of observability?

Metrics, logs and traces. Add a shared id so you can follow one request.

What is OpenTelemetry?

A vendor-neutral standard and set of libraries for traces, metrics and logs.

What are the golden signals?

Latency, traffic, errors and saturation.

What is infrastructure as code?

Define infrastructure in versioned files, such as Terraform, so environments are repeatable and reviewable.

Managed service or self-managed?

Managed by default. You trade some control and cost for less operations work and better reliability.

How do you cut cloud cost?

Tag and measure. Right-size. Autoscale. Use committed discounts for steady load. Use Spot for fault-tolerant work. Remove idle resources.

Front end for full-stack roles

Client-side or server-side rendering?

Server-side or static for fast first paint and SEO. Client-side for highly interactive apps. Many apps mix them.

What are Core Web Vitals?

LCP measures loading, INP measures responsiveness and CLS measures visual stability.

How do you speed up a slow React page?

Measure first. Split bundles, lazy load, memoise where it helps, virtualise long lists and cut re-renders by moving state down.

Server state versus client state?

Server state comes from an API and needs caching and refetching. Client state is UI-only. Use a query cache for the first.

When do you use micro-frontends?

When many teams need independent deploys. They cost duplicated dependencies and harder shared state and testing.

SVG, canvas or WebGL for charts?

SVG for hundreds of points. Canvas for thousands. WebGL for very large data. Aggregate on the server when you can.

WebSocket or Server-Sent Events?

SSE for one-way server updates, simple and works over HTTP. WebSocket for two-way, low-latency messages.

What does WCAG 2.1 AA require?

Keyboard access, enough contrast, text alternatives, labels, focus order and no information by colour alone.

How do you keep a design system healthy?

Tokens, accessible components, versioning, docs, a migration path and a clear owner.

REST or GraphQL for the front end?

GraphQL avoids over-fetching and fits varied screens. It needs query limits and caching care. REST is simpler for fixed screens.

Chapter 09

Questions to ask them

Always ask two or three. Pick the ones that match who is in the room. Add the leadership and AI questions in DevOps 2.

For the hiring manager

  1. What does the first six months look like for this role, and what would success be?
  2. Which services or platforms would I own first, and who would I pair with?
  3. How is Java expertise built on the team, for engineers who are strong in other languages?
  4. How do teams use AI tools today, and what rules do you set for AI-assisted code?
  5. How are architecture decisions made and recorded across teams?
  6. How does the team handle on-call, incidents and technical debt?

For the architect

  1. How do you isolate tenants today, and where are the hardest limits?
  2. What are the biggest scaling or reliability risks in the platform?
  3. Which data stores and messaging systems do you use, and why?
  4. How do you handle peaks such as shift change and pay period close?
  5. How are rule changes for labour compliance tested and rolled out?
  6. What does your observability stack look like, and how are SLOs set?

UKG Staff Prep Guide
