How each question works

Read the interviewer quote. Say the 30-second answer out loud, then stop. Read the full answer only when you need depth. Learn every concept card: idea, example, then the formal term.

Quiz mode

Turn on quiz mode in the toolbar. Answers blur. Say your answer first, then tap the blurred text to check it.

Track progress

Tick "Studied" on each question. The counter in the toolbar shows your progress in this browser.

PracticeActions WorkbenchWrite real GitHub Actions workflows for 22 scenarios. A checker finds mistakes as you type and explains your workflow in plain English.Open ↗

Study sessions, in this order

Do them in sequence: the Kubernetes scenarios need the K0 basics. A session can be one sitting or split across a day.

  1. Session 1Kubernetes and EKS from zero (K0), then K1. This is your biggest gap, so do it first. Watch the 10-minute EKS video, not the 4-hour course. Draw the request path from memory.
  2. Session 2K2 to K9. K9 is a hands-on lab: run your Playwright repo on minikube with kubectl. K8 is a short overview of a GitHub job in Kubernetes: learn its minikube, GKE and EKS table. Say each 30-second answer out loud. Learn the kubectl commands. Then read the GKE answers in the GCP topic: the commands are the same.
  3. Session 3GitHub Actions G1 to G7. Read every YAML snippet until you can explain each line. Then read the FAQ topic DevOps basics and pipelines, including the Jenkins pipeline.
  4. Session 4His stated focus: the FAQ topics GCP, AWS Lambda, Selenium and Playwright. Read the Lambda answer about your Joyent work, and say the honest version out loud. Map each AWS service you know to GCP. Say the Workload Identity Federation answer out loud.
  5. Session 5Design D1 to D10 and the capstone C1. Draw C1 on paper in 10 minutes.
  6. Session 6Leadership L1 to L7 and the interviewer's lens questions P1 to P13. Fill every [your number] placeholder in your stories.
  7. Last sessionRound-one fixes, the UKG frequently asked questions and the fact updates. Then turn on quiz mode and say the 30-second answers for every question.
Chapter 01

Kubernetes and EKS from zero

Kubernetes runs containers on a group of machines and keeps them in the state that you declare. You tell it what you want, for example "3 copies of results-api, version 3f2c1ab". Controllers then compare the real state with your desired state all the time, and they fix the difference.

This chapter starts with the smallest part, the pod, and adds one component at a time. After the components, it shows the architecture that runs them, and then how EKS splits that work between AWS and you. The cluster explorer below is the map. Click a box to get an explanation, and double-click it to open the box and see what is inside. Read the lessons in order first if Kubernetes is new to you, then use the explorer to test yourself.

  • Amazon EKS Explained in 10 Minutes | Complete AWS Kubernetes Guide for BeginnersNaveen Tech Hub · ~10 minWhat EKS manages (control plane) and what you run (nodes).

Part 1

The main components, from the smallest up

Lesson 01

The problem it solvesYou have a container image. You need a machine to run it on, and a unit that Kubernetes can schedule, restart and give an address to.

A node is one machine in the cluster. It can be a virtual machine (an EC2 instance on EKS) or a physical server. Each node has CPU, memory and a network address in the VPC.

A pod is the smallest unit that Kubernetes deploys. A pod wraps one or more containers. Kubernetes never runs a bare container; it always runs a pod.

Why the extra layer? The pod gives Kubernetes one interface for every container runtime. It also lets a small group of containers share resources. All containers in one pod share:

  • one IP address and one network namespace, so they talk to each other on localhost;
  • the volumes that the pod declares;
  • one life cycle: they are scheduled to the same node at the same time.

Usually one pod holds one main application container. Add a second container only when it must live next to the main one, for example a log shipper or a proxy. This pattern is a sidecar.

Each pod gets its own IP address. Pods are ephemeral: when a pod dies, Kubernetes makes a new pod, and the new pod gets a new IP address. So you cannot let other apps call a pod by its IP. The next lesson fixes this problem.

  1. Node (EC2 instance)
  2. Pod (IP 10.0.12.45)
  3. Container: api :8080
  4. Container: log-shipper
On EKS

On EKS, the Amazon VPC CNI gives each pod a real IP address from your VPC subnet. A load balancer can then send traffic directly to a pod IP. The number of pods on one node is limited by the IP addresses that its network interfaces can hold.

RememberNode = a machine. Pod = the smallest deployable unit; it wraps containers and gets an IP that changes when the pod is replaced.

Used in: K1 K7
Lesson 02

The problem it solvesPod IPs change every time a pod is replaced. Other apps need one address that does not change, and users outside the cluster need a way in.

A Service is a stable virtual IP address and a DNS name in front of a group of pods. The Service does not die with the pods. When a pod is replaced, the Service keeps the same address and sends traffic to the new pod.

A Service finds its pods with a label selector. For example, the selector app: results-api matches every pod with that label. The Service sends traffic only to matching pods that are Ready.

A Service is also a load balancer inside the cluster. With 3 matching pods, it spreads requests across the 3 pods.

Services have types. An internal Service (ClusterIP, the default) is reachable only inside the cluster. A database must stay internal. An external Service (NodePort or LoadBalancer) opens a way in from outside. Lesson 16 explains each type.

An external Service gives you an IP and a port, which is not good for users. An Ingress adds HTTP routing rules in front of Services: a host name such as results.example.com, a path such as /api, and TLS. The Ingress forwards each request to the correct Service.

An Ingress object is only a set of rules. An Ingress controller must read the rules and do the routing. Without a controller, the Ingress does nothing.

  1. Browser
  2. Ingress: results.example.com
  3. Service: results-api
  4. Ready pods only
On EKS

On EKS, the AWS Load Balancer Controller is the usual Ingress controller. It reads each Ingress and creates an AWS Application Load Balancer (ALB) with listeners, rules and a target group. The community ingress-nginx controller is retired since March 2026, so use the AWS controller or Gateway API for new work.

RememberService = a stable address and load balancer for a set of ready pods. Ingress = HTTP rules (host, path, TLS) that forward external traffic to Services.

Used in: K1 K5
Lesson 03

The problem it solvesThe database URL, feature flags and passwords change between environments. You must not rebuild the image for each change, and you must not put passwords in the image.

A ConfigMap holds plain configuration as key-value pairs, for example DB_HOST=postgres.test-platform.svc. A pod reads it as environment variables or as files in a volume.

A Secret holds sensitive values, for example a password or an API token. It works like a ConfigMap. It is a separate object type, so RBAC can limit who reads it.

A Secret is only base64-encoded by default. Base64 is an encoding, not encryption. Anyone who can read the Secret object can decode it. To protect it, encrypt Secrets at rest in etcd and limit read access with RBAC.

Configuration changes do not restart pods automatically. Environment variables from a ConfigMap are read only when the container starts. A mounted ConfigMap file updates after some delay, but the app must reload it. A rollout (kubectl rollout restart) applies the change safely.

On EKS

On EKS, turn on envelope encryption of Secrets with an AWS KMS key. Many teams keep the real values in AWS Secrets Manager. The External Secrets Operator or the Secrets Store CSI driver syncs them into the cluster.

RememberConfigMap = plain settings. Secret = sensitive settings, base64 only, so protect it with encryption at rest and RBAC.

Used in: K2 K6
Lesson 04

The problem it solvesA container file system is lost when the container restarts. A database that loses its data on every restart is useless.

A volume attaches storage to a pod. The containers in the pod mount it at a path, for example /var/lib/postgresql/data.

Some volumes live only as long as the pod. An emptyDir volume is scratch space that two containers in one pod can share. It is deleted with the pod.

Other volumes are persistent. Their data lives outside the pod and outside the node: on a cloud disk or a network file system. When the pod is replaced, the new pod mounts the same data.

Kubernetes does not manage your data for you. It does not back up, replicate or repair the data. That is your job, or the job of a managed database.

On EKS

On EKS, persistent volumes are usually Amazon EBS disks through the EBS CSI driver. An EBS volume lives in one Availability Zone, so a pod that uses it must run on a node in that same zone.

RememberVolume = storage mounted into a pod. Persistent volumes keep data when the pod is replaced. Kubernetes does not back up your data.

Used in: K3
Lesson 05

The problem it solvesOne pod is a single point of failure. You need copies of the app, rolling updates and automatic replacement, without managing each pod by hand.

You almost never create pods directly. You create a Deployment: a blueprint that says which pod to run and how many copies (replicas) to keep. The Deployment adds a layer of abstraction on top of pods.

The Deployment creates a ReplicaSet, and the ReplicaSet creates the pods. If a pod dies, the ReplicaSet makes a new one. When you change the image, the Deployment creates a new ReplicaSet and moves pods from the old one to the new one, step by step. This is a rolling update. The old ReplicaSet stays, so kubectl rollout undo can go back.

  1. Deployment (replicas: 3)
  2. ReplicaSet (one per version)
  3. Pod
  4. Pod
  5. Pod

Deployments are for stateless apps: every replica is the same and can be replaced by any other. Databases are stateful. Each replica has its own data and its own role, for example a primary and replicas.

A StatefulSet runs stateful apps. It gives each pod a stable name (postgres-0, postgres-1), a stable DNS name, and its own persistent volume. It starts and stops the pods in order. Lesson 15 explains it in depth.

Two more controllers complete the set:

  • A DaemonSet runs one pod on every node (or on selected nodes). Use it for node agents: log collectors, the VPC CNI, kube-proxy.
  • A Job runs pods until they finish successfully. A CronJob creates Jobs on a schedule. Test shards and nightly cleanups are Jobs.
On EKS

StatefulSets are harder to operate than Deployments. Many teams run stateless apps on EKS and use a managed database such as Amazon RDS. For a test platform, this is usually the right choice.

RememberDeployment → ReplicaSet → pods for stateless apps. StatefulSet for stateful apps (stable names and own volumes). DaemonSet = one pod per node. Job/CronJob = run to completion.

Used in: K2 K5 K3
Part 2

The architecture that runs the components

Lesson 06

The problem it solvesPods run on nodes. Something on each node must start the containers, report back to the cluster, and route Service traffic.

Every worker node runs three processes:

  1. Container runtime. It pulls images and runs containers. EKS uses containerd. Docker is not required on the node.
  2. kubelet. It is the Kubernetes agent on the node. It gets the pods for its node from the API server and tells the runtime to start them. It also runs the probes and reports pod and node status.
  3. kube-proxy. It implements Services on the node. It programs iptables or IPVS rules, so a call to a Service IP goes to one ready pod. It prefers a pod on the same node when it can, which saves network hops.

A node also needs a CNI plugin (Container Network Interface). The CNI gives each pod its IP address and connects pod networking across nodes.

Worker nodes do the real work. Production clusters have many worker nodes. A node that stops sending status becomes NotReady, and its pods are rescheduled to other nodes after a timeout.

On EKS

On EKS, the CNI is the Amazon VPC CNI (the aws-node DaemonSet). kube-proxy and CoreDNS run as EKS add-ons. The kubelet is part of the EKS-optimized AMI or Bottlerocket.

RememberEvery node runs: container runtime (containerd), kubelet (agent that runs and reports pods), kube-proxy (Service routing). Plus a CNI for pod IPs.

Used in: K7 K1
Lesson 07

The problem it solvesSomeone must decide where each pod runs, notice failures, and store the state of the whole cluster.

The control plane (the master nodes in older texts) runs four processes:

  1. kube-apiserver. It is the only entry point to the cluster. kubectl, the kubelets, controllers and CI pipelines all talk to it. It authenticates the caller, authorizes the request with RBAC, validates it, and stores it.
  2. kube-scheduler. It decides which node gets a new pod. It looks at the pod resource requests, the free capacity on each node, taints, affinity rules and topology. It only decides; the kubelet on that node starts the pod.
  3. kube-controller-manager. It runs the controllers: the ReplicaSet, Deployment, Node, Job and EndpointSlice controllers, and more. Each one watches the state and fixes the difference from the desired state. When a pod dies, a controller notices and asks for a new pod.
  4. etcd. It is a distributed key-value store that holds the whole cluster state: every object, its spec and its status. It is the cluster brain. If you lose etcd, you lose the cluster. Application data is not in etcd.

A fifth process, the cloud-controller-manager, connects Kubernetes to the cloud provider, for example to manage node lifecycle with EC2.

What happens when you run kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml:

  1. kubectl sends the Deployment to the API server.
  2. The API server authenticates you, checks RBAC, validates the object and writes it to etcd.
  3. The Deployment controller sees the new Deployment and creates a ReplicaSet. The ReplicaSet controller creates 3 pod objects, still with no node.
  4. The scheduler sees 3 unscheduled pods and assigns each one to a node.
  5. The kubelet on each node sees its new pod, pulls the image with containerd and starts the containers.
  6. The kubelet runs the probes and reports the status. When the readiness probe passes, the EndpointSlice controller adds the pod IP to the Service.

Everything goes through the API server, and every component watches for changes. No component calls another one directly. This design is why the system heals itself.

On EKS

On EKS, AWS runs and scales the control plane for you across 3 Availability Zones. You do not see or patch these machines, and you cannot SSH to them. You pay a fixed fee per cluster per hour.

RememberAPI server = the single front door. Scheduler = picks a node. Controller manager = keeps desired state. etcd = the cluster state store.

Used in: K2 K7
Lesson 08

The problem it solvesIn the interview, you must say which layer you own when something fails.

Amazon EKS is managed Kubernetes. AWS owns the control plane. You own the data plane, the workloads and the integration with your AWS account.

LayerWho owns it on EKSExamples
Control planeAWSAPI server, etcd, scheduler, controller manager, upgrades of these
Worker nodesYou (or AWS with Auto Mode / Fargate)Managed node groups, self-managed nodes, Karpenter NodePools
Cluster add-onsYou choose and upgradeVPC CNI, CoreDNS, kube-proxy, EBS CSI driver, Pod Identity Agent
WorkloadsYouDeployments, Services, Ingress, ConfigMaps, Secrets
AWS integrationYouVPC and subnets, IAM roles, ALB through the Load Balancer Controller, ECR

Ways to get worker nodes:

  • Managed node groups: AWS creates an EC2 Auto Scaling group with EKS AMIs and handles node updates.
  • Self-managed nodes: you run the EC2 instances yourself. Most control, most work.
  • Karpenter: an open-source autoscaler that starts the right EC2 instance for pending pods, including Spot. It is GA since v1.0.
  • Fargate: AWS runs each pod on its own isolated compute. No nodes to manage, but no DaemonSets and some limits.
  • EKS Auto Mode: AWS manages the nodes, autoscaling (based on Karpenter), load balancing and storage for you.
On EKS

A short answer for the interview: "EKS runs the control plane. We own the nodes, the add-ons, IAM and the network. When I debug, I first decide which of those layers fails."

RememberAWS: control plane. You: nodes, add-ons, workloads, IAM, VPC.

Used in: K6 K7 G4
Part 3

Working with a cluster: kubectl and YAML

Lesson 09

The problem it solveskubectl is how you, and CI, talk to the API server. In a debugging question, the interviewer wants to hear the exact commands in the correct order.

kubectl is the command-line client for the API server. It reads a kubeconfig file (~/.kube/config) that lists clusters, users and contexts. A context is one cluster plus one user plus a default namespace.

On EKS, aws eks update-kubeconfig writes the kubeconfig entry. kubectl then gets a short-lived token from your AWS identity. EKS maps that IAM identity to Kubernetes permissions with access entries (or the older aws-auth ConfigMap).

For local practice, use minikube or kind. Both run a full cluster on your laptop, with the control plane and a worker on one machine.

CommandWhen and why
aws eks update-kubeconfig --name <cluster> --region ap-south-1Do this first. It adds the EKS cluster to your kubeconfig so that kubectl can connect.
kubectl config current-contextDo a check of which cluster you talk to before you change anything.
kubectl get pods -n <ns> -o wideShows each pod, its state, READY count, restarts, pod IP and node. Start every investigation here.
kubectl get pods -A --field-selector=status.phase=PendingFinds all Pending pods in all namespaces. Use it during a capacity problem.
kubectl describe pod <name> -n <ns>Shows the full spec, the container last state, the exit code and the Events. Most answers are in the Events section at the bottom.
kubectl logs <pod> -c <container> -n <ns>Shows the log of the current container. Add -c when the pod has more than one container.
kubectl logs <pod> --previousShows the log of the container before the last restart. Use it for CrashLoopBackOff, because the current container has no useful log yet.
kubectl logs -f deploy/<name> --since=10mFollows the log of one pod of a Deployment for the last 10 minutes.
kubectl get events -n <ns> --sort-by=.lastTimestampShows recent events in time order: scheduling failures, probe failures, image pulls and evictions.
kubectl exec -it <pod> -- shOpens a shell inside the container. Use it to test DNS, call a dependency, or run aws sts get-caller-identity.
kubectl top pods -n <ns> / kubectl top nodesShows live CPU and memory use. It needs metrics-server. Compare the numbers with requests and limits.
kubectl port-forward svc/<service> 8080:80 -n <ns>Connects your laptop port 8080 to the Service. Use it to test the app without the ALB, so you can find which layer fails.
kubectl get endpointslices -n <ns> -l kubernetes.io/service-name=<service>Shows the ready pod IPs behind a Service. An empty list explains a 503.
kubectl describe node <node>Shows node conditions (MemoryPressure, DiskPressure, Ready), allocated requests and the pods on the node.
kubectl rollout status deploy/<name> / kubectl rollout undo deploy/<name>Watches a rollout. undo goes back to the previous ReplicaSet when a new version fails.
kubectl auth can-i create jobs -n <ns> --as=system:serviceaccount:<ns>:<sa>Checks an RBAC permission for a ServiceAccount. Use it when CI gets forbidden errors.
kubectl diff -f <file> / kubectl apply -f <file>diff shows what will change. apply sends the desired state to the cluster.
On EKS

Always run kubectl config current-context before a change. The most common serious mistake is a command against the wrong cluster.

Rememberkubectl → API server, with the identity and cluster from the current kubeconfig context.

Used in: K1 K2 K7
Lesson 10

The problem it solvesEvery scenario answer refers to fields in a manifest. You must read YAML fast and know which field causes which behavior.

Every Kubernetes object has the same shape:

  • apiVersion and kind: which type of object this is, for example apps/v1 and Deployment.
  • metadata: the name, the namespace, labels and annotations.
  • spec: the desired state that you write. Each kind has its own spec.
  • status: the actual state. Kubernetes writes it, and it comes from etcd. You never write it.

Controllers compare spec with status all the time and fix the difference. This loop is the core of Kubernetes. It is called reconciliation.

Labels connect objects. The Deployment selector must match the labels in the pod template. The Service selector must match the same pod labels. A label mismatch is a classic cause of a Service with no endpoints, which gives a 503.

Connect ports correctly: the Service port is what clients call, and the Service targetPort must equal the container containerPort. The Ingress backend uses the Service port, not the container port.

On EKS

Store manifests in Git, deploy with a pipeline or GitOps (Argo CD, Flux), and never change production with hand edits. Then git log is your change history.

Remembermetadata (name, labels) + spec (desired) + status (actual). Labels and selectors connect objects; ports connect Service to container.

Used in: K1 K2 K5
Part 4

Each component in more depth

Lesson 11

The problem it solvesHundreds of teams on one cluster need separate names, separate permissions and limits on what each team can use.

A namespace is a virtual cluster inside the cluster. Most objects live in exactly one namespace. Names must be unique only inside a namespace.

A new cluster has these namespaces: default, kube-system (cluster components such as CoreDNS and the CNI), kube-public and kube-node-lease (node heartbeats).

Use namespaces to:

  • group the resources of one team or one app;
  • give each team permissions only in its namespace, with RBAC Role and RoleBinding;
  • limit total usage with a ResourceQuota, and set default requests and limits with a LimitRange;
  • control traffic between namespaces with a NetworkPolicy.

Some objects are cluster-scoped and belong to no namespace: nodes, PersistentVolumes, StorageClasses, ClusterRoles and namespaces themselves.

A pod can call a Service in another namespace with the full DNS name: <service>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local. A ConfigMap or Secret cannot be shared across namespaces; each namespace needs its own copy.

On EKS

Namespaces are a soft boundary. All pods still share the same nodes and kernel. For strong isolation between untrusted workloads, use separate node pools with taints, or separate clusters.

RememberNamespace = a name, permission and quota boundary. Not a security wall by itself.

Used in: K4
Lesson 12

The problem it solvesThe 503 question needs this exact path. You debug by walking the path one hop at a time.

flowchart LR
  U["Client"] --> D["Route 53 DNS"]
  D --> A["ALB listener :443 (TLS)"]
  A --> R{"Listener rule: host + path"}
  R --> T["Target group: pod IPs"]
  T --> P["Pod 10.0.12.45"]
  P --> C["Container :8080"]
  L["AWS Load Balancer Controller"] -. "creates from Ingress" .-> A
  L -. "registers ready pods" .-> T
  1. A test or a user calls https://results.test-platform.example.com/runs.
  2. DNS (Route 53) returns the address of the ALB. ExternalDNS can create this record from the Ingress host.
  3. The ALB listener gets the request on port 443 and ends TLS with an ACM certificate.
  4. The ALB checks its listener rules. The host and path match, so the rule forwards to one target group.
  5. The AWS Load Balancer Controller made this ALB, rule and target group from the Ingress object.
  6. With target type ip, the target group holds pod IPs, for example 10.0.12.45:8080. The controller updates the list when pods change.
  7. The ALB sends the request only to targets that pass the target group health check.
  8. The packet goes straight to the pod. This works because the VPC CNI gives each pod a real VPC IP address.
  9. The packet arrives at the container port (targetPort 8080). The app handles it and sends the response back the same way.
  10. With target type instance, there is one more hop: the ALB sends to a NodePort on a node, and kube-proxy forwards to a pod.
  11. Inside the cluster, pod-to-pod calls do not use the ALB. A pod calls the Service name, CoreDNS gives the ClusterIP, and kube-proxy picks a ready pod.

Two target types matter. With target-type: ip, the ALB sends traffic straight to pod IPs. With target-type: instance, it sends to a NodePort on each node, and kube-proxy forwards to a pod. Use ip on EKS: one hop less, and the target health follows the pods.

The ALB has its own health check. It can disagree with the Kubernetes readiness probe. Point the ALB health check path to the same endpoint as the readiness probe.

On EKS

Use alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/group.name to share one ALB across many Ingress objects. Each ALB costs money, and 200 teams with one ALB each is expensive.

RememberDNS → ALB listener → rule → target group (pod IPs) → pod → container port. The controller builds the ALB from the Ingress.

Used in: K1 K5
Lesson 13

The problem it solvesA real app is 10 to 20 YAML files, repeated for each environment with small changes. Copying them by hand causes drift.

Helm is the package manager for Kubernetes. A chart is a package of YAML templates plus a values.yaml file with defaults. You install a chart with your own values, and Helm renders the final YAML.

Each install is a release with a version history. helm upgrade changes a release, and helm rollback returns to an earlier revision.

Teams use public charts for common software, for example the AWS Load Balancer Controller, Karpenter, KEDA, Prometheus and the Actions Runner Controller. They write their own charts for their apps.

An alternative is Kustomize, built into kubectl. It patches plain YAML for each environment instead of templating it.

On EKS

For a shared test platform, publish one chart for the runner and worker setup. Teams then change only their values file. This is the same idea as a reusable GitHub Actions workflow.

RememberHelm chart = templates + values. Release = an installed chart with history and rollback.

Used in: K3 G4
Lesson 14

The problem it solvesA pod must not know which cloud disk it uses. The cluster must create disks on demand when pods ask for them.

Kubernetes splits storage into three objects:

  • A PersistentVolume (PV) is a piece of real storage in the cluster, for example one EBS volume. It is cluster-scoped.
  • A PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC) is a request for storage by a pod: "I need 20 GiB, ReadWriteOnce". It lives in the namespace of the pod.
  • A StorageClass describes how to create PVs on demand: the provisioner (the EBS CSI driver), the disk type (gp3), and the reclaim policy.
  1. Pod
  2. PVC: 20Gi
  3. StorageClass: gp3
  4. PV
  5. EBS volume

With dynamic provisioning, a new PVC makes the StorageClass create a new PV and a new disk automatically. The pod mounts the PVC as a volume.

Access modes matter. ReadWriteOnce means one node can mount it, which is true for EBS. ReadWriteMany means many nodes can mount it at the same time, which needs a shared file system such as Amazon EFS.

The reclaim policy decides what happens to the disk when you delete the PVC. Delete removes the disk. Retain keeps it, so you can recover data.

ConfigMaps and Secrets can also be mounted as volumes. They are not persistent storage, but they use the same volumes and volumeMounts fields.

On EKS

Use the EBS CSI driver with volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer. Then the disk is created in the same Availability Zone as the node that the scheduler picks.

RememberPod → PVC (the request) → StorageClass (how to make it) → PV (the real disk).

Used in: K3
Lesson 15

The problem it solvesReplicas of a database are not interchangeable. Each one needs its own identity and its own data.

A StatefulSet gives each pod three things that a Deployment does not:

  1. A stable name with an ordinal: postgres-0, postgres-1, postgres-2. A replaced pod keeps the same name.
  2. A stable DNS name through a headless Service (clusterIP: None): postgres-0.postgres.test-platform.svc.cluster.local. Clients can address one specific replica, for example the primary.
  3. Its own PVC, from volumeClaimTemplates. When postgres-1 is replaced, the new postgres-1 mounts the same disk.

Pods start in order (0, then 1, then 2) and stop in reverse order. Updates also go in order. This order lets a database set up replication safely.

Kubernetes still does not handle the database logic: replication, failover, backups. You need an operator or your own tooling for that. This is why many teams prefer a managed database.

On EKS

Deleting a StatefulSet does not delete its PVCs by default. This protects data, but it also leaves EBS volumes that cost money. Clean them up deliberately.

RememberStatefulSet = stable name + stable DNS (headless Service) + own PVC per pod, started in order.

Used in: K3
Lesson 16

The problem it solvesThe interviewer will ask why a Service has no endpoints, or which Service type fits a case.

TypeWhat it doesWhen to use it
ClusterIP (default)A virtual IP and DNS name, reachable only inside the cluster.Service-to-service calls; anything behind an Ingress.
Headless (clusterIP: None)No virtual IP. DNS returns the pod IPs directly.StatefulSets; clients that pick a specific pod.
NodePortOpens the same port (30000–32767) on every node and forwards to the Service.Rarely directly; ALB target type instance uses it.
LoadBalancerAsks the cloud for an external load balancer. On EKS, the AWS Load Balancer Controller creates an NLB.TCP/UDP traffic from outside, or non-HTTP protocols.
ExternalNameA DNS alias (CNAME) to a name outside the cluster.Give an external database a cluster-internal name.

A Service keeps a live list of the IP addresses of its ready pods in EndpointSlice objects. The EndpointSlice controller adds a pod when it is Ready and removes it when it is not.

An empty EndpointSlice has three common causes. The selector does not match the pod labels, no pod passes the readiness probe, or the pods are in another namespace.

Each layer is built on the one before it: a LoadBalancer Service also has a NodePort and a ClusterIP.

On EKS

kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=<svc> is the fastest single check in the 503 scenario.

RememberClusterIP inside, NodePort on every node, LoadBalancer from the cloud, headless for direct pod DNS. EndpointSlices hold the ready pod IPs.

Used in: K1
Part 5

What keeps it healthy in production

Lesson 17

The problem it solves"Running but 503" and "CrashLoopBackOff" are both questions about this lesson.

A pod moves through phases: Pending (accepted, but not running yet), Running, Succeeded, Failed. kubectl get pods also shows reasons that you must recognize:

  • Pending for a long time: no node has room, a taint blocks it, or (on EKS) no free IP addresses.
  • ImagePullBackOff: the image name or tag is wrong, or the node has no permission to pull from ECR.
  • CreateContainerConfigError: a ConfigMap or Secret key that the pod needs does not exist.
  • CrashLoopBackOff: the container starts and exits again and again. Kubernetes waits longer between each restart.
  • OOMKilled (exit code 137): the container used more memory than its limit, and the kernel killed it.

Running is not Ready. Running means the containers started. Ready means the pod passes its readiness probe and can get traffic.

The kubelet runs three probes:

ProbeQuestion it asksWhen it fails
LivenessIs the app alive, or stuck?The kubelet restarts the container.
ReadinessCan the app take traffic now?The pod is removed from Service endpoints. No restart.
StartupHas the app finished starting?Liveness and readiness wait until it passes. Protects slow boots.

A liveness probe that is too strict kills a slow app before it is ready, and causes a CrashLoopBackOff. Use a startup probe for slow starts. Do not check downstream dependencies in the liveness probe, or one database problem restarts every pod.

On shutdown, the kubelet sends SIGTERM and waits terminationGracePeriodSeconds (30 seconds by default), then sends SIGKILL. A preStop hook runs before SIGTERM. Question K5 uses this to drain traffic.

On EKS

The ALB health check and the readiness probe are two separate checks. Keep them on the same endpoint, or the ALB and Kubernetes disagree about which pods are healthy.

RememberLiveness → restart. Readiness → traffic on/off. Startup → wait for boot. Running ≠ Ready.

Used in: K1 K2 K5
Lesson 18

The problem it solvesShared clusters fail when one team's pods take all the CPU or memory. The noisy-neighbor question is about this lesson.

Each container can set two values for CPU and memory:

  • A request is the amount that the scheduler reserves. The scheduler places a pod only on a node with enough unreserved capacity. CPU is in millicores: 250m is a quarter of one core.
  • A limit is the maximum at runtime. Above the CPU limit, the container is throttled (slowed). Above the memory limit, the container is killed (OOMKilled, exit code 137).

Kubernetes gives each pod a QoS class from these values. When a node runs out of memory, the kubelet evicts pods in this order:

  1. BestEffort: no requests or limits. Evicted first.
  2. Burstable: requests lower than limits. Evicted next, the largest users first.
  3. Guaranteed: requests equal limits for every container. Evicted last.

A ResourceQuota caps the total requests and limits in a namespace. A LimitRange sets defaults for containers that do not declare values. Together they stop one team from starving the others.

A PriorityClass lets important pods preempt less important ones when the cluster is full. A PodDisruptionBudget limits how many pods of an app can be down during voluntary disruptions, such as a node drain. It does not protect against eviction from memory pressure.

On EKS

Requests decide cost on EKS: Karpenter and Cluster Autoscaler add nodes for pending requests, not for real usage. Requests that are too high waste money. Requests that are too low cause eviction and noisy neighbors.

RememberRequest = reserved, used by the scheduler. Limit = the ceiling: CPU throttles, memory kills. QoS decides who is evicted first.

Used in: K4 K3 K7
Lesson 19

The problem it solvesA pod that gets AccessDenied from S3, or a CI job that gets "forbidden" from the API server, is a question about this lesson.

There are two separate permission systems. Keep them apart in your answer:

  • Kubernetes RBAC controls what a caller can do inside the cluster: list pods, create Jobs, read Secrets.
  • AWS IAM controls what a pod can do in AWS: write to S3, read from SQS.

A ServiceAccount is the identity of a pod inside Kubernetes. Each pod runs as one ServiceAccount.

RBAC uses four objects. A Role lists allowed verbs on resources in one namespace. A ClusterRole does the same for the whole cluster. A RoleBinding or ClusterRoleBinding gives the role to a user, group or ServiceAccount.

To give a pod AWS permissions on EKS, connect its ServiceAccount to an IAM role. Do not use the node instance role for app permissions, because every pod on the node then gets those permissions. Two methods exist:

  • IRSA (IAM Roles for Service Accounts): annotate the ServiceAccount with a role ARN. The role trusts the cluster OIDC provider.
  • EKS Pod Identity: create a pod identity association for the namespace and ServiceAccount. No annotation and no OIDC provider. AWS recommends it for new work.
On EKS

Debug from inside the pod: kubectl exec -it <pod> -- aws sts get-caller-identity. If it shows the node role, the pod did not get its own role.

RememberRBAC = permissions inside the cluster. IAM via IRSA or Pod Identity = permissions in AWS. Both attach to the ServiceAccount.

Used in: K6 G3
Lesson 20

The problem it solvesThe question about 2,000 browser sessions at 9 AM and near zero at night is about this lesson.

Scaling has two layers. Pod scaling adds pods. Node scaling adds machines for those pods.

  • The HorizontalPodAutoscaler (HPA) changes the replica count of a Deployment from metrics, usually CPU as a percentage of the request. It needs metrics-server.
  • KEDA scales on event sources: the length of an SQS queue, a Selenium Grid session queue, a Kafka lag. It can scale to zero, which HPA alone cannot do.
  • When new pods do not fit, they stay Pending. The Cluster Autoscaler then grows a node group, or Karpenter starts the best-fit EC2 instance directly, including Spot. When nodes are empty, both remove them.
  1. Queue grows
  2. KEDA adds pods
  3. Pods Pending
  4. Karpenter adds nodes
  5. Pods Running

Placement controls which pods go to which nodes:

  • A taint on a node repels pods. Only pods with a matching toleration can run there. Use it to keep a node pool for browsers only.
  • A nodeSelector or node affinity attracts a pod to certain nodes, for example by instance type or zone.
  • Pod anti-affinity and topology spread constraints spread replicas across nodes and zones, so one failure does not take all replicas.
On EKS

Spot nodes can be taken back with 2 minutes of notice. Run only interruptible work on Spot, such as test shards that can retry, and keep the platform services on On-Demand nodes.

RememberHPA/KEDA scale pods. Cluster Autoscaler/Karpenter scale nodes for Pending pods. Taints repel, tolerations allow, affinity attracts.

Used in: K3 K4 K7
Chapter 02

GitHub Actions

GitHub Actions runs workflows when events happen in a repo. A workflow has jobs, and each job runs on a runner and has steps. On this team, your job is to make CI a shared, safe and fast product for hundreds of teams.

PracticeWrite these workflows yourselfThe Actions Workbench has a scenario for each topic in G1 to G7, with a live checker and hints.Open ↗
UKG-G1

Interviewer

We have about 300 repos. Every team copy-pasted its own E2E workflow, so we have 300 slightly different YAML files. A security fix takes months to reach everyone. How would you centralize this?

What this tests The interviewer tests if you can design CI as a shared product with versions, ownership and a rollout plan.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

I move the common E2E logic into one reusable workflow that the platform team owns. Each repo keeps a short caller file that uses workflow_call with a version tag. I pin every third-party action to a commit SHA, and an org ruleset makes the shared check required. I roll out in waves with automated pull requests and give the old YAML a clear end date. After that, a security fix is one release, not 300 pull requests.

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. Find out what exists

    Inventory the 300 workflows first. Use the GitHub code search API or a script to group them by shape. Usually 4 or 5 patterns cover more than 80% of the repos. Note the real differences, such as the Node version, the test command and the browsers.

  2. 2. Build the shared layer

    Use two building blocks:

    • A reusable workflow (on: workflow_call) for whole jobs: checkout, setup, shard, test, report.
    • Composite actions for small step groups that teams mix into their own jobs, for example "setup test env".

    Put both in one repo, for example ukg/test-platform-workflows. Expose only the real differences as inputs.

  3. 3. Version it like a product

    Release with SemVer tags such as v3.2.0 and a moving major tag v3. Teams call @v3 to get fixes, or a commit SHA when they need full immutability. Inside the shared workflow, pin all third-party actions to a full commit SHA. Use Dependabot or Renovate to raise the SHA pins.

  4. 4. Enforce the minimum with rulesets

    Use organization rulesets to require the shared workflow to pass before merge on protected branches. This sets the floor for every repo. It does not force every team to use the same detail.

  5. 5. Roll out and deprecate

    Start with 3 to 5 friendly pilot repos. Then open automated pull requests that replace the old YAML with the caller file. Add a warning annotation to the old patterns and publish a removal date. Track adoption on a dashboard: repos on the shared workflow, and which version.

  6. 6. Make ownership clear

    The platform team owns the shared workflow, with CODEOWNERS, a changelog and an on-call rotation. Teams can contribute through pull requests and an RFC for big changes. Provide a template repo so new services start on the shared workflow from day one.

Concepts you must own 11

Reusable workflow
Idea

A reusable workflow is a whole workflow that other workflows call, like a function.

Example

Team A writes 8 lines that call ukg/test-platform-workflows/.github/workflows/e2e.yml@v3. All jobs come from the shared file.

Term

The called file has on: workflow_call with inputs, secrets and outputs. The caller uses jobs.<id>.uses: owner/repo/.github/workflows/file.yml@ref. Nesting depth is limited.

workflow_call inputs
Idea

Inputs are the parameters that a caller gives to the reusable workflow.

Example

with: { node-version: "20", test-command: "npm run e2e" }.

Term

Inputs have a type (string, number, boolean), an optional default and required. Read them as ${{ inputs.name }}.

secrets: inherit
Idea

secrets: inherit passes all the caller's secrets to the reusable workflow, so you do not list each one.

Example

The caller has TEST_USER_PASSWORD. The shared workflow can read it without an explicit mapping.

Term

It works only when the caller and the called workflow are in the same organization or enterprise. Explicit secrets: mapping is safer because it shows exactly what passes.

Composite action
Idea

A composite action is a group of steps packed as one step.

Example

uses: ukg/actions/setup-test-env@v2 installs Node, restores caches and installs browsers in one line.

Term

It has runs: using: composite in action.yml. It runs inside the caller job, so it cannot set runs-on or own jobs. It cannot read secrets directly; pass them as inputs.

Reusable workflow vs composite action
Idea

Use a reusable workflow to share whole jobs. Use a composite action to share a few steps inside a team's own job.

Example

The full E2E pipeline is a reusable workflow. "Upload results to the results service" is a composite action.

Term

Reusable workflows control runners, matrices, environments and permissions. Composite actions are more flexible but give less control and less visibility in the UI.

Versioning by tag or SHA
Idea

A version reference decides which copy of the shared workflow a repo runs.

Example

@v3 follows the newest v3 release. @v3.2.1 is fixed. @9f3e... is fixed and cannot move.

Term

Tags can be moved or deleted, so a commit SHA is the only immutable reference. Many platforms use a major tag for speed and a SHA for high-risk repos.

Organization rulesets and required workflows
Idea

A ruleset is an org-wide rule. It can make a workflow a required check before merge in many repos at one time.

Example

The ruleset says: on main in all repos with property tier=prod, the e2e workflow must pass.

Term

Organization rulesets target repos by name or custom property. The "require workflows to pass before merging" rule replaced the older "required workflows" feature.

Template repository
Idea

A template repo is a starter repo. New repos copy it, including the workflow caller file.

Example

A new service made from ukg/service-template has CI on day one.

Term

Mark a repo as a template in its settings. A copy does not follow later changes, so keep the logic in the reusable workflow, not in the template.

Pin third-party actions to a commit SHA
Idea

A tag on a third-party action can change. If an attacker changes it, your CI runs their code with your secrets.

Example

In March 2025, the tj-actions/changed-files tags were moved to malicious code. Repos pinned to a SHA were safe.

Term

Use uses: owner/action@<40-char-sha> # vX.Y.Z. Use Dependabot or Renovate to update the pins. An org policy can allow only listed actions.

Rollout and deprecation of old YAML
Idea

Move teams in waves and give the old way an end date. Do not switch all 300 repos in one day.

Example

Wave 1: 5 pilot repos. Wave 2: automated pull requests to 100 repos. Wave 3: the rest, with help.

Term

Use automated pull requests (a script or Renovate), warning annotations (::warning::) in the old pattern, an adoption dashboard and a published removal date.

Ownership of the shared workflow
Idea

One team must own the shared workflow, or it will rot.

Example

The test platform team owns it, reviews changes and answers incidents when it breaks CI for many teams.

Term

Use CODEOWNERS, a changelog, SemVer releases, an RFC for breaking changes and a support channel. Contributors outside the team can still send pull requests.

Code to know

Follow-up questions

  • A team needs a step that the shared workflow does not have. What do you do?

    Add an extension point, such as an optional pre-test-command input or a separate job that runs before or after the reusable workflow. If many teams need it, put it in the shared workflow. I do not want teams to fork the shared file.

  • How do you ship a fix to all teams fast, for example a security fix?

    Release a PATCH version and move the v3 tag, so every @v3 caller gets it on the next run. Repos that pin a SHA get an automated pull request from Renovate. For a severe issue, I also announce it and track which repos still run the old version.

  • Why not use only composite actions?

    Composite actions cannot own the runner, the matrix, the environment or the job permissions. So each repo still writes most of the job, and drift comes back. Composite actions are good building blocks inside the reusable workflow.

  • How do you test a change to the shared workflow before release?

    The shared repo has its own CI that calls the workflow against a few sample repos. Then I release an RC tag and ask canary teams to point at it for a few days. Only then do I move the major tag.

Caution
  • Some candidates say "put the YAML in a template repo". A template is a one-time copy, so drift starts again on day two.
  • Some candidates pin shared actions to @main. Then any merge changes 300 pipelines with no version and no rollback.
  • Some candidates use secrets: inherit everywhere without thought. It passes every secret, so a bug in the shared workflow can expose all of them.
  • Some candidates force the change on all repos in one day. This breaks many teams and destroys trust in the platform.
Staff signal

A Staff answer treats the shared workflow as a product. It has an owner, versions, a contribution path, an adoption metric and a deprecation plan, not only a YAML file.

  • Reusable Workflow and Composite Actions in GitHub ActionsMayank SoniReusable workflows vs composite actions: when to use each.
  • Introduction to GitHub Actions - Part 6 - Repository RulesetsMickey GoussetRulesets, the current home of org-level 'require workflows to pass'.
UKG-G2

Interviewer

The E2E pipeline for a large monorepo takes 45 minutes and developers bypass it. Get it under 10 minutes without losing coverage.

What this tests The interviewer tests if you measure first and then use parallelism, caching and test selection with clear trade-offs.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

First I measure the time of each job and step, because I need to know where the 45 minutes go. Then I fix the biggest costs: caches for dependencies and browsers, sharding with a matrix, and path filters so a PR runs only affected tests. I add tiers: a fast smoke set on each PR, the full set on merge, and the long set nightly. Coverage stays the same because every test still runs at some tier.

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. Measure before you change anything

    Get the time of each job and step from the run logs or the GitHub API. Split the 45 minutes into queue time, setup time and test time. Also find the 20 slowest test files. A small number of files usually take most of the time.

  2. 2. Remove waste in setup
    • Cache dependencies with actions/setup-node cache: npm or actions/cache keyed on the lockfile hash.
    • Cache browser binaries and build outputs.
    • Build the app one time, upload it as an artifact, and download it in each test job.

    This often saves 5 to 10 minutes per job.

  3. 3. Run tests in parallel

    Use a strategy.matrix to split the suite into shards, for example 8 shards with --shard=i/8. Use the needs graph: one build job fans out to many test jobs, then one report job fans in. Balance shards by test duration, not by file count.

  4. 4. Run only what the change affects

    Use paths triggers or dorny/paths-filter so a change in apps/billing does not run the apps/hr suite. In a monorepo, a tool such as Nx or Turborepo can compute the affected projects. Always run a small smoke set, so a bad filter cannot hide a total break.

  5. 5. Add test tiers
    • PR: smoke tests plus affected tests, target under 10 minutes.
    • Merge to main: the full suite, sharded.
    • Nightly: slow, cross-browser and long-running tests.

    Every test still runs at some tier, so coverage is the same. Only the time of feedback changes.

  6. 6. Stop waste and decide on runners

    Add a concurrency group with cancel-in-progress: true so a new push cancels the old run on that PR. Use larger runners for CPU-heavy jobs if the cost is lower than the developer time saved. Choose fail-fast on purpose: off for full reports, on for quick PR feedback.

  7. 7. Protect the result

    Put the pipeline time on a dashboard with a budget, for example p90 under 10 minutes. Alert when the trend goes up. Without this, the time grows back in six months.

Concepts you must own 11

Measure per job and per step
Idea

You cannot fix time that you have not measured.

Example

The data shows 12 minutes for npm ci and browser install in every shard. Test time is only 20 minutes.

Term

Get timings from the Actions UI, the REST API (/actions/runs/{id}/jobs has step start and end times) or OpenTelemetry export. Separate queue time from run time.

Sharding with a matrix
Idea

Split the tests into equal parts and run the parts at the same time on different runners.

Example

8 shards of 4 minutes each instead of one run of 32 minutes.

Term

strategy.matrix.shard: [1..N] with npx playwright test --shard=${{ matrix.shard }}/${{ strategy.job-total }}. Each matrix entry is a separate job. The maximum is 256 jobs per matrix.

Test impact and path filters
Idea

Run only the tests for the code that changed.

Example

A PR changes only apps/web/**. The API contract tests do not run.

Term

Use on.pull_request.paths to skip whole workflows. Use dorny/paths-filter to skip single jobs, because it gives outputs that if: can read. Nx and Turborepo compute affected projects from the dependency graph.

Caching with actions/cache
Idea

A cache saves files from one run and gives them back in the next run, so you do not download them again.

Example

~/.cache/ms-playwright is restored, so browsers are not downloaded again.

Term

key is an exact match, for example a hash of package-lock.json. restore-keys are prefix fallbacks for a partial hit. Caches are scoped by branch, and a PR can read the cache of the base branch.

Dependency cache vs build cache
Idea

A dependency cache keeps downloaded packages. A build cache keeps compiled output.

Example

Dependency cache: ~/.npm. Build cache: .next/cache or the Nx cache.

Term

Key the dependency cache on the lockfile. Key the build cache on source hashes. A wrong key gives stale builds, so include every input that changes the output.

Artifacts between jobs
Idea

An artifact is a file that one job uploads and another job downloads.

Example

The build job uploads dist/. Eight test jobs download it and do not build again.

Term

actions/upload-artifact@v4 and actions/download-artifact@v4. Artifacts are for passing results and reports. Caches are for speed. In v4, artifact names must be unique in a run.

needs graph, fan-out and fan-in
Idea

needs sets the order of jobs. One job can start many jobs, and many jobs can feed one job.

Example

build → 8 e2e shards → report.

Term

Jobs without needs run in parallel. needs can read outputs (needs.build.outputs.x). Use if: ${{ !cancelled() }} on the fan-in job so it runs after failures too.

Concurrency groups with cancel-in-progress
Idea

A concurrency group lets only one run per group continue. A new run can cancel the old one.

Example

A developer pushes 3 commits in 2 minutes. Only the last commit runs to the end.

Term

concurrency: { group: ${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}, cancel-in-progress: true }. Do not cancel runs on main deploys, or you can lose a deploy.

Larger runners
Idea

Larger runners are GitHub-hosted machines with more CPU and memory.

Example

A 16-core runner runs 4 Playwright workers per shard instead of 2.

Term

They are set up at org level with a label and cost more per minute. Compare cost per run and developer wait time. Self-hosted runners are the other option.

Test tiering
Idea

Run fast, important tests often and slow tests less often.

Example

PR: 150 smoke tests. Merge: 2,000 tests. Nightly: 6,000 tests on 3 browsers.

Term

Use tags (@smoke, @regression) with --grep. Each tier has an owner and a time budget. A failed nightly test must create a ticket, or the tier has no value.

fail-fast trade-offs
Idea

With fail-fast on, the first failed shard cancels the other shards.

Example

On a PR, a failure in shard 2 stops shards 3 to 8 and gives fast feedback.

Term

strategy.fail-fast is true by default. Set it to false when you need the full list of failures, for example on main and nightly.

Code to know

Follow-up questions

  • Shards are unequal. One shard takes 9 minutes and the others take 3. What do you do?

    Split by test duration, not by file count. Store the timing of each file from earlier runs and give each shard an equal total. Also split very large spec files, because one file cannot cross shards in many tools.

  • How do you make sure path filters do not hide a real break?

    Always run a small smoke set on every PR. Run the full suite on merge to main and nightly. Also review the filter map when shared packages change, because a shared package affects everything.

  • Does more shards always help?

    No. Each shard pays a fixed setup cost, so after some point extra shards only add cost and queue time. Find the point where setup time is a small part of each shard.

  • How much will this cost?

    Total runner minutes can go up a little, because setup repeats in each shard. But wall-clock time goes down a lot, and caches cut the repeated setup. I show the cost and the developer hours saved in one table.

Caution
  • Some candidates start with "add more runners". Without measurement, you can pay more and still wait for a slow setup step.
  • Some candidates delete or skip slow tests to hit the target. That loses coverage, which the question forbids.
  • Some candidates use caches with keys that ignore some inputs. Stale caches give wrong results that are very hard to debug.
  • Some candidates turn on retries to make the suite green faster. That hides flaky tests and does not save time.
Staff signal

A Staff answer starts with data, gives a tiered strategy that keeps coverage, and adds a time budget with monitoring so the gain stays.

Watch

  • Matrix Builds & Parallel Jobs in GitHub Actions | Speed Up Your CI/CD!DevTips DailyMatrix strategy to fan out jobs in parallel.
  • Caching Dependencies to SPEED UP Workflows in GitHub ActionsCoderDaveactions/cache keys and restore-keys.
  • Playwright Sharding with Merged Reports in GitHub Actions - Step-by-Step GuideQA RoutineSharding E2E tests with a matrix, then merging reports in a fan-in job.
UKG-G3

Interviewer

A test log printed a production API key. The run came from a pull request built off a fork. Contain it, and redesign so this cannot happen again.

What this tests The interviewer tests if you act in the right order in an incident and know the GitHub Actions trust model.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

First I rotate the key, because a key in a log is already compromised. Then I check the audit logs and the provider logs for use of the key, and I delete the logs that contain it. The likely root cause is pull_request_target or a self-hosted runner that gave secrets to fork code. For the redesign I use OIDC to AWS instead of long-lived keys, and I put prod secrets behind an environment with required reviewers. I also set least-privilege permissions: and turn on secret scanning with push protection.

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. Contain now
    • Revoke and rotate the key immediately. Do not wait for the investigation.
    • Delete the workflow run logs that show the key.
    • Disable the workflow or block fork runs until the fix is in.
    • Tell security, because a production key is an incident.
  2. 2. Find out the impact

    Check the provider logs for use of the key from unknown IPs. Check the GitHub audit log for who triggered the run and who viewed or downloaded logs and artifacts. Check whether the PR changed the workflow or the test code that printed the key.

  3. 3. Find the root cause

    Fork PRs do not get secrets with the pull_request trigger. So something gave them access:

    • pull_request_target that checks out the fork code and runs it with secrets.
    • An org setting that sends secrets to fork PRs.
    • A test that printed an encoded or derived value that masking did not catch.
  4. 4. Remove long-lived secrets

    Use GitHub OIDC to AWS. The job asks for a short-lived token, and AWS STS gives temporary credentials. The IAM trust policy accepts only one repo and one environment, for example repo:ukg/app:environment:prod. Then no long-lived AWS key exists to leak.

  5. 5. Put a human gate in front of prod

    Store prod secrets only in a prod environment with required reviewers and branch restrictions. Tests that run on PRs use test credentials with no prod access. Set permissions: to the minimum, for example contents: read, as the org default.

  6. 6. Detect and prevent

    Turn on secret scanning and push protection for the org. Add a log lint that fails a job if it prints known secret patterns. Write a short postmortem and a rule for pull_request_target: it must never check out and run PR code.

Concepts you must own 10

Rotate first
Idea

A secret that appeared in a log is compromised. Replace it before you investigate.

Example

You revoke the old API key and issue a new one. Then you look at who used the old key.

Term

Incident order: contain (revoke, rotate), then assess (logs), then fix the root cause, then prevent. Deleting the log alone does not help, because someone can have copied it.

pull_request vs pull_request_target
Idea

pull_request runs the PR code with no secrets for forks. pull_request_target runs in the context of the base repo, with secrets.

Example

A workflow on pull_request_target checks out github.event.pull_request.head.sha and runs npm test. The fork's test code can now read secrets.

Term

pull_request_target uses the workflow from the base branch and gets a write token and secrets. It is safe only when it does not run untrusted code, for example for labeling. This danger is called a "pwn request".

Fork PRs get no secrets by default
Idea

GitHub does not give secrets to workflows that run from a fork PR.

Example

A contributor opens a PR from a fork. ${{ secrets.API_KEY }} is empty.

Term

With pull_request from a fork, secrets are not passed (except GITHUB_TOKEN, which is read-only). Org settings can change this for private repos, so check them.

Masking limits
Idea

GitHub hides registered secret values in logs with ***. It cannot hide every changed form of a secret.

Example

The test prints the key in base64, or prints only part of it. The log shows the real value.

Term

Masking matches exact strings. Encoded, split or transformed values are not masked. Use ::add-mask:: for values that you make at runtime, and do not print secrets at all.

Environments with required reviewers
Idea

An environment is a named target, such as prod, with its own secrets and its own rules.

Example

A job with environment: prod waits until a person from the release group approves it.

Term

Environment protection rules include required reviewers, wait timers and deployment branch or tag rules. Environment secrets are only available to jobs that reference that environment.

Least-privilege GITHUB_TOKEN with permissions:
Idea

Each job gets an automatic GITHUB_TOKEN. Give it only the rights that the job needs.

Example

A test job needs contents: read only. It cannot push code or change releases.

Term

Set permissions: at workflow or job level. Unlisted scopes become none. Set the org default to read-only.

OIDC to AWS
Idea

The job proves who it is with a short-lived signed token. AWS trusts that proof and gives temporary keys.

Example

The deploy job gets 1-hour credentials for gha-results-deploy. No AWS key is stored in GitHub.

Term

Add permissions: id-token: write. Use aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials with role-to-assume. AWS calls AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity against the IAM OIDC provider token.actions.githubusercontent.com.

Trust policy scoped to repo, branch or environment
Idea

The IAM role says which GitHub workflows may use it. Make that list as small as possible.

Example

Only repo:ukg/results-service:environment:prod can assume the prod deploy role.

Term

The condition key token.actions.githubusercontent.com:sub takes values such as repo:ORG/REPO:ref:refs/heads/main or repo:ORG/REPO:environment:prod. Always check aud = sts.amazonaws.com. Never use a wildcard for the whole org on a prod role.

Secret scanning and push protection
Idea

GitHub finds known secret formats in code. Push protection blocks a push that contains one.

Example

A developer commits an AWS key. The push fails with a message before the key reaches the repo.

Term

Part of GitHub Advanced Security. It covers partner patterns and custom patterns. Alerts go to repo and org admins.

Audit logs
Idea

The audit log records who did what in the organization.

Example

It shows who re-ran the workflow, who changed a secret and who changed a ruleset.

Term

Use the org audit log (UI, API or streaming to a SIEM). The cloud provider logs, such as AWS CloudTrail, show where a leaked key was used.

Code to know

Follow-up questions

  • When is pull_request_target safe to use?

    It is safe when the workflow does not run code from the PR. Examples are adding labels or posting a comment. If you must test fork code with secrets, use a two-step design: run tests without secrets, then a trusted workflow_run job that only reads artifacts.

  • How do fork contributors run E2E tests that need credentials?

    They run with test credentials that have no prod access, or a maintainer approves the run through an environment. The best option is an ephemeral test environment where a leaked token has no value.

  • Does OIDC remove all secrets?

    No. It removes cloud access keys. Some third-party tokens, such as a Slack bot token, still need secrets. Keep those in environments or org secrets scoped to selected repos, and rotate them on a schedule.

  • How do you stop teams from copying this mistake again?

    The shared reusable workflow gets OIDC and minimal permissions by default. An org policy allows only approved actions. A lint check flags pull_request_target with a checkout of the PR head.

Caution
  • Some candidates start with the root cause analysis. A leaked key must be rotated first, because each minute adds risk.
  • Some candidates say "GitHub masks secrets, so this cannot happen". Masking misses encoded or derived values.
  • Some candidates fix it by moving the key to another secret store. A long-lived key still exists; OIDC removes it.
  • Some candidates write a trust policy with repo:ukg/*. Then any repo in the org can assume the prod role.
Staff signal

A Staff answer handles the incident in the right order and then changes the platform default, so every team is safe without extra work.

UKG-G4

Interviewer

Our E2E tests must call services inside a private VPC on EKS. GitHub-hosted runners cannot reach them. What are your options?

What this tests The interviewer tests if you know the network options, the runner model and the security and cost trade-offs.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

I put self-hosted runners inside the VPC. My first choice is Actions Runner Controller on EKS with runner scale sets. Each job gets a fresh, ephemeral runner pod, so no state or secret stays between jobs. Runners scale on the job queue and go to zero at night. They get AWS access through OIDC or Pod Identity, not stored keys. Another option is to run the tests inside the cluster as a Kubernetes Job.

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. Name the problem

    GitHub-hosted runners run on the internet. They have no path to private subnets. So the tests must run inside the VPC, or a network path must come to the runner.

  2. 2. Compare the options
    • Self-hosted runners in the VPC (EC2 VMs or ARC on EKS). This is the usual answer.
    • A VPN or bastion from hosted runners. This is fragile and opens the network.
    • Run the tests inside the cluster as a Kubernetes Job. CI only starts the Job and reads results.
    • Expose a private endpoint with strict IP rules. This increases the attack surface.
    • GitHub Azure private networking exists, but it does not apply to an AWS VPC.
  3. 3. Choose ARC with runner scale sets

    Install Actions Runner Controller on EKS. Create one runner scale set per purpose, for example e2e-private. ARC watches the job queue and creates a runner pod for each job. Workflows use runs-on: e2e-private.

  4. 4. Make runners ephemeral

    Each runner pod runs one job and is then deleted. This stops state bleed, such as left-over files, caches or logged-in sessions. It also limits damage if a job is compromised.

  5. 5. Control access

    Put runner scale sets in runner groups that only some repos can use. Give the runner pods AWS access with IRSA or Pod Identity, or with OIDC from the workflow. Never let public or fork PRs use runners inside the VPC.

  6. 6. Control cost and blast radius

    Set minRunners: 0 and a maxRunners limit. Put runner pods on their own node pool, with Spot nodes for test work. Use a separate namespace with quotas and NetworkPolicies. Runners must reach the test environment, not prod.

Concepts you must own 9

Self-hosted runner
Idea

A self-hosted runner is a machine that you run, which takes jobs from GitHub.

Example

An EC2 instance in the private subnet runs the runner agent and calls the private services.

Term

The runner makes an outbound HTTPS connection to GitHub, so you do not open inbound ports. You own patching, scaling and security.

Runner on a VM vs Actions Runner Controller
Idea

You can run runners on plain VMs or as pods on Kubernetes.

Example

VM: an Auto Scaling group of EC2 runners. ARC: runner pods on EKS that start per job.

Term

VMs are simple and good for Docker-in-Docker. ARC gives fast scaling, pod isolation and use of the existing cluster. ARC is the GitHub-supported Kubernetes operator.

Runner scale sets
Idea

A runner scale set is a group of identical runners that ARC grows and shrinks with the job queue.

Example

The e2e-private scale set goes from 0 to 40 runner pods at 9 AM and back to 0.

Term

Install with the gha-runner-scale-set-controller and gha-runner-scale-set Helm charts. The installation name is the runs-on value. Settings include minRunners, maxRunners and the pod template.

Ephemeral vs persistent runners
Idea

An ephemeral runner does one job and is deleted. A persistent runner does many jobs and keeps its disk.

Example

A persistent runner keeps ~/.npmrc with a token from job 1. Job 2 from another repo can read it.

Term

Ephemeral runners stop state bleed and limit the effect of a compromised job. ARC scale sets are ephemeral by default. Use caches for speed instead of a dirty disk.

Runner groups and labels
Idea

A runner group decides which repos may use a set of runners. Labels decide which job goes to which runner.

Example

Only repos in the qa-platform group can use the e2e-private runners.

Term

Runner groups are set at org or enterprise level. With ARC scale sets, the runs-on value is usually the scale set installation name.

Scaling runners on demand
Idea

Start runners only when jobs wait, and stop them when the queue is empty.

Example

Overnight there are no jobs, so there are 0 runner pods and fewer nodes.

Term

ARC scales on queued jobs for the scale set. Karpenter or Cluster Autoscaler adds nodes for the new runner pods. Set limits so a bad workflow cannot start 1,000 runners.

OIDC and IAM for runners
Idea

The runner needs AWS access without stored keys.

Example

The job uses OIDC to assume e2e-test-role. Or the runner pod uses a ServiceAccount with Pod Identity.

Term

OIDC gives per-workflow scoping through the sub claim. Pod Identity or IRSA gives per-runner-pool scoping. Do not use the node instance role for job access.

Alternatives: VPN, bastion, in-cluster Job, private endpoint
Idea

There are other ways to reach a private network, but each has costs.

Example

A Kubernetes Job inside the cluster runs Playwright and writes results to S3. CI only waits for the Job.

Term

VPN or bastion: adds a network path from the internet. In-cluster Job: no runner in the VPC, but CI must start and watch the Job. Private endpoint exposure: more attack surface. Choose by security, speed and effort.

Cost and blast radius
Idea

Blast radius is how much damage one failure or attack can do.

Example

If a runner can reach prod databases, a malicious test can harm prod. A runner that only reaches the test VPC has a small blast radius.

Term

Reduce it with a separate namespace, a node pool, NetworkPolicies, security groups, scoped IAM and ephemeral runners. Show cost per team with labels and AWS cost allocation tags.

Code to know

Follow-up questions

  • Why not keep a few persistent runners? They are simpler.

    Persistent runners keep files, tokens and processes between jobs. One bad job can affect the next job, which gives flaky results and a security risk. Ephemeral runners cost a little start time, and caches cover most of it.

  • Can fork PRs use these runners?

    No. A fork PR can change the workflow and run any code inside the VPC. Restrict the runner group to selected private repos. Require approval for workflows from outside contributors.

  • How does a runner pod run Docker builds?

    ARC supports Docker-in-Docker mode and a Kubernetes mode for container jobs. Docker-in-Docker needs a privileged container, which is a security cost. Many teams build images on separate VM runners and keep test runners unprivileged.

  • When would you choose the in-cluster Job option?

    I choose it when the tests need very low latency to the services. I also choose it when security does not allow CI runners in that VPC. The cost is more glue code to start the Job, stream logs and collect results.

Caution
  • Some candidates open the private services to the internet for the tests. That moves a test problem into a security problem.
  • Some candidates use persistent runners shared by all repos. One job can read secrets or files from the last job.
  • Some candidates give the runner nodes an admin IAM role. Every job can then do everything in the AWS account.
Staff signal

A Staff answer compares the options, picks one with a clear reason, and designs isolation, scaling limits and cost visibility for hundreds of teams.

  • Deploying GitHub self-hosted runners on Kubernetes with ARC - Karan Thakur | PlatformCon 2024Platform EngineeringConference talk: running ARC in production.
UKG-G5

Interviewer

About 8% of CI runs fail with timeouts, mostly on Thursdays. No code change correlates with it. How do you investigate?

What this tests The interviewer tests if you debug with data and look for shared causes outside the code.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

A weekly pattern with no code change points to something shared in the environment. I compare good runs and bad runs by time, runner, test and environment. Then I check what else runs on Thursdays, such as other teams' batch jobs, data refreshes or rate limits. I add diagnostics to each run so the next failure tells us more. Retries can help in the short term, but the report must record each retry, so they do not hide the cause.

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. Get the data

    Export the last few hundred runs with time, conclusion, runner, job, test name and duration. Group the failures by weekday and hour. Confirm the pattern is real and find the exact time window.

  2. 2. Compare good and bad runs

    Put a passing Thursday run next to a failing one. Look at:

    • Which tests time out, and at which step.
    • Runner type, image version and region.
    • Test environment response times.
    • Dependency and image download times.
  3. 3. Check shared causes
    • Other teams' nightly or weekly jobs that hit the same environment.
    • A weekly database refresh, backup or deploy window.
    • Rate limits: GitHub API, Docker Hub pulls, or a third-party API.
    • Test data collisions when many runs use the same accounts at the same time.
  4. 4. Add diagnostics now

    Add timing per step, a dump of runner and environment facts, and a health check of the environment at start. Collect Playwright traces on failure. Send this data to the results store so you can query it.

  5. 5. Classify the failures

    Mark each failure as a product bug, a test bug, an infra issue or flaky. A test that fails and then passes on retry with no code change is flaky. Track the flaky rate per test over time.

  6. 6. Fix and set a retry policy

    Fix the root cause, for example move the other team's batch job or isolate test data. Allow one retry for known infra errors only. Record every retry as "flaky" in the report, and quarantine tests above a flaky threshold.

Concepts you must own 8

Compare good vs bad runs
Idea

Put a passing run and a failing run side by side, and look for the difference.

Example

Failing runs all start between 09:00 and 11:00 UTC on Thursday. Passing runs do not.

Term

This is differential diagnosis. Compare time, runner, image, environment, data and dependency versions. Change one variable at a time to confirm.

Runner type and region
Idea

Different runners can have different speed and network paths.

Example

All failures ran on one self-hosted runner pool that shares a NAT gateway with a batch system.

Term

Record RUNNER_NAME, RUNNER_OS, RUNNER_ARCH, the image version and the network path. Hosted runner images also update every week.

Shared environment contention
Idea

Many users of one environment slow each other down.

Example

A data team runs a big weekly import on Thursday into the same staging database.

Term

Contention shows as higher latency and timeouts in many unrelated tests at the same time. Check the environment metrics and the schedule of other jobs.

Rate limits
Idea

A service refuses or slows requests after a limit per hour or per IP.

Example

Many runners behind one NAT IP pull images from Docker Hub and hit the pull limit.

Term

GitHub API limits are per token. Docker Hub limits anonymous pulls per IP. Use an authenticated mirror or Amazon ECR pull-through cache. Read response headers such as X-RateLimit-Remaining.

Test data collisions under concurrency
Idea

Two runs use the same test account at the same time and break each other.

Example

Run A deletes a shared user while run B logs in with it. Run B waits and times out.

Term

Collisions grow with parallelism, so they appear on busy days. Use unique data per run, or a lease on shared accounts.

Flaky classification
Idea

A flaky test passes and fails on the same code.

Example

checkout.spec.ts failed, then passed on retry with the same commit. It is flaky.

Term

The usual signal is fail-then-pass on one commit. Classes are product bug, test bug, infra and flaky. Each class has a different owner.

Adding diagnostics
Idea

Make each failure carry the facts that you need to explain it.

Example

Each run writes start time, runner name, environment latency and API rate limit to the job summary.

Term

Collect step timings, Playwright traces, screenshots, HAR files, an environment dump and distributed trace IDs. Send them to a central store for queries.

Retry policy that records retries
Idea

A retry can make a run green, but the report must still say that a retry happened.

Example

Playwright with retries: 1 marks the test as flaky in the report, not passed.

Term

Allow retries only for known transient errors. Count retries per test. Quarantine tests that pass the flaky threshold. A retry that hides failures makes the problem invisible.

Code to know

Follow-up questions

  • What if you find no cause in the CI data?

    Then I look at the environment side: database load, deploy logs and other teams' schedules for that window. I talk to the owners of the shared environment. I can also run a synthetic test every 10 minutes on Thursday to see when the latency starts.

  • Would you just add retries?

    Only as a short-term step for known transient errors, and only with the retries recorded. Retries alone hide the cause and make the suite slower. The root cause still needs a fix.

  • The cause is another team's batch job. They will not move it. What now?

    I show the data: the time window, the failure rate and the developer hours lost. Then I offer options: move the job, give it its own capacity, or give tests a separate environment. If no agreement comes, I take the trade-off to the owners of both teams.

Caution
  • Some candidates increase all timeouts. The tests then fail later and slower, and the cause stays.
  • Some candidates blame the code first. The question says no code change correlates, so look at the environment.
  • Some candidates add silent retries. The dashboard then shows green while the real problem grows.
Staff signal

A Staff answer finds the cross-team cause, adds diagnostics that help every team, and sets a retry and quarantine policy for the platform.
