UKG-G6

Interviewer

Our release pipeline rebuilds the image for staging and again for prod. A prod bug did not reproduce in staging. What is wrong and how do you fix it?

What this tests The interviewer tests if you know immutable artifacts, environment promotion and safe deploy and rollback.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

A rebuild for each environment makes a different artifact, so staging tests do not prove anything about prod. I build the image one time, tag it with the commit SHA, and promote the same digest to staging and then prod. Prod uses a GitHub environment with required reviewers. Rollback is a redeploy of the previous digest. For many services I prefer GitOps with Argo CD, where CI only changes the image digest in a Git repo.

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. Explain the cause

    Each rebuild can pull a different base image, a different dependency version or a different build flag. So the prod image is not the image that staging tested. The bug lived in the difference.

  2. 2. Build once

    Build the image one time on merge to main. Tag it with the commit SHA. Push it to ECR and record the digest (sha256:...). Turn on tag immutability in ECR.

  3. 3. Promote the same digest

    Staging and prod deploy results-api@sha256:..., not a tag. Environment differences come only from config, such as ConfigMaps and secrets, not from the image.

  4. 4. Gate prod

    The prod deploy job uses environment: prod with required reviewers. The gate also needs green staging tests on the same digest.

  5. 5. Deploy with a safe strategy

    Use a rolling update for most services. Use blue/green or canary for high-risk services, with automatic checks on error rate and latency. Argo Rollouts or the load balancer weights can control a canary.

  6. 6. Roll back fast

    Rollback is a redeploy of the previous known-good digest. It needs no rebuild. With GitOps, rollback is a revert of one commit in the config repo.

Concepts you must own 9

Build once, tag by commit SHA
Idea

Make the image one time, and name it after the exact code it contains.

Example

Commit 3f2c1ab gives image results-api:3f2c1ab.

Term

A SHA tag gives traceability from a running pod back to the commit. Do not use latest for deploys.

Promote the same digest
Idea

Move the exact same bytes from staging to prod.

Example

Staging runs results-api@sha256:9a1c.... Prod runs the same digest after approval.

Term

A digest is a content hash. A tag can move, but a digest cannot. Deploy by digest to guarantee identity.

Immutable artifacts
Idea

An immutable artifact never changes after you publish it.

Example

ECR tag immutability stops someone from pushing a new image with the old tag 3f2c1ab.

Term

Immutable artifacts make deploys repeatable and audits possible. The same idea applies to npm packages and test-framework releases.

Environments and approvals
Idea

A GitHub environment adds rules and secrets for one deploy target.

Example

environment: prod waits for a release manager to approve in the UI.

Term

Protection rules include required reviewers, wait timers and branch rules. The run history shows who approved each deploy.

Rolling deploy
Idea

A rolling deploy replaces old pods with new pods a few at a time.

Example

With maxSurge: 1 and maxUnavailable: 0, Kubernetes adds one new pod, waits until it is ready, then removes one old pod.

Term

It is the Deployment default. It is cheap, but old and new versions serve traffic together for a short time.

Blue/green deploy
Idea

Blue/green runs a full new copy next to the old one, then switches all traffic at one time.

Example

Green runs v2. Tests pass. The ALB rule moves 100% of traffic from blue to green.

Term

Rollback is a fast switch back. It needs double capacity during the switch.

Canary deploy
Idea

A canary sends a small part of the traffic to the new version first.

Example

5% of traffic goes to v2 for 15 minutes. Error rate stays flat, so it goes to 25%, then 100%.

Term

Use weighted target groups, a service mesh or Argo Rollouts. Automatic analysis on metrics decides to continue or roll back.

Rollback by previous digest
Idea

Go back by deploying the last good image. Do not build old code again.

Example

Prod fails on digest B. The pipeline redeploys digest A in two minutes.

Term

Keep a record of the deployed digest per environment. kubectl rollout undo works too, but a GitOps revert keeps Git as the source of truth.

GitOps vs push-based deploy
Idea

Push-based: CI calls the cluster and deploys. GitOps: CI writes the new version to Git, and a tool in the cluster pulls it.

Example

With Argo CD, CI opens a commit that changes the digest in envs/prod/values.yaml. Argo CD syncs the cluster.

Term

GitOps (Argo CD, Flux) gives drift detection, an audit trail in Git and no cluster credentials in CI. Push-based is simpler for a few services.

Code to know

Follow-up questions

  • How do you handle different config per environment?

    The image is the same everywhere. Config comes from ConfigMaps, Secrets or a Helm values file per environment. Config changes go through the same review and pipeline as code.

  • How does this apply to the test framework itself?

    A framework release is also an immutable artifact, for example an npm package or a container image with browsers. Teams pin a version, and we never change a published version.

  • When would you pick canary over blue/green?

    Canary is better when real traffic shows problems that tests miss, and when you have good metrics. Blue/green is better for a fast, full switch with a simple rollback, if you can pay for double capacity.

Caution
  • Some candidates say "use the same Dockerfile". The same Dockerfile can still give a different image on a different day.
  • Some candidates deploy by the latest tag. The tag moves, so nobody knows what really runs.
  • Some candidates roll back by rebuilding the old commit. That is slow and can give a different image again.
Staff signal

A Staff answer makes immutability a platform rule for images and framework releases, and links promotion gates to test results on the same digest.

UKG-G7

Interviewer

Hundreds of teams want their test results in Slack and in a dashboard, not buried in CI logs. How do you build that?

What this tests The interviewer tests if you design reporting that scales to many teams and gives signal, not noise.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

Every run writes a short job summary and uploads a standard JUnit file and an HTML report as artifacts. The shared workflow also sends the results to a central results service, which feeds a Grafana dashboard. For Slack I use one Slack app with a bot token, stored as an org secret, and each team sets its channel. I notify only on a change of state, such as main going from green to red, to avoid alert fatigue.

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. Standardize the output

    Every framework writes JUnit XML and a JSON summary in a fixed schema. This gives one format for all teams, whatever the tool.

  2. 2. Show results where the developer looks

    Write a Markdown table to $GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY with pass, fail, flaky and a link. Upload the HTML report and traces as artifacts with a retention period.

  3. 3. Send results to a central store

    The shared workflow posts the JSON summary to a results service, or uploads it to S3 for ingestion. Each record has team, repo, branch, commit, test ID, status, duration and retry count.

  4. 4. Build dashboards on the store

    Grafana shows pass rate, flaky rate, duration and top failing tests per team. Leaders get a cross-team view. Teams get their own view.

  5. 5. Notify with care

    Use one Slack app with a bot token. It can post to any channel where it is a member. Each team sets its channel as a repository variable. Send a message only on a state change or a new failure cluster, not on every red run.

Concepts you must own 7

Slack incoming webhook
Idea

An incoming webhook is a URL that posts messages to one fixed channel.

Example

Team A's webhook posts to #team-a-ci only.

Term

It is simple, but each channel needs its own URL to store and rotate. For hundreds of channels it does not scale.

Slack app with a bot token
Idea

A Slack app is one identity that can post to many channels with one token.

Example

The bot test-platform posts to #team-a-ci and #team-b-ci with chat.postMessage.

Term

The bot token (xoxb-...) needs the chat:write scope. It must be a member of each channel. One token is easier to rotate and audit than many webhooks.

Tokens as org or environment secrets
Idea

Store the Slack token once at org level, and share it only with the repos that need it.

Example

The org secret SLACK_BOT_TOKEN has access policy "selected repositories".

Term

Org secrets can be scoped to all, private or selected repositories. Environment secrets add approval rules. Rotate on a schedule.

Job summaries ($GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY)
Idea

A job summary is Markdown that appears on the run page.

Example

A table with 812 passed, 3 failed, 5 flaky and a link to the report.

Term

Append Markdown to the file at $GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY. Each step has its own file, and the run page shows them together.

JUnit, Allure and HTML report artifacts
Idea

Reports are files that show each test result in detail.

Example

The Playwright HTML report with traces is uploaded as html-report and kept 14 days.

Term

JUnit XML is the common machine format. Allure gives rich history and steps. HTML reports are for humans. Set retention-days to control storage cost.

Central results store
Idea

One place keeps the results of all teams, so you can compare and see trends.

Example

A results service writes each test result to a database. Grafana reads from it.

Term

Use an API or S3 plus an ingest job. The store needs a fixed schema, a team ID and indexing by test ID and time. This store also feeds flaky detection and failure triage.

Alert fatigue
Idea

Too many alerts make people ignore all alerts.

Example

A channel gets 40 red messages a day. The team mutes it and misses a real outage.

Term

Notify on state change (green to red, red to green), on new failure groups, or on a threshold. Do not notify on every failure. Give a daily digest for the rest.

Code to know

Follow-up questions

  • How does the job know if the state changed?

    The results service keeps the last status per repo and branch. The workflow asks the service, or the service sends the Slack message itself. Moving notification logic into the service also keeps the workflow simple.

  • Why not build a custom dashboard UI?

    Grafana or an existing tool gives most of the value fast. I build custom UI only for workflows that Grafana cannot do, such as failure triage with known-issue links.

  • How do you keep the cost of reports under control?

    Set artifact retention per type, for example traces 7 days and summaries 90 days. Store raw data in S3 with lifecycle rules. Keep aggregated metrics longer in the database.

Caution
  • Some candidates create a webhook per team and store hundreds of URLs. That is hard to manage, audit and rotate.
  • Some candidates post every failed run to Slack. Teams then mute the channel.
  • Some candidates parse logs for results. Logs change format, so a standard report file is more reliable.
Staff signal

A Staff answer defines one result schema for all teams and builds notification, dashboards and triage on top of it, with clear rules against noise.

Chapter 03

Kubernetes and EKS

Read K0 first. Each answer uses the same method. Find the layer that fails and show the evidence with kubectl. Fix it, then change the platform so it does not happen again. Say the honest line early: you have not run EKS in production, but you know the model and how you would debug it.

UKG-K1

Interviewer

Pods show Running, the nodes are healthy, but users get a 503 from the ALB. Debug it.

What this tests The interviewer tests if you know the request path and debug it layer by layer, not by guess.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

Running does not mean Ready, so I check the READY column first. Then I check if the Service has endpoints. An empty EndpointSlice means no pod passes readiness, or the selector does not match the pod labels. If endpoints exist, I check the ALB target group health and compare its health check path and port with the readiness probe. I also find out who returns the 503: the ALB, the ingress controller, or the app.

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. Find who returns the 503

    Look at the response headers and body. An ALB 503 has an AWS page and no app headers. An app 503 has the app's own headers and body. The ALB access logs show elb_status_code and target_status_code separately.

  2. 2. Check Running vs Ready

    kubectl get pods shows 0/1 Running when the readiness probe fails. kubectl describe pod shows Readiness probe failed in Events. A failed readiness probe removes the pod from the Service endpoints.

  3. 3. Check the Service endpoints

    Run kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=<svc>. If the list is empty but pods are Ready, compare the Service selector with the pod labels. One typo, such as app: result-api, breaks the link with no error.

  4. 4. Check the ports

    The Service targetPort must be the port that the container listens on. The Ingress backend must use the Service port. Use kubectl port-forward svc/<svc> and curl to test the Service without the ALB.

  5. 5. Check the ALB target group

    Run aws elbv2 describe-target-health. Targets can be unhealthy even when the pods are Ready. A common cause is a health check path such as / that returns 404 or a redirect. Set alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/healthcheck-path to the same path as the readiness probe.

  6. 6. Check the dependencies of the app

    The readiness endpoint can fail because a database or downstream API is down. Then all pods drop out together and the ALB returns 503. Readiness can check critical local state, but a shared outage then removes every pod at one time.

Concepts you must own 8

Running vs Ready
Idea

Running means the container process is alive. Ready means the pod can take traffic.

Example

results-api-7d9 0/1 Running 0 5m: alive, but not Ready.

Term

Ready is a pod condition set from the readiness probe. Only Ready pods receive Service traffic.

Readiness probe failing removes the pod from endpoints
Idea

When readiness fails, Kubernetes takes the pod IP out of the Service list. The pod is not restarted.

Example

The /ready endpoint returns 500 because the DB pool is not ready. Traffic stops to that pod.

Term

The EndpointSlice controller marks the address ready: false. The AWS Load Balancer Controller can also deregister the target.

Empty EndpointSlices
Idea

An empty endpoint list means the Service has nowhere to send traffic.

Example

kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=results-api shows <unset> for addresses.

Term

Two causes: no matching pod is Ready, or the selector matches no pod. Both give a 503 at the ingress layer.

ALB target group health check path and port mismatch
Idea

The ALB has its own health check. It can disagree with the Kubernetes probe.

Example

The readiness probe uses /ready on 8080. The ALB checks / and gets a 302 redirect, so it marks targets unhealthy.

Term

Set alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/healthcheck-path, healthcheck-port and success-codes. With target type ip, the health check goes straight to the pod.

Selector and label mismatch
Idea

The Service finds pods by label. A different label means the Service finds no pod.

Example

The Service selects app: results-api. The new Deployment template has app: results-api-v2.

Term

Compare kubectl get svc -o jsonpath='{.spec.selector}' with kubectl get pods --show-labels. Kubernetes gives no error for this.

Wrong targetPort
Idea

The Service sends traffic to a port where nothing listens.

Example

The app moved from 8080 to 3000. The Service still has targetPort: 8080.

Term

Use a named port (targetPort: http, with ports.name: http in the container) so a port change happens in one place.

App failing a dependency check
Idea

The app says "not ready" because something it needs is down.

Example

The test-results DB is in maintenance. Every pod fails /ready. All targets go unhealthy.

Term

Deep readiness checks give cascading failures. Check only what the pod needs to serve. Use timeouts and circuit breakers for dependencies. Never put dependency checks in liveness.

Who returns the 503
Idea

Different layers return a 503 for different reasons. Find the layer first.

Example

ALB 503: no healthy targets. ingress-nginx 503: no endpoints. App 503: the app is overloaded.

Term

Read the ALB access logs (elb_status_code vs target_status_code), the ingress controller logs and the app logs. The response body and headers often name the layer.

Code to know

Follow-up questions

  • Endpoints exist and targets are healthy, but users still get some 503s. What next?

    Look at timing. A 503 during deploys points to a shutdown race between the ALB and the pod. A 503 under load points to app overload or too few pods. Compare the 503 times with deploys and traffic.

  • Should the readiness probe check the database?

    Only if the pod truly cannot serve any request without it. If all pods check the same database, one database issue removes every pod. Often it is better to stay Ready and return a clear error for that request.

  • What is the difference between a 502, 503 and 504 from an ALB?

    502 means the target sent a bad response or closed the connection. 503 means no healthy target is registered. 504 means the target did not answer in the idle timeout.

Caution
  • Some candidates restart the pods first. That loses evidence and does not fix a selector or health-check mismatch.
  • Some candidates say "the pods are Running, so Kubernetes is fine". Running is not Ready.
  • Some candidates look only at the app logs. A 503 from the ALB never reaches the app, so the app logs are empty.
Staff signal

A Staff answer debugs by layer with a clear order, and then fixes the class of problem. Examples are named ports, aligned health checks in the shared Helm chart, and an alert on empty endpoints.

UKG-K2

Interviewer

A team made a "harmless" config change and now the pods are in CrashLoopBackOff. Walk me through it.

What this tests The interviewer tests if you can read pod evidence fast, restore service, and fix the process.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

First I restore service with kubectl rollout undo or a revert of the config in Git. Then I read kubectl logs --previous for the crash message and kubectl describe pod for the exit code and events. Common causes are a missing env var or Secret key, a liveness probe that kills a slow start, or OOMKilled with exit code 137. The process fix is that config changes go through the same pipeline and review as code.

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. Restore service first

    If the change was in the Deployment, run kubectl rollout undo. If the change was only in a ConfigMap, revert it and run kubectl rollout restart. A ConfigMap change does not make a new ReplicaSet, so rollout undo cannot revert it.

  2. 2. Read the crashed container's log

    Use kubectl logs <pod> --previous. The current container has just started and has no useful log. Look for errors such as "missing env var" or "cannot parse config".

  3. 3. Read the pod details

    Use kubectl describe pod. Look at Last State, Reason and Exit Code, and the Events at the bottom.

    • OOMKilled, exit code 137: memory limit.
    • Exit code 1: app error.
    • Liveness probe failed events: probe killed the app.
    • CreateContainerConfigError: missing ConfigMap, Secret or key.
  4. 4. Check the probes

    A config change can make start-up slower, for example a bigger cache. A liveness probe with a short delay then kills the app again and again. Add a startup probe that allows the full boot time.

  5. 5. Check the image

    Confirm that the running image tag is the one that the change expected. A config that needs a newer app version fails on an older image.

  6. 6. Fix the process

    Config lives in Git and goes through review and CI, like code. Validate it with a schema check before deploy. Add a hash of the config to the pod annotations, so a config change makes a normal, reversible rollout.

Concepts you must own 9

kubectl logs --previous
Idea

This command shows the log of the container that crashed, not the new one.

Example

The new container shows nothing yet. --previous shows Error: DB_URL is not defined.

Term

Kubernetes keeps the log of the last terminated container. Add -c <name> for multi-container pods.

kubectl describe events
Idea

Events are short messages from Kubernetes about what happened to the pod.

Example

Back-off restarting failed container, Liveness probe failed: HTTP probe failed with statuscode: 503.

Term

Events show scheduler, kubelet and controller decisions. They are kept for about one hour by default, so collect them early.

Bad ConfigMap or Secret key, or missing env var
Idea

The pod asks for a setting that does not exist, or the app gets a value it cannot use.

Example

The change renamed db-password to db_password in the Secret. The pod still asks for db-password.

Term

A missing key in configMapKeyRef or secretKeyRef gives CreateContainerConfigError. A key that exists but has a bad value lets the container start and then crash. Use optional: true only on purpose.

Liveness probe too aggressive
Idea

A liveness probe that checks too early kills a slow app before it finishes the boot.

Example

The app now needs 70 seconds to start. Liveness starts at 10 seconds and fails 3 times, so the kubelet restarts it forever.

Term

This gives restarts with exit code 137 or 143 and Liveness probe failed events. Increase the thresholds or add a startup probe.

Startup probe
Idea

A startup probe gives the app time to boot. Liveness waits until it passes.

Example

failureThreshold: 30, periodSeconds: 5 allows up to 150 seconds to start.

Term

startupProbe stops liveness and readiness checks until it succeeds. After success, liveness can be strict again.

OOMKilled, exit code 137
Idea

The container used more memory than its limit, so the kernel killed it.

Example

A new config turns on a bigger in-memory cache. The pod hits 512Mi and dies.

Term

Last State: Terminated, Reason: OOMKilled, Exit Code: 137. 137 = 128 + 9 (SIGKILL). Raise the limit or fix the memory use. Exit code 143 = SIGTERM.

Image tag mismatch
Idea

The config expects one app version, but the pod runs another.

Example

The new config key exists only in v2.4. The Deployment still uses :2.3.

Term

Check kubectl get pod -o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[*].image}'. Deploy config and image together, or make the app accept both configs.

kubectl rollout undo
Idea

This command goes back to the previous version of the Deployment.

Example

kubectl rollout undo deploy/results-api brings back the last ReplicaSet in seconds.

Term

It works on changes to the pod template, such as image, env and probes. It does not revert ConfigMap or Secret content. With GitOps, revert in Git instead, or Argo CD will undo your fix.

Config changes through the same pipeline as code
Idea

A config change can break prod like a code change. So it gets the same review, tests and rollout.

Example

The ConfigMap is in Git. A pull request runs a schema check and deploys to staging first.

Term

Use GitOps or Helm and a config schema check in CI. A checksum/config annotation makes a config change start a rolling update that you can undo.

Code to know

Follow-up questions

  • The log is empty, even with --previous. What then?

    The process may die before it writes anything, for example a bad entrypoint or a missing binary. Check the exit code and the events. Run the image locally, or start a debug copy with kubectl debug and a shell as the command.

  • How do you make config changes roll out like code?

    Put a hash of the ConfigMap in a pod annotation, for example checksum/config in Helm. A config change then changes the pod template, which makes a new ReplicaSet. So readiness gates the rollout, and rollout undo works.

  • Exit code 137, but no OOMKilled. What else?

    137 means SIGKILL. It can also come from a liveness probe kill after the grace period, or from a node eviction. The reason field and the events tell you which.

Caution
  • Some candidates read kubectl logs without --previous. They see the log of the new container, which has not crashed yet.
  • Some candidates say rollout undo reverts a ConfigMap edit. It does not, because the pod template did not change.
  • Some candidates raise the liveness timeout to a very large number. That hides a real hang; a startup probe is the correct tool.
Staff signal

A Staff answer restores service first and finds the cause from evidence. Then it changes the platform so config changes are reviewed, validated and reversible for every team.

Watch

  • Troubleshooting Kubernetes Pods in CrashLoopBackOff, Pending and ImagePullBackOff state.TechyWithLornadescribe, logs --previous, events for common pod failures.
  • ConfigMaps and Secrets in KubernetesPavan ElthepuHow config reaches a pod and how a bad key breaks startup.
UKG-K3

Interviewer

Teams need 2,000 parallel browser sessions at 9 AM and almost none overnight. Design Selenium Grid or Playwright workers on EKS for this.

What this tests The interviewer tests if you can design elastic, isolated and cost-aware infrastructure for a bursty workload.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

I run each browser as a pod, and I scale on the length of the test queue with KEDA, not on CPU. Karpenter adds Spot nodes in a dedicated, tainted node pool, so browsers never starve app workloads. Each browser pod has a fixed request and limit and a memory-backed /dev/shm. Sessions have a hard timeout and Jobs clean up after themselves. I tag everything by team, so we can show cost per team.

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. Choose the unit of work
    • Selenium Grid 4: a hub (router, distributor, session queue) and browser node pods. Good for existing Selenium suites.
    • Playwright: each worker is a Kubernetes Job that runs one shard and exits. No grid is needed.

    Either way, one browser session is one isolated pod, or one container with a fixed number of sessions.

  2. 2. Size the browser pods

    A Chrome session needs about 1 CPU and 1 to 2 GiB of memory. Measure it on your real tests. Set the memory limit equal to the request, so the scheduler never overcommits memory. Mount an emptyDir with medium: Memory at /dev/shm. The 64Mi default crashes Chrome tabs.

  3. 3. Scale pods on the queue

    CPU is a bad signal, because an idle browser uses little CPU while tests wait. KEDA reads the Selenium Grid session queue or an SQS queue of shards. It scales browser pods or Jobs from zero to the needed number.

  4. 4. Scale nodes fast and cheap

    Karpenter sees Pending browser pods and starts right-sized nodes in about a minute. Use Spot instances for most of the capacity, with On-Demand as a fallback. Consolidation removes idle nodes after the peak.

  5. 5. Handle Spot interruptions

    Karpenter drains a node on the 2-minute interruption notice. Each test shard must be retryable, so a lost node only re-runs a few shards. Record these re-runs as infra retries, not as test failures.

  6. 6. Isolate the browser pool

    Put a taint workload=browsers:NoSchedule on the browser nodes and a matching toleration on browser pods. Use a separate namespace with a ResourceQuota per team. Then 2,000 browsers cannot evict the results API or other apps.

  7. 7. Clean up and control cost

    Set activeDeadlineSeconds and session timeouts so a stuck browser dies. Set ttlSecondsAfterFinished to delete finished Jobs. Label pods by team and use cost allocation tags or Kubecost to show cost per team.

Concepts you must own 10

Browsers as pods
Idea

Each browser runs in its own pod, so one crash or one memory leak does not affect other tests.

Example

One Chrome pod per Selenium session, or one Playwright Job per shard with 2 workers inside.

Term

Selenium Grid 4 on Kubernetes uses the hub components and node pods (the official Helm chart supports KEDA). Playwright needs no grid: the test runner and browser run in the same pod.

Selenium Grid 4 nodes vs Playwright workers as Jobs
Idea

A grid keeps browsers that remote tests connect to. Playwright workers run the tests and the browser together.

Example

Selenium: tests in CI call the hub URL. Playwright: CI puts 200 shards on a queue, and 200 Jobs pick them up.

Term

Grid gives a shared remote browser pool for many languages. Jobs give simpler isolation and no network hop per command. Many platforms support both during a migration.

Requests and limits for browsers
Idea

Browsers use a lot of CPU and memory in bursts. Set clear numbers, or nodes become overloaded.

Example

requests: {cpu: 1, memory: 2Gi}, limits: {memory: 2Gi}.

Term

Equal memory request and limit avoids OOM surprises. A CPU limit can throttle browsers and cause timeouts, so many teams set only a CPU request.

/dev/shm for browsers
Idea

Chrome uses shared memory for page rendering. The container default is too small.

Example

Without a larger /dev/shm, Chrome tabs crash with "Aw, Snap" or the session dies.

Term

Mount emptyDir: {medium: Memory, sizeLimit: 1Gi} at /dev/shm. This memory counts against the pod memory limit.

Autoscaling on queue length with KEDA
Idea

Scale on the work that waits, not on how busy the machines look.

Example

300 sessions wait in the grid queue. KEDA asks for 300 more browser pods.

Term

KEDA has a Selenium Grid scaler and an AWS SQS scaler. ScaledObject scales a Deployment. ScaledJob creates one Job per message. Both can scale to zero.

Karpenter or Cluster Autoscaler for nodes
Idea

Pods need nodes. A node autoscaler adds nodes when pods are Pending.

Example

At 9 AM, 400 browser pods are Pending. Karpenter starts 30 nodes. At 11 AM it removes them.

Term

Karpenter is faster and picks instance types per need. Cluster Autoscaler scales fixed node groups. Set limits on the NodePool as a cost ceiling.

Spot instances and interruption handling
Idea

Spot nodes are cheap, but AWS can take them back with a 2-minute warning.

Example

A Spot node goes away during a run. Its 6 shards return to the queue and run again on another node.

Term

Use several instance types for better Spot availability. Karpenter handles interruption events through an SQS queue. Make every test shard idempotent and retryable.

Node pools with taints and tolerations
Idea

A taint keeps all pods off a node unless they have the matching toleration.

Example

Browser nodes have workload=browsers:NoSchedule. Only browser pods tolerate it, and a nodeSelector keeps them there.

Term

A taint keeps other pods out. A toleration lets a pod in. A nodeSelector or node affinity makes the pod go there. You need both directions.

Session cleanup
Idea

Stuck or forgotten sessions waste nodes and money.

Example

A test crashes and never closes the browser. The session timeout ends it after 5 minutes.

Term

Use Grid session-timeout and node drain-after-session-count, Job activeDeadlineSeconds and ttlSecondsAfterFinished, and a sweeper for orphan pods.

Cost visibility
Idea

Teams change behavior when they see their own cost.

Example

A dashboard shows team A used 4,000 browser-hours last month.

Term

Label pods with team. Use AWS split cost allocation data for EKS, Kubecost or OpenCost. Report cost per test run and per team.

Code to know

Follow-up questions

  • Why not scale on CPU with an HPA?

    Browser CPU use does not show the waiting work. At 9 AM the queue can hold 500 sessions while current pods are idle at login screens. Queue length is a direct signal of demand, and KEDA can also scale to zero.

  • How do you handle the 9 AM cold start?

    Nodes need about a minute, and image pulls add more. Pre-warm with a scheduled minimum before 9 AM, and keep browser images small and cached on nodes. A small buffer of warm nodes is cheaper than 2,000 slow first sessions.

  • Would you run a grid or Jobs for Playwright?

    For Playwright, I prefer Jobs, because the runner and browser are in the same pod and there is no remote hop. For existing Selenium suites, I run Selenium Grid during the migration window.

  • How do you stop one team from taking all 2,000 sessions?

    Use a ResourceQuota per team namespace, or a fair-share queue with per-team limits. Show the use per team on a dashboard.

Caution
  • Some candidates use a fixed fleet sized for the peak. That wastes money for about 20 hours each day.
  • Some candidates scale on CPU. Browsers wait on the network a lot, so CPU does not show demand.
  • Some candidates forget /dev/shm. Chrome then crashes at random, and the tests look flaky.
  • Some candidates put browsers on the same nodes as shared services. A burst can starve or evict important pods.
Staff signal

A Staff answer connects capacity, isolation, retries on Spot and cost per team into one design, and gives teams fair limits and visibility.

UKG-K4

Interviewer

One team's test job keeps evicting other teams' pods on a shared cluster. Fix it.

What this tests The interviewer tests if you know multi-tenant controls in Kubernetes and can apply them fairly.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

The usual cause is pods with no requests or very low requests that then use far more memory. The node runs out of memory, and the kubelet evicts pods, with BestEffort and over-request pods first. I give each team a namespace with a ResourceQuota and a LimitRange for default requests and limits. Platform services get a higher PriorityClass and a PodDisruptionBudget. Heavy test jobs go to a dedicated node pool, and we show each team its cost.

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. Confirm the mechanism

    Look at the evicted pods: kubectl get events shows Evicted with The node was low on resource: memory. Compare the requests of the noisy pods with their real use in kubectl top pods. Usually the noisy job requests little and uses a lot.

  2. 2. Set defaults and limits per team

    Give each team its own namespace. A LimitRange sets default requests and limits for containers that set nothing. A ResourceQuota caps the total CPU, memory and pods per namespace.

  3. 3. Make requests honest

    Requests must be close to real use. Then the scheduler does not overpack nodes. Use Guaranteed QoS (requests equal limits) for important services. Use VPA in recommendation mode to suggest values.

  4. 4. Protect critical pods

    Give shared platform services a PriorityClass that is higher than test jobs. Add a PodDisruptionBudget for voluntary disruptions such as node drains.

  5. 5. Separate heavy work

    Put heavy test jobs on a dedicated node pool with taints and tolerations. Then their spikes cannot touch other workloads.

  6. 6. Make cost visible

    Show use and cost per namespace. Chargeback or showback makes teams care about honest requests.

Concepts you must own 9

Namespace per team
Idea

Each team gets its own space in the cluster. Rules and limits apply per space.

Example

team-a-tests, team-b-tests, platform.

Term

ResourceQuota, LimitRange, RBAC and NetworkPolicy are namespaced. A namespace is not a hard security boundary on its own.

ResourceQuota
Idea

A ResourceQuota is a budget for one namespace.

Example

Team A can request at most 100 CPU and 200Gi memory, and run at most 300 pods.

Term

When a quota covers a resource, each new pod must set requests or limits for it, or the API server rejects it. The API server rejects pods that go over the quota.

LimitRange
Idea

A LimitRange sets default and maximum resources for each container in a namespace.

Example

A pod with no resources gets 250m CPU and 256Mi memory requests automatically.

Term

It is applied by an admission controller at pod creation. It sets default, defaultRequest, min, max and a max limit-to-request ratio.

Requests, limits and QoS classes
Idea

Requests and limits set how Kubernetes treats a pod when memory is short.

Example

A test job with no requests is BestEffort. It is evicted first.

Term

Guaranteed: requests = limits for every container. Burstable: at least one request. BestEffort: none. Under memory pressure, the kubelet evicts BestEffort pods, then Burstable pods above their requests.

Eviction under node pressure
Idea

When a node runs low on memory or disk, the kubelet removes some pods to save the node.

Example

The node reaches memory.available < 100Mi. The kubelet evicts the pods that use most above their requests.

Term

This is node-pressure eviction. It uses QoS, use above requests and priority to rank pods. It is different from an OOM kill of one container at its limit.

PriorityClass
Idea

A PriorityClass tells Kubernetes which pods are more important.

Example

The results API has priority 100000. Test jobs have the default 0.

Term

Higher-priority Pending pods can preempt lower-priority pods. Priority also affects node-pressure eviction order. Do not let teams use high priority classes freely; limit it with a quota on PriorityClass.

PodDisruptionBudget
Idea

A PDB says how many pods of an app must stay up during voluntary disruptions.

Example

minAvailable: 2 for the grid hub. A node drain waits until another hub pod is ready.

Term

PDBs protect against voluntary disruptions, such as drains, upgrades and Karpenter consolidation. They do not stop node-pressure eviction or crashes.

Dedicated node groups
Idea

Give heavy or risky workloads their own nodes.

Example

The browser and load-test pool is tainted. Only test jobs with the toleration run there.

Term

Use taints, tolerations and node selectors, or a separate Karpenter NodePool with its own limits.

Chargeback
Idea

Each team sees, or pays, the cost of what it uses.

Example

A monthly report shows team A at 40% of the cluster cost.

Term

Showback shows the cost. Chargeback bills the cost. Base it on requests, not only use, because requests reserve capacity.

Code to know

Follow-up questions

  • Is a namespace enough to isolate teams?

    No. It isolates names, quotas and RBAC, but pods still share nodes and the kernel. For stronger isolation, add dedicated nodes, NetworkPolicies and pod security rules, or a separate cluster for high-risk tenants.

  • What is the difference between eviction and preemption?

    Eviction happens when a node runs out of a resource; the kubelet removes pods to protect the node. Preemption happens at scheduling time; the scheduler removes lower-priority pods to place a higher-priority pod.

  • How do you introduce quotas without breaking teams?

    Measure current use first and set quotas above it. Announce the change, start with warnings on dashboards, then enforce. Give a simple process to ask for more.

Caution
  • Some candidates give the noisy team its own cluster at once. That is expensive and avoids the real fix of honest requests.
  • Some candidates think a PDB stops evictions from memory pressure. PDBs only cover voluntary disruptions.
  • Some candidates add a ResourceQuota without a LimitRange. Pods without requests are then rejected, and teams see sudden failures.
Staff signal

A Staff answer sets fair multi-tenant defaults for every team, with quotas, priorities, dedicated pools and showback, and rolls them out without surprise.

UKG-K5

Interviewer

Our rolling update should be zero downtime, but we drop requests for about 30 seconds on every deploy. Why, and how do you fix it?

What this tests The interviewer tests if you understand pod shutdown timing and the race with the load balancer.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

The pod and the ALB do not agree about time. Kubernetes sends SIGTERM to the pod while the ALB still sends it traffic for some seconds. I add a preStop sleep so the pod keeps serving while it is removed from the target group. The app must handle SIGTERM and drain its open connections. I set maxUnavailable: 0, align the ALB deregistration delay with terminationGracePeriodSeconds, and turn on the ALB pod readiness gate.

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. Explain the race

    When a pod stops, two things happen in parallel. The kubelet sends SIGTERM to the container. At the same time, the endpoint is removed, and the controller deregisters the target from the ALB. The ALB change takes several seconds, so the ALB still sends requests to a pod that already shuts down.

  2. 2. Keep the pod alive a little longer

    Add a preStop hook that sleeps for 15 to 20 seconds. The kubelet runs preStop before it sends SIGTERM. During the sleep, the ALB and kube-proxy remove the pod.

  3. 3. Shut down gracefully

    The app must catch SIGTERM, stop new connections, finish open requests and then exit. Set terminationGracePeriodSeconds larger than the preStop sleep plus the drain time. After the grace period, the kubelet sends SIGKILL.

  4. 4. Align the ALB

    Set the ALB deregistration_delay.timeout_seconds to a value that fits inside the grace period, for example 30 seconds. The default of 300 seconds is longer than most grace periods.

  5. 5. Start new pods safely

    Use maxUnavailable: 0 and maxSurge: 1 so capacity never drops. Turn on the AWS Load Balancer Controller pod readiness gate. Then a new pod is Ready only after the ALB marks its target healthy, so the rollout does not move too fast.

  6. 6. Cover node drains

    Add a PodDisruptionBudget, so node upgrades and Karpenter consolidation do not stop too many pods at once. Test the result with a load test during a deploy and count the errors.

Concepts you must own 8

maxSurge and maxUnavailable
Idea

These two numbers control how fast a rolling update swaps pods.

Example

maxSurge: 1, maxUnavailable: 0: add one new pod, wait until it is ready, then remove one old pod.

Term

Defaults are 25% each. maxUnavailable: 0 keeps full capacity during the rollout, at the cost of one extra pod.

Readiness gates
Idea

A readiness gate adds an extra condition before a pod counts as Ready.

Example

A new pod is Ready only when its ALB target is healthy, not only when its own probe passes.

Term

The AWS Load Balancer Controller injects the gate when the namespace has the label elbv2.k8s.aws/pod-readiness-gate-inject=enabled. It works with target type ip.

preStop hook
Idea

A preStop hook runs a command inside the container just before Kubernetes asks it to stop.

Example

preStop: exec: sleep 20 keeps the pod serving for 20 seconds while traffic moves away.

Term

The kubelet runs preStop first, then sends SIGTERM. The preStop time counts against terminationGracePeriodSeconds. Newer Kubernetes versions also have a built-in sleep action.

terminationGracePeriodSeconds
Idea

This is the total time that a pod gets to stop before a forced kill.

Example

With a value of 60: preStop sleeps 20 seconds, the app drains for up to 40 seconds, then SIGKILL.

Term

The default is 30 seconds. It must cover the preStop time plus the app drain time.

ALB deregistration delay vs pod shutdown race
Idea

The ALB keeps a removed target for a while, so open requests can finish. If the pod dies first, those requests fail.

Example

Deregistration delay is 300 seconds, but the pod dies after 30 seconds. Requests in that window get 502 errors.

Term

Set deregistration_delay.timeout_seconds with the Ingress annotation alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/target-group-attributes. Keep it at or below the pod grace period.

Graceful SIGTERM handling
Idea

The app must react to SIGTERM by finishing its work, not by dying at once.

Example

A Node.js app calls server.close() on SIGTERM. It stops new connections and waits for open requests.

Term

SIGTERM is the polite stop signal. The process must be PID 1 or forward signals. A shell wrapper can swallow the signal, so use exec or an init such as tini.

Connection draining
Idea

Draining means that no new requests go to the pod, but open requests can finish.

Example

A long test-results upload completes before the old pod exits.

Term

Draining happens at the load balancer (deregistration delay) and in the app (graceful shutdown). Keep-alive connections need extra care: send Connection: close during shutdown.

PodDisruptionBudgets during node drains
Idea

A PDB stops a node drain from taking down too many pods at one time.

Example

During an EKS node upgrade, minAvailable: 3 lets only one of four pods stop at a time.

Term

kubectl drain, managed node group upgrades and Karpenter respect PDBs through the eviction API.

Code to know

Follow-up questions

  • Why do we need a sleep? It looks like a hack.

    Kubernetes has no built-in signal that says "every load balancer has removed this pod". The sleep covers that propagation time. It is the standard pattern, and Kubernetes added a native sleep action for it.

  • How do you prove the fix works?

    Run a steady load with a tool such as k6 during a deploy. Count non-2xx responses before and after the fix. Put this check into the platform's deploy pipeline.

  • Does this also matter for test infrastructure?

    Yes. A Selenium hub or results API that drops requests during a deploy shows up as flaky tests for hundreds of teams.

Caution
  • Some candidates only increase terminationGracePeriodSeconds. Without preStop, the app still gets SIGTERM while the ALB sends traffic.
  • Some candidates say readiness probes solve it. Readiness helps new pods start; it does not fix the shutdown race.
  • Some candidates forget that a shell entrypoint can swallow SIGTERM. The app never drains, and SIGKILL ends it.
Staff signal

A Staff answer explains the race precisely and puts the fix into the shared Helm chart, so every service gets safe shutdown by default.

UKG-K6

Interviewer

A test-results service on EKS gets AccessDenied when it writes to S3. It works from a developer laptop. Debug and fix it.

What this tests The interviewer tests if you know how pods get AWS identity and how to debug IAM step by step.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

The laptop uses the developer's own credentials, so it proves nothing about the pod. I run aws sts get-caller-identity inside the pod to see which role it really uses. If it shows the node role, IRSA or Pod Identity is not set up: the ServiceAccount annotation, the association, or the trust policy is wrong. The fix is a dedicated IAM role with only s3:PutObject on the bucket path, bound to the pod's ServiceAccount. I never bake access keys into the image.

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. Explain the difference

    The laptop uses a developer profile with wide rights. The pod uses whatever identity the AWS SDK finds in the pod. So the test from a laptop does not show the pod's permissions.

  2. 2. Find the real identity

    Run aws sts get-caller-identity from inside the pod, or log it at app start. If it shows the node instance role, the pod does not get its own role.

  3. 3. Check the pod identity setup
    • IRSA: the ServiceAccount has the eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn annotation. The pod uses that ServiceAccount. The pod has AWS_ROLE_ARN and AWS_WEB_IDENTITY_TOKEN_FILE.
    • Pod Identity: an association exists for the cluster, namespace and ServiceAccount. The agent add-on runs.
    • Pods created before the change must restart to get the identity.
  4. 4. Check the trust policy

    For IRSA, the role trust policy must name the cluster OIDC provider and the exact system:serviceaccount:<ns>:<sa>. For Pod Identity, the principal is pods.eks.amazonaws.com. A typo in the namespace gives an AssumeRole error.

  5. 5. Check the permission policy

    If the identity is right, the policy can still deny. Check the action, the resource ARN, the bucket policy and KMS key permissions if the bucket uses SSE-KMS. CloudTrail shows the denied call and the reason.

  6. 6. Apply least privilege

    Give only s3:PutObject on the needed prefix. Never put access keys in the image or in env vars. Limit pod access to the node role through the instance metadata settings.

Concepts you must own 7

IRSA or Pod Identity vs node instance role
Idea

The pod can use its own role, or it can fall back to the role of the node it runs on.

Example

Without IRSA, the SDK uses the node role eks-node-role, which has no S3 write, so AccessDenied.

Term

The SDK default credential chain finds pod credentials first (web identity token or container credentials). The node role from IMDS is the fallback. Per-pod roles give least privilege.

ServiceAccount annotation (IRSA)
Idea

The annotation tells EKS which IAM role the pod's ServiceAccount maps to.

Example

eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/results-api-s3-writer.

Term

The EKS pod identity webhook sees the annotation and injects a projected token and env vars into new pods. Existing pods do not change until they restart.

EKS Pod Identity association
Idea

Pod Identity maps a ServiceAccount to an IAM role with an EKS API call, not an annotation.

Example

aws eks create-pod-identity-association --namespace test-platform --service-account results-api --role-arn ....

Term

It needs the eks-pod-identity-agent add-on. The SDK gets credentials from the agent through AWS_CONTAINER_CREDENTIALS_FULL_URI. It needs a recent AWS SDK version.

IAM trust policy
Idea

The trust policy says who may assume the role. The permission policy says what the role may do.

Example

The trust policy allows only system:serviceaccount:test-platform:results-api from this cluster's OIDC provider.

Term

IRSA: Federated = the OIDC provider, sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity, conditions on sub and aud. Pod Identity: Service: pods.eks.amazonaws.com, sts:AssumeRole and sts:TagSession.

Least privilege
Idea

Give the minimum rights needed for the job, and nothing more.

Example

Allow s3:PutObject on arn:aws:s3:::ukg-test-results/team-*/*. Do not allow s3:* on *.

Term

Scope by action, resource and condition. Use IAM Access Analyzer to find unused permissions.

Never bake access keys into images
Idea

Keys in an image are visible to anyone who can pull the image, and they do not expire.

Example

A developer adds AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID to the Dockerfile. The image goes to a shared registry.

Term

Use IRSA or Pod Identity for short-lived, automatically rotated credentials. Scan images for secrets in CI.

Debug with sts get-caller-identity from inside the pod
Idea

This one command shows the AWS identity that the pod really uses.

Example

The output shows assumed-role/eks-node-role, so the pod identity setup failed.

Term

Run kubectl exec <pod> -- aws sts get-caller-identity, or call the SDK equivalent. If the image has no CLI, run a debug pod with the same ServiceAccount.

Code to know

Follow-up questions

  • IRSA or Pod Identity: which would you pick for a new platform?

    For new EKS clusters I prefer Pod Identity, because setup is simpler and one role works across clusters without editing trust policies. IRSA is still valid and works in more places, for example outside EKS. Both are fine if the team uses them consistently.

  • The identity is correct, but it still gets AccessDenied. What next?

    Check the bucket policy, an SCP in AWS Organizations, a permissions boundary and KMS key policy. CloudTrail shows which policy type denied the call.

  • How do you stop pods from using the node role?

    Set the instance metadata hop limit to 1 and require IMDSv2 on nodes. Then pods on the pod network cannot reach IMDS. Keep the node role minimal, only what the node needs.

Caution
  • Some candidates add S3 permissions to the node role. Then every pod on every node can write to the bucket.
  • Some candidates create an IAM user and put the keys in a Kubernetes Secret. That gives long-lived keys that someone must rotate by hand.
  • Some candidates trust the laptop test. The laptop uses a different identity, so it proves nothing about the pod.
Staff signal

A Staff answer fixes the case and then makes per-workload identity the default in the platform templates, with a check that blocks static keys.

  • Comparing Pod Identities and IRSA in EKSDevOps WorldEKS Pod Identity vs IRSA side by side.
  • #ContainersFromTheCouch - EKSWorkshop.com - IRSA for EKSContainers from the CouchIRSA walkthrough: OIDC provider, ServiceAccount annotation, trust policy.

UKG-K7

Interviewer

During a load test, several nodes go NotReady and pods pile up in Pending. What is going on and what do you do?

What this tests The interviewer tests if you can separate node health, scheduling and network capacity problems under pressure.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

I check the node conditions first: memory pressure, disk pressure, or a kubelet that stopped reporting. Then I read the Pending reasons with kubectl describe pod. They can be insufficient CPU, a taint, or no free IP addresses. On EKS, the VPC CNI gives each pod a real VPC IP, so pods per node and the subnet size can run out. Fixes are prefix delegation, larger subnets, correct requests, and system reserves for the kubelet. I watch all of this in Container Insights or Prometheus.

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. Stabilize

    Pause or slow down the load test. Cordon the bad nodes, so no new pods go there. Let the autoscaler add healthy capacity.

  2. 2. Read node conditions

    Use kubectl describe node. Look for MemoryPressure, DiskPressure, PIDPressure and Ready=False. If the kubelet stopped posting status, the node may be out of memory itself, because pods had no limits.

  3. 3. Read Pending reasons

    Use kubectl describe pod on a Pending pod. Typical messages:

    • Insufficient cpu or Insufficient memory: the nodes are full by requests.
    • untolerated taint: no node accepts the pod.
    • failed to assign an IP address: the VPC CNI has no free IPs.
  4. 4. Check IP capacity

    With the VPC CNI, each pod uses one VPC IP. The instance type limits the number of ENIs and IPs, so it limits pods per node. The subnet can also run out of free addresses. Turn on prefix delegation and use larger subnets or secondary CIDRs.

  5. 5. Check the autoscaler

    Read the Karpenter or Cluster Autoscaler logs. It can be at its limit, blocked by a NodePool limit, unable to get Spot capacity, or out of subnet IPs.

  6. 6. Protect the nodes

    Set requests and limits on all pods, so the node is not overcommitted. Keep kube-reserved and system-reserved so the kubelet has room. Add alerts for node conditions, Pending time and free subnet IPs.

Concepts you must own 8

kubelet health
Idea

A node is Ready only while its kubelet reports to the control plane.

Example

The kubelet runs out of memory and stops sending heartbeats. After about 40 seconds the node becomes NotReady.

Term

The kubelet updates a Lease object in kube-node-lease. If updates stop, the node controller marks the node Unknown/NotReady. After a timeout, pods on it are evicted.

Disk and memory pressure
Idea

When a node is low on memory or disk, the kubelet sets a pressure condition and evicts pods.

Example

Browser screenshots and videos fill the node disk. DiskPressure=True, and images are garbage-collected.

Term

Conditions are MemoryPressure, DiskPressure and PIDPressure. They add taints such as node.kubernetes.io/disk-pressure that block new pods.

IP exhaustion with VPC CNI
Idea

Every pod needs a real VPC IP. When the node or subnet has none left, new pods cannot start.

Example

An m5.large supports at most 29 pods with the default VPC CNI mode, whatever its free CPU.

Term

Max pods is based on ENIs per instance and IPs per ENI. Errors appear as failed to assign an IP address to container in pod events and aws-node logs.

Subnet sizing
Idea

The subnet is the pool of IP addresses for nodes and pods. A small subnet fills fast.

Example

A /24 subnet has 251 usable IPs. 2,000 browser pods need far more.

Term

Plan pod subnets large, for example /19 or more per AZ. You can add secondary CIDRs (such as from 100.64.0.0/10) with VPC CNI custom networking.

Prefix delegation
Idea

Prefix delegation gives each ENI slot a block of 16 IPs instead of one IP.

Example

With prefix delegation, an m5.large can run 110 pods instead of 29.

Term

Set ENABLE_PREFIX_DELEGATION=true on the VPC CNI. It needs Nitro instances and free contiguous /28 blocks in the subnet. Set max pods to match.

Pending reasons through kubectl describe
Idea

The scheduler writes why it cannot place a pod.

Example

0/40 nodes are available: 12 Insufficient memory, 28 node(s) had untolerated taint {workload: browsers}.

Term

Main reasons: insufficient resources, taints, node affinity or selector mismatch, an unbound PVC, and no IPs. The message counts nodes per reason.

Autoscaler behavior
Idea

The node autoscaler adds nodes only for pods that could fit on a new node.

Example

Karpenter does not add nodes because the NodePool reached its CPU limit.

Term

Karpenter and Cluster Autoscaler act on unschedulable pods. They cannot fix IP exhaustion in a full subnet. Check their logs, limits and Spot availability.

Observability: Container Insights, Prometheus and Grafana
Idea

You need metrics to see the problem before nodes fail.

Example

A Grafana panel shows node memory at 95% and free subnet IPs at 12 before the storm.

Term

CloudWatch Container Insights gives managed cluster metrics and logs. Prometheus with kube-state-metrics and node-exporter gives detailed metrics for Grafana. Alert on node conditions, Pending pods and IP use.

Code to know

Follow-up questions

  • Why did the node go NotReady and not just evict pods?

    If pods have no memory limits, they can use memory faster than the kubelet can evict them. The kubelet itself then starves and stops reporting. System reserves and limits prevent this.

  • How do you plan IP capacity for 2,000 browser pods?

    Count the peak pods and add room for nodes and rolling updates. Use prefix delegation and large pod subnets in each AZ. Alert when free IPs fall below a threshold.

  • How would you run load tests so they do not break the shared cluster?

    Run them on a dedicated node pool with its own limits, in a scheduled window, with alerts. Even better, run them in a separate cluster that matches production size.

Caution
  • Some candidates only add more nodes. If the subnet has no free IPs, new nodes cannot help.
  • Some candidates restart the NotReady nodes at once. That loses the evidence of the cause.
  • Some candidates look at CPU use only. Pending pods depend on requests, IPs and taints, not live CPU use.
Staff signal

A Staff answer turns the incident into capacity planning: IP and node limits, alerts before the failure, and a safe place to run load tests.

Watch

  • Choosing the right CNI for EKS: Navigating IP exhaustion and network challengesDoiTIP exhaustion, prefix delegation, secondary CIDRs.

UKG-K8

Interviewer

Your Cypress suite runs today as a GitHub Actions job in a container. How would you run it in Kubernetes? What differs between minikube, GKE and EKS?

What this tests The interviewer tests if you can map a CI job to Kubernetes objects and set up a cluster for it. He also tests if you know what changes between a local and a managed cluster.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

A GitHub job becomes a Kubernetes Job, and a schedule becomes a CronJob. The container image stays the same. GitHub secrets become a Kubernetes Secret. The Job exit code is the test result. The Job and CronJob manifests are the same on minikube, GKE and EKS. What changes is the cluster setup: where the image comes from, how the pod gets cloud identity, where results are stored, and how traffic leaves the cluster.

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. Map the GitHub flow to Kubernetes

    See the first table. In short, the workflow becomes a Job, the matrix becomes one Job per row, the cron schedule becomes a CronJob, and GitHub secrets become a Secret.

  2. 2. Create the cluster

    Pick the platform. Use minikube on your laptop to test the manifests. Use GKE or EKS for real runs. See the commands below and the second table.

  3. 3. Prepare the namespace

    Create one namespace for the tests, for example e2e. Create the Secret from your .env file. Add a resource quota if the cluster is shared.

  4. 4. Get the image to the cluster

    Build the same image you use in CI. Push it to the registry of your cloud. On minikube, load it with minikube image load.

  5. 5. Run the Job

    Apply the Job. Read the logs with kubectl logs. Wait for the result with kubectl wait. A non-zero exit code makes the Job fail.

  6. 6. Keep the results

    The pod filesystem is deleted with the pod. Upload reports and videos to a bucket before the container exits.

  7. 7. Schedule it

    Use a CronJob with concurrencyPolicy: Forbid. Use Helm or Kustomize to make one CronJob per tier and region.

  8. 8. Choose the trigger

    Keep GitHub Actions as the front door if you like. A workflow step creates the Job and waits for it. Another option is Actions Runner Controller, which runs the GitHub runners inside the cluster.

Concepts you must own 2

Job
Idea

Runs a pod until it finishes and keeps the result.

Example

One Job for the iam suite on dev2.

Term

batch/v1 Job with restartPolicy: Never, backoffLimit and activeDeadlineSeconds.

CronJob
Idea

Creates a new Job on a schedule.

Example

The uptime check every 30 minutes.

Term

batch/v1 CronJob with schedule and concurrencyPolicy.

Code to know

Follow-up questions

  • What is the same on all three clusters?

    The Job, CronJob, Secret and kubectl commands. Only the platform around them changes.

  • Why a Job and not a Deployment?

    A test run starts, finishes and gives one result. A Deployment keeps pods running.

  • What can minikube not show you?

    It cannot show cloud identity, egress allow-lists or autoscaling delays. Test those on a real cluster.

Caution
  • Using latest as the image tag. A run cannot be repeated.
  • Forgetting /dev/shm. Electron crashes under load.
  • Not saving results before the pod ends. A failed run leaves no video.
  • Setting backoffLimit above 0. Retries hide real failures.
Staff signal

A Staff answer keeps the test code unchanged and changes only the platform around it. It names what minikube cannot prove. It ends with a safe rollout: pin the image, start with dev2, then move to the next tier.

UKG-K9

Hands-on lab

You have a Playwright repo that passes on your laptop. Run it on a local Kubernetes cluster with plain kubectl, with no extra test tool. Then show how the same run changes on GKE and EKS, and what Testkube would add.

What this tests The interviewer tests if you have really run tests on Kubernetes. He listens for sharding, shared report storage, image handling and the local versus cloud differences.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

I build one image that has the code and the Playwright browsers. I run it as an Indexed Job. Each pod runs one shard and writes its report to its own folder. A second Job merges the reports into one HTML report. On minikube I share one disk. On GKE and EKS I upload to a bucket, because pods can land on different nodes. Testkube automates the same flow. I use it only when the team wants its history and UI.

Local Option A: minikube + kubectl (start here)

Everything runs on your laptop. No cloud account. No extra tools. About 30 minutes the first time.

  1. Install the tools

    You need Docker Desktop (or another Docker engine), minikube and kubectl. You also need the repo with its tests. You already ran them locally, so Node is ready.

    Give Docker Desktop at least 6 GB of memory. Minikube cannot start with less than what you ask for.

  2. Start the cluster

    This makes a one-node cluster inside a Docker container. It takes about one minute. The last command must show one node in the Ready state.

  3. Add a Dockerfile

    The pod needs your code, node_modules and the browsers. The official Playwright image has the browsers. Your Dockerfile adds the code on top.

    The image tag must match the Playwright version in package-lock.json. This repo uses 1.63.0. A mismatch gives the error Executable doesn't exist.

  4. Build the image inside minikube

    Minikube has its own Docker engine. Point your terminal at it, then build. The image is then already inside the cluster, so you need no registry.

    The eval line only affects this terminal window. If you open a new window later, run it again.

  5. Make a namespace

    A namespace keeps the test objects in one place. Make it the default for your terminal. Then you can leave out -n pw in every command below.

  6. Smoke test with one pod

    Run the whole suite in one pod first. If this fails, the sharded run will fail too. Fix problems here, where there is only one pod to look at.

    You should see 144 passed. The app under test starts inside the pod, because the Playwright config starts it.

  7. Create shared storage for reports

    Every shard pod writes a small report file. You need one place that all pods can write to. A PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC) gives you that. Minikube makes the disk for you.

  8. Run the sharded Job

    This is the main step. It starts 4 pods at once. Pod 0 runs shard 1 of 4, pod 1 runs shard 2 of 4, and so on. Kubernetes sets JOB_COMPLETION_INDEX in each pod.

    Each pod writes to its own folder. This is important. The blob reporter clears its output folder when it starts. Shards that share one folder would delete each other's reports.

  9. Watch it run

    Open a second terminal for the watch command. Pods go from Pending to Running to Completed. Each pod should print 36 passed. Four pods give 144 tests.

  10. Merge the reports

    The merge Job copies all four report files into one folder. Then it builds one HTML report on the same disk.

  11. Copy the report to your laptop and open it

    A finished Job pod cannot be copied from. So start a small helper pod that mounts the same disk and sleeps. Copy the report out with kubectl cp. Then delete the helper.

  12. Run it again with other settings

    Change completions, parallelism and the /4 in the command together. They must show the same number. Delete the PVC first when you lower the shard count. Old blob-N folders would stay and get merged.

    For the big suite, set TEST_DIR to ./tests-large. Add it to the env list.

  13. Fix common problems

    Use kubectl describe pod <name> first. Read the Events at the bottom.

    • ErrImageNeverPull: the image is not in minikube. Run the eval line again and rebuild.
    • Pending: not enough CPU or memory. Lower the requests or start minikube with more.
    • OOMKilled: a browser used too much memory. Lower WORKERS or raise the memory limit.
    • Executable doesn't exist: the image tag and the Playwright version differ.
    • Pod stuck at ContainerCreating with a PVC message: check kubectl get pvc. It must say Bound.
    • Resource use: run minikube addons enable metrics-server, wait a minute, then kubectl top pods.
  14. Clean up

    Stop the cluster to keep it for later. Delete it to free the disk space. Run the last command in any terminal where you used the eval line.

GCP Option B: GKE + kubectl

The same Jobs on a real cluster. Only the image, storage and identity change.

  1. Create the cluster and push the image

    Build for linux/amd64. Most cloud nodes use that CPU type. An Apple silicon Mac builds arm64 by default, and that image fails on amd64 nodes with exec format error.

    If your registry is private and outside GCP, you also need an image pull secret. Artifact Registry in the same project needs none.

  2. Change three things in the YAML
    1. Set image: to europe-west1-docker.pkg.dev/<project>/pw/pw-tests:1.
    2. Delete the imagePullPolicy: Never line.
    3. Do not use the PVC. See the next step.

    On Autopilot, always set resource requests. The manifest already does. Autopilot bills for the requests.

  3. Send reports to a bucket, not a disk

    On minikube there is one node, so all pods can share one disk. On GKE the pods can land on different nodes. A normal GKE disk attaches to one node only. Pods on other nodes would be stuck.

    So each shard uploads its report file to a Cloud Storage bucket before it exits. Return the test exit code after the upload. The pod needs permission to write to the bucket. Use Workload Identity Federation for GKE. Do not put keys in the pod.

  4. Merge and open the report

    The simplest merge is on your laptop. Download the four files, then merge. This needs no merge Job and no helper pod.

AWS Option C: EKS + kubectl

The same as GKE, with ECR and S3.

  1. Create the cluster and push the image

    The steps match GKE. The registry is ECR. The worker nodes pull from ECR with their IAM role, so you need no pull secret for ECR in the same account.

  2. Change the YAML

    Set image: to <account>.dkr.ecr.<region>.amazonaws.com/pw-tests:1 and delete imagePullPolicy: Never. Keep the resource requests. They decide how many pods fit on the nodes.

  3. Send reports to S3, not a disk

    The reason is the same as on GKE. An EBS volume attaches to one node only. Pods on other nodes cannot use it. EFS can be shared, but it adds a driver and a cost for a small file.

    Give the pod an IAM role with s3:PutObject on the bucket. Use EKS Pod Identity or IRSA. Do not put keys in the pod.

  4. Merge and open the report

    Download the files and merge on your laptop. The commands are in the GKE option above. Use the S3 line.

Testkube Option D: Testkube on GKE or EKS

What the cloned repo does. It adds a tool, an agent and a control plane.

  1. What Testkube adds

    Testkube is a tool that runs tests as Kubernetes workflows. It starts the shard pods, collects the reports, merges them and keeps a history. The repo you cloned does exactly this with k8s/testworkflow.yaml.

    The cost is more to install and run. It needs an agent in the cluster. It also needs a control plane, which can be hosted by Testkube or run by you. Standalone mode cannot run the parallel workflow in this repo.

  2. Get a cluster first

    Use the GKE or EKS cluster commands from the options above. Skip the image and bucket steps. Testkube pulls the public Playwright image and the code from Git.

  3. Connect the agent

    Follow the Testkube documentation for your environment. Then check that the CLI points to the same agent.

    Do not pass the agent secret with helm --set. Shell history and process lists can leak it. Use a protected values file or an existing Kubernetes Secret.

  4. Point the workflow at your code

    The workflow downloads the tests from a Git repo at a fixed commit. It does not use your local files. Change content.git.uri and revision to your fork and your commit. Push first.

    The workflow also pins the Playwright image by digest. Check that the digest fits your node CPU type.

  5. Register and run

    Register again after every change to the YAML. kubectl apply alone does not register it in the control plane.

  6. Open the report

    List the runs, pick one, then download its files.
