Follow-up questions

  • Why an Indexed Job and not four separate Jobs?

    One object gives you one status and one place to wait. Each pod still gets its own number in JOB_COMPLETION_INDEX, so it knows which shard to run.

  • Why does each shard write to its own folder?

    The blob reporter clears its output folder at the start. Shards that share a folder delete each other's report files.

  • Do most companies use Testkube?

    I cannot say that. It is one option. Many teams run plain Jobs, start tests from their CI system, or use a workflow engine such as Argo Workflows. Know the plain Job version first. Then Testkube is only a wrapper you can explain.

  • What would you do for 1,440 tests?

    Set TEST_DIR to the big suite. Raise the shard count to 8. Watch CPU and memory first, then add nodes. Do not raise WORKERS before you measure.

Caution
  • Using an image tag that differs from the Playwright version in package-lock.json. The browser is not found.
  • Building on an Apple silicon Mac and pushing to amd64 nodes. The pod fails with exec format error.
  • Letting all shards write to one report folder. They delete each other's files.
  • Using one shared disk on a multi-node cloud cluster. Pods on other nodes cannot mount it.
  • Forgetting eval $(minikube docker-env) in a new terminal. The cluster cannot find the image.
Staff signal

A Staff answer starts with the smallest working run: one pod. Then it adds sharding and report merging. It names the one-folder-per-shard trap and the one-node disk trap before they cause a failure. It treats Testkube as a choice with a cost, not as the default.

Chapter 04

Software design: framework and platform

Design questions test how you make decisions, not which tool you like. Start each answer with the criteria, give a clear recommendation, and show the extension points and the rollout. Use your Cypress framework ownership as proof that you have built these layers before.

UKG-D1

Interviewer

Design one API-testing layer for REST, SOAP and GraphQL that 100 teams can use. Related, from round one: hundreds of teams use Selenium today. Do we build a custom framework, keep Selenium, or move to Playwright, and how do we support REST, SOAP and GraphQL API testing?

What this tests The interviewer tests if you decide with criteria and design clean extension points, not if you name a favorite tool.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

I do not start from a tool. I start from criteria: maintenance cost, reliability, speed, hiring, ecosystem, migration cost and time to value. For UI tests, those criteria usually point to Playwright plus a thin UKG layer, not a full custom framework and not more Selenium. Selenium stays for existing suites during a planned migration. For APIs, I build one client interface with protocol adapters for REST, SOAP and GraphQL, a common response model, and auth plugins. Then assertions are the same for every protocol, and language choice is secondary.

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. Correct the round-one answer

    "Selenium, in Java, because it is compatible with everything" answers the wrong question. Compatibility is only one criterion. The real question is which option gives the lowest total cost and the best signal for hundreds of teams over the next few years.

  2. 2. Decide with explicit criteria

    Compare the options on:

    • Reliability: auto-wait and less flakiness.
    • Speed and parallelism, and the cost of infrastructure.
    • Debugging: traces, video and network logs.
    • Maintenance cost for the platform team.
    • Ecosystem, hiring and community.
    • Language fit with the teams.
    • Migration cost and time to value.
  3. 3. Give the recommendation
    • Build a full custom framework: no. It has a high cost, it is hard to hire for, and it re-invents what tools already do.
    • Keep Selenium for everything: no for new work. It needs more custom wait and grid code and gives weaker debugging.
    • Playwright plus a thin UKG layer: yes. It has auto-wait, built-in tracing, sharding, browser contexts and API testing in the same runner.

    Selenium stays supported for existing suites while teams migrate. I validate the choice with a spike on 2 or 3 real team suites.

  4. 4. Design the API layer

    One ApiClient interface that tests use. Behind it, one adapter per protocol:

    • REST adapter: HTTP verbs, JSON, status codes.
    • GraphQL adapter: one endpoint, query and variables, reads the errors array.
    • SOAP adapter: XML envelopes from the WSDL, reads SOAP Faults.

    Config selects the adapter per service, so tests do not contain protocol code.

  5. 5. Normalize the response

    Every adapter returns the same model: status, ok, data, errors, headers and timing. Assertions such as toBeOk() or toRespondWithin(800) then work for every protocol. This is where most of the value comes from.

  6. 6. Add auth plugins and extension points

    Auth is a plugin: OAuth client credentials, API key, mTLS, or a team-specific SSO token. Teams can add their own adapter or auth plugin through a documented interface. They do not need to change the core.

  7. 7. Address language

    Language is secondary. If most teams write TypeScript, Playwright with TypeScript is the natural choice. If many teams are Java, Playwright also has a Java binding, and the same adapter design works in Java. The architecture matters more than the language.

Concepts you must own 10

Decision criteria (Selenium vs Playwright vs custom)
Idea

Choose a framework by a short list of criteria with weights, not by habit.

Example

Playwright scores high on reliability and debugging. Selenium scores high on existing investment. Custom scores low on maintenance cost.

Term

Write a decision matrix and an ADR (Architecture Decision Record). Validate with a time-boxed spike on real suites. Revisit the decision on a set date.

Playwright plus a thin layer
Idea

Use a strong open-source tool, and add only the UKG-specific parts on top.

Example

The UKG layer adds login fixtures, test data, the API client, reporting and environment config.

Term

A thin layer follows the tool's own patterns (fixtures, projects, reporters). It is easy to upgrade, because it does not wrap every tool call.

Protocol adapters behind one client interface
Idea

Each protocol has its own small translator. Tests talk only to one common interface.

Example

api('payroll').call({operation: 'GetPayslip'}) uses the SOAP adapter. api('people').call(...) uses the GraphQL adapter.

Term

This is the Adapter pattern with a Strategy selected by config. Adding gRPC later means one new adapter, with no test changes.

Common response model
Idea

Every protocol returns the same shape of result, so assertions are generic.

Example

{status, ok, data, errors, headers, timingMs, raw} for REST, SOAP and GraphQL.

Term

Normalize errors into one list. Keep the raw body for reports. Timing supports SLA assertions.

GraphQL returns 200 with an errors array
Idea

A GraphQL call can fail and still return HTTP 200. The errors are inside the body.

Example

{"data": {"employee": null}, "errors": [{"message": "Not authorized"}]} with status 200.

Term

The GraphQL adapter must set ok = false when errors is not empty. A test that checks only status === 200 gives a false pass.

SOAP faults, WSDL and XML
Idea

SOAP sends XML messages in an envelope. A WSDL file describes the operations. Errors come as a Fault element.

Example

The payroll service returns <soap:Fault><faultcode>soap:Client</faultcode>....

Term

SOAP 1.1 faults usually come with HTTP 500. The adapter builds envelopes from the WSDL, parses XML to an object and maps the Fault to the common error list.

Config-driven adapter selection
Idea

A config file says which protocol and auth each service uses.

Example

services.yaml: payroll: {protocol: soap, wsdl: ./payroll.wsdl, auth: mtls}.

Term

Config is validated with a schema at start. Environment variables fill URLs per environment. Tests never hard-code protocol or URL.

Auth plugins (OAuth, API key, mTLS)
Idea

Authentication is a pluggable step that runs before each request.

Example

The OAuth plugin gets a client-credentials token, caches it and refreshes it before it expires.

Term

One AuthPlugin interface with apply(request). Secrets come from the CI secret store or a vault, never from the repo. mTLS loads a client certificate.

Extension points for team-specific needs
Idea

Give teams a safe place to add what they need without a change to the core.

Example

One team adds a custom header plugin for its legacy gateway.

Term

Expose interfaces (adapters, auth plugins, reporters, fixtures) and a registry. Document them. Promote popular extensions into the core.

Language choice is secondary
Idea

The design of the layers matters more than the language.

Example

The same adapter design works in TypeScript with Playwright or in Java with Playwright for Java or REST Assured.

Term

Choose the language by team skills and ecosystem. Avoid two full implementations; if you must support two languages, share the contracts and the config format.

Code to know

Follow-up questions

  • Why not a fully custom in-house framework?

    A custom framework re-builds waiting, browser control, reports and parallelism that Playwright already gives. The platform team then owns all of it forever, and new hires must learn a private tool. A thin layer gives the UKG-specific value at a small part of the cost.

  • Teams have years of Selenium Java code. Does this not waste it?

    No. Existing suites keep running, and the shared Selenium support stays during the migration. New tests start in Playwright, and we move old tests by value and risk, not all at once.

  • How do you test the API layer itself?

    Each adapter has contract tests against mock servers, for example WireMock for REST and SOAP and a schema mock for GraphQL. We also run the layer against 2 or 3 real services in CI.

  • Would you use Playwright for API tests too?

    Yes, Playwright request gives an HTTP client in the same runner, with the same fixtures and reports. The adapters can use it as their HTTP transport. Pure API teams can still use the layer without a browser.

Caution
  • Some candidates pick a tool because it is familiar or "compatible with everything". The interviewer wants criteria and trade-offs.
  • Some candidates check only HTTP 200 for GraphQL. Errors in the body then pass as success.
  • Some candidates build one giant abstraction over every tool. It fits nobody and blocks upgrades.
  • Some candidates make language the main decision. The adapter design and the response model matter more.
Staff signal

A Staff answer makes a reversible decision with explicit criteria and a spike. It designs a small core with extension points that 100 teams can grow without the core team.

UKG-D2

Interviewer

We have 10,000 Selenium tests. Plan a migration to Playwright that does not stall the teams.

What this tests The interviewer tests if you can plan a large migration by value, with data, safety checks and no big-bang rewrite.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

From a cutover date, all new tests are written in Playwright. Then I triage the old tests: delete stale and duplicate ones, and migrate the rest by run frequency, flakiness, business criticality and maintenance cost. If CI does not have that data, I mine the logs and git history and ask teams, and I add instrumentation for the future. LLM-assisted conversion speeds up the work, but every converted test passes a validation harness that runs old and new side by side. I turn off a Selenium suite only after its Playwright version is stable.

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. Stop the growth

    From a cutover date, all new tests are written in Playwright on the shared fixtures. The Selenium code base gets no new tests, only fixes.

  2. 2. Triage before you migrate

    Not all 10,000 tests deserve migration:

    • Delete tests that are stale, disabled, or duplicate other tests.
    • Move some UI tests down to API tests, because they are faster and more stable.
    • Migrate the rest in order of value.
  3. 3. Rank by data

    Rank each suite by run frequency, flakiness, business criticality and maintenance cost. High-flaky, high-value suites move first, because the migration gives them the biggest gain. Stable, rarely-changed suites can wait.

  4. 4. Get the data when CI does not have it
    • Mine CI logs and JUnit files for fail-then-pass on the same commit. That gives a flakiness estimate.
    • Use git history: files that change often have a high maintenance cost.
    • Send a short survey to teams about the most painful suites.
    • Add instrumentation now, so the data is better each week.

    Timebox this to about two weeks. Good-enough data is better than a perfect plan that starts late.

  5. 5. Convert with tools and a safety check

    Use LLM-assisted conversion and codemods for the mechanical part. Upgrade locators to getByRole and getByTestId during conversion. Every converted test goes through human review and a validation harness: it runs next to the Selenium test and must give the same result.

  6. 6. Run in parallel, then turn off

    Keep both versions in CI for a set window, for example two to four weeks. Turn off the Selenium version only when the Playwright version meets a stability bar. Decommission the Grid capacity as use drops.

  7. 7. Make it easy for teams

    The platform team provides shared fixtures, a migration guide, office hours and pairing. Track progress per team on a dashboard. Celebrate teams that finish.

Concepts you must own 12

New tests in Playwright from the cutover date
Idea

Stop adding to the old system, so the migration has an end.

Example

From 1 March, a lint rule fails a PR that adds a new Selenium test file.

Term

This is the "strangler fig" pattern: the new system grows around the old one until the old one can be removed.

Triage: delete stale or redundant tests
Idea

Some tests have no value. Do not spend money to migrate them.

Example

800 tests were disabled for more than a year. 400 tests check the same login flow.

Term

Find tests with no runs, permanently skipped, or covering the same path. Confirm with owners, then delete. Each deleted test is a test that you never need to maintain again.

Migrate by frequency, flakiness, criticality and maintenance cost
Idea

Migrate first the tests that give the most value per hour of work.

Example

The checkout suite runs on every PR, fails 6% of the time and covers revenue. It goes first.

Term

Score each suite on these four factors. High score first. Low-value and stable suites go last, or stay until they are replaced.

Getting the data when CI does not have it
Idea

If the CI system does not store history, collect evidence from other places.

Example

A script reads 3 months of JUnit files, finds fail-then-pass pairs, and counts them per test.

Term

Sources: CI logs and artifacts, git churn (git log --format= --name-only | sort | uniq -c), bug tracker links and a team survey. Each source has bias, so combine them.

Instrument going forward
Idea

Start to collect good data now, even while you use rough data for the first decisions.

Example

The shared reporter sends every test result with run ID, retry count and duration to the results store.

Term

Each week of data improves the ranking. Re-rank the backlog every month.

Timebox the "perfect data" instinct
Idea

A perfect dataset can take months. Set a fixed time, decide with what you have, and adjust later.

Example

Two weeks of data mining and a survey are enough to pick the first 10 suites.

Term

Decide with the data available, label the confidence, and revisit. Migration order is a reversible decision.

LLM-assisted conversion with human review
Idea

An LLM can do the first draft of a conversion fast. A person must still check it.

Example

The LLM turns a Selenium page object into Playwright with getByRole locators. The owner reviews the diff.

Term

Give the LLM the shared fixtures and style rules as context. Use it for mechanical work. Never merge without review and a passing validation run.

Validation harness: run both and compare
Idea

Run the old and the new test against the same build and compare the results.

Example

Both pass on a good build. Both fail on a build with a known injected bug.

Term

Compare results over many runs and on purpose-broken builds. A new test that never fails is suspect: it may assert nothing.

Parallel execution window
Idea

For a set time, both versions run, so you can compare them and fall back.

Example

For 3 weeks, the Selenium and Playwright checkout suites both run on main.

Term

Only one version should block merges, usually the old one at first. Switch the blocking role when the new one is stable.

Decommission only after stability
Idea

Turn off the old test only when the new one has proved itself.

Example

The Playwright suite has a flaky rate under 1% for 3 weeks. The Selenium suite is removed.

Term

Set the exit bar in advance: pass rate, flaky rate and catch of known bugs. Then remove code, jobs and Grid capacity.

Locator upgrade: getByRole and getByTestId
Idea

Find elements the way a user sees them, not by page structure.

Example

Old: By.xpath("//div[3]/button"). New: page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Approve' }).

Term

Role-based locators follow the accessibility tree and survive layout changes. getByTestId uses data-testid for elements with no good role or name.

Shared Playwright fixtures as the framework surface
Idea

Fixtures are the main thing that teams import. They give login, data, API client and setup in one place.

Example

A test gets loggedInPage and data from the fixture. It does not write login code.

Term

Playwright test.extend() defines fixtures with setup and teardown. Version them as a package. They replace the old base classes and page-object helpers.

Code to know

Follow-up questions

  • How long will this take?

    I do not promise a single date for 10,000 tests. I plan in waves, measure the speed of the first waves, and then give a forecast. Many old tests are deleted, so the real number to migrate is smaller.

  • How do you stop the LLM from producing bad tests?

    Every converted test needs review by the owning team and must pass the validation harness. A test must also fail on a broken build, so it really asserts something. We track the review rejection rate to improve the prompts.

  • What if teams have no time for the migration?

    The platform team does the first conversion and the team only reviews. The gain is visible: faster and more stable suites. We also connect the migration to work the team already plans, such as a feature in that area.

Caution
  • Some candidates plan a big-bang rewrite of all 10,000 tests. That stops feature work and moves dead tests too.
  • Some candidates wait months for perfect data before they start. The team loses momentum.
  • Some candidates trust LLM output without a validation run. The new tests may pass while they test nothing.
  • Some candidates turn off Selenium as soon as the new test passes once. One pass does not prove stability.
Staff signal

A Staff answer ranks work by value with imperfect data and builds safety checks into the process. It makes the migration cheap for teams instead of only telling them to do it.

UKG-D3

Interviewer

Your framework release broke three consumer teams. How do you handle it now, and how do you release so it does not happen again?

What this tests The interviewer tests if you can run a shared library like a product with SemVer, safe rollout and fast rollback.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

Right now I help the teams pin back to the last good version, and I ship a PATCH that restores the old behavior. I never change a version that is already published. For the future, I define what "breaking" means for a test framework, such as a changed default timeout or a renamed helper. Breaking changes go only into a MAJOR version, after a deprecation window with warnings, a migration guide and codemods. Every release candidate runs against canary consumer suites before a staged rollout.

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. Stop the damage

    Tell the three teams to pin the previous version in their lockfile. Then ship a PATCH release that reverts the breaking change. Do not unpublish or overwrite the bad version.

  2. 2. Find the gap

    Ask why the release was not marked MAJOR. Usually the change looked harmless inside the framework but changed behavior for consumers. Write a short blameless postmortem.

  3. 3. Define "breaking" for a test framework

    Breaking includes more than API signatures:

    • A renamed or removed helper.
    • A changed default timeout, retry count or wait behavior.
    • A renamed config key.
    • A new minimum Node, Java or browser version.
    • A changed report format that dashboards read.
  4. 4. Deprecate before you remove

    Add the new API in a MINOR release. Mark the old API deprecated, with a runtime warning and a removal version. Remove it only in the next MAJOR, after a fixed window. Provide a migration guide and a codemod where possible.

  5. 5. Test against real consumers

    Publish a release candidate. Run the test suites of 5 to 10 canary consumer repos against it in CI. A change in their results blocks the release.

  6. 6. Roll out in stages

    Renovate or Dependabot opens upgrade PRs, first to canary teams, then to all. Teams pin with lockfiles, so nothing changes until they merge. Track the version spread on a dashboard.

Concepts you must own 10

SemVer
Idea

A version number MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH tells consumers how risky an upgrade is.

Example

4.6.1 → 4.6.2 is a fix. 4.6 → 4.7 adds features. 4 → 5 can break you.

Term

Semantic Versioning: MAJOR for incompatible changes, MINOR for compatible features, PATCH for compatible fixes. Pre-releases use 5.0.0-rc.1.

What "breaking" means in a test framework
Idea

In a test framework, a change of behavior is breaking even if no function signature changes.

Example

The default action timeout goes from 30 seconds to 10 seconds. Slow tests in three teams fail.

Term

Breaking includes renamed helpers, changed defaults (timeout, retry), config keys, runtime or browser baselines, and report formats. List these in the contribution guide.

Deprecation with warnings and a removal window
Idea

Tell users early that something will go away, and give them time to move.

Example

login() prints a warning in 4.6 and is removed in 5.0, three months later.

Term

Use @deprecated JSDoc for IDE warnings and a once-per-run console warning. Publish the removal version and date in the changelog.

Pinning and lockfiles
Idea

A lockfile records the exact version that a repo uses, so updates happen only on purpose.

Example

package-lock.json has @ukg/test-core 4.6.1. A new 4.7.0 does not change anything until a PR updates the lock.

Term

Always commit lockfiles and use npm ci in CI. A caret range (^4.6.0) without a lockfile can pull a new MINOR with no review.

Renovate and Dependabot
Idea

Bots open pull requests that update dependency versions.

Example

Renovate opens one grouped PR for all @ukg/test-* packages every Monday. CI runs the team's tests on it.

Term

Both support grouping, schedules and auto-merge rules. Auto-merge only PATCH updates, and only if tests pass.

Canary-consumer testing against an RC
Idea

Before a release, run real teams' test suites against the new version.

Example

5.0.0-rc.1 runs against 8 canary repos. Two fail, so the release waits.

Term

Pick canary repos that cover different usage patterns. Automate it in the framework CI with a matrix of consumer repos.

Staged rollout
Idea

Release to a few teams first, then to more teams.

Example

Week 1: canary teams. Week 2: 30% of repos. Week 3: all repos.

Term

Control the rollout with Renovate schedules or the moving major tag. Watch error and flaky rates per version on the dashboard.

Rollback by pinning back and a PATCH
Idea

To roll back, consumers go to the last good version, and you release a fix as a new version.

Example

Teams pin 4.6.1. You publish 4.7.1 that reverts the change. They upgrade again.

Term

Rollback is always forward in version numbers. Mark the bad version with npm deprecate and a message.

Never mutate a published version
Idea

A published version must always contain the same code.

Example

If you overwrite 4.7.0, two teams with the "same" version run different code.

Term

npm does not allow republishing a version. Git tags and container tags can move, so protect them. Immutability keeps builds reproducible.

Changelog, migration guide and codemods
Idea

Tell users what changed, how to move, and give them a tool that does the move.

Example

The 5.0 migration guide lists each change. A codemod rewrites login(u, p) to loginAs(role) in all tests.

Term

Keep a changelog (for example with Conventional Commits and release tooling). Write codemods with jscodeshift or ts-morph. Ship them with the MAJOR release.

Code to know

Follow-up questions

  • A team says it cannot wait for a MAJOR to get a fix. What do you do?

    If the fix is compatible, release it as a PATCH on the current MAJOR line. Support the previous MAJOR for a fixed time with security and critical fixes only.

  • How many MAJOR versions do you support at once?

    Usually the current one and the previous one for a published period, for example six months. The adoption dashboard shows who is still on old versions, so we can help them before support ends.

  • How do you know a default change is breaking before you ship it?

    The canary consumer run shows it. Also, any change to a default value needs a note in the PR template and a reviewer check against the list of breaking change types.

Caution
  • Some candidates fix the bad version in place. Then nobody knows which code a version contains.
  • Some candidates ship breaking changes in a MINOR release because "it is a small change". Consumers trust SemVer to protect them.
  • Some candidates tell consumers to always use the latest version. That gives surprise breaks with no review.
Staff signal

A Staff answer handles the incident calmly. Then it builds a release system with clear rules, consumer testing and adoption metrics that protects hundreds of teams.

  • Automating dependency updates - Dependabot vs RenovateAna's Dev ScribblesHow consumers get framework updates automatically.
UKG-D4

Interviewer

Hundreds of tests run in parallel against shared environments, and they keep breaking each other's data. Design the test-data approach.

What this tests The interviewer tests if you can make tests isolated and repeatable when they share an environment.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

Each test creates its own data with a unique prefix that includes the run ID. It creates the data through the API, not the UI, because the API is faster and more stable. Teardown deletes the data, and the cleanup is idempotent. A startup sweep removes orphans from crashed runs. Shared reference data is seeded and read-only. For high-risk work, we use a tenant per team or an ephemeral environment per PR.

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. Separate two kinds of data
    • Reference data: products, tax tables, org structure. Seed it one time and treat it as read-only.
    • Per-test data: the employee, the timesheet, the order that the test changes. Each test creates its own.
  2. 2. Make data unique and traceable

    Give every created record a prefix with the run ID and a short random part, for example e2e-8812-a1b2-emp. Two parallel tests can never pick the same record. A person can see which run created it.

  3. 3. Set up through the API

    Create data through APIs or data factories, not by clicking in the UI. A UI setup takes minutes and fails for reasons that the test does not care about. Test the UI only for the feature under test.

  4. 4. Clean up in layers
    • Teardown in a fixture that runs even when the test fails.
    • Cleanup that is idempotent: a 404 on delete counts as success.
    • A startup sweep that deletes prefixed records older than a few hours.
    • A nightly job as a last safety net.
  5. 5. Isolate more where needed

    Use a tenant or org per team where the product supports it. For risky changes, create an ephemeral environment per PR, for example a namespace per PR on EKS. Weigh the cost: each ephemeral environment uses compute and needs seed data.

  6. 6. Share this from my experience

    At Joyent, our Cypress tests created real cloud resources such as compute instances. Unique names and cleanup kept tests isolated. A startup cleanup removed stale resources from failed runs.

Concepts you must own 8

Unique data per test (prefix and run ID)
Idea

Each test makes its own records with a name that no other test can use.

Example

e2e-8812-w3-emp-a1b2c3 = run 8812, worker 3, random part.

Term

Use the CI run ID, worker index and a random suffix. The prefix also allows safe bulk cleanup and debugging.

API-based setup over UI setup
Idea

Create test data by calling the API. Use the UI only for the behavior that you test.

Example

One API call creates an employee in 200 ms. The UI flow takes 40 seconds.

Term

API setup is faster, more stable and easier to parallelize. It also tests that the API contract stays stable.

Teardown and startup sweep for orphans
Idea

Delete data after each test, and also delete left-over data from runs that crashed.

Example

A runner died, so its data stayed. The next run's global setup deletes e2e-* records older than 2 hours.

Term

Use fixture teardown (runs on failure), a sweep in global setup, and a scheduled cleanup job. Only touch records with the test prefix.

Idempotent cleanup
Idea

Running the cleanup twice gives the same result as running it once.

Example

The delete call gets 404 because another sweep already removed the record. The cleanup still succeeds.

Term

Treat "not found" as success. Delete children before parents. Log failures, but do not fail the test on cleanup errors.

Seeded reference data vs per-test data
Idea

Some data is shared and never changed by tests. Other data belongs to one test.

Example

The department QA-SANDBOX is seeded. Tests add employees to it but never edit it.

Term

Seed reference data with a versioned script. Protect it with permissions if possible. Per-test data comes from factories.

Data factories and builders
Idea

A factory makes a valid record with good defaults, and the test changes only what matters.

Example

data.employee({ status: 'TERMINATED' }) creates a full employee with one special field.

Term

This is the Builder or Factory pattern (like Factory Bot). It hides required fields and keeps tests short.

Tenant or namespace isolation
Idea

Give each team its own space in the product or the cluster.

Example

Team A tests in tenant qa-team-a. Team B cannot see that tenant's data.

Term

Multi-tenant products can give a test tenant per team. On Kubernetes, a namespace per team isolates services and quotas.

Ephemeral environments per PR
Idea

Create a short-lived copy of the app for one pull request, and delete it when the PR closes.

Example

PR 4512 gets namespace pr-4512 on EKS with the changed service and its dependencies.

Term

Use Helm or Argo CD ApplicationSets with a PR generator. Costs include compute, seed time and dependency mocks. Use them for high-risk changes, with TTLs and auto-delete.

Code to know

Follow-up questions

  • Some flows need a shared, limited resource, such as one admin account. What do you do?

    Use a lease. A test takes a lock on the account from a small pool and returns it after the test. If possible, add more accounts to the pool, so parallel tests do not wait.

  • How do you make cleanup safe in a shared environment?

    Delete only records with the test prefix, and only older than a time limit. Never use broad deletes. Run the sweep with an account that can only touch test data.

  • When is an ephemeral environment per PR worth the cost?

    When the change is high risk or touches shared data models. For most PRs, unique data in a shared environment is enough. Ephemeral environments need TTLs and cost tracking.

Caution
  • Some candidates use fixed shared test users in parallel. Tests then change each other's state.
  • Some candidates create data through the UI. It is slow and adds failures that have nothing to do with the test.
  • Some candidates rely only on teardown. A crashed runner never runs teardown, so orphans pile up.
Staff signal

A Staff answer makes isolated data the default in the framework through fixtures and factories. Then every team gets safe parallel runs without extra effort.

  • Workshop 2: Ephemeral Pull Request Environments Using vClustervClusterHands-on per-PR environments on Kubernetes.
UKG-D5

Interviewer

Leadership asks: "Is the framework working?" Design observability for the automation platform itself.

What this tests The interviewer tests if you choose metrics that drive decisions and can explain them to leaders.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

I answer with a small set of metrics that drive decisions. They are flaky rate, pipeline time, time to diagnose a failure, and adoption across teams. I classify every failure as product, test or infra, because each class has a different owner. Traces, screenshots and videos are kept as artifacts for diagnosis. Grafana shows the trends, and alerts fire on trend changes, not on single failures.

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. Define "working"

    The framework works when tests give a fast and trusted signal at low cost. So measure trust (flaky rate), speed (execution and queue time), value (bugs caught) and reach (adoption).

  2. 2. Collect the data

    The shared reporter sends each test result to the results store: team, repo, framework version, status, retries, duration, and failure class. Runner metrics give queue time and capacity.

  3. 3. Classify failures

    Each failure gets a class: product bug, test bug, infra, or flaky. Rules and the triage service set most classes automatically. People correct the rest. Infra failures are the platform team's own problem.

  4. 4. Build dashboards for each audience
    • Leaders: trends of flaky rate, pipeline time, adoption and escaped defects.
    • Teams: their top flaky tests and slow tests.
    • Platform team: queue time, infra failures and version spread.
  5. 5. Alert on trends

    Alert when the flaky rate or the queue time crosses a threshold for a period. Do not alert on one red run.

  6. 6. Separate decision metrics from vanity metrics

    "Number of tests" is vanity. "Flaky rate went from X to Y, and time to diagnose fell from A to B" drives decisions. Each metric on the dashboard must have an owner and an action.

Concepts you must own 8

Pass rate vs flaky rate (fail-then-pass)
Idea

Pass rate can look good while many tests are unreliable. Flaky rate shows how much you can trust a result.

Example

Pass rate is 97%, but 6% of tests passed only after a retry.

Term

Flaky = failed then passed on the same commit, or different results on the same code. Track it per test, per team and over time.

Execution time and queue time
Idea

Execution time is how long tests run. Queue time is how long they wait for a runner or a browser.

Example

Tests run 8 minutes, but they wait 12 minutes for a runner at 9 AM.

Term

Measure p50 and p90, not only the average. Queue time is a capacity problem; execution time is a test or infra problem.

Infra vs product vs test failures
Idea

A failure can mean the product is broken, the test is broken, or the platform is broken.

Example

"Connection refused to grid" is infra. "Expected 5, got 4" after a code change is product. A bad selector is test.

Term

Classify with rules (error patterns), signals (retry passed) and human labels. Report each class to its owner.

Time to diagnose
Idea

How long a developer needs to understand why a test failed.

Example

With traces and a grouped failure view, diagnosis takes 5 minutes instead of 40.

Term

Measure from failure to first triage action or label. It is the best measure of framework debugging quality.

Adoption and version spread
Idea

How many teams use the framework, and which versions they use.

Example

180 of 200 teams use it. 30 teams are still on version 3.

Term

Report from package lockfiles or reporter metadata. A wide version spread increases support cost and slows fixes.

Traces, screenshots and videos as artifacts
Idea

Save the evidence of each failure so people can see what happened.

Example

A Playwright trace shows each action, the DOM snapshot and the network calls at the failure.

Term

Use trace: 'retain-on-failure' or 'on-first-retry'. Store in S3 with lifecycle rules. Link from the report and Slack message.

Dashboards (Grafana) and alerting on trends
Idea

Dashboards show trends. Alerts tell you when a trend goes wrong.

Example

A Grafana alert fires when the 7-day flaky rate goes above 3%.

Term

Use Grafana on Prometheus or a SQL store. Alert on rates over time windows. Every alert has an owner and a runbook.

Decision metrics vs vanity metrics
Idea

A decision metric changes what you do. A vanity metric only looks good.

Example

"10,000 tests" is vanity. "Flaky rate 6% → 2% saved [your number] developer hours a month" is a decision metric.

Term

Ask of each metric: "What would we do if it changed?" If there is no answer, remove it from the dashboard.

Follow-up questions

  • How do you measure escaped defects?

    Link production incidents and bugs to the area of the product. Check whether an automated test covered that path. The trend shows if the suite catches the bugs that matter.

  • Leadership wants one number. Which one?

    I give the flaky rate trend with the pipeline time. Together they show trust and speed, which are the reasons teams use the framework. But I explain that one number hides a lot.

  • How do you get the data without each team doing extra work?

    The shared reporter and the reusable workflow send the data automatically. Teams get the value for free when they adopt the framework.

Caution
  • Some candidates report the number of tests or the pass rate only. These look good while trust is low.
  • Some candidates alert on every failure. Teams ignore the alerts after one week.
  • Some candidates mix infra failures with product failures. Product teams then lose time on platform problems.
Staff signal

A Staff answer picks a few metrics that lead to decisions and shows them to each audience in its own terms. The platform collects the data automatically.

  • SLIs, SLOs, SLAs, oh my! (class SRE implements DevOps)Google Cloud TechPick metrics that drive decisions.
UKG-D6

Interviewer

There are thousands of CI failures a day. Design a service that groups them so teams see 20 root causes, not 2,000 red tests.

What this tests The interviewer tests if you can design a data pipeline with normalization, grouping, idempotency and useful notifications.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

CI sends JUnit results and logs through a webhook or artifact upload. An ingest API puts each run on a queue, so spikes do not overload the processing. Workers normalize each error message and stack trace, remove IDs and timestamps, and make a fingerprint. Same fingerprint means same group. Groups link to known issues. Teams get a notification only for a new group, and an LLM can add a short summary with guardrails.

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. Ingest

    The shared workflow posts the JUnit XML and log location to an ingest API, or uploads them to S3. The API validates the request, stores the raw files and puts a message on a queue (SQS or Kafka). It answers fast, so CI never waits for processing.

  2. 2. Process idempotently

    Workers read from the queue. Each message has a key such as run ID plus test ID. If a message is delivered twice, the result is the same. Failed messages go to a dead-letter queue.

  3. 3. Normalize

    Remove noise from error messages and stack traces: UUIDs, timestamps, numbers, ports, temp paths and line numbers. Keep the error type, the message pattern and the top few stack frames.

  4. 4. Fingerprint and group

    Hash the normalized text to get a fingerprint. All failures with the same fingerprint are one group. Later, add fuzzy matching or embeddings to merge groups that are close.

  5. 5. Link and store

    Link groups to known issues, such as a Jira ticket or a quarantine entry. Store groups and occurrences in a database, for example PostgreSQL, with an index on fingerprint and time. Keep raw logs in S3.

  6. 6. Summarize and notify

    An optional LLM writes a short summary of each new group, from the normalized error and a sample log. It must quote the evidence and never guess a fix as fact. Notify only on new groups or groups that grow fast.

  7. 7. Use my experience

    At Joyent I built an experiment that used an LLM to analyze CI failures. It showed me that the LLM output is only as good as the input. Normalization and grouping must come first.

Concepts you must own 10

Ingest JUnit and logs through webhook or artifact upload
Idea

CI sends the failure data to the service at the end of each run.

Example

The reusable workflow posts {run_id, repo, junit_url} to POST /ingest.

Term

Push (a webhook or an HTTP call from CI) is fast. Pull (read artifacts through the GitHub API) needs no change in CI. Authenticate calls, for example with OIDC tokens.

Normalize stack traces and error messages
Idea

Remove the parts of a message that change each time, so that the same problem looks the same.

Example

Timeout 30000ms waiting for #order-8812 and Timeout 30000ms waiting for #order-9134 become Timeout <N>ms waiting for #order-<N>.

Term

Use regex rules for IDs, times, numbers and paths. Keep the error class and top frames. Test the rules with real samples.

Fingerprint and group
Idea

A fingerprint is a short hash of the normalized failure. Same fingerprint means same group.

Example

1,400 failures today share fingerprint a91f03c2. They are one root cause.

Term

Hash with SHA-1 or similar. Start with exact match on normalized text. Add similarity (edit distance, embeddings) later.

Dedupe
Idea

Remove repeated copies of the same event, so counts are correct.

Example

A re-run of the same CI job sends the same result again. The service counts it once.

Term

Use a unique key, such as run ID + attempt + test ID, with a unique constraint or an upsert.

Known-issue linking
Idea

Connect a group to a ticket that already explains it.

Example

Group a91f03c2 links to QA-512: payments sandbox timeout. Teams see the ticket and do not investigate again.

Term

Store the link on the group. Use it to suppress notifications and to drive quarantine.

Queue between ingest and processing
Idea

A queue holds work between the part that receives it and the part that does it.

Example

At 9 AM, 5,000 results arrive in 2 minutes. Workers process them over 5 minutes, and nothing is lost.

Term

SQS (simple, managed, with a dead-letter queue) or Kafka (high volume, replay, many consumers). The queue decouples, buffers and enables retries.

Idempotency
Idea

The same request handled twice gives the same result as once.

Example

SQS delivers a message twice. The upsert on (run_id, test_id) keeps one row.

Term

SQS standard queues deliver at least once, so consumers must be idempotent. Use idempotency keys and upserts.

Storage choice
Idea

Choose storage by how you read the data.

Example

PostgreSQL for groups and queries by team and time. S3 for raw logs. OpenSearch for full-text search.

Term

Relational for structured queries and joins. Object storage for large raw files with lifecycle rules. A search engine only if full-text search is needed.

LLM summarization with guardrails
Idea

An LLM can write a short, readable summary of a failure group. It must not invent facts.

Example

"All 1,400 failures time out on the payments sandbox after 30 seconds, since 08:52."

Term

Guardrails: give only normalized data and samples, ask it to cite evidence, and limit the length. Mark output as AI-generated. Do not let it close or label issues alone.

Notifications on new clusters only
Idea

Tell teams only about new problems, not about the same problem again.

Example

Group a91f03c2 is new today, so the team gets one Slack message. Tomorrow, it does not repeat.

Term

Notify on new groups, on regressions of closed groups and on fast growth. Send a daily digest for the rest.

Code to know

Follow-up questions

  • How do you test the normalization rules?

    Keep a set of real failure samples with the expected group for each. Run the rules against the set in CI. Measure two errors: one cause split into many groups, and many causes merged into one group.

  • Kafka or SQS?

    For this load, SQS is simpler and fully managed, with a dead-letter queue. Kafka is better if many consumers need the same stream or we need to replay history.

  • How would you code the grouping in an interview?

    Write a normalize function with a few regex rules, then group by the normalized string in a dictionary. Return groups sorted by count. Then discuss edge cases, such as multi-line stack traces.

  • How do you avoid wrong LLM summaries?

    The LLM only summarizes data that we give it, and the UI shows the raw evidence next to it. People can flag a bad summary, and we track the flag rate.

Caution
  • Some candidates group by test name. One root cause can break hundreds of different tests.
  • Some candidates hash the raw message. Every message is unique because of IDs and timestamps, so nothing groups.
  • Some candidates process inside the CI request. A spike then slows down every CI run.
  • Some candidates let the LLM decide the root cause alone. It can be confidently wrong.
Staff signal

A Staff answer designs for scale and failure from the start, with a queue, idempotency and a DLQ. It also measures the quality of the grouping.

  • Kafka vs RabbitMQ vs SQS | Message Queues ExplainedThatNotesGuyQueue choice between ingest and processing.
  • Dead Letter Queues Explained — SQS, SNS & EventBridge (+ 7 Production Rules)CloudMeatAndBonesDLQ, retries, idempotent consumers.
UKG-D7

Interviewer

CI needs to react when a deploy to a downstream environment finishes. Do you use polling, webhooks or a queue?

What this tests The interviewer tests if you know integration patterns and their trade-offs in reliability, latency and cost.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

Polling is simple but wastes calls and adds delay. A webhook pushes the event at once, but it needs a reachable endpoint, signature checks, retries and idempotency. A queue or pub/sub decouples the systems and buffers events, with retries and a dead-letter queue. For GitHub Actions, the deploy system can call repository_dispatch or workflow_dispatch when it finishes. For many consumers, I put an event bus in between.

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. State the need

    When the environment deploy finishes, the E2E suite must start against that version. The trigger must be fast, reliable, and secure.

  2. 2. Compare the options
    • Polling: CI asks "done yet?" every 30 seconds. Simple, but wasteful and slow.
    • Long-polling: the server holds the request until there is news. Fewer calls, but held connections.
    • Webhook: the deploy system calls a URL when it finishes. Fast, but needs a reachable endpoint and security.
    • WebSocket: a persistent two-way connection. Good for live UIs, too much for this.
    • Queue or pub/sub: the deploy system publishes an event. Consumers read it when ready.
  3. 3. Pick for GitHub Actions

    The deploy system calls the GitHub API: repository_dispatch with an event type and payload, or workflow_dispatch with typed inputs. GitHub is the endpoint, so we do not host one. Authenticate with a GitHub App token with minimal scope.

  4. 4. Pick for many consumers

    If several systems care about deploys, publish to an event bus such as EventBridge, SNS or Kafka. A small consumer triggers the GitHub workflow. The queue gives retries and a dead-letter queue.

  5. 5. Make it safe

    Verify webhook signatures. Make the handler idempotent with the deploy ID. Use a concurrency group per environment, so two deploys do not run E2E against a changing target.

Concepts you must own 9

Polling
Idea

The client asks again and again whether something changed.

Example

CI calls GET /deploys/123 every 30 seconds for up to 20 minutes.

Term

Simple and needs no inbound network. It wastes requests, adds up to one interval of delay, and can hit rate limits.

Long-polling
Idea

The client asks once, and the server waits to answer until there is news or a timeout.

Example

The request stays open up to 60 seconds and returns at once when the deploy ends.

Term

Fewer requests and lower delay than polling. The server holds many open connections. It is still a client pull.

Webhooks
Idea

The source system calls your URL when the event happens.

Example

The deploy tool sends POST /hooks/deploy with {env, version, status}.

Term

Push with low delay. It needs a public or reachable endpoint, HMAC signature verification, retries with backoff on the sender, and idempotent handlers.

Webhook signature verification
Idea

The receiver checks that the message really came from the sender and was not changed.

Example

GitHub sends X-Hub-Signature-256. The receiver computes HMAC-SHA256 with the shared secret and compares.

Term

Use a constant-time compare. Reject old timestamps to stop replay attacks.

Retries and idempotency for webhooks
Idea

Senders retry when they get no success answer, so the receiver can get the same event twice.

Example

The deploy tool retries after a timeout. The handler sees deploy ID d-77 again and ignores it.

Term

Store processed event IDs. Answer 2xx fast and do the work asynchronously.

WebSockets
Idea

A WebSocket is a long-lived, two-way connection between client and server.

Example

A live test dashboard gets each result the moment it finishes.

Term

Good for live UIs and chat. For a single "deploy done" event it adds connection management with no gain.

Message queues and pub/sub
Idea

A queue stores messages until a consumer reads them. Pub/sub sends one event to many subscribers.

Example

The deploy system publishes env-deployed. The E2E trigger, the release notes bot and the dashboard each get a copy.

Term

Benefits: decoupling, buffering of spikes, retries and a DLQ for failed messages. Examples: SQS (queue), SNS and EventBridge (pub/sub), Kafka (log).

Dead-letter queue (DLQ)
Idea

A DLQ holds messages that failed too many times, so they are not lost and do not block others.

Example

A malformed event fails 5 times and moves to the DLQ. An alarm tells the owner.

Term

SQS uses a redrive policy with maxReceiveCount. Monitor the DLQ depth.

repository_dispatch and workflow_dispatch
Idea

These are two ways to start a GitHub Actions workflow from outside GitHub.

Example

The deploy system calls POST /repos/ukg/e2e-suites/dispatches with event_type: env-deployed.

Term

repository_dispatch takes a custom event_type and a free client_payload, and runs on the default branch. workflow_dispatch targets one workflow and ref, with typed inputs, through POST /actions/workflows/{id}/dispatches.

Code to know

Follow-up questions

  • When is polling the correct choice?

    When the source cannot send events, when volume is low, or when the network does not allow inbound calls. Use a sensible interval with backoff and a timeout.

  • What if GitHub is down when the deploy finishes?

    With a direct call, the deploy system must retry. With a queue in between, the event waits in the queue and the consumer retries later. That is more reliable.

  • How do you secure repository_dispatch?

    Use a GitHub App with only the permission it needs on the target repo. Do not use a personal access token. Validate the payload in the workflow before you use it.

Caution
  • Some candidates say "webhooks are always better". Webhooks need security, retries and idempotency, or events get lost or repeated.
  • Some candidates use a sleep 600 in CI to wait for the deploy. That is slow and still fails when the deploy takes longer.
  • Some candidates trust the webhook payload without a signature check. Anyone can then start pipelines.
Staff signal

A Staff answer picks the simplest reliable pattern. It also explains when to move to an event bus, as more systems need the same event.
