  • Webhooks vs Polling Explained | Real-Time Events Without Wasting ResourcesSystemDR - Scalable System DesignWebhook trade-offs: public endpoint, retries, signatures.
UKG-D8

Interviewer

Our application sends email through SMTP. How do you confirm that an email was really sent? And how do you know it reached the user?

What this tests The interviewer tests if you know what an SMTP success reply really proves. They also test if you design for the steps after it: bounces, retries and monitoring.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

First I ask what 'sent' means, because there are three facts. One: our app gave the message to a mail server. Two: the recipient's server accepted it. Three: it reached the inbox. An SMTP 250 reply proves only that the next server accepted the message. So I log the SMTP reply and the message ID, and I keep a state for every email in an outbox table. Then I read the later outcome from delivery events: provider webhooks, or bounce messages. I alert on bounce rate and on emails with no final state. For a test, I send to a test inbox and check the message.

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. Define 'sent'

    There are three different facts:

    • Handed off: our app gave the message to the relay.
    • Accepted: the receiving server said yes (SMTP 250).
    • Delivered to the inbox: the user can see it.

    SMTP gives you the first fact and sometimes the second. It never gives the third. Say this first, because it shows that you know the limit of the protocol.

  2. 2. Read the SMTP reply and log it

    Log the full reply, the queue ID and the Message-ID header for every send.

    • 2xx: accepted. Not the same as delivered.
    • 4xx: temporary problem. Retry later with exponential backoff and a limit.
    • 5xx: permanent failure. Do not retry. Mark the email failed and look at the reason.

    Check the rejected list too. One send can accept some recipients and refuse others.

  3. 3. Keep a state for every email (outbox pattern)

    The web request writes a row to an outbox table. A worker sends it. States are: queued, accepted, delivered, deferred, bounced, complained, failed. This gives you three things. You can retry after a crash. You have one place to ask 'what happened to this email?'. No email is lost if the SMTP server is down. Use an idempotency key so one business event creates one email.

  4. 4. Collect the real outcome after the send

    The final result arrives later and from outside:

    • With a provider such as SES, SendGrid or Postmark, subscribe to their events (webhook or SNS). They report delivered, bounced, complained and deferred.
    • With plain SMTP, a failed delivery returns as a bounce message (a DSN) to the return-path address. Read that mailbox and parse it.

    Verify the webhook signature. Make the handler idempotent, because providers send events twice.

  5. 5. Monitor the system, not each email

    Track send success rate, bounce rate, complaint rate, time to delivered (p95) and the age of the oldest queued email. Alert when a state does not change, for example 'accepted' for 30 minutes. Hard bounces go on a suppression list, so you do not send to them again. A high bounce or complaint rate damages the sender reputation, and the provider may pause your account.

  6. 6. Verify with a test

    In the test environment, point the app to a capture server such as Mailpit and assert on the real message: recipient, subject, links. A small scheduled canary sends through the real provider to a test inbox and alerts if it does not arrive. See D9.

  7. 7. Do not use 'opened' as proof

    Open tracking uses a tiny image. Mail apps now load it automatically or block it, so it is not reliable. Use a business signal instead, for example 'the user clicked the reset link'.

Concepts you must own 6

SMTP reply codes
Idea

A three-digit answer from the mail server after each command.

Example

250 2.0.0 Ok: queued as 4F3A1 means the server took the message. 451 means 'try again later'. 550 means 'this mailbox does not exist'.

Term

2xx success, 4xx transient failure (retry), 5xx permanent failure (RFC 5321). Enhanced status codes such as 5.1.1 give more detail.

Accepted is not delivered
Idea

A server can say 'OK' and still drop the message to spam, or bounce it later.

Example

The relay accepts the message at 10:00. At 10:02 the recipient's server rejects it, and a bounce message comes back.

Term

SMTP hands over responsibility hop by hop. The sending app only sees the first hop. Later failures return asynchronously as DSNs (RFC 3464) or provider events.

Hard bounce and soft bounce
Idea

A hard bounce is a permanent failure. A soft bounce is a temporary one.

Example

Hard: the mailbox does not exist. Soft: the mailbox is full or the server is busy.

Term

Hard bounces (5.x.x) go on a suppression list at once. Soft bounces (4.x.x) are retried, and become suppressed after a set number of failures.

Outbox pattern
Idea

Save the 'send this email' request in your database first. Send it from a background worker.

Example

The signup request writes one outbox row in the same transaction as the new user. A worker sends the email.

Term

The outbox row is written in the same database transaction as the business change. A separate worker publishes it with retries. This gives at-least-once delivery, so the send step must be idempotent.

Delivery events (webhooks)
Idea

The provider calls your API when something happens to an email.

Example

SES sends 'Delivery', 'Bounce' and 'Complaint' events to an SNS topic. A Lambda updates the outbox row.

Term

Verify the signature. Treat events as at-least-once and out of order. Key updates on the message ID, so a repeat does not change state twice.

DSN (bounce message)
Idea

An automatic email that says delivery failed.

Example

A message from the mail system with a subject such as 'Undelivered Mail Returned to Sender'.

Term

A Delivery Status Notification is sent to the envelope sender (the return-path). It carries the original Message-ID and a status code, so you can match it to the outbox row.

Code to know

Follow-up questions

  • The server returned 250, but the user says the email never came. What do you check?

    I look up the message by queue ID or Message-ID in the provider log. Then I check, in this order:

    • Was there a bounce or complaint event for it?
    • Is the address on our suppression list?
    • Is the address spelled correctly?
    • Did it go to spam? Check SPF, DKIM and DMARC. See D10.
    • Was it delayed (greylisting, a deferred event)?

  • A send times out after the data was sent. Do you retry?

    I do not know if the server accepted it, so a retry can create a duplicate. For a low-risk email, I accept the rare duplicate. For a critical email, I use a provider that supports an idempotency key. Or I keep the same Message-ID, so the receiver can drop the copy. I never choose 'lose the email' over 'send twice' for a password reset.

  • How do you know the user opened the email?

    I do not rely on it. Open tracking uses a hidden image, and many mail apps load it automatically or block it. I measure the action that matters, for example a click on the verification link.

  • Why not send the email inside the web request?

    SMTP can be slow or down. The user would wait, or the request would fail after the database change. With an outbox, the request is fast, the email is not lost, and a worker retries with backoff.

Caution
  • Some candidates say 'we check that SMTP returned 250, so it was sent'. This proves only that the next server accepted it.
  • Some candidates retry every error. A 5xx reply is permanent, and repeated sends to a bad address harm the sender reputation.
  • Some candidates send inside the web request and have no stored state. A crash or a timeout then loses the email without a trace.
  • Some candidates use open tracking as proof of delivery. Mail apps make it unreliable.
Staff signal

A Staff answer separates 'accepted' from 'delivered', then builds the missing part: a state machine, delivery events, retries and alerts. It also treats the email system as something to measure, with rates and ages, not as a single call that succeeds.

UKG-D9

Interviewer

Many teams have features that send email: password reset, invoices, alerts. How do you test those emails in the automation platform, and keep the tests reliable?

What this tests The interviewer tests if you can turn a hard, asynchronous, external dependency into a simple, stable platform feature.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

I do not send test email to real inboxes. In every test environment I run a mail-capture server, for example Mailpit. The app sends through normal SMTP to it, so the code path is real. The platform gives teams a mail fixture. Each test gets a unique recipient address. It polls the capture API until the message arrives, with a timeout. Then it asserts on subject, body and links. This is fast, parallel-safe and has no external dependency. A small scheduled canary test checks the real provider path separately.

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. Split what you test

    There are two different questions:

    • Did our app create and send the right email? Test this in every environment with a capture server. It is fast and exact.
    • Does the real provider deliver to a real inbox? Test this with one small canary on a schedule. Do not run it in every pull request.
  2. 2. Capture, do not deliver

    Run Mailpit (or a similar tool) as a pod in each test environment. Set the app's SMTP host to it, for example port 1025. Mailpit accepts every message, shows it in a web page (port 8025) and exposes a REST API. No email leaves the cluster, so there is no risk of mail to real people.

  3. 3. Give every test its own recipient

    Make a unique address per test, for example reset-<run>-<worker>-<test>@test.example.com. Search the inbox by that address. Tests then run in parallel without reading each other's mail. Do not share one inbox and do not delete all messages between tests.

  4. 4. Wait with a poll, not a sleep

    Email is asynchronous. Poll the API every 0.5 to 2 seconds until the message appears. Fail with a clear message after a timeout, for example 30 seconds. A fixed sleep(5) is slow when email is fast and flaky when email is slow.

  5. 5. Assert on what matters

    Check recipient, subject, a key phrase, and the link or the one-time code. Then use the link in the same test, for example open the reset URL in the browser. This tests the whole flow. Do not compare the full HTML text, because small copy changes will break many tests.

  6. 6. Put it in the platform

    Provide one mail fixture with address() and waitFor(), plus helpers such as extractLink(). Document it with an example. Teams then write 5 lines, not their own polling code. Keep the capture server in the shared environment template, so it is there by default.

  7. 7. Add a real-provider canary

    Every 15 or 30 minutes, send one email through the real provider to a dedicated test mailbox. Check that it arrives within a set time. Alert on failure. This catches DNS, SPF, DKIM or provider problems that a capture server cannot see.

Concepts you must own 5

Mail capture server (Mailpit, MailHog)
Idea

A fake mail server that keeps all mail instead of delivering it.

Example

The app sends to mailpit:1025. A test calls GET /api/v1/search?query=to:... to read it.

Term

It implements SMTP on the receiving side and exposes the stored messages through a web UI and an HTTP API. MailHog is no longer actively developed, so Mailpit is a common current choice.

Unique recipient per test
Idea

Every test uses its own email address, so tests do not mix.

Example

reset-8812-3-ab12@test.example.com

Term

This isolates test data and allows parallel runs. The address carries the run ID, so you can also find and clean old mail.

Poll with a timeout
Idea

Ask again and again until the result is there, but stop after a time limit.

Example

Check every second for up to 30 seconds.

Term

Use the framework's polling assertion (expect.poll in Playwright) with backoff intervals. It avoids fixed sleeps and gives a readable failure.

Canary test
Idea

A small test that runs all the time in the real system and warns you early.

Example

Every 30 minutes, one email goes through the real provider to a test mailbox.

Term

Synthetic monitoring of a production-like path. It covers the part that test doubles cannot: DNS, authentication records, provider limits.

Test double at the network edge
Idea

Replace the outside service, but keep your own code the same.

Example

The app still uses real SMTP code. Only the server it talks to is fake.

Term

Replacing the dependency at the protocol boundary keeps the production code path under test, which an in-process mock does not.

Code to know

Follow-up questions

  • Why not use a real Gmail account for tests?

    It is slow, rate-limited, and shared state makes tests flaky. Google may block automated logins. It also means real mail leaves your systems. I use a capture server for the app, and one canary for the real path.

  • How do you test an email with an attachment or a link that expires?

    The capture API returns attachments and the raw message, so I assert on the file name, size and type. For an expiring link, I open it in the same test, right after the email arrives. I also add one test that waits past the expiry in a unit-level test with a controlled clock, not in the end-to-end suite.

  • The email test is flaky. How do you find the cause?

    I look at three things. Is the recipient unique, or do two tests share an inbox? Is the timeout too short for a slow queue? Is the app sending after the database transaction is committed, or before it? I log the recipient and the time the message arrived, so I can see the real delay.

  • Can a third-party test inbox service replace Mailpit?

    Yes, services such as Mailtrap, Mailosaur or MailSlurp work, and they can test real public addresses. The trade-off is cost, an external network dependency in every test, and rate limits. For 100 teams I prefer a capture server inside the environment and a few service-based canaries.

Caution
  • Some candidates use a fixed sleep. It is slow when email is fast and flaky when email is slow.
  • Some candidates share one inbox between all tests. Parallel tests then read each other's mail.
  • Some candidates mock the email function inside the app. This skips the real SMTP code and its configuration.
  • Some candidates compare the full HTML body. A small copy change then breaks many tests.
Staff signal

A Staff answer turns a hard dependency into a platform feature: one fixture, an environment default, and a documented example. It also keeps two risks apart, the app's behavior and the real provider path, and tests each in the right place.

UKG-D10

Interviewer

Our emails are accepted by SMTP, but many users say they land in spam or never arrive. How do you investigate, and how do you prevent it?

What this tests The interviewer tests if you know how receivers decide to trust a sender, and if you can use data instead of guessing.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

I start with data. I take one real message, open its headers, and check Authentication-Results for SPF, DKIM and DMARC. If one fails, I fix the DNS records or the provider setup. Then I check reputation: bounce and complaint rates, the sending IP and domain, and whether we send to old or bad addresses. Prevention has five parts. Authenticate the domain. Use a separate sending subdomain. Remove hard bounces. Add an unsubscribe header for bulk mail. Monitor rates with a dashboard and DMARC reports.

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. Get facts from one real message

    Ask an affected user for the full headers (in Gmail: 'Show original'). Read Authentication-Results. It shows spf=pass, dkim=pass, dmarc=pass, or which one failed. Also read the Received lines to see the path and the delays.

  2. 2. Check the three DNS records
    • SPF: a DNS record that lists the servers allowed to send for the domain.
    • DKIM: the provider signs each message. The receiver checks the signature with a public key in DNS.
    • DMARC: a record that tells receivers what to do when SPF and DKIM do not match the visible From domain, and where to send reports.

    The domain in the visible From must align with the SPF or DKIM domain, or DMARC fails.

  3. 3. Check reputation

    Receivers also score the sender. Look at the bounce rate, the complaint rate, the age and sharing of the sending IP, and sudden volume jumps. Use the free postmaster tools from the big mailbox providers, and a blocklist check. Sending to old, bought or mistyped addresses is a common cause.

  4. 4. Check the message itself

    Look for a missing plain-text part, broken HTML and one large image. Look for link shorteners and a mismatch between the link text and the real URL. Look for spam words in the subject. For bulk mail, include List-Unsubscribe headers and a visible unsubscribe link. Major mailbox providers now require authentication and easy unsubscribe from bulk senders.

  5. 5. Separate the types of mail

    Send transactional mail (reset, receipts) from its own subdomain, and send marketing mail from a different one. Then a marketing complaint cannot harm password reset mail. Warm up new domains and IPs with a slow increase in volume.

  6. 6. Clean the list automatically

    Put hard bounces and complaints on a suppression list at once. Stop sending to addresses that bounce. Check addresses at signup, for example with a confirmation email. This keeps the bounce rate low.

  7. 7. Monitor and add a safety net

    Set a DMARC rua address and read the aggregate reports. Alert on bounce rate, complaint rate and the canary from D9. Start DMARC with p=none, fix every legitimate sender, then move to quarantine and reject.

Concepts you must own 6

SPF
Idea

A list in DNS of the servers that may send email for your domain.

Example

v=spf1 include:amazonses.com -all says: only Amazon SES may send for this domain.

Term

Sender Policy Framework (RFC 7208). The receiver checks the connecting IP against the SPF record of the envelope-from domain. SPF breaks when a message is forwarded.

DKIM
Idea

A digital signature on each email. The receiver checks it with a public key from DNS.

Example

The provider signs the message with a private key. The public key is in selector1._domainkey.mail.example.com.

Term

DomainKeys Identified Mail (RFC 6376) signs selected headers and the body. It usually survives forwarding, unless the message is changed on the way.

DMARC
Idea

A policy that says what to do with mail that fails SPF and DKIM, and where to send reports.

Example

p=quarantine tells receivers to treat failing mail as suspicious.

Term

DMARC (RFC 7489) requires that SPF or DKIM passes and that its domain aligns with the From domain. Policies are none, quarantine and reject. Aggregate reports (rua) show every source that sends as your domain.

Sender reputation
Idea

A score that receivers keep for your domain and IP address, based on past mail.

Example

A high complaint rate and many bounces lower it. Mail then goes to spam.

Term

It is built from complaint rate, bounce rate, spam-trap hits, engagement and volume patterns. A new domain or IP has no history, so it needs a warm-up.

Suppression list
Idea

A list of addresses that you must not send to.

Example

Every hard bounce and every spam complaint is added at once.

Term

Providers keep an account-level suppression list. Keeping your own list too prevents repeat sends when you change provider.

Transactional and bulk mail
Idea

Transactional mail answers a user action. Bulk mail goes to many people.

Example

Transactional: a password reset. Bulk: a product newsletter.

Term

Use separate subdomains and, for volume, separate IP pools. Bulk mail needs List-Unsubscribe and one-click unsubscribe support.

Code to know

Follow-up questions

  • SPF passes, but DMARC fails. Why?

    DMARC needs alignment. SPF can pass for the provider's own domain, while the visible From domain is yours. If the DKIM signature also uses the provider's domain, nothing aligns. The fix is to set up a custom domain with the provider, so DKIM signs with your domain.

  • Why do forwarded emails fail SPF?

    The forwarding server has a different IP address, and it is not in your SPF record. DKIM usually survives forwarding, because the signature travels with the message. This is why DMARC accepts either SPF or DKIM that aligns.

  • How do you roll out DMARC safely?

    Start with p=none and read the reports for a few weeks. List every system that sends as your domain, for example the app, the CRM and the support tool. Fix their SPF or DKIM. Then move to quarantine with a percentage (pct), and at the end to reject.

  • A marketing campaign got many complaints. How do you protect password reset mail?

    That is the reason to use separate subdomains and, if volume is high, separate IP pools for transactional and marketing mail. Reputation is tracked per domain and IP. I also pause the campaign, check the list source, and add the complaints to the suppression list.

Caution
  • Some candidates guess ('maybe it is the subject line') before they read the headers. The headers show the real SPF, DKIM and DMARC result.
  • Some candidates fix SPF only. DMARC needs alignment, and DKIM is the safer path for forwarded mail.
  • Some candidates send all mail from one domain. A marketing complaint then harms password reset mail.
  • Some candidates set DMARC to reject on day one. A forgotten system that sends as your domain is then blocked.
Staff signal

A Staff answer starts from evidence: the headers and the rates. It explains the trust chain in plain words. Then it designs prevention: separate domains, automatic suppression and monitoring. It also shows a safe rollout path for DMARC.

Watch

  • Stop going to Spam: DMARC, SPF and DKIM Explained - Syntax #732SyntaxHow SPF, DKIM and DMARC work, and how to set them up.
Chapter 05

Leadership and Staff scope

A Staff engineer is an individual contributor who leads through influence, not authority. Each answer shows that you understand people first, use data, make the good path easy, and escalate only as a clear trade-off.

UKG-L1

Interviewer

A large, influential team says the Playwright migration is a waste of time and refuses to do it. What do you do?

What this tests The interviewer tests if you can influence a strong team without authority and without a fight.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

First I listen, because they may have a real cost or constraint that I do not see. Then I show their own data, such as flaky rate and pipeline time, not general claims. I offer help: pairing, codemods and migration tooling, so the cost for them is small. If they still have a good reason, I agree an exception with an end date. I escalate only with a clear trade-off for leadership, not as a complaint.

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. Understand their position

    Meet the tech lead and ask about their costs and constraints. Maybe they have a release deadline, a huge suite, or a bad experience with an earlier migration. Write down their concerns and confirm them back.

  2. 2. Show their own data

    Bring numbers about their suites: flaky rate, pipeline time, time spent on test maintenance. Compare with a pilot team that already migrated. Data about their own work is stronger than a general argument.

  3. 3. Make the migration cheap

    Offer pairing for the first suites, codemods and LLM-assisted conversion, and a migration guide. Make the new path the easy path: better reports, faster runs, and shared fixtures that remove their custom code.

  4. 4. Agree on a plan that fits them

    Start with their most painful suite, where the gain is fastest. Fit the work around their release dates.

  5. 5. Allow an exception with an end date

    If the timing is truly bad, agree an exception with a date and a condition. Write it down, so it does not become permanent.

  6. 6. Escalate only as a trade-off

    If there is still no agreement, write a short note for both sets of leaders. It states the options, the cost of each, and my recommendation. Leadership then decides the trade-off. It is not a complaint about the team.

Concepts you must own 6

Understand their cost and constraints first
Idea

Resistance often has a real reason. Find it before you argue.

Example

The team ships a big release in 6 weeks and cannot spare two engineers now.

Term

Use active listening and restate their view. This builds trust and often changes the plan.

Show data (flakiness, runtime)
Idea

Numbers about their own work convince better than opinions.

Example

"Your suite failed 9% of runs last month with no code change. The pilot team went from 8% to [your number]."

Term

Use the results store. Compare before and after for a similar team. Be honest about uncertainty.

Offer help over mandates
Idea

Help people do the work instead of only telling them to do it.

Example

A platform engineer pairs with them for two days and converts their top 3 suites.

Term

Pairing, codemods, migration tooling, office hours. A mandate without help creates resentment and low-quality work.

Make the new path the easy path
Idea

If the new way is easier and better, people move by choice.

Example

New fixtures give login and data in one line. The new reports show traces. Old code needs more work.

Term

Invest in developer experience: docs, templates, defaults and tooling. Adoption follows value.

Exceptions with an end date
Idea

Allow a delay, but make it temporary and written down.

Example

"Team X migrates after the Q3 release, by 30 November."

Term

Record the exception, the reason, the end date and the owner. Review it on the date.

Escalate with a clear trade-off framed for leadership
Idea

When you escalate, give leaders a decision, not a conflict.

Example

"Option A: they migrate now and the release slips one week. Option B: they migrate in Q4, and we keep Selenium Grid for one more quarter at [cost]."

Term

A short written note with options, costs and a recommendation. Share it with the team first, so there is no surprise.

Follow-up questions

  • What if their reason is just "we like Selenium"?

    Then I focus on outcomes, not tools. I show their maintenance time and flaky rate. I also make clear the Selenium path will lose shared support after a published date, so the cost of staying grows.

  • They are influential and other teams follow them. Does that change your approach?

    Yes. I spend more time with them, because if they agree, others follow. I ask them to help shape the migration tooling, so it becomes their success too.

  • Would you ask your manager to force it?

    Not as a first step. A forced migration gives poor quality and lost trust. I escalate only when the trade-off is real, and then I frame it as a decision for leaders.

Caution
  • Some candidates say "I would escalate to their manager" as the first step. That shows no influence skills.
  • Some candidates argue with general claims such as "Playwright is better". The team needs evidence about its own work.
  • Some candidates give a permanent exception. Then the platform must support two stacks forever.
Staff signal

A Staff engineer changes the incentives and lowers the cost for the team, and uses escalation only as a clear, shared decision.

Watch

  • Being Glue | Tanya Reilly | athenahealth Tech TalkathenahealthInfluence without authority; the non-coding work of senior ICs.
UKG-L2

Interviewer

Every framework change needs your review, and 20 teams are waiting on you. How do you fix this?

What this tests The interviewer tests if you scale yourself through systems and people instead of more effort.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

I replace my review with written standards and automated checks such as lint and CI. Big changes go through a short RFC or ADR process, so decisions do not depend on me. I spread ownership with CODEOWNERS across trusted contributors and mentor them into reviewers. I also add extension points, so most teams do not need core changes at all.

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. Find out what I really review

    Look at the last 50 reviews. Group them: style, correctness, API design, risk. Most are usually small and repeatable, so a tool or a document can handle them.

  2. 2. Turn rules into automation

    Write the standards down. Turn the repeatable ones into lint rules, type checks, tests and CI gates. Then a pull request gets fast feedback without me.

  3. 3. Use a light RFC or ADR process for big changes

    A short template: problem, options, decision, consequences. Review happens in writing, with a time limit. Recorded decisions mean people do not need to ask me again.

  4. 4. Spread ownership

    Set CODEOWNERS by area, with two or more owners each. Choose trusted contributors from other teams. Pair-review with them at first, then let them review alone.

  5. 5. Remove the need for core changes

    Add extension points such as plugins, custom fixtures and reporters. Teams can then build what they need in their own repos.

  6. 6. Measure the result

    Track review wait time and the share of reviews that I do. My target is to review only the high-risk changes.

Concepts you must own 6

Documented standards plus automated checks
Idea

Write the rules once, and let tools apply them to every change.

Example

A lint rule blocks page.waitForTimeout() in shared code. A person no longer needs to comment on it.

Term

Use ESLint with custom rules, TypeScript strict mode, unit tests and CI required checks. Keep human review for design and risk.

RFC and ADR process
Idea

An RFC asks for feedback on a proposal. An ADR records the final decision and why.

Example

RFC-012 proposes a new retry policy. After a week of comments, ADR-012 records the decision.

Term

Keep templates short. Store them in the repo. Set a review deadline and a named decider.

Contribution model
Idea

A clear path for other teams to change the framework.

Example

CONTRIBUTING.md explains how to propose, build, test and release a change.

Term

This is inner source: open code, documented process, maintainers who help contributors.

CODEOWNERS across trusted contributors
Idea

CODEOWNERS says who must review changes to each part of the code.

Example

/packages/api-client/ @ukg/api-test-maintainers lists four people from three teams.

Term

A GitHub CODEOWNERS file with branch protection makes their review required. Use teams, not single people.

Extension points so teams do not need core changes
Idea

Give teams safe places to add behavior without editing the core.

Example

A team adds its own reporter plugin. The core team never reviews it.

Term

Plugin interfaces, fixture extension, config hooks and a registry. Document the contract and keep it stable.

Mentoring others into reviewers
Idea

Teach other engineers to review as well as you do.

Example

For one month, a new reviewer reviews first and I review their review.

Term

Shadow, then pair, then review alone. Write a review checklist. Thank and recognize reviewers in public.

Follow-up questions

  • How do you keep quality when others review?

    The automated checks keep a quality floor. The checklist and the ADRs give shared judgment. I still review the high-risk areas, and I sample other reviews for a while.

  • What if nobody wants to be a reviewer?

    I make it visible and valued: recognition, a line in their growth plan, and a fair rotation. I also make reviews easier with small PRs and good automation.

  • How do you decide which changes still need your review?

    I keep review for changes with high risk or wide effect, such as public APIs, defaults and security. CODEOWNERS points those paths to a small senior group. Everything else goes to area owners.

Caution
  • Some candidates say "I would work longer hours". That does not scale and burns out the reviewer.
  • Some candidates remove review entirely. Quality then drops, and teams lose trust in the framework.
  • Some candidates add more process for every change. Small changes then wait as long as big ones.
Staff signal

A Staff engineer measures success by how much the system can do without them, through automation, written decisions and new reviewers.

Watch

  • Technical leadership and glue work - Tanya Reilly | #LeadDevNewYorkLeadDevScaling yourself through others instead of gatekeeping.
UKG-L3

Interviewer

A Principal engineer wants to build a fully custom in-house framework. You think Playwright plus a thin layer is better. How do you handle it?

What this tests The interviewer tests if you can disagree with a senior person using evidence and still keep the relationship.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

I move the discussion from opinions to criteria: maintenance cost, hiring, ecosystem and time to value. I ask what problem the Principal wants the custom framework to solve, because there may be a real need. Then I propose a short spike to test both options on a real suite. I write a trade-off document with the results. When the decision is made, I commit to it fully, even if it is not my option.

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. Understand the goal

    Ask what the custom framework must do that Playwright cannot. Maybe it is control over the roadmap, a special protocol or a security rule. That need may be real, and it changes the design.

  2. 2. Agree on criteria first

    Agree on the criteria before the options: maintenance cost, hiring and onboarding, ecosystem, time to value, and risk. When people agree on criteria, the decision often becomes clear.

  3. 3. Get evidence

    Propose a time-boxed spike, for example two weeks. Build the hardest real scenario both ways. Measure effort, stability and debugging time.

  4. 4. Write the trade-off document

    Show the options, the evidence, the costs and the risks, including the risks of my own option. Share it with the Principal first, then with the wider group.

  5. 5. Disagree and commit

    When the decider decides, I support the decision in public and in my work. If new evidence appears later, I bring it back through the same process.

  6. 6. Keep the relationship

    Talk in private before public meetings. Give credit for good points. The goal is the best result for the teams, not winning.

Concepts you must own 8

Frame by criteria
Idea

Compare options with a shared list of what matters, not by personal preference.

Example

Criteria: maintenance cost, hiring, ecosystem, time to value. Each option gets a score with evidence.

Term

A weighted decision matrix. Agree on criteria and weights before you score the options.

Maintenance cost
Idea

The cost to keep a framework working over years, not only to build it.

Example

A custom framework needs a team to fix browser changes, write docs and support users forever.

Term

Total cost of ownership: build, maintain, support, upgrade, and the opportunity cost of what the team does not build.

Hiring and ecosystem
Idea

Popular tools are easier to hire for, and have plugins, answers and community fixes.

Example

New hires know Playwright already. Nobody knows an in-house tool on day one.

Term

Consider the community size, release activity, docs, plugins and the learning curve for new engineers.

Time to value
Idea

How soon teams get a real benefit.

Example

Playwright plus fixtures helps teams in weeks. A custom framework needs months before the first team uses it.

Term

Plan in increments that deliver value early. Long, all-or-nothing builds carry high risk.

Prototype or spike to resolve with evidence
Idea

A short experiment answers the question better than a long debate.

Example

Two engineers build the hardest login and data scenario in both approaches in two weeks.

Term

Set the goal, the time box and the success measures before the spike starts.

Trade-off document
Idea

A short written comparison of options, costs and risks, with a recommendation.

Example

Four pages: context, criteria, options, evidence from the spike, recommendation, and open risks.

Term

Also called a design doc or decision doc. It leads to an ADR that records the final decision.

Disagree and commit
Idea

After the decision, support it fully even if you argued for another option.

Example

The group picks the custom route for one module. I help build it well.

Term

Commit in action and in public. Raise new evidence through the agreed process, not through quiet resistance.

Keep the relationship
Idea

You will work with this person for years. Protect trust.

Example

I share my document with the Principal first and ask for feedback before the group meeting.

Term

Disagree in private first, give credit in public, and focus on ideas, not people.

Follow-up questions

  • What if the spike shows that the Principal is right?

    Then I support the custom approach and say so openly. The goal is the best decision, and the spike did its job.

  • What if the Principal refuses a spike and just decides?

    I write my concerns down once, with the risks and how we would notice them. Then I commit. I suggest checkpoints to review the decision with data.

  • How do you keep this from becoming personal?

    I talk about criteria and evidence, not about who is right. I meet the Principal one-to-one before any group meeting. I also say clearly which of their points are strong.

Caution
  • Some candidates say they would go to the manager to overrule the Principal. That damages trust.
  • Some candidates say they would just follow the Principal. A Staff engineer is expected to give an independent view.
  • Some candidates argue only for their own option. A fair document also shows the weak points of your option.
Staff signal

A Staff engineer turns a disagreement into a decision process with criteria, evidence and a written record, and commits once it is decided.

Watch

  • LeadDev Bookmarked - The Staff Engineer’s Path: Tanya Reilly in conversationLeadDevStaff-level judgement, disagreement, and big-picture thinking.
UKG-L4

Interviewer

It is 6 PM before a launch. The automation suite is red and blocks the release. Product wants you to skip the failing suite. What do you do?

What this tests The interviewer tests if you can make a fast, risk-based call with the right people and a clear process.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

I triage fast: is it a real bug, a flaky test, or an infra problem? Traces, failure history and a re-run on the same build usually tell me in 15 minutes. I do not make the call alone. I bring the risk to the release owner and the engineering owner, and we use the documented override policy with sign-off. Known-flaky tests go into quarantine with a ticket. After the launch, we hold a postmortem and fix the cause.

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. Triage fast

    Look at which tests fail and why. Check the failure history: did these tests fail before on green builds? Check infra: runner, grid, environment health. Re-run the failed tests one time on the same build.

  2. 2. Classify
    • Real bug: the release waits, or the feature is turned off with a flag.
    • Flaky test: known flaky, with history. It can be quarantined.
    • Infra: fix or re-run on healthy infra.
  3. 3. Make a risk-based call with owners

    Bring the facts to the release owner and the engineering owner of the area. Explain what the failing tests cover and what the risk is. The owners decide, using the override policy.

  4. 4. Follow the override policy

    An override needs named sign-off, a written reason and a follow-up ticket. Add manual checks for the uncovered area if needed. Record it, so it is visible later.

  5. 5. Quarantine, do not delete

    Move known-flaky tests to a quarantine list with an owner and a due date. They still run and report, but they do not block.

  6. 6. Learn

    Hold a short postmortem after the launch. Fix the root cause, and check why the problem appeared so late in the cycle.

Concepts you must own 6

Triage fast: real bug vs flaky vs infra
Idea

Find out quickly what kind of failure it is, because each kind needs a different action.

Example

The failing test passed 50 times on the last builds and fails only on one runner. That points to infra.

Term

Use traces, failure history, the triage service groups and a single re-run. Timebox the triage, for example to 30 minutes.

Risk-based call with owners, not alone
Idea

The decision belongs to the people who own the risk.

Example

The payments owner decides with the release manager. I give them the facts.

Term

Present what the tests cover, what is unknown, the options and your recommendation. The release owner signs the decision.

Documented override policy with sign-off
Idea

A written rule says when and how a red suite can be overridden, and who must approve.

Example

Override needs approval from the release manager and the area tech lead, plus a ticket.

Term

Agree the policy in calm times, not at 6 PM. Technically, this can be a GitHub environment with required reviewers.

Quarantine mechanism for known-flaky tests
Idea

A quarantine list holds tests that still run but cannot block a release.

Example

checkout.retry.spec.ts is in quarantine with owner Team B, due in 2 weeks.

Term

A config file or tag (@quarantine) read by the runner. Each entry has an owner, ticket and expiry. Report the quarantine size as a metric.

Postmortem
Idea

A blameless review after an incident to learn and improve.

Example

The team finds that the environment was refreshed at 5 PM, which broke test data.

Term

Write the timeline, impact, root cause and actions with owners. Focus on the system, not on people.

Prevent recurrence
Idea

Make changes so the same situation does not happen again.

Example

Run the full suite on the release branch two days before launch, not on the last day.

Term

Actions can include earlier test stages, better test data, flaky budgets and a freeze on environment changes before launches.

Follow-up questions

  • Product insists, and the owners are not reachable. What do you do?

    I do not approve the override alone if the policy names someone else. I give Product the facts and the risk in writing and follow the escalation path. Often a feature flag can turn off the risky part, so the rest can ship.

  • What if it is a real bug?

    Then the release waits, or the feature is turned off with a flag. The test did its job. I make that clear to everyone.

  • How do you stop a quarantine list from growing forever?

    Each entry has an owner, a ticket and an expiry date. An expired entry blocks again, or the owner must renew it with a reason. I report the quarantine size as a platform metric.

Caution
  • Some candidates skip the suite to help Product. That removes the safety net without an owner's decision.
  • Some candidates refuse every override. That ignores real cases of flaky or infra failures and blocks the business.
  • Some candidates delete the flaky test. That loses coverage and hides the problem.
Staff signal

A Staff engineer gives clear facts fast, lets the right owners decide under a known policy, and fixes the system afterwards.

UKG-L5

Interviewer

How do you measure the success of the framework, or justify headcount for the platform team?

What this tests The interviewer tests if you connect engineering work to business outcomes with honest metrics.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

I use outcome metrics, not output metrics. Outcomes are developer time saved, escaped defects, CI time, flaky rate trend and adoption. I set a baseline before the change, so I can show the difference. Then I connect the numbers to developer productivity and release frequency, which leaders care about. For headcount, I show the cost of the problem and the value per engineer.

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. Choose outcomes, not outputs

    Outputs are things we made: features, tests, docs. Outcomes are what changed for teams: less waiting, fewer flaky failures, fewer escaped bugs. Leaders fund outcomes.

  2. 2. Set a baseline first

    Measure the current state before the change: CI time, flaky rate, time to diagnose, maintenance hours. Without a baseline, you cannot prove an improvement.

  3. 3. Measure the change

    Compare after with before, for the same teams. Use pilot teams and compare them with teams that did not adopt yet.

  4. 4. Translate to business terms

    Developer hours saved per month times the number of developers. Faster pipelines mean more releases per week. Fewer escaped defects mean fewer incidents.

  5. 5. Make the headcount case

    Show the current cost of the problem, the gain each platform engineer delivers, and the work that waits. Be honest about what is an estimate.

Concepts you must own 8

Outcome metrics vs output metrics
Idea

An output is what you produce. An outcome is the change that it causes.

Example

Output: "we shipped 12 fixtures". Outcome: "pipeline time fell from 45 to 12 minutes for 40 teams".

Term

Leaders fund outcomes. Use outputs only to explain how you got the outcome.

Time saved
Idea

The developer time that the framework gives back.

Example

Less waiting for CI and less time on flaky failures saves [your number] hours per developer per month.

Term

Estimate with: wait time saved per run × runs per day × developers, plus triage time saved. State the method.

Escaped defects
Idea

Bugs that reach production even though tests exist.

Example

Escaped defects in the payroll area fell from 6 per quarter to 2 after the new API layer.

Term

Link incidents to product areas and test coverage. Track the trend, not a single month.

CI time
Idea

How long developers wait for pipeline feedback.

Example

The p90 PR pipeline time went from 45 minutes to 10 minutes.

Term

Use p50 and p90 from the CI data. Shorter feedback loops increase deployment frequency.

Flaky rate trend
Idea

The share of results that change without a code change, over time.

Example

The flaky rate fell from 6% to 1.5% in two quarters.

Term

Flaky = fail-then-pass on the same commit. A falling trend means more trust in red builds.

Adoption
Idea

How many teams use the framework and its current version.

Example

160 of 200 teams are on the shared workflow, 140 on the current major version.

Term

Adoption by choice is strong evidence of value. Track it from lockfiles and reporter metadata.

Baseline before change
Idea

Measure where you start, so you can prove where you end.

Example

Before the migration: 45 minutes CI, 7% flaky rate. These are the baseline numbers.

Term

Record the baseline, the date and the method. Keep the method the same for later measurements.

Tie to developer productivity and release frequency
Idea

Connect your metrics to what the business cares about.

Example

Faster CI and fewer flaky failures let teams release twice a week instead of once.

Term

DORA metrics (deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate, time to restore) are a common shared language.

Follow-up questions

  • What if you have no baseline because nobody measured before?

    I collect the best proxy data now, for example from logs and git history. I start measuring today, and I label early numbers as estimates.

  • How do you avoid gaming the metrics?

    Use several metrics that balance each other, such as CI time together with escaped defects. Fast CI with more escaped bugs is not success.

  • How do you justify one more platform engineer?

    I show the current cost of the problem in developer hours, and the gain that one engineer gave last quarter. I also list the work that waits, with its expected value. I label every estimate as an estimate.

Caution
  • Some candidates report the number of tests or features built. That shows effort, not value.
  • Some candidates claim big savings with no baseline. Leaders do not trust numbers without a method.
  • Some candidates use one metric only. One metric is easy to game and hides side effects.
Staff signal

A Staff engineer sets a baseline before the work, measures outcomes honestly, and speaks in the language of business impact.

  • Will Larson Reflects on Staff EngineerBook OverflowStaff archetypes and showing impact.
UKG-L6

Interviewer

Fifteen teams each wrote their own login, retry and test-data helpers. How do you fix the duplication?

What this tests The interviewer tests if you can consolidate shared code without forcing a bad abstraction on everyone.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

First I take an inventory of the 15 versions and find the common 80%. I upstream that common part into the framework, with the best ideas from the teams. Then teams move gradually: the old copies get a deprecation note, and we help with the switch. I give an inner-source path for teams to add what they need. I avoid a giant abstraction that tries to fit every case and fits nobody.

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. Inventory

    Search the repos for login, retry and data helpers. List each version, its features and its users. Talk to the owners about why they built it.

  2. 2. Find the common 80%

    Most helpers do the same core work. Pick the best design from the team versions, and give credit to the teams.

  3. 3. Upstream it

    Build the shared version in the framework, with tests and docs. Keep it small and clear. Use extension points for the special cases.

  4. 4. Deprecate local copies gradually

    Mark local copies as deprecated, with a link to the shared helper. Offer codemods or pairing. Track the number of local copies on a dashboard.

  5. 5. Open an inner-source path

    Teams can propose changes to the shared helpers through pull requests. This stops new copies from growing.

  6. 6. Avoid the giant abstraction

    Do not try to cover every case in one helper with 30 options. Cover the common case well and let teams extend for the rest.

Concepts you must own 6

Inventory
Idea

Find and list every version that exists before you design anything.

Example

A code search finds 15 login helpers, 9 retry helpers and 12 data factories.

Term

Use GitHub code search, a dependency graph or a short survey. Record features, users and owners.

Find the common 80%
Idea

Most of the needs are the same. Solve those first.

Example

12 of 15 login helpers use the same SSO flow with a role. Only 3 have special needs.

Term

Pareto principle. Design for the common path, and give hooks for the long tail.

Upstream into the framework
Idea

Move the shared code into the central framework, with tests and an owner.

Example

loginAs(role) lands in @ukg/test-core 4.7 with docs and examples.

Term

Upstreamed code follows SemVer, has an owner and is covered by the framework CI and canary consumers.

Deprecate local copies gradually
Idea

Move teams one by one, with help and a timeline, not all at once.

Example

A lint rule warns when a test imports the local login helper. Teams switch over two months.

Term

Use warnings, codemods, a dashboard and a target date. Remove support for old patterns only after most teams move.

Inner-source contribution path
Idea

Teams can change the shared code through a clear, open process.

Example

Team C adds MFA support to loginAs with a pull request and a review from the maintainers.

Term

Inner source applies open-source practices inside a company: open repo, CONTRIBUTING guide, maintainers and timely reviews.

Avoid a giant abstraction that fits nobody
Idea

One helper that tries to do everything becomes hard to use and hard to change.

Example

A doLogin(options) with 30 flags is worse than 15 copies, because nobody understands it.

Term

Prefer small, composable helpers and extension points. Duplication is cheaper than the wrong abstraction.

Follow-up questions

  • A team says its helper is better than yours. What do you do?

    If it is better, I take its design into the shared version and credit the team. The goal is one good helper, not my helper.

  • How do you stop new copies from appearing?

    Make the shared helper easy to find and easy to extend. Add a lint rule that warns on new local copies. Answer contribution PRs fast, so teams prefer to contribute.

  • When is duplication acceptable?

    When the needs are truly different, or when the helper is small and stable. A shared helper also has a cost: versions, reviews and coupling. I share code when the common part is large and changes often.

Caution
  • Some candidates design a new helper alone and force it on all teams. They lose the teams' knowledge and their support.
  • Some candidates try to support every special case in the core. The result is complex and fragile.
  • Some candidates delete local copies at once. Many test suites break on the same day.
Staff signal

A Staff engineer turns 15 local efforts into one shared asset that teams feel they own. It stays small and has a path to extend it.

UKG-L7

Interviewer

Tell me about a time you owned a framework, drove a CI change, ran an experiment, fixed a hard problem, influenced without authority, or made a mistake.

What this tests The interviewer tests if your real experience shows Staff-level scope, judgment and ownership.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

Use STAR: situation, task, action, result. Then add the Staff framing: scope, your decision, the trade-off, the measurable result, and what you would do differently. Keep each story to about two minutes. Use only true facts, and fill each [your number] before the interview. Say the Selenium transparency line when Selenium comes up.

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. Use the structure
    • Situation: one or two sentences of context.
    • Task: what you owned.
    • Action: what you decided and did. Say "I", not "we", for your part.
    • Result: a measurable result.
    • Staff framing and what you would do differently.
  2. 2. Be exact about scope

    Say clearly what you owned and what you contributed to. For the CI migration, you contributed; you did not own all CI/CD infrastructure. Honest scope builds trust.

  3. 3. Fill in your numbers

    Every place that says [your number] needs a real value from your memory. If you do not know a number, give a range or say it was not measured. Do not invent it.

  4. 4. Say the transparency line

    "My Selenium experience is more limited, but I have substantial experience designing and owning E2E automation frameworks, particularly with Cypress, and the underlying framework concepts transfer."

  5. 5. Map stories to questions

    One story can answer several questions. Prepare the 5 stories below and know which question each one fits.

Your stories (fill every placeholder first)

Owning the Joyent Cypress E2E framework

Use for Framework ownership; technical leadership; design questions D1, D3, D4.

Situation

At Joyent (a Samsung company), we built a private-cloud console on Samsung SPC and AWS. The UI needed reliable end-to-end tests across many features.

Task

I owned a significant part of the Cypress E2E automation. This included the shared layer that other engineers used to write tests.

Action
  • I built custom commands and helpers, and custom queries, so tests read at a high level.
  • I set the selector strategy, so tests did not break on layout changes.
  • I added tagging and filtering, so CI could run the correct subset of tests.
  • I managed the config, test data, cleanup and visual regression checks.
Result

The framework gave the team one shared way to write tests. Add your real result here: [your number] tests or engineers, and [your number] for time saved or flaky rate change.

Staff framing

I treated the framework as a product for other engineers, with shared commands, conventions and filtering. Name the scope: [your number] engineers or teams used it.

Do differently

I would add usage and flaky-rate metrics from the start, so I could show the value with data and decide priorities faster.

Isolated tests that create real cloud resources

Use for Hard technical problem; test data design (D4); debugging.

Situation

Our E2E tests created real cloud resources, such as compute instances. Then they validated those resources. When tests ran together or failed, resources collided or were left behind.

Task

I needed tests to be isolated and repeatable, even when a run failed in the middle.

Action
  • I gave each test unique data, so two runs did not use the same resources.
  • I added cleanup after each test to delete what the test created.
  • For runs that crashed, I sometimes ran a startup cleanup that removed stale resources from earlier failed runs.
Result

Tests stayed isolated, and stale resources from failed runs were removed. Add [your number] for the drop in collisions or failures, if you know it.

Staff framing

The decision was to design for failure. A crashed test never runs its teardown, so the startup sweep was the safety net. This is the same pattern that a shared platform needs for hundreds of teams.

Do differently

I would make the cleanup fully idempotent and automatic from the start, with a scheduled sweep, so it did not depend on a manual run.

Contributing to the Jenkins to GitHub Actions migration

Use for CI/CD experience; GitHub Actions questions; working across teams.

Situation

Joyent moved its CI/CD from Jenkins to GitHub Actions.

Task

I contributed to the migration, mainly the E2E integration and the runner and build setup. I did not own all CI/CD infrastructure.

Action
  • I moved the E2E test stages into GitHub Actions workflows.
  • I helped with the runner and build setup for the test jobs.
  • I worked with the engineers who owned the CI/CD infrastructure.
Result

The E2E tests ran in GitHub Actions as part of the pipeline. Add [your number] if you know the pipeline time or another result.

Staff framing

I made E2E a first-class part of the new pipeline, not an afterthought. I also learned how CI changes affect every developer, which is the daily reality of this UKG team.

Do differently

I would push earlier for shared, reusable workflows, so each repo did not keep its own copy. That is how I would design it at UKG.

LLM-based CI failure-analysis experiment

Use for Innovation; failure triage (D6); influencing without authority.

Situation

CI failures took engineers a long time to understand. Many failures had the same cause but looked different.

Task

I chose to test if an LLM could help analyze CI failures and suggest fixes.

Action
  • I built an experiment that sent CI failure data to an LLM for analysis.
  • The experiment also tried self-healing: the LLM suggested a fix for the failure.
  • [Add one real detail: what input you gave it, and who saw the results.]
Result

The experiment showed where an LLM helps and where it does not. Add [your number] or one real example of a failure that it explained well.

Staff framing

I ran a small, cheap experiment to answer a question with evidence, before anyone invested in a full tool. It also showed others a new way to work, without a mandate.

Do differently

I would first normalize and group the failures, and give the LLM only clean data. I would also measure the accuracy of its suggestions.

Supporting QA and Selenium automation at ADP

Use for Selenium question; transparency; supporting other teams.

Situation

At ADP, the QA team used Selenium automation for the apps that I worked on.

Task

I supported the QA team and their Selenium automation. I was not the primary owner of the Selenium framework.

Action
  • I supported the QA engineers with their Selenium automation.
  • [Add one or two real examples of the support that you gave.]
Result

[Add the real result of your support, or a real example. Keep it small and true.]

Staff framing

Say the transparency line here. "My Selenium experience is more limited, but I have substantial experience designing and owning E2E automation frameworks, particularly with Cypress, and the underlying framework concepts transfer."

Do differently

[Add a real lesson. If you have none, say what you would now do: for example, agree stable test IDs with QA as a team standard.]

Concepts you must own 6

STAR
Idea

A simple order for a behavioral answer: Situation, Task, Action, Result.

Example

Situation: tests left cloud resources behind. Task: make tests isolated. Action: unique data and cleanup. Result: fewer collisions.

Term

Keep Situation and Task short. Spend most of the time on Action and Result.

Staff framing: scope
Idea

Show how far the effect of your work reached.

Example

"The Cypress framework was used by [your number] engineers across [your number] teams."

Term

Scope beyond your own team is the main difference between Senior and Staff stories.

Staff framing: your decision
Idea

Show a choice that you made, not only tasks that you did.

Example

"I decided to create test data through the API instead of the UI."

Term

Name the options that you considered and why you chose one.

Staff framing: trade-off
Idea

Show what you gave up to get what you wanted.

Example

"Unique data per test cost more setup time, but it removed collisions between parallel runs."

Term

Every real decision has a cost. Naming it shows judgment.

Staff framing: measurable result
Idea

Give a number that shows the effect.

Example

"Flaky failures went from [your number] to [your number] per week."

Term

Use real numbers or honest ranges. If you did not measure, say what you would measure now.

What you would do differently
Idea

Show that you learn from your own work.

Example

"I would have added metrics from day one, so I could show the gain to leaders."

Term

Pick a real lesson that changed how you work. It shows growth, not weakness.

Follow-up questions

  • Tell me about a mistake.

    Use the "what I would do differently" line from the Cypress or cleanup story. Say what happened, what you changed, and how you work now. Keep it real and short.

  • How did you influence people who did not report to you?

    Use the LLM experiment or the Cypress framework story. Explain that you showed value with a working example and made the shared way easier than the old way.

  • What was your exact role in the GitHub Actions migration?

    Be exact: you contributed the E2E integration and parts of the runner and build setup. Other engineers owned the overall CI/CD infrastructure.

Caution
  • Some candidates say "we" for everything. The interviewer cannot see what you did yourself.
  • Some candidates invent numbers. If the interviewer asks one more question, the story falls apart.
  • Some candidates claim ownership of work they only contributed to. Exact scope is more credible.
  • Some candidates tell long stories with no result. End every story with a result and a lesson.
Staff signal

A Staff story shows a decision with a trade-off and an effect beyond your own work, and an honest lesson that changed how you work.

Chapter 06

Capstone: the whole platform

This question joins all other sections. Start with requirements, walk through the components in the order of a test run, and end with security, cost and adoption.
