UKG-C1

Interviewer

Design the full test platform on AWS for 200 teams: GitHub Actions orchestration, test runners on EKS, framework distribution and versioning, the results pipeline, observability, cost controls, security with OIDC, IRSA and secrets, the rollout plan, and how you get teams to adopt it.

What this tests The interviewer tests if you can connect every part into one coherent platform, with clear trade-offs and a realistic adoption plan.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

Teams add one small caller file that uses a versioned reusable workflow. The workflow runs fast checks on ephemeral ARC runners inside the VPC. It sends browser shards to an SQS queue, and KEDA and Karpenter scale Playwright workers on Spot nodes in EKS. The framework ships as versioned packages and images, and Renovate keeps teams current. Results flow to a central store that feeds triage, Grafana dashboards and Slack alerts on state change. Security uses OIDC from GitHub, Pod Identity in EKS and no long-lived keys, and I roll out with pilot teams over 90 days.

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. Clarify requirements first

    Ask and state assumptions:

    • 200 teams, a mix of Selenium today and Playwright tomorrow, plus API tests.
    • Peak of about 2,000 parallel browser sessions at 9 AM, near zero at night.
    • Test environments live in private VPCs.
    • Goals: PR feedback under 10 minutes, flaky rate down, cost visible per team.
    • Constraints: security review, existing Jenkins or Selenium suites, team autonomy.
  2. 2. Orchestration with GitHub Actions

    A platform repo holds reusable workflows (on: workflow_call) and composite actions, released with SemVer tags. Teams keep an 8-line caller file. An org ruleset requires the shared workflow on protected branches. Tiers: smoke on PR, full suite on merge, cross-browser nightly. Concurrency groups cancel old runs on the same PR.

  3. 3. Runners and execution on EKS

    Two layers of compute:

    • CI runners: Actions Runner Controller with runner scale sets in the VPC. Each job gets an ephemeral runner pod.
    • Browser farm: the runner splits the suite into shards and puts them on an SQS queue. A KEDA ScaledJob creates one Playwright Job per shard. Selenium Grid 4 runs beside it during the migration.

    Karpenter adds Spot nodes in a tainted browsers NodePool with a CPU limit. Each team has a namespace with a ResourceQuota.

  4. 4. Framework distribution and versioning
    • @ukg/test-core: Playwright fixtures, test data builders, loginAs, reporters.
    • @ukg/test-api: the API client with REST, SOAP and GraphQL adapters.
    • A worker image with pinned browsers, tagged with the framework version and commit SHA.

    Packages live in a private registry such as CodeArtifact or GitHub Packages. SemVer, deprecation windows, canary consumers for each RC, and Renovate PRs keep teams current.

  5. 5. Results pipeline

    Each worker writes JUnit, a JSON summary and traces. Large files go to S3 with lifecycle rules. The summary goes to a results ingest API, which puts it on a queue. Workers normalize failures, fingerprint them, group them and store them in PostgreSQL. The CI job reads the final status and writes a job summary.

  6. 6. Observability and cost controls

    Grafana dashboards per audience: flaky rate, pipeline time p50 and p90, queue time, failure classes, adoption and version spread. Prometheus and Container Insights watch the cluster: Pending pods, node pressure and free subnet IPs. Slack alerts go out only on state change and new failure groups. The platform has its own SLOs, for example queue time under 2 minutes at p90. Cost controls:

    • Scale to zero overnight with KEDA and Karpenter consolidation.
    • Spot for retryable test shards, On-Demand for shared services.
    • NodePool limits and per-team quotas as hard ceilings.
    • Test impact selection so a PR runs only the affected tests.
    • Cost per team from pod labels and AWS split cost allocation data, shown on the dashboard.
  7. 7. Security
    • GitHub to AWS: OIDC with id-token: write and trust policies scoped to repo, branch or environment.
    • Pods to AWS: EKS Pod Identity or IRSA, one role per workload, least privilege.
    • Secrets: AWS Secrets Manager for test credentials, environments with reviewers for anything prod-like.
    • Runners: ephemeral, in runner groups limited to private repos, never for fork PRs.
    • Supply chain: actions pinned to SHAs, signed images, secret scanning and push protection.
  8. 8. Adoption

    Make the platform the easy path: one file to adopt, faster runs, better reports and less maintenance. Start with pilot teams and publish their before and after numbers. Offer migration tooling, office hours and pairing. Track adoption on a dashboard, and agree exceptions with end dates.

Components

  • Product team repo: an 8-line caller workflow that uses the shared reusable workflow with a version tag.
  • Platform workflows repo: reusable workflows and composite actions, released with SemVer tags, owned by the platform team.
  • GitHub organization: rulesets that require the shared workflow, runner groups, org secrets, and secret scanning.
  • AWS IAM OIDC provider: trusts GitHub tokens. Roles are scoped by repo, branch or environment.
  • Amazon EKS cluster in a private VPC, with these parts:
  • ARC controller and runner scale sets: ephemeral CI runner pods in namespace arc-runners.
  • Amazon SQS shard queue, with a dead-letter queue.
  • KEDA: scales Playwright worker Jobs on queue length, and Selenium Grid nodes on the grid queue.
  • Browser farm: Playwright worker Jobs and Selenium Grid 4, on a tainted browsers NodePool.
  • Karpenter: NodePools for runners, browsers (Spot first) and platform services (On-Demand).
  • Team namespaces: ResourceQuota, LimitRange and labels for cost.
  • Platform services: results ingest API, triage workers, and the results UI, behind an internal ALB.
  • EKS Pod Identity: one IAM role per workload, for SQS, S3 and Secrets Manager access.
  • Amazon ECR: worker and service images, with tag immutability and image scanning.
  • Package registry (CodeArtifact or GitHub Packages): @ukg/test-core and @ukg/test-api.
  • Amazon S3: traces, videos and raw reports, with lifecycle rules.
  • Results queue (SQS) and PostgreSQL (Amazon RDS): test results, failure groups and known-issue links.
  • AWS Secrets Manager: test-account credentials, synced to pods.
  • Observability: Prometheus, Container Insights and Grafana dashboards and alerts.
  • Slack app: posts to team channels on state change and new failure groups.
  • Renovate: opens framework upgrade PRs in consumer repos.
  • Cost reporting: AWS split cost allocation data for EKS, or Kubecost, by team label.

Data flow

  1. A developer opens a PR. The caller workflow starts the shared reusable workflow at @v3.
  2. GitHub assigns the job to the e2e-private runner scale set. ARC creates an ephemeral runner pod in EKS.
  3. The job gets an OIDC token. AWS STS returns short-lived credentials for the submit role.
  4. The job runs lint, unit and API tests on the runner pod.
  5. The job splits the E2E suite into shards and sends one SQS message per shard.
  6. KEDA sees the queue length and creates one Playwright worker Job per shard.
  7. Pending worker pods trigger Karpenter. It starts Spot nodes in the browsers NodePool.
  8. Each worker pulls its image from ECR, gets test credentials from Secrets Manager through Pod Identity, and runs its shard against the private test environment.
  9. Each worker uploads traces and reports to S3 and posts a JSON summary to the results ingest API.
  10. The ingest API puts the summary on the results queue. Triage workers normalize, fingerprint and group failures, and write to PostgreSQL.
  11. The CI job polls the results API until all shards finish. Then it writes the job summary and passes or fails the check.
  12. The results service compares the state with the last run. On a change or a new failure group, the Slack app posts to the team channel.
  13. Grafana reads PostgreSQL and Prometheus for the dashboards. Alerts fire on trend changes and on platform SLO breaches.
  14. After the peak, KEDA scales workers to zero and Karpenter removes empty nodes.
  15. When the framework releases a new version, canary consumer suites run first, then Renovate opens upgrade PRs in all repos.

30-60-90 day rollout

Days 0–30
  • Listen first: interview 8 to 10 teams about their pain, and collect baseline numbers (pipeline time, flaky rate, cost).
  • Write a short RFC for the platform design and review it with the Principal engineers and security.
  • Build the minimum path: one reusable workflow, ARC runners in the VPC, OIDC roles, and the results ingest to S3 and PostgreSQL.
  • Onboard 2 or 3 pilot teams that volunteer, including one Selenium team and one Playwright team.
  • Exit criteria: pilots run on the platform with PR feedback under the target and no security findings.
Days 31–60
  • Add the browser farm: SQS shards, KEDA ScaledJob, Karpenter Spot NodePool and Selenium Grid for existing suites.
  • Add the triage service, Grafana dashboards and Slack notifications on state change.
  • Publish @ukg/test-core and @ukg/test-api with SemVer, docs and a migration guide.
  • Expand to about 20 teams in waves, with automated PRs and office hours.
  • Publish the pilot before and after numbers.
  • Exit criteria: platform SLOs met for 2 weeks, cost per team visible, pilot teams would recommend it.
Days 61–90
  • Open self-service onboarding for all teams, with a template repo and a one-command setup.
  • Turn on the org ruleset for the shared workflow on protected branches, with announced dates.
  • Start the Selenium-to-Playwright migration program: cutover date, triage data and LLM-assisted conversion with validation.
  • Grow the contributor model: CODEOWNERS across teams, the RFC process and extension points.
  • Report to leadership with outcome metrics against the baseline, and set the next quarter's goals.

Concepts you must own 6

Platform as a product
Idea

Treat the test platform like a product with users, a roadmap and support.

Example

The platform team runs office hours, publishes a changelog and measures adoption and satisfaction.

Term

Platform engineering creates paved roads: a supported default path that is easier than building your own.

Control plane vs data plane of the test platform
Idea

Separate the parts that decide (orchestration, config) from the parts that do the work (runners, browsers).

Example

GitHub Actions and the shared workflows decide. EKS runner and browser pods execute.

Term

This split lets each part scale and fail separately. A browser farm outage does not change workflow config.

Queue-based sharding
Idea

Put the units of work on a queue, and let workers take them when they are free.

Example

200 shards go on SQS. 200 Jobs start, and a lost Spot node's shard returns to the queue.

Term

The queue gives buffering, retries, a DLQ and a clear scaling signal for KEDA. Use the visibility timeout to return unfinished shards.

Multi-tenancy for 200 teams
Idea

Many teams share one platform, but they must not hurt each other.

Example

Each team has a namespace with quotas, its own cost line and its own Slack channel.

Term

Namespaces, ResourceQuota, LimitRange, PriorityClass, dedicated NodePools and per-team IAM scoping. Consider separate clusters only for strong isolation needs.

Platform SLOs
Idea

Promises that the platform makes to its users, with numbers.

Example

"p90 queue time under 2 minutes" and "infra-caused failures under 0.5% of runs".

Term

SLO = a target on an SLI (a measured indicator). An error budget tells the team when to stop features and fix reliability.

30-60-90 day rollout
Idea

Deliver value in steps with a check at each step, not one big launch.

Example

Day 30: pilot with 3 teams. Day 60: 20 teams. Day 90: open to all, with self-service.

Term

Each phase has exit criteria. Measure before the change, so you can prove the gain.

Code to know

Follow-up questions

  • Why not run the browsers on the CI runners directly?

    For small suites, that is fine, and the shared workflow allows it. For 2,000 sessions, a separate browser farm scales on its own signal, uses Spot, and keeps CI runners small and cheap.

  • What breaks first at 10 times the load?

    Likely the subnet IPs and the GitHub API rate limits, then the results database writes. I would plan prefix delegation and larger subnets, use a GitHub App with higher limits, and batch the result writes.

  • One cluster or many?

    One cluster per environment tier is simpler to start, with namespaces per team. I would split clusters for a strong isolation need, a different region, or a blast-radius limit.

  • You have no hands-on EKS experience. How would you deliver this?

    I am honest about it. I know the model and the debugging method, and I have learned the core objects for this role. I would pair with the platform engineers who run EKS today and own the framework and adoption parts, where my experience is strongest.

  • How do you avoid building too much before teams use it?

    The first 30 days deliver only the minimum path for pilot teams. Each later part is built because a pilot needs it, and pilot feedback drives the order.

Caution
  • Some candidates start drawing boxes before they ask about scale, constraints and goals.
  • Some candidates design only the technology and forget adoption. A platform that nobody uses has no value.
  • Some candidates use long-lived AWS keys in CI or node roles for app access. Security review stops the design.
  • Some candidates size for the peak with fixed capacity. The cost then stays high all night.
Staff signal

A Staff answer links every component to a goal and a trade-off, and designs for failure, cost and security from the start. It plans adoption as carefully as the technology.

Watch

  • Platform Engineering - Internal Developer Platform Reference ArchitectureVirtual ElephantPlatform layers and golden paths for many teams.
  • Kubernetes CI/CD: Build a Pipeline (ArgoCD + Github Actions)Rayan SlimEnd-to-end CI on Actions, CD to Kubernetes.
Chapter 07

Interviewer's lens: a UKG Sr. Principal Software Engineer

This lens uses the public profile PDF that you supplied. The interviewer is a Sr. Principal Software Engineer at UKG in Noida, with more than 12 years at the company. He started as an automation engineer: Selenium UI frameworks, Sauce Lab runs, API tests and code coverage. He then moved to DevOps and cloud work: Kubernetes, Docker, Terraform, Jenkins, GCP, zero-downtime upgrades and cloud-agnostic design. His top skills are Site Reliability Engineering, technical discussions and architecture. The listed points are inferences from this background. They are not facts about how he interviews. He also told you his focus for this round: basic DevOps, pipelines, GCP, GitHub, Kubernetes, and testing frameworks with Selenium and Playwright. That list is a fact from the interview, not an inference.

What he listens for

Stated focus

He said the round covers basic DevOps, pipelines, GCP, GitHub, Kubernetes, and Selenium and Playwright frameworks. Basic means he checks the fundamentals first. Answer simply and correctly. Then go deeper if he asks.

Test framework depth

He built Selenium frameworks himself. Expect follow-up questions on waits, flakiness, reporting and cost of license tools. A name-drop will not pass. Explain how you built or fixed the part.

Cloud-agnostic design

His mission is solutions that run on more than one cloud. Say which parts of your design depend on AWS. Say how you would move them. Name the abstraction layer, for example Terraform modules or a runner interface.

Zero-downtime change

He worked on zero-downtime upgrades. For each change to a shared framework or runner, say how you stage it, check it and roll it back.

SRE thinking

Site Reliability Engineering is his top skill. Use SLOs, error budgets and alerts for the test platform. Say what you measure, not only what you build.

Pipeline ownership

He managed the product build flow and the continuous testing step. Be ready to say where tests run in the pipeline, how long they take and who owns a red build.

Honesty about gaps

He knows Kubernetes and Jenkins well. Do not bluff on EKS. Say what you have run in production, say what you studied, and show the method you use to reason.

Fix the round-one answers

UKG-D1 Selenium, Playwright or custom framework, with REST, SOAP and GraphQL APIs

Round oneSelenium, in Java, because Java is compatible with everything.
Say now

The choice depends on criteria, not on the language. For new UI tests I lean to Playwright with a thin internal layer, because of auto-waiting, tracing and parallel runs. I keep Selenium where teams have a large stable investment and migrate in phases. For APIs, I put REST, SOAP and GraphQL adapters behind one client interface with one response model. Then the assertions, reporting and auth are the same for every team.

UKG-D2 Migrate 10,000 Selenium tests to Playwright

Round onePartly covered in practice.
Say now

New tests go to Playwright from a cutover date. I triage the old tests: delete the stale ones and migrate by frequency, flakiness and criticality. LLM-assisted conversion drafts the code, and a human reviews it. Both suites run in parallel until the new tests are stable. Then I retire the old ones.

UKG-K1 Pods are Running but users get 503

Round oneNot answered.
Say now

Running does not mean Ready. I check the Service endpoints first. If they are empty, the readiness probe fails or the labels do not match. Then I check the ALB target group health, because its health check can differ from the Kubernetes probe. Then I read the app logs for a failing dependency.

Questions he would add

UKG-P1

Interviewer

Our products calculate shifts, overtime and pay. A shift can cross midnight, a DST change or a pay-period boundary. How does the framework let teams test time-dependent logic reliably?

What this tests He tests if you connect the framework to UKG's real domain risk: time and money.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

Time-dependent tests fail when they use the real clock. The framework must let a test set the time. I give teams a test-clock API that sets the time in the app under test and in the browser. I add shared fixtures for the dangerous dates: DST changes, month end, leap day and pay-period boundaries. I run these tests in more than one time zone in CI.

Full Staff-level answer

  1. Control the clock

    Do not let tests read the real system time. Give a test-clock API in the framework. In Playwright, page.clock sets the browser time. On the backend, use an injectable clock (for example java.time.Clock) or a test-only time endpoint.

  2. Name the dangerous dates

    Make a shared library of boundary dates. Include the DST start and end for each supported region, midnight, month end, year end, leap day and pay-period edges. Teams use the library. They do not invent dates.

  3. Run in more than one time zone

    Set the TZ variable and the browser timezoneId in a CI matrix. Many date bugs show only when the server and the browser use different zones.

  4. Assert on business values

    Assert hours, overtime and pay amounts. Do not assert a formatted date string, because the format changes with the locale.

  5. Push most cases down

    Test the rule matrix with fast unit or API tests. Keep only a few E2E tests that prove the full flow for each boundary.

Caution
  • Tests that use new Date() or LocalDate.now() pass on most days and fail on DST days. Never let a test depend on the real clock.
  • Running all date tests only in UTC hides most time-zone bugs.
UKG-P2

Interviewer

Two hundred teams ask you to add their helpers to the framework. What do you refuse to put in it, and how do you decide?

What this tests He tests if you can protect the framework from becoming a giant abstraction that fits nobody.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

The core framework holds only what most teams need in the same way: driver or browser setup, waits, config, auth, data cleanup, reporting and CI integration. Product-specific page objects and business flows stay in the team repos. I use a simple rule: three or more teams need it in the same form, and someone commits to own it. Everything else goes through extension points.

Full Staff-level answer

  1. Define the core

    The core is infrastructure for tests: browser lifecycle, waits, config, secrets, test data helpers, reporting and CI hooks. It has a small public API with versioning.

  2. Use a rule for new additions

    Add a feature to the core only when 3 or more teams need it in the same form. The feature must have tests, docs and an owner.

  3. Give extension points

    Teams add custom fixtures, reporters and API adapters through plugins. They do not need a core change, so you do not become the bottleneck.

  4. Keep a contrib layer

    Shared but less stable helpers go to a contrib package. They can move to the core later if they prove useful.

Caution
  • Adding every request to the core makes every release risky for every team.
  • Refusing all requests pushes teams to fork the framework.
UKG-P3

Interviewer

One product area spends 70% of its CI minutes on UI E2E tests. Leadership wants to cut the cost but not the confidence. What do you do?

What this tests He tests the test pyramid, data-driven decisions and cost awareness.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

First I measure which tests cost the most and which tests find real bugs. Many UI tests check business rules that an API or unit test can check faster. I move those checks down. I keep a small set of E2E journeys for each critical flow. I run the full E2E set on merge or nightly, not on every PR. I report cost and escaped defects before and after the change.

Full Staff-level answer

  1. Measure

    Get the runtime, the failure history and the bugs found for each test. A test that never failed in a year and takes 4 minutes is a candidate.

  2. Move checks down

    Convert rule checks to API or component tests. Keep the UI test only for the user journey.

  3. Tier the runs

    Run smoke tests on PR, the affected set on merge and the full set nightly.

  4. Prove it

    Track CI minutes, PR time and escaped defects. Show leadership that confidence stayed the same.

Caution
  • Deleting tests only by runtime can remove the tests that find the most bugs.
UKG-P4

Interviewer

Who decides when a flaky test is quarantined, fixed or deleted? Describe the policy for 200 teams.

What this tests He tests ownership, policy design and automation instead of manual policing.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

The platform detects flakiness. The owning team decides the fix. A test that fails and then passes on retry is marked flaky automatically. It goes to quarantine: it still runs, but it does not block merges. A ticket goes to the owning team with a time limit. If nobody fixes it in that time, the team must fix it or delete it.

Full Staff-level answer

  1. Detect automatically

    Record every retry. Mark a test flaky when its fail-then-pass rate passes a threshold, for example 2% over 7 days.

  2. Quarantine without hiding

    A quarantined test still runs and reports. It does not block the merge. The dashboard shows the quarantine list.

  3. Assign the owner

    Use CODEOWNERS or test tags to find the owning team. Open a ticket automatically.

  4. Set an exit rule

    Give a time limit, for example 14 days. After that, the team fixes or deletes the test. The quarantine list must not grow forever.

Caution
  • Global auto-retry without recording hides real product bugs.
UKG-P5

Interviewer

Show me the code that a test author writes with your framework. What does the public API look like?

What this tests He tests if you can design a clean API, not only describe layers.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

The author writes the user intent. The framework hides setup, waits and cleanup. In Playwright, I expose this through fixtures: the test asks for a logged-in page and a data factory, and the framework gives them. The test reads like a short story of the user steps plus assertions.

Full Staff-level answer

  1. Fixtures, not base classes

    Fixtures compose. A test asks only for what it needs. Setup and cleanup live in one place.

  2. Data through a factory

    The factory creates data through the API with a unique prefix. It deletes the data after the test.

  3. Auth through stored state

    Log in once per role. Reuse the stored session in each test.

  4. Locators by role and test ID

    Use getByRole and getByTestId. These locators survive most UI changes.

Code to know

UKG-P6

Interviewer

Why would we run test runners and browsers on EKS? Why not use GitHub-hosted runners only?

What this tests He tests if you can argue both sides and not pick Kubernetes by default.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

GitHub-hosted runners are simpler, and I start there. EKS makes sense for three reasons. Tests must reach private environments. We need thousands of browsers at peak and near zero at night. We want our own cost and security controls. The cost is that we now own a cluster, so we need the skills and the on-call for it.

Full Staff-level answer

  1. Default to hosted

    Hosted runners need no maintenance. Larger runners can get static IPs and private networking on some plans.

  2. Reasons for EKS
    • Network access to private VPC services.
    • Burst scale with ARC, KEDA and Karpenter.
    • Spot instances for lower cost.
    • Central control of images, secrets and isolation.
  3. The cost

    Someone must run the cluster, patch nodes and handle incidents. Count that cost before you choose.

UKG-P7

Interviewer

Where would you use AI or LLMs in our test platform, and where would you not?

What this tests He tests judgment about AI: real value, guardrails and measurement.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

I use AI where a human reviews the output and the value is easy to measure. Good places are failure summaries, grouping of similar failures, test-conversion drafts and locator suggestions. I do not let AI change tests or skip failures without review. I built an LLM experiment for CI failure analysis at Joyent. The lesson was that the input data matters more than the model.

Full Staff-level answer

  1. Good uses
    • Summarize a failure from logs, trace and screenshot.
    • Suggest a probable cause and an owner.
    • Draft Selenium-to-Playwright conversions for human review.
    • Suggest stable locators from the DOM.
  2. Guardrails

    A human approves every code change. The model gets only redacted logs. Every suggestion links to its evidence.

  3. Measure

    Track how often teams accept the suggestion and the time to diagnose. Stop the feature if it does not help.

  4. Your story

    Use your Joyent LLM failure-analysis experiment. Say what it did, what you learned and what you would change. Do not add numbers that you cannot defend.

Caution
  • Self-healing locators that change tests silently can hide real UI regressions.
UKG-P8

Interviewer

Teams depend on your platform to merge code. What SLOs do you set for it?

What this tests He tests if you treat the test platform as a product with reliability targets.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

I set SLOs on what teams feel. Examples: 99% of CI runs start within 2 minutes, infrastructure failures cause less than 1% of red builds, and the PR smoke suite finishes in under 10 minutes for the 90th percentile. I alert on the error budget, not on single failures.

Full Staff-level answer

  1. Pick user-facing SLIs
    • Queue time: time from push to the first test.
    • Duration: p50 and p90 of the PR suite.
    • Infra failure rate: red builds caused by the platform, not by product code.
    • Flaky rate: fail-then-pass rate.
  2. Set targets with teams

    Agree on the targets with the consumer teams. Publish them on the dashboard.

  3. Use the error budget

    When the budget runs out, the platform team stops feature work and fixes reliability.

UKG-P9

Interviewer

Two hundred teams need test users, API keys and tenant credentials in several environments. How do you manage them?

What this tests He tests security design at platform scale.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

No team stores long-lived credentials in its repo. CI gets cloud access through OIDC. Test credentials live in a secrets manager, scoped per team and per environment. The framework fetches them at runtime. Where possible, the framework creates short-lived test users through an API and deletes them after the run.

Full Staff-level answer

  1. No static keys in CI

    Use GitHub OIDC to assume an IAM role. Scope the trust policy to the repo, branch and environment.

  2. One secrets store

    Put test credentials in AWS Secrets Manager or a vault. Use one path per team and per environment.

  3. Short-lived users

    Create test users through an API with a unique prefix. Delete them in teardown and in a nightly sweep.

  4. Detect leaks

    Turn on secret scanning and push protection. Mask derived values in logs.

UKG-P10

Interviewer

Tell me about a technical decision you made in a framework that you would reverse today.

What this tests He tests self-awareness and learning. He wants a real story with a real cost.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

Pick a true decision from your Joyent Cypress work. Say what you chose and why it made sense then. Say what it cost later. Say what you would do now, and what you changed after you saw the cost.

Full Staff-level answer

  1. Choose a real example

    Candidates from your experience: a helper API that grew too large, a selector convention that teams did not follow, or a cleanup design that left orphans. Use only what really happened.

  2. Structure
    • The decision and the reason at the time.
    • The signal that showed the cost.
    • What you changed.
    • What you would do from the start now.
  3. Stop there

    Give the story in 90 seconds. Let him ask follow-ups.

UKG-P11

Interviewer

UKG runs on more than one cloud. How do you design the test platform so that it does not depend on one cloud provider?

What this tests He built cloud-agnostic solutions. He tests if you can separate the platform logic from the provider.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

I keep the platform logic in containers and a small runner interface. The cloud-specific parts sit behind modules: cluster, storage, secrets and identity. Terraform modules give the same shape on each cloud. I accept some loss of native features for portability. I test the portable path in CI on a second cloud on a schedule, so drift shows early.

Full Staff-level answer

  1. Containers first

    Package the test runner and its browsers as one image. The image runs on any Kubernetes cluster. Pin versions so that results do not change by cloud.

  2. Hide the provider

    Put a thin interface in front of storage, secrets, identity and queues. Each cloud has one adapter. The test code never calls a cloud API directly.

  3. Use Terraform modules

    Write one module per capability. Each module has one implementation per cloud. Teams ask for a capability, not for a provider service.

  4. Name the cost

    Portability costs native features and some speed. Say this. Use a native service only when the gain is large and the exit path is clear.

  5. Prove it

    Run a small smoke suite on the second cloud every night. A portable design that nobody runs is not portable.

Caution
  • Saying 'we use Kubernetes, so we are portable'. Storage, identity and networking still tie you to one cloud.
  • Building a full abstraction for every service. Abstract only the few services that tests use.
UKG-P12

Interviewer

You must ship a breaking change to the shared test framework. Two hundred teams run tests all day. How do you upgrade with no outage for them?

What this tests He worked on zero-downtime upgrades. He tests staged rollout and rollback for a shared tool.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

I never force a big-bang upgrade. I ship the new version beside the old one with semantic versions. A compatibility layer keeps old tests running. Canary teams move first, and I watch failure rate and run time. Then I widen the rollout in waves. The old version stays for a set time, and I can pin any team back in minutes.

Full Staff-level answer

  1. Version and isolate

    Publish the new version with a clear major number. Teams pin a version. The old and the new version live side by side.

  2. Add a compatibility layer

    Keep the old API working for one or two releases. Print a deprecation warning with the fix. Provide a codemod for the common change.

  3. Canary first

    Pick 3 to 5 friendly teams with different stacks. Compare failure rate, flake rate and run time against their old runs.

  4. Widen in waves

    Move teams in groups. Stop if a metric goes past a set limit. Share the status in one visible place.

  5. Keep the way back

    A team can pin the old version with one line. Set and publish the date when the old version ends.

Caution
  • Changing a public API without a deprecation period breaks teams that you cannot see.
  • Rolling out to everyone on a Friday with no pin-back path.
UKG-P13

Interviewer

Describe how tests fit into the build flow. Which tests run on a pull request, which run after merge, and which run at night? Who owns a red build?

What this tests He managed the product build flow and the continuous testing step. He tests practical pipeline design and ownership.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

Fast checks run on every pull request: unit tests, linting and a small smoke set. The full API suite runs after merge. Broad UI suites run on a schedule or on a release branch, in parallel. Each stage has a time budget. The team that owns the failing area owns the red build. The platform team owns the pipeline itself and its flake rate.

Full Staff-level answer

  1. Stage by speed

    Pull request: under 10 minutes. Post-merge: under 30 minutes. Nightly or release: the full suite. Move a test to an earlier stage only when it is fast and stable.

  2. Select tests

    Use change-based selection when you can trust it. Always run a small smoke set. Keep a full run as a safety net.

  3. Parallelize

    Shard tests across runners. Keep test data separate per shard, so the shards do not affect each other.

  4. Assign ownership

    Tag each test with an owning team. A red build pages the owner. The platform team handles infrastructure failures and flake.

  5. Report

    Show pass rate, flake rate and queue time per team on one dashboard. Review it each week.

Caution
  • Running the full UI suite on every pull request. Developers then ignore the pipeline.
  • No clear owner for a red build. The failure stays red for days.

How he would tell you to answer

He named his focus areas

Basic DevOps, pipelines, GCP, GitHub, Kubernetes, and Selenium and Playwright frameworks. Expect fundamentals first, then depth. Read the FAQ topics 'DevOps basics and pipelines' and 'GCP for a DevOps and test platform' before the rest.

Expect framework-level depth

He began as a Selenium automation engineer. Prepare to explain how you would build a waits, retry and reporting layer yourself. Use your Cypress work as the example.

Show the cloud exit path

His work centres on cloud-agnostic design. When you name an AWS service, add one sentence: how would this move to another cloud?

Lead with a clarifying question, then a structure

Ask about scale, constraints or the current state in one sentence. Then say the three or four parts of your answer before you go into detail.

Say the 30-second answer, then stop

Give the short answer from this page. Let him pull the detail he wants. Long answers hide the main point.

Own the EKS gap in one sentence

Say: 'I have not operated EKS in production. I studied it for this role, and here is how I would debug it.' Then answer with the method. Do not apologize again.

Connect to UKG's domain

Use examples from time, scheduling and payroll. Time zones, pay periods and tenant data show that you understand where UKG's risk is.

Close every design with measure and rollback

End each design answer with the metric you track and the way you roll back. This is the most common gap between Senior and Staff answers.

Draw while you talk

In a design round, draw 5 to 8 boxes and the data flow first. Talk over the drawing. The capstone diagram on this page is a good template.

Prepare 4 true stories

Fill every '[your number]' placeholder in the L7 stories before the interview. Do not use a number that you cannot explain.

Chapter 08

Frequently asked: the rest of the syllabus

These questions are common in UKG and test-platform interviews. The scenario chapters do not cover them. Use them for the coding round and for quick factual questions.

UKG: company and interview process

What does UKG do?

UKG makes cloud software for HR, payroll and workforce management. The company name comes from the merger of Ultimate Software and Kronos. UKG says that more than 80,000 organizations use its products. The main product suites are:

  • UKG Pro: an HCM suite for enterprises (HR, payroll, talent).
  • UKG Pro Workforce Management: time, scheduling and labor. This product was named UKG Dimensions before.
  • UKG Ready: an all-in-one HR and payroll product for small and mid-size businesses.
  • UKG Bryte AI: the AI layer across the products.

Why does test automation matter so much for a product like UKG?

UKG products calculate pay, time and schedules for many workers. A defect in payroll or time rules has a direct effect on real people. Many teams ship changes to one shared platform. A shared test framework lets hundreds of teams test in the same way. It also gives one view of quality across the products. Say this in your own words. Link it to your Joyent work, where tests created and removed real cloud resources.

What do public interview reports say about UKG Noida rounds?

Reports on Glassdoor and LeetCode Discuss show a similar pattern. These are self-reports, so treat them as signals, not rules.

  • An online or written coding test. One report: 2 DSA problems plus 1 Git question on HackerRank. Another report: 2 Java programs plus 1 Selenium question.
  • 2 to 4 technical rounds. Topics: core Java, OOP, collections, multithreading, DSA, REST vs SOAP, database indexes.
  • For test roles (Lead/SDET), recent reports name Selenium, TestNG, API testing, framework design and Java fundamentals.
  • A managerial or delivery round, then HR.
  • Senior and Principal reports mention system design.

Which questions repeat in UKG test-automation interviews?

These questions appear in public reports for UKG test roles in Noida:

  • "Briefly describe the automation framework that you are currently working on."
  • "Explain your automation framework flow."
  • "What are the roles and responsibilities of an SDET?"
  • "Write a method with its JUnit test case."
  • "Which Java collections suit an in-memory cache?"

Prepare a 2-minute framework story. Use your Cypress framework at Joyent. Describe layers, data, CI, reports and what you changed.

What is the best answer shape for 'describe your framework'?

Give the structure first, then one decision and one result. Use this order:

  1. Purpose and scale: what product, how many tests, who uses it.
  2. Layers: tests, page/helper layer, custom commands, config, data, reporting.
  3. Test data: unique data per run plus cleanup. Add the startup sweep for orphans.
  4. CI: how tests run in Jenkins and GitHub Actions, and the tags for smoke vs full runs.
  5. One trade-off you made and why.
  6. One result you can measure, or one lesson.

What do UKG job posts in Noida ask for in testing?

One Noida Sr Software Engineer post lists unit tests and automated test suites as required. It lists Playwright or Selenium experience as preferred. It also lists GitHub Copilot and other AI tools as preferred. Use this as a signal. Show that you can use AI tools with review, as in your LLM failure-analysis work.

DevOps basics and pipelines

What is the difference between continuous integration, continuous delivery and continuous deployment?

Continuous integration (CI) means developers merge small changes often. Each merge builds and runs tests automatically. Continuous delivery means every change that passes is ready to release, but a person approves the release. Continuous deployment removes that approval. Every change that passes goes to production by itself.

What stages does a good pipeline have, and in what order?

Order the stages from fast to slow.

  • Build and lint: seconds to minutes.
  • Unit tests and static analysis.
  • Package: build and scan the container image.
  • Deploy to a test environment.
  • Integration, API and smoke tests.
  • Slower UI end-to-end tests, in parallel.
  • Promote to production with a gate.

Fail fast. A cheap check must fail before an expensive check starts.

What are blue/green, rolling and canary deployments?

Rolling: replace instances a few at a time. It is the Kubernetes default.

Blue/green: run the new version beside the old one. Switch the traffic all at once. Rollback is a switch back. It costs double capacity for a short time.

Canary: send a small share of traffic to the new version. Watch the metrics. Increase the share in steps. This limits the damage of a bad release.

What is infrastructure as code, and why is idempotency important?

Infrastructure as code (IaC) describes servers, networks and clusters in files that live in Git. You review, test and version them like application code. An idempotent change gives the same result when you run it once or ten times. Terraform is idempotent: plan shows the difference between the files and reality, and apply fixes only that difference.

How does Terraform keep its state, and what goes wrong with a shared state file?

Terraform stores a state file. It maps your code to real resources. For a team, keep the state in a remote backend with locking. On GCP this is a Cloud Storage bucket. On AWS it is S3 with a lock table. Without locking, two people can run apply together and corrupt the state. Never commit state to Git, because it can hold secrets.

Write a basic Jenkins declarative pipeline for a Maven test job.

Use a declarative Jenkinsfile in the repository. Choose an agent, run the tests, and always publish the test report. For shared logic across many teams, use a Jenkins shared library.

Jenkins or GitHub Actions: how do you compare them?

Jenkins is self-hosted. You manage the controller, the agents, the plugins and the upgrades. It is very flexible. GitHub Actions is managed and sits next to the code. Workflows are YAML, and the marketplace gives ready actions. The trade-off is control against operating cost. For a platform team, I would choose the one with less upkeep. I would keep pipeline logic in reusable code, so that a move stays possible.

Which Git workflow and branch rules do you use?

Short-lived branches and pull requests into one main branch. Protect main: require passing checks and at least one review. Keep branches small and merge often. Use tags for releases. Trunk-based development with feature flags works well when you deploy many times a day.

How do you keep secrets out of a pipeline?

Never put secrets in the repository or in image layers. Store them in a secret manager and inject them at run time. Prefer short-lived credentials from workload identity (OIDC) over long-lived keys. Mask values in logs. Limit each secret to the job that needs it. Rotate on a schedule.

Which Linux commands do you use first when a build agent or a container misbehaves?

  • top or htop: CPU and memory.
  • df -h and du -sh: disk space. A full disk is a common cause of build failures.
  • free -m: memory.
  • ss -tulpn: open ports.
  • journalctl -u <service> and dmesg: logs and kernel messages such as an out-of-memory kill.
  • curl -v: test a network call.
  • ps aux | grep: find a process.

What are the four golden signals?

Latency, traffic, errors and saturation. For a test platform, measure four things. How long a run waits and runs. How many runs start. How many runs fail for infrastructure reasons. How full the runner pool is. Alert on symptoms that users feel, not on every cause.

GCP for a DevOps and test platform

I know AWS well. How do the main AWS services map to GCP?

Use this map. It is close, not exact.

  • EC2 → Compute Engine.
  • EKS → GKE (Google Kubernetes Engine).
  • ECR → Artifact Registry.
  • S3 → Cloud Storage.
  • IAM roles → IAM roles and service accounts.
  • Secrets Manager → Secret Manager.
  • CloudWatch → Cloud Monitoring and Cloud Logging.
  • RDS → Cloud SQL.
  • SQS and SNS → Pub/Sub.
  • ELB → Cloud Load Balancing.
  • Fargate → GKE Autopilot, or Cloud Run.
  • Auto Scaling group → managed instance group.

Say it as: 'I know the AWS side in depth. I map it to GCP by concept.'

How is the GCP resource hierarchy different from AWS accounts?

GCP has an organization, folders and projects. A project is the unit that holds resources and billing. IAM policies and organization policies are inherited down the tree. In AWS the account is the main boundary. In GCP, a project plays that role, and folders let you apply one policy to many projects.

How does IAM work in GCP?

You grant a role to a principal on a resource. A principal is a user, a group or a service account. Roles are basic (Owner, Editor, Viewer), predefined for one service, or custom. Avoid basic roles in production, because they are too broad. Use the narrowest predefined role. A service account is an identity for a workload. Give each workload its own service account.

How does a GitHub Actions workflow log in to GCP without a stored key?

Use Workload Identity Federation. GitHub gives the job a short-lived OIDC token. GCP trusts that token through a workload identity pool and provider. The job then acts as a service account. No JSON key is stored in GitHub. Limit the trust to one repository and one branch. Check the current major version of the action before you copy this example.

What is GKE, and how does it differ from EKS?

Both are managed Kubernetes. The provider runs the control plane. GKE has two modes. In Standard mode you manage node pools. In Autopilot mode Google manages the nodes, and you pay for the resources that your pods request. GKE links Kubernetes service accounts to IAM through Workload Identity Federation for GKE. The EKS equivalent is IAM Roles for Service Accounts, or EKS Pod Identity. The kubectl commands and the YAML are the same on both.

GKE Standard or Autopilot for test runners?

Autopilot gives less node work, and it fits spiky workloads. Standard gives more control: custom machine types, Spot nodes, GPUs and special kernels. For browser test runners, I would first try Autopilot for low upkeep. I would move to Standard if I needed fine control of cost or node settings. Say that you would measure both.

How do you connect to a GKE cluster and check it?

Get credentials with the gcloud command, then use the normal kubectl commands.

Where do you store container images on GCP?

Use Artifact Registry. It stores Docker images and other package types, with IAM control per repository. Container Registry is the older service and is deprecated. Turn on vulnerability scanning. Tag images with the Git commit hash, not only latest.

Cloud Build, GitHub Actions or Jenkins on GCP?

Cloud Build is the managed CI service of GCP. Each build step runs in a container, and a cloudbuild.yaml file defines the steps. It integrates well with Artifact Registry and IAM. GitHub Actions is better when the code and the reviews are already in GitHub. Jenkins is best when you need full control or you have many existing jobs. The choice depends on where the code lives, who maintains it and the existing investment.

Compute Engine, GKE or Cloud Run for the test runners?

Cloud Run runs containers without a cluster. It scales to zero. Cloud Run jobs fit short batch work. A large UI suite with many browsers and long runs fits GKE better, because you control the pod size, the queue and the node pool. Compute Engine fits when you need a full virtual machine, for example a real device or a legacy tool. I would start with GKE for the platform and use Cloud Run for small services.

How is a VPC different in GCP?

A VPC network in GCP is a global resource. Its subnets are regional. In AWS a VPC is regional. Firewall rules apply to the network and use tags or service accounts. A private GKE cluster has nodes with no public IP. Use Cloud NAT so that private nodes can reach the internet to pull dependencies.

How do you cut the cost of test runners on GCP?

  • Run tests on Spot VMs or Spot node pools. They are cheap, but Google can reclaim them. Make the test jobs retry safely.
  • Scale node pools to zero when idle.
  • Right-size the pods from real usage.
  • Use committed use discounts for the steady base load.
  • Keep artifacts on a lifecycle rule in Cloud Storage so that old videos and traces expire.

How do you monitor workloads on GCP?

Cloud Logging collects logs from GKE automatically. Cloud Monitoring holds metrics, dashboards and alerts. Managed Service for Prometheus gives you Prometheus-style metrics without running the servers. You can still use Grafana for dashboards. Define SLOs and alert on the burn rate.

How do you run Terraform for GCP safely across teams?

Use the Google provider. Keep the state in a Cloud Storage bucket with versioning. Use one state per environment. Put reusable pieces in modules. Run plan on pull requests and apply only from the pipeline, with a service account that has the minimum roles. Review plans like code.

How do the EKS and GKE commands compare?

The kubectl part is identical. Only the login and the cluster commands differ.

  • Get credentials: aws eks update-kubeconfig --name my-cluster on EKS. gcloud container clusters get-credentials my-cluster --region <region> on GKE.
  • Create a cluster: eksctl create cluster or Terraform on EKS. gcloud container clusters create or create-auto (Autopilot), or Terraform, on GKE.
  • Pod identity: IRSA or EKS Pod Identity on EKS. Workload Identity Federation for GKE on GKE.
  • Images: ECR on EKS. Artifact Registry on GKE.

How do GKE node pools and autoscaling work?

A node pool is a group of nodes with the same machine type. A cluster can have many pools, for example a normal pool and a Spot pool for test runners. The cluster autoscaler adds nodes when pods cannot be scheduled and removes idle nodes. Node auto-provisioning can create new pools by itself for pod needs. The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler scales pods. KEDA can scale from queue length, as on EKS.

How does GKE handle upgrades?

GKE upgrades the control plane for you. Choose a release channel: Rapid, Regular or Stable. New versions reach Rapid first. Set maintenance windows so that upgrades happen at quiet times. Node pools upgrade by surge: GKE adds extra nodes, drains old ones, and keeps pods running if you set Pod Disruption Budgets. Test upgrades on a staging cluster first.

How does traffic reach a pod on GKE?

A Service of type ClusterIP gives a stable name inside the cluster. For outside traffic, use an Ingress or the Gateway API. GKE creates a Google Cloud load balancer for it. Clusters are VPC-native: each pod gets an IP from a VPC alias range. This is similar to the VPC CNI on EKS, where pods get VPC IPs. Readiness probes decide which pods receive traffic, as on EKS.

Selenium

Explain the Selenium WebDriver architecture.

Your test code uses a language binding, for example the Java client. The binding sends W3C WebDriver commands over HTTP to a driver, for example chromedriver. The driver controls the real browser. Each command is a request, and the driver sends a response. Selenium 4 uses the W3C WebDriver standard, so all major browsers speak the same protocol. Selenium also moves to WebDriver BiDi. BiDi adds a WebSocket so the browser can send events, for example console logs and network requests.

Which locator strategy do you prefer and why?

Use a stable, unique attribute first. A dedicated test attribute such as data-testid is the best choice. Then use id or name if they are stable. Use CSS selectors before XPath, because CSS is short and fast to read. Use XPath only when you must find an element by its text or by a parent. Do not use absolute XPath or index-based locators. They break when the layout changes.

Explain implicit, explicit and fluent waits.

An implicit wait is a global timeout for findElement. An explicit wait (WebDriverWait) waits for one condition on one element, for example "clickable". A fluent wait is an explicit wait with a custom poll interval and a list of exceptions to ignore. Use explicit waits. Do not mix implicit and explicit waits. If you mix them, the timeouts can add up and the wait time becomes hard to predict. Never use Thread.sleep as a wait.

What is the Page Object Model? What is Page Factory?

The Page Object Model puts the locators and actions of one page in one class. Tests call methods such as loginPage.login(user). They do not touch locators directly. When the UI changes, you change one class, not many tests. Page Factory is a Selenium helper that fills @FindBy fields with lazy proxies. Many teams now prefer plain page objects with By locators and explicit waits, because Page Factory proxies can hide stale-element problems.

What causes StaleElementReferenceException and how do you fix it?

The driver keeps a reference to one DOM node. If the page re-renders that node, the old reference becomes stale. A click on the old reference then fails. To fix it, find the element again just before you use it. Wait for the re-render to finish with an explicit wait. Store By locators, not WebElement objects, in page objects.

How do you handle iframes, windows and alerts?

  • iframe: call driver.switchTo().frame(...) before you find elements inside it. Call switchTo().defaultContent() after.
  • New window or tab: get getWindowHandles(), then switchTo().window(handle). Selenium 4 also has switchTo().newWindow(WindowType.TAB).
  • JavaScript alert: wait with ExpectedConditions.alertIsPresent(). Then call accept(), dismiss() or getText().

Explain Selenium Grid 4 components.

Grid 4 splits the old hub into parts that can run alone:

  • Router: the entry point. It sends new-session requests to the queue and other requests to the correct Node.
  • New Session Queue: holds new-session requests in FIFO order.
  • Distributor: knows all Nodes and their capabilities. It takes requests from the queue and gives each one to a Node.
  • Session Map: maps a session ID to the Node that runs it.
  • Event Bus: carries messages between the parts.
  • Node: runs browsers and manages slots.

You can run Grid in standalone, hub-and-node, or fully distributed mode.

What is Selenium Manager?

Selenium Manager ships with Selenium since version 4.6. It finds, downloads and caches the correct driver for your browser. Since 4.11 it can also download Chrome for Testing, and later Firefox and Edge. You do not need WebDriverManager or manual driver paths in most cases. The Selenium docs still mark it as beta. Grid can use it with --selenium-manager true.

How do you run Selenium tests in parallel safely?

Give each test thread its own WebDriver. Keep the driver in a ThreadLocal. Do not share static driver fields. Use unique test data per test. Set TestNG parallel="methods" or "classes" and a thread-count. Run browsers on a Grid or in containers so the machine does not run out of resources.

Playwright

Explain the Playwright architecture.

The test runner talks to the browser through one persistent connection. It does not send one HTTP request per command as classic WebDriver does. Playwright uses CDP for Chromium and its own patched protocols for Firefox and WebKit. Playwright downloads browser builds that match each release. One browser process can hold many browser contexts. Each context is like a new, clean browser profile.

What is auto-waiting and actionability?

Before an action, Playwright checks that the element is ready. For a click, it waits until the element is attached, visible, stable, enabled and able to get events. If a check fails, Playwright retries until the timeout. Web-first assertions such as expect(locator).toBeVisible() also retry. Because of this, you do not need manual waits in most tests.

Which locators does Playwright recommend?

Use locators that match what a user sees. Prefer getByRole with an accessible name, for example getByRole('button', { name: 'Save' }). Use getByLabel, getByPlaceholder and getByText for forms and content. Use getByTestId when there is no good user-facing locator. Use CSS or XPath only as a last choice. Locators are lazy and strict: an action fails if the locator matches more than one element.

What are browser contexts and why do they matter?

A browser context is an isolated session with its own cookies, storage and cache. Playwright Test gives each test a new context. Tests do not share state, so they can run in parallel. A new context is much faster than a new browser. You can open two contexts in one test to test two users at the same time.

What are fixtures in Playwright Test?

A fixture gives a test something that it needs, for example page, context or request. You can write custom fixtures for a logged-in page, a test user or an API client. A fixture runs setup before the test and teardown after it. Tests ask for fixtures by name, so setup is shared without base classes. For a framework team, custom fixtures are the main public surface that other teams use.

How do workers, parallelism and sharding work?

Playwright runs test files in parallel worker processes. Set the count with workers. Set fullyParallel: true to run tests inside one file in parallel too. Sharding splits the suite across machines with --shard=1/4. With fullyParallel, shards split by test, so they are more even. Use the blob reporter on each shard, then npx playwright merge-reports to make one HTML report.

How do you handle flaky tests and debug failures (retries, trace viewer, UI mode)?

Set retries in the config, for example 2 in CI. A test that fails and then passes is marked "flaky" in the report. Track the flaky count over time. Use --fail-on-flaky-tests when flakiness must block a run. Set trace: 'on-first-retry' to record actions, DOM snapshots, network and console for a retried test. Open the trace in the HTML report or with npx playwright show-trace. Use UI mode (--ui) to run and step through tests. Use --last-failed to run only the tests that failed in the previous run.

How do you mock or intercept network calls?

Use page.route(urlPattern, handler). In the handler, call route.fulfill() to return fake data, route.abort() to block, or route.continue() to change and pass the request. Mock only to test UI states that are hard to create, for example errors. Keep some tests against the real backend, so that the mocks do not hide contract changes.

How do you test APIs and reuse login with Playwright?

The request fixture gives an APIRequestContext. Use it to call REST APIs directly, for API tests or for fast test setup. For login, run a setup project once. Save cookies and local storage with context.storageState({ path }). Other projects load that file with use: { storageState }, so tests start logged in.

Compare Playwright, Selenium and Cypress.

  • Selenium: W3C standard, many languages, very large ecosystem, Grid for scale. You must build waits, reports and fixtures yourself.
  • Cypress: runs inside the browser, very good developer experience, JavaScript/TypeScript only. Multi-tab and multi-origin support is more limited.
  • Playwright: auto-wait, contexts, tracing, sharding and API testing built in. It supports TypeScript/JavaScript, Java, Python and .NET.

For a new platform, Playwright gives most features out of the box. Selenium still fits large Java suites that already exist.

Java test stack: Maven, TestNG, JUnit 5

Explain the Maven build lifecycle.

The default lifecycle runs phases in order. The main phases are validate, compile, test, package, verify, install and deploy. When you run a phase, Maven runs all earlier phases first. Plugins attach goals to phases. For example, Surefire attaches to test. mvn clean verify is a common CI command.

What is the difference between Surefire and Failsafe?

Surefire runs unit tests in the test phase. By default it finds classes named *Test. Failsafe runs integration tests in the integration-test phase and checks results in verify. By default it finds classes named *IT. Failsafe lets post-integration-test run even when tests fail, so cleanup can happen. Put E2E and API tests in Failsafe.

Compare TestNG and JUnit 5.

  • Annotations: TestNG has @BeforeSuite, @BeforeTest, @BeforeClass, @BeforeMethod. JUnit 5 has @BeforeAll, @BeforeEach.
  • Grouping: TestNG uses groups. JUnit 5 uses @Tag.
  • Data-driven: TestNG uses @DataProvider. JUnit 5 uses @ParameterizedTest with sources.
  • Parallel: TestNG sets it in testng.xml. JUnit 5 sets it in junit-platform.properties.
  • Dependencies: TestNG has dependsOnMethods. JUnit 5 does not, by design.

TestNG is common in Selenium suites. JUnit 5 is common in new Java projects.

Write a TestNG data provider.

A data provider returns rows of arguments. TestNG runs the test once for each row. Set parallel = true on the provider to run rows in parallel.

Why use ThreadLocal for WebDriver?

In parallel runs, many threads run tests at the same time. If they share one static driver, one test can click in another test's browser. ThreadLocal gives each thread its own driver instance. Always call remove() after quit(). If you do not, thread pools can reuse an old driver.

How do you manage dependency versions in a shared test framework?

Publish the framework as a versioned artifact. Use a BOM (dependencyManagement) so that consumers get compatible versions of Selenium, TestNG and REST Assured together. Pin plugin versions. Use mvn dependency:tree to find conflicts. Let Renovate or Dependabot open update pull requests, and let CI test them.

Which Java collection fits an in-memory cache?

Use ConcurrentHashMap for a thread-safe key-value cache. Collections.synchronizedMap locks the whole map on each call, so it is slower under load. For a size-limited LRU cache, extend LinkedHashMap with access order and override removeEldestEntry. For production caches, a library such as Caffeine gives expiry and eviction.

API testing

Compare REST, SOAP and GraphQL.

  • REST: resources and HTTP verbs. Status codes tell the result. The payload is usually JSON.
  • SOAP: an XML envelope with a WSDL contract. Errors come as SOAP faults. It usually uses HTTP POST.
  • GraphQL: one endpoint. The client asks for the exact fields that it needs. Errors often come in an errors array with HTTP 200.

A test layer must check GraphQL errors and SOAP faults. A status code check alone is not enough.

Which HTTP status codes must you know?

  • 200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content.
  • 301/302 redirect, 304 Not Modified.
  • 400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthorized (no valid identity), 403 Forbidden (identity known, no permission), 404 Not Found, 409 Conflict, 422 Unprocessable Entity, 429 Too Many Requests.
  • 500 Internal Server Error, 502 Bad Gateway, 503 Service Unavailable, 504 Gateway Timeout.

What is idempotency?

A request is idempotent when many identical calls have the same effect as one call. GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent. POST is not idempotent by default. Many APIs accept an idempotency key so that a retried POST does not create a duplicate. Test this: send the same request twice and check that the system has one record.

Show a REST Assured test.

REST Assured uses a given/when/then style. given sets headers, auth and body. when sends the request. then checks the status and the body.

What is consumer-driven contract testing?

The consumer writes tests that state what it needs from the provider. Pact records these needs as a contract file. The provider runs the contract against its real code in its own CI. If the provider breaks the contract, its build fails before deploy. Contract tests are faster and more stable than full E2E tests between services.

When do you mock an API with WireMock?

Mock a dependency when it is slow, costly, unstable or not built yet. Mock it also to create hard cases, for example a timeout or a 500 error. WireMock runs a fake HTTP server with stubbed responses. Do not mock everything. Keep a smaller set of tests against real services, so that mocks do not drift from reality.

Explain the test pyramid.

Have many fast unit tests at the bottom. Have fewer service and API tests in the middle. Have a small number of slow UI E2E tests at the top. Most checks belong in lower layers, where they are fast and stable. Use E2E tests for the main user journeys only. For a platform team, the pyramid guides where to spend framework effort.

Explain OAuth2 and JWT for test automation.

OAuth2 is a protocol to get an access token. Test suites often use the client-credentials flow, because there is no user in the loop. A JWT is a signed token with three parts: header, payload (claims) and signature. The server checks the signature and the expiry. In tests, get a token once per run, cache it, and refresh it before it expires. Never print tokens in logs.

AWS basics

Explain IAM users, roles and policies.

A user is a long-term identity for a person or app. A role is an identity that has no long-term keys. Something assumes the role and gets temporary credentials from STS. A policy is a JSON document that allows or denies actions on resources. A trust policy on a role says who can assume it. Prefer roles with temporary credentials for CI and for pods.

Explain a VPC with public and private subnets.

A VPC is your private network in AWS. A public subnet has a route to an internet gateway. A private subnet has no direct route from the internet. Resources in a private subnet use a NAT gateway for outbound internet access. EKS worker nodes and test runners usually run in private subnets. Load balancers for public traffic run in public subnets.

Compare security groups and network ACLs.

A security group is a stateful firewall on an ENI, for example an EC2 instance. It has allow rules only. Return traffic is allowed automatically. A network ACL is a stateless firewall on a subnet. It has allow and deny rules, and you must allow return traffic yourself. Most teams use security groups as the main control.

What are S3 and ECR used for in a test platform?

S3 stores objects, for example test reports, screenshots, videos and traces. Use lifecycle rules to delete old artifacts and control cost. ECR is the AWS container registry. Store test-runner and browser images there. Pull from ECR inside AWS to avoid Docker Hub rate limits.

Compare ALB and NLB.

An ALB works at layer 7 (HTTP/HTTPS). It routes by host and path, and it can end TLS. An NLB works at layer 4 (TCP/UDP). It is very fast and can keep static IPs. On EKS, the AWS Load Balancer Controller creates an ALB for an Ingress. It creates an NLB for a Service of type LoadBalancer.

What is CloudWatch?

CloudWatch collects metrics and logs from AWS services and apps. You can make dashboards and alarms on metrics. CloudWatch Logs Insights lets you query logs. Container Insights adds cluster, node and pod metrics for EKS.

Compare EC2 and Fargate for running tests.

On EC2, you manage the instances, and you pay for them while they run. You get full control, for example over /dev/shm size, GPUs and DaemonSets. Fargate runs each pod or task on its own managed compute, and you pay per pod. Fargate is simple, but it has limits, for example no DaemonSets. Browser-heavy test fleets often use EC2 nodes with Karpenter and spot instances.

AWS Lambda and serverless

What is AWS Lambda, and how does it work?

Lambda runs your code in response to an event. You upload a function. AWS runs it in a managed micro virtual machine (microVM) and scales the number of copies for you. You do not manage servers. You pay for the number of requests and the run time, in milliseconds, multiplied by the memory you set. When no events arrive, you pay nothing.

What is a cold start, and how do you reduce it?

A cold start is the extra time Lambda needs to create a new execution environment. It downloads the code, starts the runtime and runs your initialization code. A warm start reuses an environment that already exists.

To reduce it:

  • Keep the package small, and import only what you need.
  • Do slow setup (SDK clients, database connections) outside the handler, so warm calls reuse it.
  • Use provisioned concurrency to keep environments ready. It costs money all the time.
  • Use SnapStart for runtimes that support it (for example Java).
  • Choose a faster runtime. Add memory, because CPU grows with memory.

What are the main Lambda limits that you must know?

  • Timeout: 15 minutes at most.
  • Memory: 128 MB to 10,240 MB. CPU grows with memory. At 1,769 MB a function has about one vCPU.
  • Temporary disk (/tmp): 512 MB to 10,240 MB.
  • Package: 50 MB zipped, 250 MB unzipped. A container image can be up to 10 GB.
  • Payload: 6 MB for a synchronous call. 1 MB for an asynchronous call.
  • Concurrency: 1,000 concurrent executions per region by default. You can ask for more.

AWS can change quotas. Check the current quota page before you give exact numbers in an interview.

Compare synchronous and asynchronous invocation, and the retry behavior of each.

Synchronous: the caller waits for the result. API Gateway and a function URL work this way. Lambda does not retry. The caller must handle the error.

Asynchronous: Lambda puts the event in an internal queue and returns at once. S3 and EventBridge work this way. On error Lambda retries two more times by default. You can send failed events to a dead-letter queue or an on-failure destination.

Event source mapping (poll-based): Lambda polls SQS, Kinesis or DynamoDB streams for you. Retry rules depend on the source. For SQS, a failed batch returns to the queue after the visibility timeout.

Lambda retries can run your code twice. How do you make a function safe?

Make the function idempotent. Running it twice must give the same result as running it once. Use a unique ID from the event as an idempotency key. Store the key with a conditional write in DynamoDB before you do the side effect. Powertools for AWS Lambda has an idempotency utility. For SQS, return partial batch failures, so that one bad message does not retry the whole batch.

Write a Lambda handler that processes an SQS batch and reports partial failures.

Return the IDs of the messages that failed. Lambda then retries only those. Turn on ReportBatchItemFailures in the event source mapping.

How does concurrency work, and what do reserved and provisioned concurrency do?

One execution environment handles one request at a time. If ten requests arrive together, Lambda needs ten environments. The total of running environments is your concurrency.

Reserved concurrency sets a maximum and a guaranteed share for one function. It protects other functions from this one, and it protects a database from too many connections.

Provisioned concurrency keeps environments warm and ready. It removes cold starts, and it costs money while it is on.

If you pass the limit, Lambda throttles. A synchronous caller gets an error. An asynchronous event waits and retries.

Which triggers do you use with Lambda, and for what?

  • API Gateway or a function URL: HTTP APIs.
  • S3: react when a file arrives, for example a test report or a video.
  • SQS: buffer work and process it at a safe speed.
  • EventBridge: react to events, and run scheduled jobs (cron).
  • SNS: fan out one event to many targets.
  • DynamoDB or Kinesis streams: react to data changes.

A queue between producer and function protects you from spikes.

How does security work for Lambda?

Each function has an execution role. It is the identity of the function. Give it only the permissions that the code needs. A separate resource policy says who may invoke the function. Put secrets in Secrets Manager or Parameter Store, not in environment variables in plain text. To reach private resources, attach the function to a VPC. Then give it a route out (NAT gateway or VPC endpoints) if it also needs the internet.

How do you deploy Lambda safely?

Publish a version (an immutable copy) and point an alias (for example prod) at it. Use a weighted alias to send 10% of traffic to the new version first. CodeDeploy can shift traffic in steps and roll back on a CloudWatch alarm. Define everything as code: AWS SAM, CDK or Terraform. Keep the deployment in a pipeline, with tests first.

How do you observe and debug a Lambda function?

Lambda sends logs to CloudWatch Logs and metrics to CloudWatch. Watch invocations, errors, duration, throttles and concurrent executions. Turn on AWS X-Ray or OpenTelemetry for traces. Use structured JSON logs with a request ID. Powertools for AWS Lambda adds logging, metrics and tracing helpers. Alarm on error rate and on throttles, not only on errors.

When is Lambda the wrong choice for a test platform?

Lambda is a poor fit in four cases. The job runs longer than 15 minutes. It needs a lot of memory or disk. It needs a GPU. It needs a real browser for a long UI session. Playwright can run in Lambda with a container image. It works for short checks, but a large UI suite fits Kubernetes, ECS or Fargate better. Lambda fits the small event-driven glue around the platform.

Lambda, Fargate or EKS: how do you choose?

Choose Lambda for short, event-driven tasks with spiky load and no server work. Choose Fargate or ECS for container jobs that run longer, with no node management. Choose EKS when you need the Kubernetes ecosystem, fine control over scheduling, or one platform for many teams. Cost also changes the answer: Lambda is cheap for low volume, and constant heavy load is often cheaper on containers.

What is the GCP counterpart of AWS Lambda?

The direct counterpart is Cloud Run functions (the new name of Cloud Functions). It runs a single function in response to HTTP or an event. Events come through Eventarc. A function runs on Cloud Run under the hood. For a whole container, use Cloud Run services or Cloud Run jobs.

One key difference: Lambda handles one request per environment. Cloud Run can handle many requests at the same time in one instance. This can lower cost and cold starts for busy services.

Map the rest like this. EventBridge becomes Eventarc. SQS becomes Pub/Sub or Cloud Tasks. Step Functions becomes Workflows. EventBridge Scheduler becomes Cloud Scheduler. API Gateway becomes API Gateway or a load balancer.

Where could you have used AWS Lambda in your Joyent experience?

Be honest first. You did not run Lambda at Joyent. Samsung's private cloud was AWS-API compatible, and your modules were EC2, VPC, MKS, KMS, Secrets Manager and quota. Say that. Then show where you would use Lambda on public AWS. These are design ideas, not claims of past work.

  • Test fixtures for Cypress: you found failures caused by missing pre-seeded cy-* resources in dev2. A scheduled function (EventBridge schedule) can check that the fixtures exist, re-seed them, and delete orphans.
  • Release tool: the old release flow had version-bump pull requests, tags and Artifactory checks. A GitHub webhook can call a function that verifies the artifacts after a tag and posts the result.
  • Uptime and pipeline data: your pipeline ran EC2 uptime tests and fed Grafana. A scheduled function can run the lightweight probes. A webhook function can send workflow run results to Grafana.
  • Dependabot and lockfile alerts across 13 microfrontends: a function can collect the alerts and send one weekly summary.
  • Self-healing test tool: a function can receive the failed-run event and start the analysis. The heavy model work should stay on a container, because of the time and memory limits.
  • API Gateway work: you set up an API Gateway trust store with mTLS. API Gateway with a Lambda integration is the natural next step.

Say it as: 'I have not run Lambda in production. On my platform the closest work was X. With Lambda I would do Y, and here is the trade-off.'

Docker

What is the difference between an image and a container?

An image is a read-only template. It has the file system and the start command. A container is a running instance of an image with a thin writable layer on top. You can start many containers from one image. When you delete a container, its writable layer goes away.

How do layers and the build cache work?

Each Dockerfile instruction makes a layer. Docker reuses a cached layer if the instruction and its inputs did not change. A change to one layer rebuilds that layer and all layers after it. So put steps that change rarely first, for example dependency install. Put steps that change often last, for example COPY of source code.

What is a multi-stage build?

A multi-stage build uses one stage to build and a second stage to run. The final image copies only the build output from the first stage. Build tools and source code stay out of the final image. The image becomes smaller and has fewer vulnerabilities.

Name Dockerfile best practices.

  • Use a small, trusted base image with a pinned version.
  • Copy the dependency file first, install, then copy source code.
  • Use multi-stage builds.
  • Run as a non-root user.
  • Add a .dockerignore file.
  • Do not put secrets in the image or in build arguments.
  • Combine related RUN steps and clean package caches in the same step.

What is the difference between an image tag and a digest?

A tag is a name, for example app:1.4.0 or latest. Someone can move a tag to a different image. A digest (sha256:...) is the hash of the image content. A digest never changes. Deploy and promote by digest, so that staging and production run the exact same image.

How does Docker Hub rate limiting affect CI?

Docker Hub limits pulls in a 6-hour window. Unauthenticated pulls get 100 per IPv4 address or IPv6 /64. Authenticated Personal accounts get 200. Pro, Team and Business accounts are unlimited under fair use. Many CI runners can share one IP and hit the limit. To fix it, log in for pulls, use a pull-through cache, or mirror images to ECR.
