CI/CD fundamentals

What is the difference between continuous integration, continuous delivery and continuous deployment?

Continuous integration means that developers merge small changes often, and CI builds and tests each change. Continuous delivery means that every change that passes is ready to release, but a person starts the production release. Continuous deployment means that every change that passes goes to production automatically. Each step needs more trust in the tests.

What are typical pipeline stages?

  1. Checkout and install dependencies (with cache).
  2. Lint and static analysis.
  3. Unit tests.
  4. Build the artifact or image once, and tag it with the commit SHA.
  5. Security scan.
  6. Deploy to a test environment.
  7. API and E2E tests.
  8. Promote the same artifact to staging, then production, with approvals.

How do you handle flaky tests in CI?

First, measure. A test that fails and then passes on retry is flaky. Record each retry. Move a known-flaky test to a quarantine group. The quarantine group still runs, but it does not block merges. Give each quarantined test an owner and an end date. Fix the cause: waits, shared data, test order or environment. Then return the test to the main group.

What is trunk-based development?

Developers merge small changes into one main branch often, at least daily. Branches live for a short time. Unfinished features hide behind feature flags. This needs fast and reliable CI, because main must stay green. Long-lived branches cause large merges and late test failures.

How do feature flags affect testing?

A feature flag turns code on or off without a deploy. Tests must cover the important flag states, not only the default. Set flag values per test or per environment in a controlled way. Remove old flags, because each flag adds test combinations.

Compare Jenkins and GitHub Actions.

  • Jenkins: self-hosted server, Groovy pipelines, very many plugins. You manage upgrades, security and agents.
  • GitHub Actions: YAML workflows next to the code, events from GitHub, a marketplace of actions, and hosted or self-hosted runners.
  • Actions has reusable workflows, OIDC to clouds and environments with approvals built in.

You contributed to a Jenkins to GitHub Actions migration at Joyent. Say what you did, and say that you did not own all CI infrastructure.

Which Slack user sends the message when a GitHub Actions job posts to Slack?

No human user sends it. The message comes from a Slack app. The app has its own identity, with a name and an icon.

There are three ways to do it:

  • Incoming webhook. The message appears as the app. The webhook URL is tied to one channel.
  • Bot token (xoxb-). The message appears as the app's bot user. This is the usual choice.
  • User token (xoxp-). The message appears as a real person. Avoid it. It breaks when that person leaves, and it acts with that person's rights.

So the answer is: a bot user that belongs to a Slack app.

How do you set up GitHub Actions to post to Slack, step by step?

  1. In Slack, open api.slack.com/apps and choose Create New App, then From scratch. Name it, for example CI Bot, and pick the workspace.
  2. Open OAuth & Permissions. Under Bot Token Scopes, add chat:write. Add chat:write.public if the bot must post in public channels without joining them.
  3. Choose Install to Workspace. An admin may need to approve it. Copy the Bot User OAuth Token. It starts with xoxb-.
  4. In Slack, find the channel ID. Open the channel details. The ID is at the bottom and starts with C.
  5. For a private channel, invite the bot with /invite @CI Bot. Public channels need no invite if you added chat:write.public.
  6. In GitHub, open Settings, then Secrets and variables, then Actions. Add the token as SLACK_BOT_TOKEN. Use an environment or organization secret if many repos share it.
  7. Add the step to the workflow. Use if: failure() to post only on failure, or if: always() to post every time.
  8. Run the workflow once on purpose with a failing step. Check that the message arrives.

Incoming webhook or bot token: which do you choose?

Choose by what the message must do.

  • Incoming webhook. It is the simplest. There is one URL, with no scopes and no channel ID. It posts to one fixed channel. It cannot reply in a thread, edit a message or upload a file. Anyone who has the URL can post, so treat it as a secret.
  • Bot token. It needs a little more setup. It can post to any channel the bot can reach. It can reply in a thread, update a message when the run finishes, and upload files. You can also give it narrow scopes.

For one alert to one channel, a webhook is enough. For a message that starts as running and turns into passed or failed, use a bot token with chat.update.

How do you keep a GitHub to Slack integration safe?

  • Store the token or webhook URL as a GitHub secret. Never write it in the workflow file or print it in a log.
  • Give the bot the fewest scopes it needs. Usually that is chat:write.
  • Use environment secrets for production channels, so that only approved jobs can read them.
  • Pin the action to a full commit SHA, not a moving tag. A tag can change after you trust it.
  • Pull requests from forks do not get secrets. This is a feature. Do not work around it with pull_request_target without a careful review.
  • Rotate the token if a person who had access leaves. Use a bot token owned by the app, not a token owned by a person.
  • Send the link to the run, not the log text. Logs can contain data you do not want in Slack.

Tell me how your own E2E workflow notified Slack.

The workflow ran a shared internal action as its last step, only when a job failed. It was given a secret and a channel ID. It posted the suite name, the tier, the region, the job status and a link to the run.

I have not read the source of that action in this review. A secret plus a channel ID fits a bot-token design. In an interview, say what the workflow showed. Then say how you would build it yourself: a Slack app, a bot token with chat:write, a GitHub secret and slackapi/slack-github-action.

One improvement to offer: send one message per run and update it when the run ends, instead of posting a new message for every failure.

Observability

What are logs, metrics and traces?

Logs are records of single events with details. Metrics are numbers over time, for example request rate or test pass rate. They are cheap to store and good for alerts. Traces follow one request across services as a tree of spans. Use metrics to find that something is wrong. Use traces to find where. Use logs to find why.

How do Prometheus and Grafana work together?

Prometheus pulls (scrapes) metrics from /metrics endpoints on a schedule. It stores them as time series with labels. You query them with PromQL. Alertmanager sends alerts from Prometheus rules. Grafana connects to Prometheus and other sources and shows dashboards.

Explain SLI, SLO and error budget.

An SLI is a measured value, for example the percent of CI runs that finish in under 10 minutes. An SLO is the target for that SLI, for example 95 percent over 28 days. The error budget is the allowed miss, here 5 percent. When the budget is used up, the team works on reliability before new features. An SLA is a contract with a customer, and it usually has a lower target than the SLO.

What is OpenTelemetry?

OpenTelemetry is an open standard and a set of SDKs for traces, metrics and logs. Apps send data in the OTLP format to an OpenTelemetry Collector. The collector processes the data and sends it to a backend, for example Prometheus, Jaeger or a vendor tool. You do not lock your code to one vendor.

Which metrics show the health of a test platform?

  • Pass rate and flaky rate per suite and per team.
  • Queue time and run time (p50 and p95).
  • Failure classes: product bug, test bug, infrastructure.
  • Time to diagnose a failure.
  • Adoption: number of teams and framework version spread.
  • Cost per run.

Alert on trends, not on each single failure.

System design (platform-focused)

What are micro-frontends?

A micro-frontend architecture splits one web UI into parts that different teams build and deploy alone. A shell app loads the parts at runtime, for example with Module Federation. Each team owns its part from end to end. Shared design-system components keep the UI consistent. The risks are larger bundles, version conflicts and harder E2E tests across parts.

What is event-driven architecture?

Services publish events when something happens, for example "test run finished". Other services subscribe and react. The publisher does not know the subscribers. This decouples teams and lets you add consumers without changes to the publisher. You must handle duplicate events, event order and schema changes.

Where do you use caching, and what are the risks?

Use a cache to keep the results of slow or frequent reads, for example in Redis or in memory. Common patterns are cache-aside (read the cache, on a miss read the database and fill the cache) and write-through. Set a TTL on each entry. The main risks are stale data and a large load on the database when many entries expire at the same time.

How does rate limiting work?

A rate limiter caps how many requests a client can make in a time window. Common algorithms are token bucket, leaky bucket, fixed window and sliding window. A token bucket allows short bursts and keeps a steady average. When a client is over the limit, return HTTP 429 with a Retry-After header. In a cluster, keep the counters in a shared store such as Redis.

Why put a queue between services?

A queue buffers work between a producer and a consumer. The producer stays fast when the consumer is slow or down. You can scale consumers on queue depth. Failed messages go to a dead-letter queue after a set number of retries. Consumers must be idempotent, because most queues deliver a message at least once.

Coding problems likely for this role

Parse a log file and count errors by type.

Read the file line by line. Use a regular expression to find lines with ERROR and get the error type. Count each type in a map. Sort the map by count, high to low. The time is O(n) for the scan plus O(k log k) for the sort.

Group CI failures by root cause (normalize and dedupe).

Make a fingerprint for each failure message. Replace numbers, IDs, UUIDs and timestamps with placeholders. Use the result as a map key. Put each test name into the list for its key. Sort groups by size so that the biggest root cause comes first.

Retry an operation with exponential backoff.

Call the operation. If it fails, wait and try again. Double the wait after each failure, up to a maximum. Add random jitter so that many clients do not retry at the same time. Stop after a set number of attempts and throw the last error. Retry only errors that can be temporary.

Write a polling wait helper (wait until a condition is true).

Check the condition. If it is true, return. If not, sleep for the poll interval and check again. Stop with a clear error when the timeout passes. Include the last value in the error message, so that the failure is easy to diagnose.

Deep-merge two config objects (defaults plus overrides).

Start with a copy of the defaults. For each key in the overrides: if both values are plain objects, merge them recursively. In all other cases, the override value wins. Arrays are replaced, not merged. Do not change the input objects.

Longest substring without repeating characters (sliding window).

Keep a window with a left and a right pointer. Move right one step at a time. Keep the last index of each character in a map. If the character is already in the window, move left past its last index. Record the largest window size. The time is O(n).

Check if a string is a palindrome (two pointers).

Put one pointer at the start and one at the end. Skip characters that are not letters or digits. Compare the characters without case. Move the pointers toward the center. If two characters are different, return false. The time is O(n) and the space is O(1).

Reverse a linked list.

Keep three references: previous, current and next. For each node, save the next node. Point the current node back to the previous node. Then move previous and current one step forward. At the end, previous is the new head. The time is O(n) and the space is O(1).

Binary tree: root-to-leaf path sum, and level-order traversal (BFS).

Path sum: subtract the node value from the target as you go down. At a leaf, check if the rest is zero. Use recursion (DFS). Level order: use a queue. Take all nodes of the current level from the queue, record their values, and add their children. A UKG Noida report asked the path-sum problem.

Print the prime numbers from 1 to N efficiently.

Use the Sieve of Eratosthenes. Mark all numbers as prime at the start. For each prime p, starting at 2, mark p*p, p*p+p and so on as not prime. Stop when p*p is larger than N. The time is O(N log log N). A UKG Noida report asked this for N = 200.

2025–2026 fact updates

These facts changed recently. Older blog posts and videos can teach the old version. Use the statement in the middle column in the interview.

TopicSay thisSource
GitHub required workflowsThe old "required workflows" feature no longer exists. GitHub retired it on October 18, 2023, and moved it into repository rulesets. Use an organization ruleset with the "Require workflows to pass before merging" rule. Say "rulesets", not "required workflows", in the interview.GitHub Actions: Required Workflows will move to Repository Rules (GitHub Changelog, 2023-08-02)
Reusable workflow limitsSince November 2025, a workflow run can nest reusable workflows up to 10 levels deep. One run can call up to 50 workflows in total. The old limits were 4 levels and 20 workflows. Loops in the workflow tree are not permitted.New releases for GitHub Actions – November 2025 (GitHub Changelog)
secrets: inherit and versioning reusable workflowssecrets: inherit passes the caller's secrets implicitly. It works only for callers in the same organization or enterprise. Secrets go only to the directly called workflow. A nested workflow gets a secret only if the middle workflow passes it on. Reference a shared workflow by a commit SHA, a tag or a branch. GitHub says that a commit SHA is the safest option.Reuse workflows (GitHub Docs)
Action pinning and blocking policySince August 2025, an admin can require that all actions are pinned to a full commit SHA. A workflow that uses an unpinned action then fails. An admin can also block an action or a version with a ! prefix in the allowed-actions policy. The block list overrides the allow list.GitHub Actions policy now supports blocking and SHA pinning actions (GitHub Changelog, 2025-08-15)
Secure use: pinning, masking, GITHUB_TOKENA full-length commit SHA is the only way to use an action as an immutable release. Structured data, for example JSON, can make secret masking fail in logs. Register a derived or generated secret value as a secret, so that the log masks it. Set the default GITHUB_TOKEN permission to read-only and add write scopes per job.Secure use reference (GitHub Docs)
Fork PRs and secretsWhen a fork triggers a pull_request workflow, GitHub does not pass secrets to the runner. The only exception is GITHUB_TOKEN. The GITHUB_TOKEN is read-only for pull requests from forks.Events that trigger workflows (GitHub Docs)
pull_request_target guidance (2025 change)pull_request_target runs in the context of the base repository and can use secrets. Do not build or run code from the pull request in this trigger. Since December 8, 2025, the workflow file and checkout always come from the default branch. Environment branch rules for pull_request now check the merge ref (refs/pull/N/merge). For pull_request_target, they check the default branch.Actions pull_request_target and environment branch protections changes (GitHub Changelog, 2025-11-07)
OIDC from GitHub Actions to AWSGive the job permissions: id-token: write (and contents: read for checkout). Create an IAM OIDC provider for https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com with audience sts.amazonaws.com. Use aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials with role-to-assume. Limit the trust policy sub claim, for example repo:org/repo:environment:prod. id-token: write lets the job request a token only. It does not give write access to resources.Configuring OpenID Connect in Amazon Web Services (GitHub Docs)
OIDC subject claim format (2026)Repositories created after July 15, 2026 use immutable IDs in the sub claim, for example repo:org@123/repo@456:ref:refs/heads/main. Repositories that opt in also use this format. Check the claim format before you write an IAM trust policy for a new repository.Configuring OpenID Connect in Amazon Web Services (GitHub Docs)
GitHub-hosted larger runnersLarger runners are available only on the GitHub Team and GitHub Enterprise Cloud plans. They support autoscaling and GPU options. Linux and Windows larger runners can get static IP ranges and Azure private networking. Static IPs let you add the runners to a firewall allow list.Larger runners (GitHub Docs)
GitHub Actions pricing 2026GitHub cut hosted-runner prices by up to 39% on January 1, 2026. GitHub announced a $0.002 per-minute platform charge for self-hosted runners for March 1, 2026. On December 15, 2025, GitHub postponed that charge with no new date. Public repositories stay free.Pricing changes for GitHub Actions (GitHub Resources)
Actions Runner Controller (ARC)ARC is a Kubernetes operator for self-hosted runners. GitHub supports only the Autoscaling Runner Sets mode (gha-runner-scale-set Helm charts). The community supports the legacy ARC mode, and GitHub Support does not. A listener pod long-polls GitHub and scales ephemeral runner pods. Each runner runs one job and is then deleted.About Actions Runner Controller / Support for ARC (GitHub Docs)
ARC 0.14.0 (March 2026)ARC 0.14.0 lets one runner scale set have many labels. Workflows can target it with combined labels in runs-on. ARC now uses the public actions/scaleset Go client.Actions Runner Controller release 0.14.0 (GitHub Changelog, 2026-03-19)
Artifact actions v4actions/upload-artifact and actions/download-artifact v3 stopped working on January 30, 2025. Use v4 or later. v4 has breaking changes, so read the migration guide before you upgrade shared workflows.Deprecation notice: v3 of the artifact actions (GitHub Changelog)
Docker Hub pull rate limitsDocker Hub counts pulls in a 6-hour window. Unauthenticated users get 100 pulls per IPv4 address or IPv6 /64 subnet. Authenticated Personal users get 200 pulls. Pro, Team and Business users have no pull limit, under fair use. Many CI runners behind one IP can share the unauthenticated limit.Docker Hub pull usage and limits (Docker Docs)
EKS Pod Identity vs IRSAAWS recommends EKS Pod Identity for new workloads when possible. Pod Identity needs no OIDC provider. The role trusts one service principal, pods.eks.amazonaws.com, so one role works in many clusters. A Pod Identity Agent DaemonSet gives credentials to pods on its node. IRSA still works and is required for Fargate, Windows nodes, EKS Anywhere and self-managed clusters.Grant Kubernetes workloads access to AWS / EKS Pod Identity (Amazon EKS User Guide)
EKS Pod Identity limitsPod Identity works only on Linux EC2 nodes. It does not support Fargate pods or Windows EC2 nodes. A cluster can have up to 5,000 associations. Associations are eventually consistent, so do not create them in a critical code path. For cross-account access, chain to a role in the other account.Learn how EKS Pod Identity grants pods access to AWS services (Amazon EKS User Guide)
AWS Load Balancer Controller: target type ipUse the AWS Load Balancer Controller, not the legacy in-tree controller. Use target type ip: alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/target-type: ip for an ALB, or service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-nlb-target-type: ip for an NLB. With ip, the load balancer sends traffic directly to pod IPs, and target health matches pod health. With instance mode, traffic goes through a NodePort and can cross nodes and zones.Load Balancing (Amazon EKS Best Practices Guide)
Zero-downtime on EKS: deregistration and readiness gatesThe ALB deregistration delay is 300 seconds by default. Add a preStop hook, for example sleep 10, so the pod keeps serving while the load balancer and iptables catch up. Enable pod readiness gates from the AWS Load Balancer Controller. With readiness gates, a rollout does not stop old pods until new pods are healthy in the target group.Load Balancing (Amazon EKS Best Practices Guide)
Karpenter statusKarpenter is stable. Version 1.0 was released in August 2024. The stable APIs are NodePool and EC2NodeClass (older names were Provisioner and AWSNodeTemplate). Consolidation uses WhenEmptyOrUnderutilized. Drift is on by default. Disruption budgets can be set per reason and on a cron schedule.Announcing Karpenter 1.0 (AWS Blog)
EKS Auto ModeEKS Auto Mode lets AWS manage nodes, autoscaling (built on Karpenter), load balancing, block storage, pod networking and the Pod Identity Agent. Nodes use locked-down Bottlerocket-based AMIs and live 21 days at most. You still own the application, the VPC and the cluster configuration. Mention it as an option that reduces node operations for a platform team.Automate cluster infrastructure with EKS Auto Mode (Amazon EKS User Guide)
KEDA Selenium Grid scalerThe KEDA Selenium Grid scaler adds browser nodes for the requests that wait in the Grid session queue. It reads the queue from the Grid GraphQL endpoint (url). Set browserName to match the queued requests. Set nodeMaxSessions to match the node --max-sessions value. Volvo Cars and SeleniumHQ maintain the scaler. The current KEDA release line is 2.21.Selenium Grid Scaler (KEDA docs)
VPC CNI prefix delegationSet ENABLE_PREFIX_DELEGATION=true on the VPC CNI (v1.9.0 or later). Each ENI slot then gets a /28 prefix (16 IPs) instead of one IP. This lets a node run many more pods. Prefixes need contiguous free blocks, so a fragmented subnet can fail with InsufficientCidrBlocks. Use a new subnet or CIDR reservations, and roll out with new node groups.Prefix Mode for Linux (Amazon EKS Best Practices Guide)
Kubernetes sidecar containersNative sidecar containers are stable since Kubernetes v1.33. A sidecar is an init container with restartPolicy: Always. It starts before the main containers and keeps running with them. The feature gate is locked on.Sidecar Containers (Kubernetes docs)
Kubernetes probesKubernetes has three probes. A liveness probe failure restarts the container. A readiness probe failure removes the pod from Service endpoints, and it runs for the whole life of the container. A startup probe stops liveness and readiness checks until the app has started. All three are stable features.Liveness, Readiness, and Startup Probes (Kubernetes docs)
In-place pod resizeIn-place pod resize is stable since Kubernetes v1.35. You can change CPU and memory requests and limits of a running pod without a restart in many cases.Kubernetes 1.35: In-Place Pod Resize Graduates to Stable (Kubernetes blog)
Ingress NGINX retirementThe community Ingress NGINX controller is retired. Best-effort maintenance ended in March 2026, and it gets no more releases or security fixes. The Kubernetes Ingress API still exists. Kubernetes recommends Gateway API for new work. On EKS, use the AWS Load Balancer Controller for ALB and NLB.Ingress NGINX Retirement: What You Need to Know (Kubernetes blog)
Playwright sharding and merged reportsRun npx playwright test --shard=x/y on each machine. With fullyParallel: true, shards split by test, so they are balanced. Without it, shards split by file. Use the blob reporter in CI. Merge the shard results with npx playwright merge-reports --reporter html ./all-blob-reports.Sharding (Playwright docs)
Playwright CLI features--last-failed runs only the tests that failed in the last run (added in v1.44). --only-changed runs only test files changed since a git ref (added in v1.46). --ui opens UI mode (added in v1.32). Recent releases add Test Agents (v1.56) and aria snapshots (toMatchAriaSnapshot, v1.49). The release notes list v1.64 as the latest version.Playwright release notes (playwright.dev) and v1.44.0 release (GitHub)
Selenium Grid 4 componentsGrid 4 has these components: Router (the entry point), New Session Queue (FIFO of new-session requests), Distributor (assigns requests to Nodes), Session Map (session ID to Node), Event Bus (messages between components), and Node (runs browsers in slots). There is no single "hub" process in fully distributed mode.Grid components (selenium.dev)
Selenium ManagerSelenium Manager ships with Selenium since 4.6. It finds, downloads and caches the correct driver. Since 4.11 it can also download Chrome for Testing. Firefox support came in 4.12 and Edge in 4.14. The Selenium docs still call it beta (version 0.x). It is the official driver manager, so you do not need WebDriverManager for most setups.Selenium Manager (selenium.dev)
Selenium WebDriver BiDiSelenium moves from WebDriver Classic to the W3C WebDriver BiDi protocol. BiDi adds a WebSocket so the browser can stream events, for example network and console events. Selenium says that its CDP support is temporary until BiDi is complete.WebDriver BiDi (selenium.dev)
Semantic VersioningSemVer 2.0.0 uses MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH. Increase MAJOR for incompatible API changes, MINOR for backward-compatible features, and PATCH for backward-compatible fixes. When you mark public API as deprecated, increase MINOR. Never change the contents of a published version. Version 0.y.z means that anything can change.Semantic Versioning 2.0.0 (semver.org)
Renovate and GitHub Actions digestsRenovate can pin GitHub Actions to commit SHAs with the helpers:pinGitHubActionDigests preset. It then updates the SHA and the version comment together, for example @<sha> # v4.0.0. Renovate does not update a bare SHA that has no version comment.GitHub Actions manager (Renovate docs)
Dependabot optionsDependabot supports the github-actions ecosystem. Use groups to put many updates in one pull request. Use cooldown to wait a set number of days before Dependabot proposes a new version. cooldown applies to version updates, not to security updates.Dependabot options reference (GitHub Docs)
UKG product namesUKG Dimensions is now named UKG Pro Workforce Management, part of the UKG Pro suite. UKG Ready is the HR and payroll suite for small and mid-size businesses. Use the current names in the interview.UKG Dimensions is now UKG Pro Workforce Management (ukg.com)
Chapter 10

Glossary

AWS Load Balancer Controller
The controller that makes an ALB from an Ingress and an NLB from a LoadBalancer Service.
Cluster
A group of machines that Kubernetes controls as one system.
Cluster Autoscaler
A tool that changes the size of node groups when pods cannot fit.
ConfigMap / Secret
Objects that hold settings and sensitive values outside the image.
Control plane
The part of the cluster that makes decisions: API server, etcd, scheduler and controller manager.
DaemonSet
An object that runs one pod on every node.
Deployment
An object that keeps N copies of a stateless pod and does rolling updates.
EKS Pod Identity
The newer way to map a ServiceAccount to an IAM role through an association and an agent.
EndpointSlice
The live list of ready pod IPs behind a Service.
Exit code 137
The process got SIGKILL; with reason OOMKilled, it used more memory than its limit.
HPA
The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler; it changes the pod count from a metric.
Ingress
HTTP routing rules from outside the cluster to Services.
IRSA
IAM Roles for Service Accounts: a pod assumes an IAM role through an OIDC token.
Job / CronJob
A Job runs pods to completion; a CronJob makes Jobs on a schedule.
Karpenter
A node autoscaler that starts right-sized EC2 instances directly for Pending pods.
KEDA
An event-driven autoscaler that scales pods on queue length and can scale to zero.
kubelet
The agent on each node that starts containers and runs probes.
Liveness probe
A check that decides if a container must be restarted.
Namespace
A folder in the cluster that separates teams and holds quotas and RBAC.
Node
A machine, usually an EC2 instance, that runs pods.
Pod
The smallest unit in Kubernetes: one or more containers that share one IP.
PodDisruptionBudget
A rule that limits how many pods of an app a voluntary drain can stop at one time.
QoS class
Guaranteed, Burstable or BestEffort; it sets the eviction order under node pressure.
RBAC
Roles and bindings that allow actions on Kubernetes objects.
Readiness probe
A check that decides if a pod gets traffic.
ReplicaSet
An object that keeps an exact number of identical pods; a Deployment makes it.
Request / limit
A request reserves resources for scheduling; a limit caps use at runtime.
Service
A stable name and IP in front of a group of ready pods.
ServiceAccount
The identity of a pod for RBAC and AWS permissions.
Startup probe
A check that gives a slow app time to boot before liveness starts.
StatefulSet
An object for pods that need stable names and their own disks.
Taint / toleration
A taint on a node keeps pods away unless the pod has a matching toleration.
Target group
The AWS list of targets that a load balancer sends traffic to and checks for health.
VPC CNI
The EKS network plugin that gives each pod a real VPC IP address.

Staff Engineer · P4 · Noida · DevOps 2

DevOps 2: Architecture and Leadership

The next round is with the hiring manager. It may also include an architect. This view prepares for both. It does not repeat the DevOps 1 test platform content. It covers system architecture, design prompts, AI in production and Claude Code, Staff leadership and the pressure follow-ups that interviewers add.

How each question works

Read the interviewer quote. Say the 30-second answer out loud, then stop. Read the full answer only when you need depth. Learn each concept card.

Do this first

Fill the story bank in LD10 with your real stories. Leadership answers fail when the examples are vague. Never use a story that did not happen to you.

Switch tabs

Use the Development, DevOps 1 and DevOps 2 buttons in the toolbar. Your studied marks, theme and settings are shared across all three tabs.

Study sessions, in this order

  1. Session 1Read Who is in the room. Then architecture lessons 1 to 3: trade-offs, how to split a system, and how services talk. Draw the strangler fig from memory.
  2. Session 2Architecture lessons 4 to 9: resilience, data, scale, reliability, security and platform design. Then say AR1 to AR4 out loud.
  3. Session 3Say AR5 to AR11 out loud. For each one, name the trade-off you accept. Then do the architecture quick-fire list.
  4. Session 4Do the system design prompts AR12 to AR17 on paper, with a timer of 35 minutes each. Then do the pressure drill in AR18.
  5. Session 5Read UKG and AI: what is public. Then the five AI lessons. Say AI1 to AI9 out loud. Be ready to explain MCP versus APIs in 30 seconds.
  6. Session 6Read the leadership lessons. Then fill the story bank in LD10 with real stories. Do this on paper before you speak.
  7. Session 7Say LD1 to LD9 and LD11 to LD20 out loud. Pick five questions to ask them.
Chapter 01

Who is in the room

You do not know which of the two will lead the round. Prepare one set of answers and change the angle. The hiring manager asks if you can lead and deliver. The architect asks if you can design and defend a system.

Hiring manager and architect compared
WhoCares aboutTypical questionsYour moveRed flags
Hiring managerCan this person lead, deliver and fit my team? Will they raise the bar and not create drama?Career story, why Staff, influence, conflict, failure, prioritising, first 90 days.Give outcomes and people impact. Use real stories. Show judgement and calm.Vague stories. Blaming others. No numbers. Wants to be the hero.
ArchitectDoes this person think in trade-offs? Can they design, defend and evolve a system?Design a system, monolith or services, resilience, data, security, build or buy.State requirements first. Compare options. Name the trade-off and the risk. Draw a simple picture.One answer with no alternatives. Buzzwords. Ignores cost, failure and operations.

Tips

  • Ask at the start: "What would you like me to focus on?" The answer tells you who you have.
  • Use the same story for every audience. Change the first sentence. For the architect, start with the design choice. For the manager, start with the people and the result.
  • If the interviewer is an architect, expect a whiteboard or a verbal design. Say your assumptions out loud.
  • Both of them score the same six signals: framing the problem, justified choices, depth on the riskiest part, simplicity, technical depth and decisiveness. Show them in every answer.
Chapter 02

Architecture concepts

Nine short lessons. Each one has the problem it solves, a table or diagram, and one line to remember. Read them before the architecture questions.

Lesson 01

The problem it solvesAn architect is asked why, not what. Every design is a bundle of trade-offs. If you name the trade-off before you are asked, you sound senior.

Start every design with the qualities that matter. Ask which two or three are most important. You cannot maximise all of them.

QualityQuestion to askWhat it often costs
PerformanceHow fast must a request be? At what percentile?More caches, more memory, more complexity
ScalabilityHow many users and how much data in one year?Distributed design, harder debugging
AvailabilityHow much downtime can the business accept?Redundancy, more cost, harder data rules
ConsistencyWhat happens if two users see different data for a moment?Lower availability or higher latency
SecurityWhat data is sensitive? Who is the attacker?Friction, slower delivery
CostWhat is the budget per user or per run?Fewer safety margins
OperabilityWho runs it at 3 AM?More tooling, more training
ChangeabilityHow often will this change, and who changes it?Extra layers, more interfaces
TestabilityCan we test it fast and in isolation?Design for seams and fakes

Write down big decisions in a short record. An Architecture Decision Record (ADR) takes ten minutes and saves months of arguing.

Draw the system at the right zoom level. The C4 model gives four levels.

  1. Context: the system and the people and systems around it
  2. Containers: the apps, services and data stores
  3. Components: the parts inside one container
  4. Code: classes or modules, only when needed

RememberName the two or three qualities that matter. Compare options. Record the decision and when to revisit it.

Lesson 02

The problem it solvesTeams split systems too early or too late. Both cost a lot. You need a clear rule for when to split.

StyleGood whenMain cost
MonolithSmall team, unclear domain, fast changeOne deploy unit. Can become tangled
Modular monolithMedium team, clear modules, one deployNeeds discipline to keep module walls
MicroservicesMany teams, different scale or release needsNetwork, data splits, tracing, many pipelines

Conway's law says that a system copies the communication structure of the organisation that builds it. Design the teams and the boundaries together.

Good signs that a split is worth it:

  • Two parts need very different scaling or availability.
  • Two teams block each other on every release.
  • One part needs a different technology or security zone.
  • A part has its own clear data and its own business owner.

Bad signs: you split to look modern, or the pieces share one database and always change together. That is a distributed monolith. It has all the cost and none of the benefit.

To change a legacy system, use the strangler fig pattern. Put a facade in front. Move one slice at a time behind it. Remove the old slice when the new one is proven.

flowchart LR
  U[Users] --> F{Facade or router}
  F -->|old routes| L[Legacy system]
  F -->|moved routes| N[New service]
  L --> DB1[(Legacy DB)]
  N --> DB2[(New DB)]
  DB1 -. sync or CDC .-> DB2

RememberStart modular. Split for a reason: scale, team, security or data ownership. Migrate with a facade, one slice at a time.

Lesson 03

The problem it solvesThe way services talk decides how they fail. Pick sync or async on purpose, per interaction.

StyleUse it whenWatch out for
Request and response (REST, gRPC)The caller needs the answer nowCaller slows down when the callee is slow
Queue (SQS, RabbitMQ)Work can wait. One consumer group takes each job.Duplicates, poison messages, no replay
Event log (Kafka, Kinesis)Many consumers. You need replay and ordering per key.Operations cost, partition design
Pub/sub (SNS, EventBridge)Fan out an event to many subscribersSubscribers must handle duplicates and order

Most brokers deliver at least once. A message can arrive twice. So the consumer must be idempotent. Exactly-once delivery in the whole system is not a safe thing to promise.

Idempotency key
Idea

A repeat of the same request has the same result as one request.

Example

A payment call carries a unique key. The server stores the key and the result.

Term

The server keeps a key-to-result record and returns the stored result for a repeated key.

Dead-letter queue (DLQ)
Idea

A side queue for messages that keep failing.

Example

After five failed tries, the message moves to the DLQ. A person looks at it.

Term

A queue configured with a maximum receive count and a target for failed messages.

Outbox pattern
Idea

Write the event and the data change in one local transaction. A relay sends the event later.

Example

An order row and an OrderCreated row are saved together. A worker publishes the event.

Term

A transactional outbox table plus a relay or change-data-capture process.

Saga
Idea

A long business action made of local steps. Each step has an undo step.

Example

Reserve stock, take payment, ship. If payment fails, release the stock.

Term

Choreography (events) or orchestration (a coordinator) with compensating actions.

RememberSync when the caller needs the answer. Async when work can wait. Always design for duplicates.

Lesson 04

The problem it solvesIn a distributed system, something is always failing. A slow dependency is worse than a dead one, because it eats threads and memory until everything stops.

  • Timeouts. Every call has one. No timeout means a thread waits forever.
  • Retries with backoff and jitter. Wait longer after each try, and add random time. Retry only safe calls. Set a retry budget so retries cannot triple the load.
  • Circuit breaker. After many failures, stop calling for a while. Then test with a few calls.
  • Bulkhead. Separate pools for separate dependencies, so one slow part cannot use all the threads.
  • Load shedding and rate limits. Reject extra work early, with a clear error, so the core keeps working.
  • Graceful degradation. Serve a cached or reduced answer when a part is down.
  • Back-pressure. Tell the sender to slow down, or let the queue grow safely.
stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> Closed
  Closed --> Open: failures pass the threshold
  Open --> HalfOpen: wait time ends
  HalfOpen --> Closed: test calls succeed
  HalfOpen --> Open: a test call fails

A retry storm is a common cause of big outages. A service slows down. Every client retries. The load triples. The service never recovers. Backoff, jitter and a retry budget stop it.

RememberTimeout, limited retry, breaker, bulkhead, shed load, degrade. Prove it with a failure test.

Lesson 05

The problem it solvesData decisions are the hardest to change later. Architects are judged on how well they choose and explain them.

CAP theorem
Idea

When the network splits, a system must choose between consistency and availability.

Example

A bank ledger may refuse writes during a split. A product page may show slightly old data.

Term

In a partition, a distributed store cannot give both linearizable consistency and full availability.

PACELC
Idea

Even with no split, you trade latency against consistency.

Example

A replica read is fast but may be slightly old.

Term

If Partition: choose A or C. Else: choose Latency or Consistency.

Eventual consistency
Idea

Replicas agree after some time if writes stop.

Example

A new profile photo shows on one device a few seconds before another.

Term

Convergence of replicas in the absence of new updates.

ACID and BASE
Idea

ACID protects each transaction. BASE accepts temporary inconsistency for scale and uptime.

Example

A bank transfer needs ACID. A like counter can be BASE.

Term

Atomicity, consistency, isolation, durability versus basically available, soft state, eventual consistency.

TechniqueHelps withCost
Cache-asideRead-heavy dataStale data. You must invalidate
Write-through cacheFresh reads after writesSlower writes
Read replicasMore read capacityReplica lag
ShardingMore write capacity and data sizeHard queries across shards. Hot shards
CQRS (separate read model)Very different read and write needsTwo models to keep in sync

Pick the shard key with care. A good key spreads load evenly and keeps related rows together. A bad key makes a hot shard.

RememberSay which data needs strong consistency and which can be stale. Cache with an invalidation plan. Choose shard keys for even load.

Lesson 06

The problem it solvesArchitects must give a number. Saying that the system scales is not an answer. Show a simple estimate and the first bottleneck.

  • Keep services stateless. Put state in a database, cache or queue. Then you add instances to add capacity.
  • Scale on the right signal. CPU works for web servers. Queue depth or age works for workers.
  • Use queue-based load levelling. A queue absorbs a spike, and workers drain it at a safe rate.
  • Find the first bottleneck. It is often the database, a shared lock or a slow downstream call.

Back-of-envelope math that you can do in your head:

  • 1 million requests per day is about 12 requests per second on average (1,000,000 divided by 86,400).
  • Peak is often 3 to 10 times the average. Ask for the real peak.
  • Little's law: the number in the system equals the arrival rate times the time each one spends. 100 requests per second at 0.2 seconds each means about 20 in flight.
  • Storage: rows per day times row size times days kept times copies.

Known peaks can be pre-scaled. If the load rises every Monday at 9 AM, add capacity at 8:45 and do not wait for the autoscaler.

RememberStateless services, the right scaling signal, queues for spikes, and a simple estimate.

Lesson 07

The problem it solvesReliability is a business choice with a price. SLOs turn it into numbers that product and engineering can agree on.

SLI, SLO, SLA
Idea

An SLI is a measurement. An SLO is the target. An SLA is a contract with a penalty.

Example

SLI: share of requests under 300 ms. SLO: 99.5% over 30 days. SLA: a refund if you miss it.

Term

Service level indicator, objective and agreement.

Error budget
Idea

The amount of failure your SLO allows. Spend it on change.

Example

A 99.9% SLO allows about 43 minutes of bad time in 30 days.

Term

Error budget = 1 minus the SLO. Burn-rate alerts warn when it is used too fast.

RTO and RPO
Idea

RTO is how long you can be down. RPO is how much data you can lose.

Example

RTO 1 hour, RPO 5 minutes.

Term

Recovery time objective and recovery point objective.

DR strategyRTO and RPOCost
Backup and restoreHoursLowest
Pilot lightTens of minutes to hoursLow
Warm standbyMinutesMedium
Active-active in two regionsNear zeroHighest, and hard data rules

Safe release methods: blue-green (two full copies, switch traffic), canary (a small share first), feature flags (ship dark, turn on later), and a fast rollback. Pair them with automatic checks on error rate and latency.

RememberAgree the SLO, then spend the error budget on change. Pick DR by RTO, RPO and cost. Release in small steps.

Lesson 08

The problem it solvesA platform that holds sensitive data, such as employee records, needs security by design. A review that finds a flaw late is expensive.

  • Least privilege. Each person, job and service gets only what it needs.
  • Zero trust. Do not trust a request because it comes from inside the network. Check identity every time.
  • Short-lived identity. Use OIDC and workload identity. Avoid long-lived keys.
  • Secrets. Keep them in a secret manager. Rotate them. Never put them in code or logs.
  • Encrypt data in transit and at rest. Use a key service with an audit trail.
  • Audit. Log who did what, to which record, and when.
  • Supply chain. Pin versions, scan images, sign artifacts and keep a list of components.
STRIDE threatExampleTypical control
SpoofingA fake service calls your APIStrong authentication
TamperingData changed in transitTLS, signatures
RepudiationA user denies an actionAudit logs
Information disclosureOne tenant reads another tenant's dataIsolation, encryption, tests
Denial of serviceA flood of requestsRate limits, quotas
Elevation of privilegeA user becomes adminLeast privilege, review
Tenant modelMeaningTrade-off
SiloSeparate stack or database per tenantStrong isolation. High cost and ops load
PoolShared stack. Tenant ID on every rowLow cost. Needs strict checks and noisy-neighbour control
BridgeShared compute, separate data storeMiddle path

RememberLeast privilege, short-lived identity, encrypted data, audit logs, and a tenant model that you can test.

Lesson 09

The problem it solvesA Staff engineer on a platform or tools team builds things that other teams choose to use. That needs product thinking.

  • Golden path. The easiest way is also the safe and supported way. Teams can leave it, but they take on the cost.
  • Platform as a product. Know your users. Measure adoption. Take feedback. Write docs.
  • Guardrails, not gates. Automate the rule in the pipeline instead of asking for a review.

A healthy test strategy is a pyramid. Many fast unit tests. Fewer service and contract tests. Few end-to-end tests for the key journeys.

  • Contract tests (for example Pact) check that a consumer and a provider agree, without a full environment.
  • Ephemeral environments give each pull request a clean, short-lived copy.
  • Test data must be owned, isolated and cheap to create.
  • Flaky tests are tracked, quarantined with an owner and fixed. A flaky test that is ignored teaches teams to ignore red.

Measure delivery with the four DORA metrics: deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate and time to restore service. Add platform measures such as time to green and flake rate.

RememberMake the right way the easy way. Measure adoption and delivery, not activity.

Chapter 03

Architecture and system design questions

Design questions for an architect or a hiring manager. Use the same shape each time: ask about the needs, name the trade-offs, choose, then say how you would check it works. AR12 to AR17 are design prompts. AR18 is the pressure drill.

UKG-AR1

Interviewer

A SaaS product serves thousands of customer companies. Every company runs a heavy job at the same time each week. Design the architecture.

What this tests The architect tests if you ask for requirements first, choose a tenancy model on purpose and plan for peaks and noisy neighbours.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

I would ask for the peak load, the data sensitivity and the recovery targets first. Then I would use a pooled, stateless service tier with a tenant ID on every request and row. Heavy jobs go through queues with per-tenant limits. Workers scale on queue depth, and I pre-scale for the known weekly peak. Large or regulated customers can get a silo. I would measure everything per tenant.

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. Ask for the requirements

    How many tenants and users? What is the peak per second and how long does it last? What data is sensitive? What are the RTO and RPO? Do any customers need a fixed region? Write the answers as numbers.

  2. 2. Choose the tenancy model

    Start with a pool: shared compute and shared data, with a tenant ID in every table. Offer a silo for the few customers who need it. Say the trade-off: pool is cheap but needs strict isolation checks.

  3. 3. Draw the request path

    Edge and gateway, then stateless API services, then a queue for heavy work, then workers, then the database. The tenant ID comes from the signed token. It is never taken from the request body.

  4. 4. Protect against noisy neighbours

    Use per-tenant rate limits and quotas. Use separate queues or priorities for big tenants. Use fair scheduling in the workers, so one tenant cannot use all of them.

  5. 5. Scale for the peak

    Scale workers on queue depth and message age. The peak is known, so add capacity 15 minutes before it. Test with a load test that copies the real pattern, not a flat one.

  6. 6. Isolate and protect the data

    Add row-level security or a mandatory tenant filter in the data layer. Use per-tenant encryption keys for sensitive data. Write tests that prove tenant A cannot read tenant B.

  7. 7. Observe by tenant

    Tag logs, metrics and traces with the tenant ID. Show the top tenants by load and by errors. This shows who is a noisy neighbour in minutes.

Concepts you must own 3

Noisy neighbour
Idea

One tenant uses so much that others slow down.

Example

One company starts a huge job and every other company waits.

Term

A resource contention problem in shared infrastructure.

Queue-based load levelling
Idea

A queue holds a spike. Workers take jobs at a steady rate.

Example

10,000 jobs arrive at 9:00. Workers finish them by 9:20.

Term

A buffering pattern that decouples producer rate from consumer rate.

Row-level security
Idea

The database only returns rows that belong to the caller's tenant.

Example

A policy adds tenant_id = current_tenant() to every query.

Term

A database feature that enforces a policy per row.

Follow-up questions

  • How do you move one big tenant from pool to silo?

    Use the tenant ID as the key. Copy the tenant's data to the new stack. Run both in parallel and compare. Then switch the router entry for that tenant. Keep a rollback for a week.

  • What if the weekly peak doubles?

    Check the first bottleneck with a load test. It is often the database. Add read replicas, caching or sharding by tenant. Also move some work to off-peak, if the business allows it.

  • How do you price the cost per tenant?

    Tag all usage by tenant. Share the fixed cost by usage. Report the cost per tenant each month. It shows which plans lose money.

Caution
  • Taking the tenant ID from the request and not from the token.
  • One queue for all tenants. A single large tenant blocks the rest.
  • Scaling only on CPU. A queue backlog can grow while the CPU is low.
  • Skipping the isolation tests.
Staff signal

A Staff answer starts with numbers, picks a tenancy model and names its cost. It plans for the noisy neighbour and for the known peak, and it proves isolation with tests.

UKG-AR2

Interviewer

A team of 12 engineers owns a large monolith. Releases are slow. A director says: "Let's move to microservices." What do you say?

What this tests The architect tests if you can resist a fashion, find the real problem and choose the smallest change that fixes it.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

I would first find out what hurts: slow builds, team conflicts, scale or risk. Twelve engineers rarely need microservices. I would start with a modular monolith, clear module boundaries and a faster pipeline. I would split out a service only for a clear reason, such as different scaling or a separate owner. Each split needs its own data and its own team.

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. Find the real problem

    Ask what the director wants to fix. Collect data: build time, deploy frequency, change failure rate, and where the team waits. The cause may be a slow pipeline or a tangled code base, not the deployment shape.

  2. 2. Compare the options

    Option A: keep the monolith and fix the pipeline. Option B: a modular monolith with enforced boundaries. Option C: extract services. Show the cost and benefit of each.

  3. 3. Explain the cost of services

    Services add network calls, partial failure, data that is split, versioning, many pipelines and more on-call work. A 12-person team pays this cost with few people to share it.

  4. 4. Set the split rules

    Split only if one of these is true. The part needs different scale or availability. A separate team owns it. It sits in a different security zone. It needs a different release speed. Do not split if the parts share one database and change together.

  5. 5. Plan the first extraction

    Pick a part with clear edges. Use the strangler fig pattern. Add a facade, move one slice, run in parallel, then remove the old code. Measure build time and incidents before and after.

  6. 6. Protect the module walls now

    Add automated checks that fail when a module reaches into another module's internals. This gives most of the benefit and keeps the option to split later.

Concepts you must own 3

Modular monolith
Idea

One deployable unit with strict internal modules.

Example

Billing and Orders are separate modules. They talk through public interfaces only.

Term

A single deployment with enforced module boundaries.

Distributed monolith
Idea

Many services that must change and deploy together.

Example

Five services share one database. One schema change breaks all five.

Term

An anti-pattern with the cost of distribution and the coupling of a monolith.

Conway's law
Idea

The system copies how people communicate.

Example

Three teams build a compiler with three passes.

Term

Systems mirror the communication structure of the organisation.

Follow-up questions

  • What if the director insists?

    Offer a pilot with a clear success measure. Extract one low-risk service. Agree the numbers up front, such as build time or deploy frequency. Decide with data after one quarter.

  • How do you keep module walls in a monolith?

    Use build tools that forbid cross-module imports, or architecture tests. Fail the pipeline on a break. Review the rule when it blocks real work.

Caution
  • Saying yes to microservices because it sounds modern.
  • Splitting the code and keeping one shared database.
  • Extracting with no owner for the new service.
  • Doing a big-bang rewrite.
Staff signal

A Staff answer questions the premise, uses data, offers a smaller first step and names clear rules for when to split.

UKG-AR3

Interviewer

A payment-status service becomes slow. Soon the checkout service, the API gateway and the web app all fail. How do you stop this from happening again?

What this tests The architect tests if you understand cascading failure and know the standard resilience patterns and how to prove them.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

A slow dependency uses up threads and connections until the callers fail too. I would set timeouts on every call, limit retries with backoff and a budget, and add a circuit breaker. I would add bulkheads so one dependency cannot use every thread. For non-critical data I would return a cached or reduced answer. Then I would prove it with a failure test.

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. Explain the failure

    The slow service holds each request open. The caller's threads wait. The pool is full. New requests queue and time out. Callers retry, and the load grows. This is a cascading failure.

  2. 2. Timeouts everywhere

    Set a connect and a read timeout on every call. The timeout is shorter than the caller's own limit. Use a deadline that passes down the call chain.

  3. 3. Careful retries

    Retry only safe, idempotent calls. Use exponential backoff and random jitter. Set a retry budget, for example no more than 10 per cent extra load.

  4. 4. Circuit breaker

    After many failures, open the breaker and fail fast. After a wait, let a few test calls through. Close the breaker when they succeed.

  5. 5. Bulkheads and load shedding

    Give each dependency its own pool. When the system is full, reject low-priority requests early with a clear error. Keep the core path alive.

  6. 6. Degrade on purpose

    For a payment status, show "Checking" and keep the order flow going. Use cached data for non-critical reads. Decide these fallbacks with the product owner in advance.

  7. 7. Prove it

    Run a failure test. Add latency to the dependency in a test environment. Check that the breaker opens, the alerts fire and the core path survives. Repeat after big changes.

Concepts you must own 3

Cascading failure
Idea

A failure in one part spreads to others.

Example

A slow service makes callers slow, and they slow their callers.

Term

A failure mode where overload or latency propagates through dependencies.

Retry budget
Idea

A limit on how many retries a client may add.

Example

Retries may add at most 10 per cent to the request rate.

Term

A cap on the ratio of retries to original requests.

Bulkhead
Idea

Separate resource pools for separate dependencies.

Example

The payment client has 20 threads. The search client has its own 20.

Term

Isolation of resources to contain failures.

Follow-up questions

  • Why add jitter to retries?

    Without jitter, all clients retry at the same moments. They create waves of load. Random time spreads the retries out.

  • How do you choose the timeout value?

    Look at the real latency of the dependency. Use a value near the 99th or 99.9th percentile, plus a small margin. It must be lower than the time your own caller will wait.

  • When is it wrong to retry?

    When the call is not idempotent, when the error is permanent (a 400), or when the system is already overloaded. Use idempotency keys when you must retry a write.

Caution
  • No timeout, or a timeout longer than the caller's.
  • Retrying on every error, with no backoff.
  • A fallback that was never tested.
  • One shared thread pool for all dependencies.
Staff signal

A Staff answer links the patterns to the failure mechanism, agrees fallbacks with the business and proves them with a failure test.

UKG-AR4

Interviewer

A team asks you to design how an order service tells five other services that an order was placed. Which style do you choose, and which technology?

What this tests The architect tests if you choose a communication style from the requirements and know the real differences between queues and logs.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

First I ask who needs the answer now. If a service needs it before it replies, I use a direct call. If others only react, I publish an event. For fan-out with replay and ordering per key, I would choose an event log such as Kafka. For simple job processing, a queue such as SQS is cheaper to run. In both cases consumers must be idempotent, and failures go to a dead-letter queue.

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. Split the interactions

    Which ones need a result now? Which ones only react later? Use a direct call for the first group. Use events for the second.

  2. 2. List the needs

    How many consumers? Do new consumers need old events (replay)? Is order important, and per what key? What volume? How long must data stay?

  3. 3. Choose the tool

    A queue (SQS, RabbitMQ) fits one consumer group, simple jobs, and low operations cost. A log (Kafka, Kinesis) fits many consumers, replay and ordering per partition key. Pub/sub (SNS, EventBridge) fits a simple fan-out.

  4. 4. Design the event

    Make it a fact in the past tense, such as OrderPlaced. Add an ID, a time, a version and the minimum data. Decide how the schema can change without breaking old consumers.

  5. 5. Handle failure

    Assume at-least-once delivery. Make consumers idempotent. Retry with backoff. Move poison messages to a dead-letter queue and alert on its depth.

  6. 6. Handle order and data safety

    Partition by the key that needs order, such as the order ID. Use the outbox pattern so that the data change and the event cannot get out of step.

Concepts you must own 3

Event versus command
Idea

An event says something happened. A command asks something to happen.

Example

OrderPlaced is an event. ChargeCard is a command.

Term

Events are facts with many possible consumers. Commands have one target.

Consumer group
Idea

Consumers that share the work of one stream.

Example

Five workers read one queue. Each message goes to one worker.

Term

A set of consumers that divide partitions or messages among themselves.

Schema evolution
Idea

Change an event without breaking readers.

Example

Add an optional field. Do not rename or remove a field.

Term

Backward and forward compatible changes, often enforced by a schema registry.

Follow-up questions

  • What does exactly-once mean in practice?

    Brokers give at-least-once delivery. Some give exactly-once processing inside their own system. Across systems, you get the same effect with idempotent consumers or a deduplication key.

  • How do you replay events after a bug?

    A log keeps events for a set time. Reset the consumer offset and reprocess. The consumer must be idempotent, or it will repeat side effects.

  • When would you not use events?

    When the caller needs a result at once, when the flow is simple and has one consumer, or when the team cannot run the platform. A direct call is easier to reason about.

Caution
  • Using a log when a simple queue is enough, then paying for its operations.
  • No plan for duplicates.
  • Putting the whole order in every event, so that the schema is hard to change.
  • No alert on the dead-letter queue.
Staff signal

A Staff answer chooses per interaction, states the delivery guarantee honestly and plans for schema change and failure.

UKG-AR5

Interviewer

When a customer places an order, the order, inventory and billing services must all change. Two-phase commit is not available. How do you keep the data correct?

What this tests The architect tests if you know the saga pattern, the outbox pattern and idempotency, and if you accept eventual consistency honestly.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

I would use a saga: a series of local transactions with an undo step for each. Each service saves its change and its event together with the outbox pattern. Every step is idempotent, so a retry is safe. If billing fails, the saga sends compensating actions, such as releasing stock. I would also add a reconciliation job that finds and fixes drift.

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. State the problem

    Each service has its own database. A single transaction cannot span all three. Two-phase commit is slow, fragile and often not supported. So the system will be eventually consistent.

  2. 2. Model the steps

    Order created, stock reserved, payment taken, order confirmed. For each step, define the undo: cancel order, release stock, refund.

  3. 3. Choose orchestration or choreography

    Choreography: services react to events. It is simple for few steps. Orchestration: a coordinator runs the steps. It is easier to follow and debug for long flows.

  4. 4. Make each step safe

    Use the outbox pattern. Save the data and the outgoing event in one local transaction. A relay publishes the event. Use idempotency keys, so a repeated message does nothing new.

  5. 5. Show the state to the user

    Show "Order received" first. Update to "Confirmed" or "Failed" later. Never promise more than you know.

  6. 6. Add reconciliation

    A nightly job compares the three services. It finds orders that are stuck or out of step. It either repairs them or raises an alert.

Concepts you must own 3

Compensating action
Idea

An undo step for a completed step.

Example

Payment failed, so release the reserved stock.

Term

A business operation that semantically reverses an earlier step.

Orchestration
Idea

A coordinator tells each service what to do next.

Example

A workflow engine runs the order steps.

Term

A central component drives the saga steps.

Choreography
Idea

Services react to each other's events.

Example

Billing listens for StockReserved.

Term

Decentralised coordination through events.

Code to know

Follow-up questions

  • What if the undo step fails?

    Retry it with backoff. If it still fails, alert a person. Keep the saga state so that someone can finish it by hand. Design undo steps to be safe to repeat.

  • When is a single database better?

    When the data is small and owned by one team. Then use one ACID transaction. Do not split data across services without a reason.

Caution
  • Dual writes: saving to the database and publishing in two separate steps.
  • Forgetting that undo steps can fail.
  • Promising the user an instant final result.
  • No reconciliation, so errors stay hidden.
Staff signal

A Staff answer accepts eventual consistency, names the patterns that make it safe and adds a safety net for the failures that remain.

UKG-AR6

Interviewer

A ten-year-old system runs a core business flow. It must be replaced. The business cannot accept a long freeze or a risky cut-over. What is your plan?

What this tests The architect tests if you can plan a safe, incremental migration with data, traffic, rollback and clear success measures.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

I would use the strangler fig pattern. Put a facade in front, move one slice at a time to the new system and keep both running. Data is the hard part, so I would sync it with change data capture and run the new path in shadow mode first. Each slice has a rollback and a success measure. When all slices are moved and stable, I remove the old system.

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. Understand the old system

    Map the features, the data and the users of each route. Find the hidden rules in the old code. Write tests that capture today's behaviour, even if it is odd.

  2. 2. Add the facade

    Put a router in front of the old system. At first it passes everything through. Now you can move traffic route by route, or user by user.

  3. 3. Pick the first slice

    Choose a slice with low risk, clear edges and visible value. Prove the method on it before you take the hard parts.

  4. 4. Handle the data

    Options: the new system reads from the old data store first. Then it uses change data capture to copy data to its own store. Then it becomes the owner. Avoid long dual writes. They drift.

  5. 5. Prove it before you switch

    Run in shadow mode. Send real traffic to both and compare the answers. Then move a small percentage with a flag. Watch the error rate and latency.

  6. 6. Keep a rollback

    For each slice, keep the old path working until the new one has run well for an agreed time. The rollback is a flag, not a deployment.

  7. 7. Define done

    Measure each slice. When traffic is 100 per cent on the new path and stable, remove the old code and the old data. Many migrations never finish this step. Put it in the plan.

Concepts you must own 3

Strangler fig
Idea

Grow the new system around the old one until the old one can be removed.

Example

Move the /invoices route first. Then /payments.

Term

An incremental replacement pattern that uses a facade or router.

Change data capture (CDC)
Idea

Read the database change log and send changes to another system.

Example

Every update to the old table appears in the new store seconds later.

Term

A technique that streams row-level changes from a database log.

Shadow traffic
Idea

Send a copy of real traffic to the new system. Ignore its answers for users. Compare them.

Example

The new pricing service gets a copy of each request. The team compares prices.

Term

A way to test with production load without user impact.

Follow-up questions

  • How do you handle the old system's odd behaviour?

    Decide for each case: copy it, fix it or remove it. Get the business owner to decide. Record the choice. Tests should capture the chosen behaviour.

  • How do you keep the team motivated in a long migration?

    Show progress with a simple chart of slices moved. Ship value in each slice. Retire the old parts as you go, so that the team sees the cost fall.

Caution
  • A big-bang rewrite with a hard cut-over date.
  • Long dual writes with no way to compare the data.
  • No success measure, so no one knows when it is done.
  • Never removing the old system.
Staff signal

A Staff answer is incremental. It treats data as the hard part, proves each step with real traffic, and plans the end of the old system.

UKG-AR7

Interviewer

Leadership says: "The platform should be reliable." There are no numbers and many noisy alerts. How do you fix this?

What this tests The architect tests if you can turn a wish into SLIs and SLOs, use error budgets and build alerts that people trust.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

I would pick the key user journeys and define SLIs for each one, such as success rate and latency. Then I would agree SLOs with product, for example 99.9 per cent over 30 days. The error budget decides how fast we can ship. I would alert on budget burn rate, not on every blip. Logs, metrics and traces share one request ID. Dashboards show each journey and each tenant.

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. Choose the journeys

    List what users do that matters: sign in, submit a form, run a report. Start with three. Each one gets its own SLI.

  2. 2. Define SLIs

    Good SLIs: the share of requests that succeed, the share that finish within a set time, and freshness for data pipelines. Measure at the edge, as the user sees it.

  3. 3. Agree SLOs with product

    Show what each level costs. 99.9 per cent allows about 43 minutes of bad time in 30 days. 99.99 per cent allows about 4 minutes. Ask what the business needs, not what sounds best.

  4. 4. Use the error budget

    If the budget is healthy, ship faster. If it is spent, slow down and fix reliability. Write this policy down and get leaders to sign it.

  5. 5. Alert on burn rate

    Page when the budget burns fast, for example at 14 times the normal rate for one hour. Send a ticket when it burns slowly. Remove alerts that nobody acts on.

  6. 6. Build the three signals

    Metrics tell you that something is wrong. Logs tell you what happened. Traces tell you where. Use one correlation ID in all three.

  7. 7. Review

    Review SLO misses monthly. Link each one to a fix with an owner. Retire SLOs that no one uses.

Concepts you must own 3

Golden signals
Idea

Four basic signals: latency, traffic, errors and saturation.

Example

A dashboard with these four for each service.

Term

The four signals recommended for monitoring user-facing systems.

Burn rate
Idea

How fast you use the error budget.

Example

A burn rate of 1 uses the whole budget in the window. A rate of 10 uses it in a tenth of the time.

Term

The ratio of the current error rate to the error rate the SLO allows.

Correlation ID
Idea

One ID that follows a request through every service.

Example

The same ID appears in the gateway log and the payment log.

Term

A unique identifier propagated in headers and logged by each service.

Follow-up questions

  • What is wrong with an alert on CPU above 80 per cent?

    It is a cause, not user pain. It may fire when users are fine and stay silent when they hurt. Alert on user-facing symptoms, then use CPU as a diagnostic.

  • How do you start if you have no data?

    Start with logs from the load balancer. They give success rate and latency per route. Set a first SLO from the last 30 days. Improve the measurement later.

Caution
  • Setting the SLO to 100 per cent.
  • Alerting on causes, not symptoms.
  • Measuring inside the service and missing what the user sees.
  • An error budget policy that no one enforces.
Staff signal

A Staff answer links reliability to business trade-offs, uses the error budget to decide pace and keeps alerts few and trusted.

UKG-AR8

Interviewer

You are designing a platform that holds employee and payroll data for many companies. How do you design its security?

What this tests The architect tests if you think in threats, identity, data protection and proof, not only in tools.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

I would start with a threat model using STRIDE. Then I would build on strong identity: SSO for people and short-lived workload identity for services. Access follows least privilege with roles and checks on every request. Data is encrypted in transit and at rest with managed keys. Everything is logged for audit. I would add tests that prove one tenant cannot read another's data, and I would secure the build pipeline too.

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. Classify the data and the threats

    List the data types and how sensitive each is. Draw the system. For each part, ask the STRIDE questions. Rank the risks by impact and likelihood.

  2. 2. Identity

    People sign in with SSO and multi-factor authentication. Services use workload identity and short-lived tokens. No long-lived keys in code or in config.

  3. 3. Authorisation

    Use roles for common access and attribute rules for fine access. Check on the server for every request. Keep a deny-by-default rule.

  4. 4. Data protection

    Encrypt in transit with TLS. Encrypt at rest with keys in a key service. Use separate keys per tenant for the most sensitive data. Mask data in logs and in test environments.

  5. 5. Tenant isolation

    Choose silo, pool or bridge by risk and cost. In a pool, enforce the tenant filter in one place. Add automated tests that attempt cross-tenant reads.

  6. 6. Audit and detection

    Log every access to sensitive records, with who, what and when. Send logs to a protected store. Alert on odd patterns, such as mass export.

  7. 7. Secure the supply chain

    Pin dependencies and base images. Scan them. Sign build artifacts. Give CI jobs short-lived cloud identity with OIDC and least privilege.

  8. 8. Prove and practise

    Run penetration tests. Run an incident drill. Track findings to closure with owners and dates.

Concepts you must own 3

Zero trust
Idea

Check identity and permission on every request, even inside the network.

Example

A service call carries a signed token. The receiver checks it.

Term

A model that removes implicit trust based on network location.

Workload identity
Idea

A service proves who it is with a short-lived token, not a stored key.

Example

A pod gets a role through its service account.

Term

Federated, short-lived credentials bound to a workload.

Envelope encryption
Idea

A data key encrypts the data. A master key in a key service encrypts the data key.

Example

Each tenant has a data key. The key service wraps it.

Term

A two-layer scheme that allows key rotation without re-encrypting all data.

Follow-up questions

  • How do you test tenant isolation?

    Write automated tests that sign in as tenant A and try to read tenant B's records through every API. Run them in the pipeline. Add a test for each new endpoint.

  • How do you handle a leaked secret?

    Revoke and rotate at once. Find where it was used with audit logs. Fix the leak path, for example a log or a repo. Then add a scanner to catch the next one.

Caution
  • Security as a review at the end.
  • Long-lived keys in CI.
  • Trusting the tenant ID sent by the client.
  • Real data in test environments.
Staff signal

A Staff answer is threat-led and layered, and it proves the controls with tests. It includes the pipeline as part of the attack surface.

UKG-AR9

Interviewer

The team needs a browser grid for cross-browser tests. Options: build on Kubernetes, adopt Selenium Grid, or pay for a cloud vendor. How do you decide?

What this tests The architect tests if you use a clear decision method with cost, risk and exit, and do not choose by habit.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

I would first decide if this is core to our product. If not, I prefer to buy or adopt. Then I compare total cost over three years, including people, not only licence price. I check security, lock-in, support and how hard it is to leave. I run a short proof of concept with real tests and write the decision in an ADR with a date to revisit.

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. Is it core or context?

    Core work makes the product different. Context work is needed but not special. Build core. Buy or adopt context.

  2. 2. List the requirements

    Browsers and versions, parallel sessions, video and traces, private network access, data location, uptime, support hours, budget.

  3. 3. Compare total cost of ownership

    Licence or cloud cost, engineers to run it, on-call, upgrades, training and the cost of delay. People cost is often the largest part.

  4. 4. Assess risk

    Security review, vendor stability, lock-in, data handling, and what happens if the vendor changes the price or closes.

  5. 5. Run a proof of concept

    Use your real tests and real network. Measure speed, flake rate, setup effort and debug ease for each option. Keep it to two weeks.

  6. 6. Decide and record

    Write an ADR with the options, the scores, the decision and the date to revisit. Plan the exit path, for example an abstraction over the grid client.

Concepts you must own 3

Total cost of ownership
Idea

The full cost over time, not the price tag.

Example

A free tool that needs two engineers costs more than a paid service.

Term

All direct and indirect costs over the life of a system.

Lock-in
Idea

The cost of leaving a vendor or a tool.

Example

Tests that use a vendor-only API cannot move easily.

Term

Switching cost caused by proprietary interfaces, data formats or skills.

Proof of concept
Idea

A short, real test of an option.

Example

Run 200 real tests on each grid and compare.

Term

A time-boxed experiment that answers a specific risk.

Follow-up questions

  • What if the team wants to build because it is fun?

    Respect the interest and test it against the criteria. Ask what advantage the product gets. If none, put the energy on core work.

  • How do you reduce lock-in when you buy?

    Wrap the vendor API in a thin interface. Keep your data exportable. Write the exit steps in the ADR.

Caution
  • Comparing licence cost only.
  • Choosing by brand or habit.
  • No proof of concept with real workload.
  • No exit plan.
Staff signal

A Staff answer uses a repeatable method, counts people cost and keeps an exit path. The decision is written down.

UKG-AR10

Interviewer

Ten teams are building services. They make different choices and the platform is getting messy. You do not want every decision to go through you. What do you do?

What this tests The architect and the manager test if you can scale your influence with paved roads, light review and automation.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

I would give teams a paved road: templates, libraries and pipelines that make the good choice the easy choice. I would add automated checks, called fitness functions, so rules are enforced by the pipeline and not by meetings. Teams write short ADRs for big decisions. I hold a weekly open review for hard cases. I measure adoption and the number of exceptions.

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. Find the real mess

    List the main differences: languages, logging, auth, deployment. Rank them by cost and risk. Fix the few that hurt most.

  2. 2. Build a paved road

    Service templates, shared libraries, a standard pipeline and a clear guide. Teams may leave the road, but they own the cost.

  3. 3. Automate the rules

    Fitness functions run in CI. Examples: no direct database access from another team's service, required health endpoints, dependency age limits.

  4. 4. Use light decision records

    Ask for a short ADR for one-way doors only. Review within two working days. Two-way doors need no review.

  5. 5. Hold open office hours
