    A weekly slot where teams bring designs early. Early advice is cheap. Late review is expensive.

  6. 6. Share the load

    Train two or three other engineers as reviewers. Rotate the role. This removes you as a single point of failure.

  7. 7. Measure

    Adoption of the paved road, number of exceptions, time to review, and incidents linked to off-road choices.

Concepts you must own 3

Fitness function
Idea

An automated test of an architecture rule.

Example

A pipeline step fails if a service imports another service's database code.

Term

An automated check that measures an architectural characteristic.

Paved road
Idea

The supported, easy path that most teams follow.

Example

A template that gives logging, metrics and deployment on day one.

Term

A default platform path with built-in good practice.

Tech radar
Idea

A shared list of technologies marked adopt, trial, assess or hold.

Example

Team lists a new queue as 'trial' for one project.

Term

A communication tool for technology choices.

Follow-up questions

  • A team ignores the paved road. What now?

    Ask why. They may have a real need that the road misses. Fix the road if the need is real. If not, explain the cost they accept and record the exception.

  • How do you avoid an ivory-tower reputation?

    Write code with the teams, take on on-call or a real task now and then, and ask for feedback. Share decisions and reasons, not only rules.

Caution
  • A mandatory review board for everything.
  • Rules in a wiki and not in the pipeline.
  • Being the only reviewer.
  • No measure of whether the road is used.
Staff signal

A Staff answer scales through defaults, automation and other people. It treats governance as a product with users.

UKG-AR11

Interviewer

The cloud bill grew fast. Finance asks you to cut it by 30 per cent in two quarters. How do you approach it?

What this tests The architect and the manager test if you use data, rank by return and protect reliability.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

I would first make the cost visible by team and service with tags. Then I would rank savings by size and risk. Typical wins: remove idle resources, right-size, use schedules for non-production, use commitments for steady load and Spot for fault-tolerant work. I would set guardrails so that we do not trade away reliability. I would track cost per unit, such as cost per tenant or per test run.

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. Make it visible

    Use tags or labels for team, service and environment. Build a cost dashboard. Find the top ten items. They are usually most of the bill.

  2. 2. Find the easy wins

    Idle and forgotten resources, oversized instances, old snapshots, unused load balancers and long log retention.

  3. 3. Use time and schedule

    Turn off development and test environments at night. Give short-lived environments a time to live. Scale down off-peak.

  4. 4. Match the purchase to the load

    Use savings plans or committed use for steady load. Use Spot or preemptible capacity for fault-tolerant work such as test runners and batch jobs.

  5. 5. Improve the design

    Cache more, compress data, move cold data to cheaper storage, and reduce cross-zone and egress traffic.

  6. 6. Protect reliability

    Do not cut redundancy for critical paths. Check SLOs before and after each change. Roll out changes in small steps.

  7. 7. Track a unit cost

    Track cost per tenant, per transaction or per test run. Total cost can rise while the unit cost falls, and that is good growth.

Concepts you must own 3

Right-sizing
Idea

Match the size of a resource to real use.

Example

A service uses 10 per cent of its CPU. Move it to a smaller size.

Term

Adjusting instance or container size to measured demand.

Unit cost
Idea

Cost divided by a business measure.

Example

Cost per tenant per month.

Term

A ratio that separates growth from waste.

Spot capacity
Idea

Spare cloud capacity at a lower price that can be taken back.

Example

Test runners on Spot. A reclaimed run retries.

Term

Interruptible compute offered at a discount.

Follow-up questions

  • What do you not cut?

    Redundancy on the critical path, backups, security logging and on-call tooling. Cutting them saves little and risks a lot.

  • How do you keep the saving from fading?

    Add budgets and alerts per team. Review the cost dashboard monthly. Make new services start with tags and a cost owner.

Caution
  • Cutting before measuring.
  • Saving money by removing redundancy.
  • One-off clean-up with no ongoing control.
  • Looking at total cost only, not unit cost.
Staff signal

A Staff answer starts with data, ranks by return and risk, and builds a habit so that the saving lasts.

UKG-AR12

Interviewer

Architect: "Design a deployment pipeline that 40 teams can use. Each team has its own services. We want fast, safe releases."

What this tests He tests problem framing, a platform mindset and safe delivery. You have real experience here, so go deep.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

I would first ask about the needs: how many deploys a day, which environments and what the rules are. Then I would offer one golden path: build, test, scan, deploy to staging, canary to production, and automatic rollback. Teams use shared templates and can leave the path with a reason. I would measure lead time and change failure rate.

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. Frame the problem

    Ask about the number of services, the deploy rate, the compliance rules, the runtime (containers, VMs) and what hurts today. State the top goal: safe and fast.

  2. 2. Draw the path

    Commit, build once, unit and component tests, security scan, artefact store, deploy to a test environment, end-to-end smoke tests, canary in production, full rollout.

  3. 3. Make it shared

    Reusable pipeline templates with versions. Teams pass in a small config file. The platform team owns the template and the upgrade path.

  4. 4. Make it safe

    Feature flags, canary with automatic checks on the SLO, one-click rollback and backward-compatible database changes. Approval gates only where rules need them.

  5. 5. Go deep on the riskiest part

    Say what is hardest: flaky tests that block everyone. Run tests in parallel shards, quarantine flaky tests with an owner and report flake rate per team.

  6. 6. Measure and evolve

    Track the four DORA metrics per team. Offer an escape hatch for odd cases. Review the golden path every quarter.

Concepts you must own 2

Golden path
Idea

The default, supported way to build and ship.

Example

A pipeline template that gives build, test, scan and deploy with no setup.

Term

A paved road: opinionated, self-service tooling that teams may leave with a reason.

Canary release
Idea

Send a small share of traffic to the new version first.

Example

5 per cent of users, then 25, then 100.

Term

Progressive delivery with automated analysis and rollback.

Follow-up questions

  • What if one team needs a different flow?

    Allow it through an exception with an owner. Keep the security gates the same. If many teams ask, change the golden path.

  • How do you stop a bad deploy from reaching all users?

    Canary to a small share, compare error rate and latency against the baseline, and roll back automatically on a breach.

Caution
  • Listing tools with no reasons.
  • No rollback plan.
  • Forcing one path on all teams with no escape.
Staff signal

A Staff answer treats the pipeline as a product for 40 teams, and measures adoption and safety.

UKG-AR13

Interviewer

Architect: "Design a monitoring and alerting system for a platform with hundreds of services. Alerts must help people, not wake them for nothing."

What this tests He tests whether you think about the user (the on-call engineer), signal over noise and the cost of data.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

I would collect metrics, logs and traces with one agent per host and a shared correlation id. I would define SLOs per service and alert on error-budget burn rate, not on every spike. Alerts go to the owning team with a runbook link. I would control cost with sampling and retention rules.

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. Frame the problem

    Who gets the alert? What must we detect? How fast? Ask about the data volume and the cost limit.

  2. 2. Collect

    Metrics for trends, logs for detail and traces for the path of one request. Use one open standard such as OpenTelemetry, so teams do not lock in.

  3. 3. Store

    Metrics in a time-series store. Logs and traces in a search store with short hot retention and cheap cold storage.

  4. 4. Alert on symptoms

    Use SLOs and burn-rate alerts: a fast burn pages a person, a slow burn opens a ticket. Do not page on CPU alone.

  5. 5. Route and teach

    Each alert has an owner, a severity and a runbook. Group related alerts to avoid storms. Review noisy alerts every week.

  6. 6. Control cost

    Sample traces, drop high-cardinality labels and set retention per data type. Watch the cost per service.

Concepts you must own 2

Burn rate
Idea

How fast you use the error budget.

Example

A burn rate of 10 empties a 30-day budget in 3 days.

Term

The ratio of the observed error rate to the rate the SLO allows.

Cardinality
Idea

The number of different values a label can take.

Example

A user id label creates millions of series.

Term

The count of unique label combinations in a metric.

Follow-up questions

  • What if the monitoring system itself goes down?

    Run a small independent watchdog that checks it, with a separate path to the on-call tool. Monitor the monitor.

  • How do you reduce alert fatigue?

    Track alerts per shift, remove alerts nobody acts on, and move low-urgency items to tickets.

Caution
  • Alerting on causes, not symptoms.
  • No owner for each alert.
  • Ignoring data cost.
Staff signal

A Staff answer designs for the on-call person, uses SLOs and manages cost and noise.

UKG-AR14

Interviewer

Architect: "Design a feature flag service for all our products. Teams must change flags without a deploy."

What this tests He tests API design, low latency, failure behaviour and flag hygiene.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

I would have a control plane where teams edit flags and an SDK in each service that keeps rules in memory. The SDK gets updates by streaming or polling and evaluates locally, so a flag check adds almost no latency. If the service is down, the SDK uses the last known rules or a safe default. I would add audit logs and a plan to remove old flags.

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. Frame the problem

    Ask for the flag types (release, experiment, kill switch), the scale of checks per second and who may change flags.

  2. 2. Split the planes

    A control plane: UI, API, storage and audit log. A data plane: SDKs that cache rules and evaluate locally.

  3. 3. Distribute rules

    Streaming updates with a poll fallback. A CDN or edge cache for browser clients. Version each ruleset.

  4. 4. Handle failure

    If the control plane fails, SDKs keep the last good rules. On a cold start with no data, use a safe default per flag.

  5. 5. Target users

    Rules by user, tenant, percentage or region. Use a stable hash so a user always gets the same result.

  6. 6. Keep it clean

    Each flag has an owner and an expiry date. Report stale flags. Audit every change.

Concepts you must own 1

Control plane and data plane
Idea

The control plane decides. The data plane does the work.

Example

Teams edit a flag in the UI. SDKs evaluate it in each service.

Term

Separation of configuration management from request-path execution.

Follow-up questions

  • How do you test code that uses flags?

    Test both states in CI. Keep the number of live flags low, because combinations grow fast.

  • What is the risk of a flag service?

    It becomes a single point of failure and a source of hidden complexity. Local evaluation and expiry rules limit both.

Caution
  • Calling the flag service on every request.
  • No default when the service is down.
  • Flags that live for years.
Staff signal

A Staff answer separates control and data planes, plans for failure and manages flag debt.

UKG-AR15

Interviewer

Architect: "Design an API gateway for our microservices. What does it do, and what should it not do?"

What this tests He tests boundaries: what belongs at the edge, and the risk of putting too much in one place.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

The gateway handles cross-cutting edge needs: authentication, rate limiting, routing, TLS and request logging. It does not hold business logic. I would run it as a stateless, horizontally scaled layer with config as code. I would plan for its failure, because it is on every request path.

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. Frame the problem

    Who calls the APIs: browsers, mobile apps, partners? What traffic? Which protocols?

  2. 2. Put edge concerns in

    Authentication and token checks, rate limits, routing, TLS, request size limits, CORS and access logs.

  3. 3. Keep business logic out

    No orchestration or data rules in the gateway. It becomes a bottleneck owned by one team.

  4. 4. Scale and protect it

    Stateless copies behind a load balancer in several zones. Config in version control with review. Health checks and fast rollback.

  5. 5. Design for failure

    Timeouts, retries only for safe calls, circuit breakers per backend and a clear error response.

  6. 6. Consider alternatives

    A backend-for-frontend per client type can fit better when clients need different data shapes.

Follow-up questions

  • Gateway or service mesh?

    The gateway handles north-south traffic from outside. A mesh handles east-west traffic between services. Many systems use both.

  • How do you avoid a gateway bottleneck?

    Keep it thin, scale it out, and let teams own their routes through config rather than code in the gateway.

Caution
  • Putting business rules in the gateway.
  • One gateway with no failure plan.
  • Rate limits with no per-client key.
Staff signal

A Staff answer draws a clear boundary and says what the gateway must never own.

UKG-AR16

Interviewer

Architect: "Design a notification platform for email, SMS and push. Many products will send through it."

What this tests He tests asynchronous design, reliability, user preferences and provider failure.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

Products call one API with a template id and an event. The platform checks user preferences, renders the message, puts it on a queue per channel and sends through a provider. Workers retry with backoff, and an idempotency key prevents double sends. A fallback provider handles outages. I would track delivery status and respect rate limits.

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. Frame the problem

    Volume per day, peak bursts, which channels, the delivery promise and the legal rules for consent.

  2. 2. Accept fast

    A thin API validates the request, stores it and returns at once. All heavy work is asynchronous.

  3. 3. Process

    Check preferences and quiet hours. Render the template. Put the message on a queue per channel and priority.

  4. 4. Send reliably

    Workers call the provider with retries, backoff and an idempotency key. Failed messages go to a dead-letter queue.

  5. 5. Handle provider failure

    Two providers per channel. A circuit breaker switches when the first one fails. Respect each provider rate limit.

  6. 6. Close the loop

    Store delivery status from provider callbacks. Give products a status API and metrics.

Follow-up questions

  • How do you stop duplicate messages?

    Use an idempotency key per message. The worker checks it before sending. Some providers also accept the key.

  • How do you protect urgent messages from a flood of marketing mail?

    Separate queues and worker pools by priority. Never let bulk traffic share capacity with one-time codes.

Caution
  • Sending inside the API request.
  • One provider only.
  • No separate lane for urgent messages.
Staff signal

A Staff answer is asynchronous, idempotent and isolated by priority.

UKG-AR17

Interviewer

Architect: "Design a global rate limiter. Then tell me how a distributed cache would help or hurt."

What this tests He tests algorithm choice, shared state, consistency trade-offs and cache failure modes.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

I would use a token bucket per client key, kept in a fast shared store such as Redis, with an atomic update per request. For very high scale I would allow small local counters and sync them, and accept a small error. A distributed cache cuts latency and database load, but I must plan for stale data and hot keys.

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. Frame the problem

    Per user, per API key or per IP? Hard limit or soft? What is the traffic, and what happens on a breach?

  2. 2. Choose the algorithm

    Token bucket allows bursts at a steady rate. A sliding window is smoother but costs more. A fixed window is simple but allows edge bursts.

  3. 3. Share state

    Keep counters in a shared store with an atomic script. Keys expire. Shard by client key.

  4. 4. Trade accuracy for speed

    At huge scale, use local counters with periodic sync. You allow a small overshoot and gain lower latency.

  5. 5. Decide failure behaviour

    If the store is down, fail open for low-risk APIs and fail closed for sensitive ones. Say it out loud.

  6. 6. Add the cache

    Cache-aside with a time-to-live. Avoid a stampede with request coalescing and jitter. Split a hot key across copies.

Concepts you must own 1

Token bucket
Idea

A bucket fills at a steady rate. Each request takes a token.

Example

Ten tokens per second, with a burst of 50.

Term

A rate-limiting algorithm that permits bursts up to the bucket size.

Follow-up questions

  • How do you tell clients about the limit?

    Return a clear status code and headers with the limit, the remaining count and the reset time.

  • What if one key is extremely hot?

    Replicate it across several cache nodes, add a short local cache and use request coalescing.

Caution
  • No decision on fail-open or fail-closed.
  • Ignoring clock and race issues.
  • A cache with no invalidation plan.
Staff signal

A Staff answer names the accuracy-versus-latency trade-off and the failure behaviour.

UKG-AR18

Interviewer

Architect: "Good design. Now a dependency becomes slow. Now a region goes offline. Now traffic rises ten times. Now the budget is cut in half."

What this tests He tests if you stay calm, treat pushback as new information and revise the design without panic.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

I stay calm and use one pattern. I state the new constraint and say what breaks first. I change the smallest part of the design. I name the cost and say what I would measure. I do not defend the old design. I update it.

Full Staff-level answer

  1. The pattern

    Constraint, what breaks first, smallest change, new cost, how I will check.

  2. A dependency becomes slow

    Add timeouts, a circuit breaker and a bulkhead. Serve cached or degraded data. Tell the user what is limited.

  3. A region goes offline

    Fail over with health checks and DNS or global load balancing. State the RTO and RPO. Say what data may be lost with async replication.

  4. Traffic rises ten times

    Find the first bottleneck. Scale stateless layers out, add caching, queue the heavy work and shed low-priority load. Check the database last.

  5. A message is delivered twice

    Make consumers idempotent with a key. Do not rely on exactly-once delivery.

  6. The hottest cache key disappears

    Use request coalescing and jittered expiry so one caller refills it. Add a stale-while-revalidate window.

  7. The budget is cut in half

    Rank the parts by value. Remove the extras, right-size, use Spot for fault-tolerant work and accept a lower availability target where the business agrees.

  8. A stronger consistency rule appears

    Say what you give up: latency or availability. Use a single writer or a consensus store for that data only.

Follow-up questions

  • What if you do not know the answer?

    Say what you know and what you would test. Then give a reasoned first step. Never bluff.

  • How do you show you are not rigid?

    Say: "That changes my choice. The new constraint is X, so I would change Y."

Caution
  • Defending the first design.
  • Adding many parts at once.
  • Not naming the cost of the change.
Staff signal

A Staff answer turns each shock into a small, reasoned change with a stated cost.

Chapter 05

AI in production, MCP and Claude Code

Five lessons. They cover AI in pipelines, MCP versus APIs, building MCP servers, Claude Code beyond writing code, and evaluation and governance.

Lesson 10

The problem it solvesTeams add a model to a pipeline and get surprises: random output, high cost and silent errors. You need a design that treats the model as an unreliable part.

A model is not a normal function. The same input can give different output. It can be wrong and sound sure. It costs money per call and it is slow. Design around that.

QuestionGood answer
Where does AI add value?Work with fuzzy input and a cheap check: summaries, triage, classification, draft code, log reading.
Where should it not decide alone?Money, access, legal or safety actions. Use rules, or a human approval step.
How do you keep it safe?Validate output against a schema. Run checks that do not use AI. Keep a human in the loop for risky actions.
How do you keep it reliable?Timeouts, retries, a fallback path and a way to turn the feature off.
How do you know it works?An evaluation set that runs in CI, plus production monitoring.
How do you control cost?Small model first, caching, short prompts, batch work and a budget alarm.
flowchart LR
  E[Event or input] --> P[Prepare prompt and context]
  P --> M[Model call]
  M --> V{Valid output?}
  V -->|no| R[Retry or fallback rule]
  V -->|yes| G{Risky action?}
  G -->|yes| H[Human approval]
  G -->|no| A[Act]
  H --> A
  A --> L[Log input, output and cost]

Example for a test platform: a model reads the logs of a failed run and proposes a cause. It never closes a ticket alone. A person confirms. The pipeline logs every proposal and its result.

RememberTreat the model as an unreliable helper. Validate its output, gate risky actions, log everything and measure quality with an evaluation set.

Lesson 11

The problem it solvesA plain API is made for programs that know it in advance. An AI agent must discover tools at run time and use them with little custom code. MCP standardises that.

MCP (Model Context Protocol) is an open standard that connects AI applications to tools and data. The official docs compare it to a USB-C port for AI. An MCP server wraps a system. An AI client talks to many servers in one way.

REST or SOAP APIMCP server
Made forDevelopers who write code against itAI applications that choose tools at run time
DiscoveryRead the docs, write a clientThe client asks the server for its tools and their schemas
ContractEndpoints and payloadsTools, resources and prompts with typed input and clear descriptions
Integration costOne custom integration per client and per systemWrite once, use in any MCP client
GranularityMany fine endpointsA few task-shaped tools that fit a model's context
State and sessionUsually statelessA session between client and server
SecurityAPI keys, OAuth, rate limitsThe same, plus per-tool permissions and user consent in the client
flowchart LR
  U[User] --> H[AI app: the host]
  H --> C1[MCP client 1]
  H --> C2[MCP client 2]
  C1 -->|stdio or HTTP| S1[Server: test results]
  C2 -->|stdio or HTTP| S2[Server: tickets]
  S1 --> A1[(REST API and database)]
  S2 --> A2[(Issue tracker API)]

MCP does not replace your API. An MCP server usually calls your API. It adds a model-friendly layer on top.

Tool
Idea

An action the model can call.

Example

create_ticket(title, severity).

Term

A named function with a JSON-schema input that the server runs.

Resource
Idea

Read-only data the app can load as context.

Example

A file, a log or a database row.

Term

Data exposed by URI that the client may read.

Prompt
Idea

A reusable prompt template.

Example

A triage prompt that takes a run id.

Term

A parameterised template that a user can start.

Transport
Idea

How client and server talk.

Example

stdio for a local tool. HTTP for a shared service.

Term

The channel: standard input and output, or streamable HTTP.

RememberAPIs serve programs. MCP serves AI agents. The server wraps the API and exposes a few clear tools. Choose MCP when an agent must find and use your system.

Lesson 12

The problem it solvesA badly designed server gives the model too many tools, vague descriptions and too much power. Good design makes the agent accurate and safe.

  1. Pick the job. Name the user task, for example: find the cause of a failed test run.
  2. Design a few tools that fit the task. Prefer get_failed_tests(run_id) over ten low-level endpoints.
  3. Write clear names and descriptions. The model reads them to decide when to call a tool.
  4. Return small, useful output. Trim logs. Return a summary and a link, not 5 MB of text.
  5. Mark read-only and risky tools. Require approval for writes and deletes.
  6. Use the least privilege. The server gets its own scoped credential, not the user's admin key.
  7. Add logging, rate limits and tests. Test the tools with an evaluation set of real questions.
RiskControl
Prompt injection through tool outputTreat all tool output as untrusted data. Do not let it change instructions. Limit what tools can do.
Too much powerLeast privilege. Read-only by default. Human approval for writes.
Leaked secretsKeep secrets on the server. Never return them. Redact logs.
Remote server accessUse OAuth or scoped tokens, TLS and per-user authorisation.
Runaway callsRate limits, timeouts and a budget per session.
Untrusted serversInstall only servers that you trust or have reviewed. Pin versions.

RememberFew task-shaped tools, clear descriptions, small output, least privilege, approval for writes and tests with real questions.

Lesson 13

The problem it solvesMany teams use an AI assistant as a smart autocomplete. The larger gain comes from building it into the workflow: context, automation, checks and shared tools.

Anthropic's own paper on how its teams use Claude Code shows non-coding use too. Examples: incident debugging, runbooks, Terraform plan review, onboarding to a codebase, data dashboards and test generation in self-checking loops.

FeatureWhat it doesExample for a dev and test team
CLAUDE.mdProject memory that loads each sessionCommands to run tests, code standards, naming rules, how to run the app
Plan mode and permissionsThink and propose before it edits. Allow and deny lists for commandsPlan a refactor first. Deny access to production configs
SubagentsSpecialist agents with their own context and toolsA test-writer, a security reviewer and a docs agent
SkillsPackaged instructions and scripts that load on demandHow to write a Cypress or Playwright spec the team way
HooksScripts that run at fixed points, for example before or after a tool callRun lint and tests after every edit. Block edits to protected files
MCP serversConnect to Jira, GitHub, the test-results store, dashboardsAsk: "Why did the last nightly fail?" and let it read the data
Headless modeRun it from a script or CI with claude -pTriage failed runs. Draft release notes. Review a pull request
Agent SDKBuild your own agent with the same loop and toolsAn internal bot that reads alerts and proposes a fix
PluginsShare a bundle of commands, agents, skills and hooksOne team setup that every repo can install
Parallel sessionsSeveral sessions on separate git worktreesOne session per ticket, each with its own branch

Use cases beyond writing code: explore an unknown codebase and write a map. Turn a bug report into a failing test. Migrate many files with one rule. Generate test data. Read a Terraform plan for risk. Draft a runbook from an incident. Summarise a long pull request. Keep docs in step with code.

RememberGive Claude Code context (CLAUDE.md), connections (MCP), guardrails (permissions and hooks), helpers (subagents and skills) and a place in CI. Keep a human on risky steps.

Lesson 14

The problem it solvesA model feature can get worse after a prompt edit or a model update, and nobody notices. Without tests and rules, quality drifts and risk grows.

  • Evaluation set: 50 to 200 real examples with expected results. Run it in CI on every prompt or model change.
  • Graders: exact checks first (schema, keywords, tests pass). Use a model as a judge only for fuzzy quality, and spot-check it with people.
  • Regression gate: block a release if the score drops below the agreed line.
  • Online monitoring: log inputs, outputs, latency, cost and user feedback. Sample and review each week.
  • Versioning: version prompts, models and tools like code. Roll back fast.
  • Cost control: budgets, caching, smaller models for easy work, and alarms.
Governance for AI-assisted codingRule
OwnershipThe author owns the change, whoever or whatever wrote it. Review it as normal code.
ReviewHumans review all AI-written changes. Add tests that fail without the change.
Secrets and dataNo secrets or customer data in prompts. Use approved tools and settings.
Licences and provenanceFollow company policy on generated code and dependencies.
PermissionsLeast privilege for agents. Protect production and configs with deny rules and hooks.
MeasureTrack lead time, change failure rate and review time, not lines of code.

Prompt injection is the key agent risk: text in a web page, a ticket or a log can try to give the agent new orders. Treat all external text as data. Limit the tools. Ask for approval for risky actions.

RememberTest AI features with an evaluation set. Watch them in production and version them. Govern AI-written code with the same owner, review and permission rules as other code.

Chapter 06

AI questions

Expect these from an architect or a manager who uses Claude every day. Answer with a design, a trade-off and a safety control.

UKG-AI1

Interviewer

Architect: "We want a model to read failed CI runs and suggest the cause. How do you put that into our pipeline safely?"

What this tests He tests if you treat a model as an unreliable part: validation, gates, cost, evaluation and a human in the loop.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

I would start with a narrow, low-risk job: read the failure logs and propose a likely cause as a comment. The model never changes code or closes tickets alone. I would validate output against a schema, run it on an evaluation set before release, log every call and cost, and add a kill switch. A person makes the final call.

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. Frame the problem

    What is the job, who uses the output and what is the cost of a wrong answer? Start with a task where wrong answers are cheap.

  2. 2. Draw the flow

    Event, prepare the context, model call, validate output, optional human approval, act, log.

  3. 3. Keep context small

    Send only the failing test, the error and the changed files. Strip secrets. This cuts cost and leakage.

  4. 4. Validate

    Ask for structured JSON. Check it against a schema. Retry once. Fall back to the plain log link if it fails.

  5. 5. Gate risky actions

    Comments are safe. Merges, deploys and ticket changes need approval or a rule engine.

  6. 6. Evaluate

    Build 100 past failures with known causes. Run them on every prompt or model change. Block release on a score drop.

  7. 7. Operate

    Log inputs, outputs, latency, cost and thumbs up or down. Set a budget alarm and a feature flag to turn it off.

Concepts you must own 2

Evaluation set
Idea

A fixed set of examples with known good answers.

Example

100 past failures with the true cause.

Term

A regression test suite for model behaviour.

Human in the loop
Idea

A person approves risky steps.

Example

The bot proposes. A person merges.

Term

An approval gate placed before an irreversible action.

Follow-up questions

  • What if the model is wrong often?

    Check the evaluation set first. Improve the context, split the task or use a stronger model. If it still fails, keep it as a suggestion only.

  • How do you handle cost at scale?

    Cache repeat failures, group similar ones, use a small model first and escalate hard cases.

Caution
  • Letting the model act alone.
  • No evaluation set.
  • Sending whole logs with secrets.
  • No fallback when the model is down.
Staff signal

A Staff answer picks a safe first use, adds validation, gates, evaluation and a kill switch, and measures the benefit.

UKG-AI2

Interviewer

Hiring manager or architect: "We already have REST APIs. Why would we build MCP servers? When is MCP the wrong choice?"

What this tests He tests if you understand MCP as a layer for agents, and not a hype replacement for APIs.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

A REST API is for programs written by developers who know it. MCP is for AI agents that discover tools at run time. The MCP server usually wraps the API and exposes a few task-shaped tools with clear descriptions. I would use MCP when many AI clients need the same system. For a fixed, deterministic integration, a direct API call is simpler and cheaper.

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. Say what each is

    API: a contract for developers. MCP: a standard way for AI apps to list and call tools and read resources.

  2. 2. Give the main difference

    Discovery and fit. An agent asks the server what it can do. The tool descriptions are written for a model.

  3. 3. Give the cost argument

    Without MCP, each AI client needs its own custom integration to each system. With MCP, you write one server.

  4. 4. Say when MCP is right

    Many agents or clients, tasks that vary, and a need for user consent and tool-level control.

  5. 5. Say when it is wrong

    A fixed pipeline step, a high-volume call, or a path that needs strict latency. Call the API directly.

  6. 6. Mention the risks

    More power for agents means more risk: prompt injection, over-broad tools and secret leaks. Use least privilege.

Concepts you must own 1

Model Context Protocol
Idea

An open standard that connects AI apps to tools and data.

Example

One server for test results works in many AI clients.

Term

A client-server protocol with tools, resources and prompts over stdio or streamable HTTP.

Follow-up questions

  • Does MCP replace our API gateway?

    No. The gateway still protects and routes API traffic. The MCP server sits above the API and talks to it.

  • Do you expose every endpoint as a tool?

    No. Too many tools confuse the model and waste context. Design a few tools around user tasks.

Caution
  • Saying MCP replaces APIs.
  • One tool per endpoint.
  • Ignoring security.
Staff signal

A Staff answer treats MCP as a layer on top of APIs and names when not to use it.

UKG-AI3

Interviewer

Architect: "Design an MCP server so engineers can ask an AI assistant about test results and CI runs. What tools, and how do you secure it?"

What this tests He tests API design for a model, scope control and security.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

I would write a small set of read-only tools. They get the latest runs, get failed tests for a run, get flake history and search by error text. Output is short and links to the full data. The server uses a scoped, read-only credential and logs every call. Writes, such as filing a ticket, are separate tools that need user approval.

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. Start from user tasks

    Why did the nightly fail? Is this test flaky? What changed since the last green run?

  2. 2. Choose a few tools

    list_runs, get_failed_tests, get_flake_history, search_errors. Clear names. Short descriptions that say when to use each.

  3. 3. Shape the output

    Summaries, top N, trimmed errors and a link. The model has a limited context window.

  4. 4. Pick the transport

    stdio for a local developer tool. Streamable HTTP for a shared service behind your gateway.

  5. 5. Secure it

    OAuth or scoped tokens, per-user authorisation, read-only by default, TLS and rate limits. Redact secrets in output.

  6. 6. Add write tools carefully

    Create a ticket or re-run a job only with explicit user approval. Log who approved.

  7. 7. Test it

    An evaluation set of real questions. Check that the right tool is called with the right arguments.

Code to know

Follow-up questions

  • How do you stop prompt injection through an error message?

    Treat tool output as data. Truncate and sanitise it. Do not give the agent tools that can cause harm without approval.

  • Local or remote server?

    Local for personal tools. Remote for shared data with central auth, logging and upgrades.

Caution
  • Dozens of tiny tools.
  • Returning huge logs.
  • Using an admin key.
Staff signal

A Staff answer designs few, task-shaped tools with least privilege and a test set.

UKG-AI4

Interviewer

Hiring manager: "Our teams use Claude and Claude Code a lot. How would you use them beyond \"write this code\" and \"review this PR\"?"

What this tests He tests whether you see an AI assistant as part of the engineering system: context, automation, guardrails and shared tools.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

I would build it into the workflow. Put team knowledge in CLAUDE.md and skills. Connect Jira, GitHub and test results through MCP. Use hooks for lint and tests after every edit. Use subagents for test writing and security review. Run it headless in CI to triage failures and draft notes. Keep humans on risky steps and measure results.

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. Give it context

    CLAUDE.md with how to build, test and run. Skills for team patterns, for example how we write a Playwright spec.

  2. 2. Connect it

    MCP servers for GitHub, the issue tracker, the test-results store and dashboards. It can answer: "What failed last night and why?"

  3. 3. Add guardrails

    Permission allow and deny lists. Hooks that run lint and tests, and block edits to protected files.

  4. 4. Add specialists

    Subagents: test writer, security reviewer, docs updater. Each has its own tools and context.

  5. 5. Put it in CI

    Headless runs: group failures by cause, draft a pull-request summary, check docs drift, review a Terraform plan for risk. Output goes to a person.

  6. 6. Use it for non-code work

    Explore a new codebase and write a map. Turn a bug report into a failing test. Generate test data. Draft runbooks from incidents. Plan a migration across many files.

  7. 7. Measure and govern

    Track lead time, change failure rate and review time. The author owns every change. No secrets in prompts.

Concepts you must own 3

CLAUDE.md
Idea

A file of project instructions that the tool loads each session.

Example

Test commands and code standards.

Term

Persistent project memory in the repository.

Hook
Idea

A script that runs at a set point in the tool loop.

Example

Run tests after each edit.

Term

A deterministic event handler for tool events.

Subagent
Idea

A helper agent with its own context and tools.

Example

A security reviewer.

Term

A delegated agent definition with a scoped prompt and tool set.

Follow-up questions

  • What would you not automate?

    Merges to production, access changes and customer-data actions. Those need approval.

  • How do you share the setup across teams?

    Package it as a plugin: commands, subagents, skills and hooks. Version it and review changes.

Caution
  • Only "write code" and "review code".
  • No guardrails.
  • No measure of benefit.
  • Trusting generated tests that never fail.
Staff signal

A Staff answer treats the assistant as a platform: context, connections, guardrails, automation and metrics.

UKG-AI5

Interviewer

Architect: "Our unit tests pass but the AI feature sometimes gives bad answers. How do you test it?"

What this tests He tests whether you adapt test strategy to probabilistic systems. This is close to your test-platform skills.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

I would build an evaluation set of real examples with expected results. I would grade by exact checks first. I would use a model judge only for fuzzy quality. I would run it in CI on every prompt, model or tool change and block release on a drop. In production I would log and sample outputs and watch quality, cost and latency.

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. Build the set

    Collect 50 to 200 real cases. Include hard and bad cases. Label the expected result.

  2. 2. Grade in layers

    Schema and rule checks first. Then task checks, such as "does the proposed fix compile?". Then a model judge for tone or quality, checked by people.

  3. 3. Handle randomness

    Lower the temperature where you can. Run each case several times and track the pass rate, not one result.

  4. 4. Gate releases

    A score line. Compare to the last good version. Block on a drop.

  5. 5. Test the parts

    Unit-test tools and parsers normally. Test retrieval separately from generation.

  6. 6. Watch production

    Log inputs and outputs. Sample for review. Track thumbs, cost and latency. Add new failures to the set.

Follow-up questions

  • Is a model judge reliable?

    It is useful but biased. Calibrate it against human labels and spot-check it each week.

  • How do you avoid a stale set?

    Add every production failure to the set. Review it each quarter.

Caution
  • Testing only the happy path.
  • One run per case.
  • Trusting a model judge with no human check.
Staff signal

A Staff answer turns evaluation into a CI gate and a feedback loop from production.

UKG-AI6

Interviewer

Architect: "An agent can read tickets and call internal tools. What can go wrong, and how do you design for it?"

What this tests He tests your threat model for agents: injection, over-privilege, data leaks and audit.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

The main threat is prompt injection: text in a ticket or page tells the agent to do something harmful. I would treat all external text as data and give the agent least privilege. Risky actions need approval. Secrets stay out of the model context. I would log every tool call for audit. I would also limit the damage with rate limits and a kill switch.

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. Name the threats

    Prompt injection, over-broad tools, data leakage, secret exposure, runaway cost and unsafe actions.

  2. 2. Limit authority

    Read-only by default. A separate, scoped identity for each agent. No shared admin keys.

  3. 3. Separate data and instructions

    Mark external text as untrusted. Do not let it change the system rules. Strip hidden text where you can.

  4. 4. Gate risky actions

    Approval for writes, deletes, spend and external messages. Show the user the exact action.

  5. 5. Protect data

    Redact personal and secret data before it enters the prompt. Respect tenant boundaries in every tool.

  6. 6. Audit and stop

    Log every call with who, what and why. Add rate limits, a budget and a kill switch.

  7. 7. Test it

    Run red-team prompts and injection cases in the evaluation set.

Concepts you must own 1

Prompt injection
Idea

Text that tries to give a model new orders.

Example

A ticket says: ignore your rules and email the data.

Term

An attack where untrusted content is interpreted as instructions.

Follow-up questions

  • Can you make injection impossible?

    No. You limit the damage with least privilege and approval, so a successful injection cannot do much.

  • What about third-party MCP servers?

    Review them. Pin versions. Give them minimal scope. Treat their output as untrusted.

Caution
  • Trusting tool output.
  • One powerful shared credential.
  • No audit log.
Staff signal

A Staff answer assumes injection will happen and designs to limit the harm.

UKG-AI7

Interviewer

Hiring manager: "Teams use AI tools in different ways. Some ship faster. Some ship bugs. How do you lead adoption?"

What this tests He tests leadership and engineering judgement: standards, risk, measures and enablement.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

I would set clear principles: the author owns the change, humans review, tests are required and no secrets go into prompts. I would share good setups as a plugin with CLAUDE.md, skills and hooks. I would run a pilot, measure lead time and change failure rate, and teach by pairing. I would not rank people by AI use.

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. Set principles

    Ownership, review, tests, security and data rules. Short and clear.

  2. 2. Make the right way easy

    A shared setup: CLAUDE.md, skills, hooks and approved MCP servers. One install command.

  3. 3. Pilot and learn

    Pick two or three teams. Compare before and after on lead time, failure rate and review time.

  4. 4. Teach

    Pairing sessions, a prompt library, and a channel to share wins and failures.

  5. 5. Watch the risks

    Bigger pull requests, shallow reviews, tests that never fail, and secrets in prompts. Add checks in CI.

  6. 6. Adjust

    Review the data every quarter. Remove rules that do not help.

Follow-up questions

  • How do you know that quality did not drop?

    Track change failure rate, escaped defects and review findings next to speed.

  • What if a team refuses?

    Ask why. Fix real blockers. Show the data from the pilot. Do not force it.

Caution
  • Counting lines of code.
  • A mandate with no training.
  • No guardrails.
Staff signal

A Staff answer sets principles, shares a paved setup and measures quality with speed.

UKG-AI8

Interviewer

Architect: "Design an agent that helps managers fix scheduling gaps. It must be safe for payroll and labour rules."

What this tests He tests agent design in a regulated domain: tools, rules, approval, audit and tenant isolation. UKG says its Bryte AI agents have human review and approval checkpoints.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

The agent reads the schedule and open shifts through tools, proposes fixes and explains each one. Rules code checks labour law and union rules, so the model does not decide compliance. A manager approves each change. Every proposal and approval is logged, and each tenant's data stays isolated. I would evaluate it on past schedules.

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. Frame the problem

    Who uses it? What is the cost of an error? Labour rules and pay make errors costly.

  2. 2. Split the roles

    The model proposes and explains. A rules engine checks compliance. A person approves.

  3. 3. Choose the tools

    Read: schedule, shifts, availability, rules. Write: propose a change, with a draft state only.

  4. 4. Add approval

    The manager sees the change, the reason and the rule check result. Only then does it apply.

  5. 5. Isolate tenants

    Every tool call carries the tenant and user identity. Check authorisation in the tool, not in the prompt.

  6. 6. Audit

    Log the prompt, the proposal, the rule result, the approver and the final change.

  7. 7. Evaluate and monitor

    Replay past schedules with known good fixes. Watch acceptance rate and rule violations.

Follow-up questions

  • Why not let the model check the rules?

    Rules are exact and must be provable. Code does that better. The model is good at proposing options.

  • What if the agent talks to another vendor's agent?

    Use an agreed protocol such as A2A. Authenticate each agent, limit scope and log the exchange.

Caution
  • The model decides compliance.
  • No approval step.
  • Tenant checks in the prompt only.
Staff signal

A Staff answer separates proposing from checking and approving, and logs everything.

UKG-AI9

Interviewer

Hiring manager: "You built test platforms. Where would AI help, and where would it hurt?"

What this tests He tests whether you can apply AI to your own domain with judgement. This is a strong area for you.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

AI helps with test drafts from requirements, failure triage by log reading, flake pattern spotting and test data. It hurts when it writes tests that always pass, hides real failures or "heals" a selector so a real bug passes. I would keep humans in review, make generated tests prove they can fail, and measure flake rate, escape rate and triage time.

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. Good uses

    Draft tests from a spec. Group failures by cause. Suggest likely owners. Summarise a run. Generate test data.

  2. 2. Risky uses

    Self-healing that hides real bugs. Generated tests with no real assertions. Auto-quarantine with no owner.

  3. 3. Make tests prove value

    A new test must fail when the feature is broken. Use mutation checks or run against a known-bad build.

  4. 4. Keep humans in charge

    A person reviews generated tests and approves a heal or a quarantine.

  5. 5. Measure

    Flake rate, escaped defects, time to triage and test maintenance time. Compare with the baseline.

  6. 6. Start small

    Triage comments first. Then test drafts. Then deeper automation if the data supports it.

Follow-up questions

  • Would you use self-healing locators?

    Only with a report of each heal and review. A heal can turn a real regression into a pass.

  • How do you stop generated tests from being brittle?

    Give them page objects and team patterns through skills. Review them like normal code.

Caution
  • Believing that more tests mean more quality.
  • Auto-healing with no review.
  • No baseline.
Staff signal

A Staff answer uses AI where checks are cheap, protects the signal of the test suite and measures the result.

Chapter 07

Leadership concepts

Six short lessons on Staff-level behaviour: how you decide, influence, give feedback and deliver.

Lesson 15

The problem it solvesThe hiring manager wants to know what kind of Staff engineer you are. Staff is not a senior engineer who codes more. It is a change in scope and in how you create impact.

A common model (from Will Larson) names four shapes of Staff work. Most people are one or two of these.

ShapeWhat you doExample
Tech leadGuide the technical direction of one teamOwn the design and the delivery plan for a team's big project
ArchitectOwn direction and quality across several teamsSet the standards and the paved path for many teams
SolverDive into the hardest problem, then hand it backFix a deep, cross-team failure
Right handExtend a senior leader's reachRun a cross-org initiative for a director

Your real history fits the tech lead and architect shapes. You owned a framework that many people used, and you set the direction for how tests were built. Say that. Do not claim a shape that you did not do.

  • Scope: you own an outcome that crosses team lines.
  • Multiplier: your work makes ten people better, not only you.
  • Judgement: you decide what not to build.
  • Communication: you write things down so that others can decide without you.

RememberSay which shape you are, give one proof for it, and show how you multiply other people.

Lesson 16

The problem it solvesStaff engineers move a group to a decision. The tools are simple. They are a written proposal, a named decider and a clear way to disagree.

A short design doc or RFC has: the problem, goals and non-goals, options, the recommendation, risks, a rollout plan and open questions. Circulate it before the meeting. Decide in the meeting.

DACI
Idea

Names the Driver, Approver, Contributors and Informed people for a decision.

Example

You drive. The director approves. Two teams contribute. Support is informed.

Term

A decision framework that makes one approver and one driver explicit.

One-way and two-way doors
Idea

A one-way decision is hard to undo. A two-way decision is easy to undo.

Example

A database choice is a one-way door. A library choice behind an interface is a two-way door.

Term

Decide two-way doors fast. Spend time only on one-way doors.

Disagree and commit
Idea

You state your view clearly. After the decision, you support it fully.

Example

You argued for option A. The group chose B. You help B succeed and you measure it.

Term

Dissent is voiced before the decision and full support follows it.

  • Write for a reader who was not in the room.
  • Put the recommendation first, then the reasons.
  • Name who decides and by when.
  • Record the result, so the next person does not repeat the debate.

RememberWrite it down, name the decider, decide two-way doors fast, and commit after the decision.

Lesson 17

The problem it solvesYou will lead people who do not report to you. Pushing does not work. A ladder of steps does.

  1. Listen. Learn what the other team needs and fears.
  2. Show data. Use their numbers, not yours.
  3. Run a small pilot with one willing team.
  4. Use the pilot result as proof for the next team.
  5. Make the right way the easy way: a template, a tool or a default.
  6. Escalate last, and only with the facts and a proposal.
  • Saying no: say what you will do instead. "Not this quarter. Here is what we can do now, and here is when we can revisit."
  • Managing up: give your manager a short update, the risk and the decision you need. No surprises.
  • Bad news: tell early. Bring the facts, the impact and a plan.
  • Credit: name the people who did the work. It builds trust and makes your next ask easier.

RememberListen, show data, pilot, prove, make it easy, and escalate last.

Lesson 18

The problem it solvesGood content in a bad shape sounds weak. Use a shape so the interviewer can follow you and score you.

ShapeStepsUse it for
STAR+Situation, Task, Action, Result, then what you learned or would changeAny behavioural question
Decision answerContext, options, trade-offs, choice, risks, rolloutArchitecture and design questions
SBISituation, Behaviour, ImpactGiving feedback to a person
30-second answerAnswer first, one reason, one example, then stopEvery first reply
  • Spend 10 per cent on the situation, 60 per cent on your actions and 30 per cent on the result and the lesson.
  • Say "I" for what you did and "we" for what the team did. Interviewers listen for this.
  • Give one number. For example: time saved, failures cut or people helped.
  • End on what you learned. It shows growth.

Keep every story under two minutes. Practise out loud. If you read it, it sounds read.

RememberUse STAR+ for stories and the decision shape for designs. Answer first. Then stop.

Lesson 19

The problem it solvesA Staff engineer raises the whole team. The manager will ask how you help others grow, how you give feedback and how you hire.

  • Mentoring: set a goal with the person. Meet often. Give hard problems with safety nets.
  • Delegation: hand over the outcome, not only the task. Agree how you will check in.
  • Feedback: use SBI. Give it soon, in private for hard topics and in public for praise.
  • Code and design review: teach in the review. Ask questions before you give orders.
  • Hiring: use a fixed set of questions and a scorecard. Judge evidence, not feeling.
  • Onboarding: a written first-week plan and a buddy cut ramp-up time.
  • Safety: people must be able to say "I do not know" and "I broke it" without fear.

Example of an SBI sentence: "In yesterday's review (situation), you merged without a test (behaviour). The release failed on that path and the team lost two hours (impact)."

RememberGrow people with goals, feedback, safe stretch work and clear delegation.

Lesson 20

The problem it solvesThe hiring manager needs to trust that you will deliver. That means choosing well, telling the truth about risk and leading when things break.

  • Prioritise with a simple score. RICE is reach times impact times confidence, divided by effort. Show the list and the reasons.
  • Tech debt: tie it to a business cost, such as slower delivery or more incidents. Ask for a fixed share of time, not a big rewrite.
  • Estimates: give a range and the main risks. Re-estimate when you learn something.
  • Roadmap: show outcomes and dates with confidence levels. Say what you are not doing.
  • Incidents: stabilise first, then find the cause. Keep one lead and one scribe. Write a blameless review with actions, owners and dates.
flowchart LR
  A[Detect] --> B[Stabilise]
  B --> C[Communicate]
  C --> D[Find the cause]
  D --> E[Fix]
  E --> F[Blameless review]
  F --> G[Actions with owners and dates]

RememberScore priorities, price tech debt in business terms, tell the truth about risk, and run incidents calmly.

Chapter 08

Leadership and behavioural questions

Use only true stories. Where you see [fill: ...], write your own fact. Do not invent a number.

UKG-LD1

Interviewer

Hiring manager: "Take me through your background in three minutes. Then tell me why you are ready for a Staff role."

What this tests He tests if you can tell a clear story, link it to this job and show Staff-level scope, not only years of experience.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

I am a front-end and full-stack engineer with 16 years of experience. The last seven years, at Joyent, I owned the end-to-end test framework. I also owned the pipelines that many teams used. That moved me from building features to building the platform that other engineers rely on. A Staff role at UKG is the next step: the same scope, across more teams.

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. Open with one line

    Who you are and what you are best at. Example: "I build the tools and frameworks that help many engineers ship with confidence."

  2. 2. Give three chapters, not a list of jobs

    Chapter 1: early years, building products in several domains. Chapter 2: the move to shared components and test automation. Chapter 3: owning the platform used by many teams. Spend most time on chapter 3.

  3. 3. Show the Staff signals

    Pick two or three proofs: a framework with real users, a decision that crossed team lines, an engineer you grew, a measured result. Add a number: [your number].

  4. 4. Explain why Staff now

    Say that your work already crosses teams, and you want to do it with more scope. Name the shape you fit: tech lead and architect for test and delivery platforms.

  5. 5. Link to UKG

    One sentence on why this role: the product, the scale, or the platform challenge. Use something real from your research: [fill: one real fact about UKG].

  6. 6. Stop

    End with: "That is the short version. I can go deeper on any part."

Concepts you must own 2

Narrative arc
Idea

A story with a direction, not a list of dates.

Example

From features, to shared components, to a platform for many teams.

Term

A coherent through-line that makes each move look purposeful.

Scope signal
Idea

Evidence that your work reached beyond your own tasks.

Example

A framework used by many teams.

Term

Proof of influence across team boundaries.

Follow-up questions

  • What is the difference between your Senior and Staff work?

    At Senior level I delivered well-scoped work for a team. At Staff level I chose which problem to solve, aligned several teams and measured the outcome. Give one example for each.

  • Why not a management role?

    Say what you enjoy: technical depth and multiplying people through design, review and mentoring. Say that you respect management and you can lead without it.

Caution
  • A long job-by-job list.
  • Years of experience as the main proof.
  • No link to the target role.
  • Over three minutes.
Staff signal

A Staff answer has a clear arc, proves scope with one real example and ends on why this role.

UKG-LD2

Interviewer

Hiring manager: "You were at Joyent until recently. Why did you leave? What have you been doing since?"

What this tests He tests honesty, calm, and whether you stayed sharp. He wants a short, factual answer with no blame.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

My role ended in August 2026 when the company reduced its workforce. It was a company decision and not about performance. Since then I have used the time on purpose. I learned Kubernetes and cloud platforms hands on. I prepared for roles that match my platform work. I am glad to share what I built and learned.

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. Say the fact in one sentence

    "My position was eliminated in a reduction in force in August 2026." Do not add drama. Do not blame.

  2. 2. Add one respectful line

    Say something true and kind about the work or the team. It shows maturity.

  3. 3. Show what you did since

    Only things that are true. You can say that you ran a test suite on a local Kubernetes cluster. You can say that you kept your skills sharp with a study plan. Add anything real: [fill: a project, a course, open-source work, contract work].

  4. 4. Turn to the future

    Say what you want next, and why this role fits. Keep it forward-looking.

  5. 5. Stay brief

    This answer should take under 45 seconds. Longer sounds defensive.

Follow-up questions

  • Were you affected by performance concerns?

    Answer simply and truthfully. If the answer is no, say: "No. It was a company-wide decision." Offer references from managers or peers if asked.

  • Why did it take this long to find a role?

    Say that you were selective, you used the time to deepen skills, and you want a role at the right level. Do not criticise the market or the recruiters.

Caution
  • Blaming a manager or the company.
  • Over-explaining.
  • Claiming work you did not do.
  • Sounding bitter.
Staff signal

A Staff answer is short, factual and forward-looking. It shows composure and proves that you kept learning.

UKG-LD3

Interviewer

Hiring manager: "Give me an example where you led a technical change that crossed team lines. What was the result?"

What this tests He tests scope, influence, and whether you can show a measured result and the effect on people.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

Use one real story. Start with the problem and the number. Say what you decided and how you got other teams to agree. End with the result and what you learned. For example, a shared test framework. Teams had slow and flaky tests. I proposed one framework, ran a pilot with one team, and then rolled it out. [fill: result with numbers].

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. Situation

    Name the problem and who it hurt. Give one number: [your number]. Example: slow, flaky end-to-end tests across several teams.

  2. 2. Task

    What was yours? Say if you owned the outcome or if you led without authority.

  3. 3. Actions

    Three or four steps in your own words. How you listened to teams. What you proposed. How you ran a pilot. How you handled the team that resisted.

  4. 4. Result

    A number and a human effect. Example: failures cut, time saved, fewer escalations, a team that asked to join.

  5. 5. What you learned

    One lesson and one change you would make. It shows you reflect.

Follow-up questions

  • Who did not agree, and what did you do?

    Name the concern. Say how you listened, changed the plan or showed data. Do not say that people were wrong.

  • What would you do differently?

    Choose something real and small, such as starting the pilot sooner or writing the guide first.

Caution
  • "We" for everything. He cannot see your part.
  • A story with no number.
  • A hero story with no other people in it.
  • A story that is not yours.
Staff signal

A Staff answer shows a clear owner, a pilot, proof and a result that other people agree with.

UKG-LD4

Interviewer

Hiring manager: "Tell me about a time you disagreed with a decision from an architect or a manager. What happened?"

What this tests He tests humility, how you argue, and if you commit fully after you lose.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

I would choose a real case. I made my argument with data, I heard the reasons for the other option and the decision went the other way. I committed fully. I helped it succeed. Later, [fill: what happened and what you learned]. The lesson was to separate the decision from my pride and to measure the result.

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. Set the scene

    The decision, who made it, and what you wanted. Keep it neutral and respectful.

  2. 2. Show how you argued

    You wrote your view, used data, offered a smaller test and asked what would change the decision.

  3. 3. Show the decision

    State plainly that it went the other way, and why the decider chose it. Show that you understood their reasons.

  4. 4. Show commitment

    What you did to make the chosen path work. Do not say "I told you so" later.

  5. 5. Close with the result and the lesson

    Whether you were right or wrong, name the lesson: [fill: your lesson].

Follow-up questions

  • What if the decision was harmful?

    Escalate with facts and a proposal to the right person. State the risk clearly. Do it once, in a clear way, and then accept the outcome of that process.

  • When would you not commit?

    When the decision breaks safety, law or ethics. Say so clearly and use the proper route.

Caution
  • A story where you were simply right.
  • Criticising the decider.
  • No sign of commitment.
  • A story with no lesson.
Staff signal

A Staff answer shows strong opinions, held loosely, and professional behaviour after the decision.

UKG-LD5

Interviewer

Hiring manager: "A Staff engineer should raise the whole team. Show me how you do that."

What this tests He tests if you have a method, real examples and a measure of success.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

I start with the person's goal. Then I give work that stretches them, with a safety net, and I give feedback soon and specifically. I use code and design reviews to teach. I measure growth by what they can do alone later, not by how much they ask me. For example, [fill: one real person or group and what changed].

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. Start with goals

    Ask what the person wants in the next year. Write it down together. Check it every month.

  2. 2. Give stretch work

    Hand over a real piece with a clear outcome. Agree the check-in points. Be available, but do not take it back.

  3. 3. Give good feedback

    Use SBI: situation, behaviour, impact. Give praise in public and hard feedback in private. Say what to keep doing.

  4. 4. Teach in reviews

    Ask questions in reviews. Explain the why. Link to a short guide that you write once and reuse.

  5. 5. Scale yourself

    Write guides, run a short session, and pair on hard parts. Teach others to mentor.

  6. 6. Measure

    Look for signs: the person leads a design, handles an incident alone or mentors someone else. Share the credit.

Follow-up questions

  • How do you help someone who is stuck?

    Ask where they are stuck. Split the problem into steps. Pair for the first step. Then let them do the next one.

  • How do you handle an engineer who does not want feedback?

    Ask how they like to get it. Link the feedback to their own goal. Keep it small, specific and frequent.

Caution
  • Giving answers and not questions.
  • Only helping the strongest people.
  • No example.
  • Feedback only at review time.
Staff signal

A Staff answer is a method plus a real example, and the person grows to need you less.

UKG-LD6

Interviewer

Hiring manager: "Tell me about a project that did not go well. What was your part?"

What this tests He tests ownership, honesty and learning. A story with no real failure is a warning sign.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

I would pick a real case. I would say what we planned, what went wrong, and which part was mine. Then I would say what we did to recover and what we changed in the way we work. The lesson matters more than the failure. For example, [fill: your story in two sentences].

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. State the goal and the miss

    What was planned, and what happened. Use a simple fact, such as a delay or a failed launch.

  2. 2. Own your part

    Say what you did or did not do. Examples: you did not raise a risk early, you under-estimated, or you did not check an assumption.

  3. 3. Say what the team did to recover

    Cut the scope, added a person, moved the date or fixed the cause.

  4. 4. Show the change

    A new habit: earlier risk reviews, smaller steps, a better estimate, a checklist. Show that it worked in the next project.

  5. 5. Keep it blameless

    Describe causes in the system, not in people.

Follow-up questions

  • What did you learn about estimating?

    Give ranges. List risks. Check the riskiest part first. Re-estimate when you learn something.

  • How did you tell your manager?

    Early, with facts, the impact and a plan. No surprises.

Caution
  • A fake failure, such as "I work too hard".
  • Blaming other teams.
  • No change afterwards.
  • Too much detail on the technical cause.
Staff signal

A Staff answer owns a real mistake, repairs the system and shows the habit that came out of it.

UKG-LD7

Interviewer

Hiring manager: "Three teams each say that their request is the top priority. You can do one. What do you do?"

What this tests He tests judgement, stakeholder skill and the courage to say no with a clear reason.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

I would ask each team for the impact and the deadline in numbers. I would score the options with a simple method such as impact, reach, confidence and effort. Then I would show the ranking to the stakeholders, say what I will do first and what waits, and give dates. If the ranking is a business call, I would ask the right leader to decide.

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. Get facts

    Impact, who is affected, deadline, cost of delay, and what happens if it waits.

  2. 2. Score them

    Use RICE: reach times impact times confidence, divided by effort. The score is a start. Add judgement for risk and dependencies.

  3. 3. Look for a smaller version

    Maybe a one-week fix helps two teams. Offer partial help to the others.

  4. 4. Communicate the choice

    Show the list in the open. Say what you do first, what waits and when you will review. People accept a clear no more than a vague yes.

  5. 5. Escalate when needed

    If the choice is a business trade-off, bring the options to the manager or the product owner. Ask for a decision by a date.

  6. 6. Review

    Check the plan weekly. Priorities change.

Follow-up questions

  • What if a senior leader pushes a request?

    Show the trade-off: "If we do this, X moves by two weeks." Let the leader choose with full information.

  • How do you protect time for tech debt?

    Agree a fixed share, such as 15 per cent. Tie each item to a business cost, such as incidents or slower delivery.

Caution
  • Saying yes to all.
  • Prioritising by who is loudest.
  • Saying no with no reason or alternative.
  • A private list no one can see.
Staff signal

A Staff answer uses a visible method, offers options and makes the trade-off the decision-maker's choice.

UKG-LD8

Interviewer

Hiring manager: "One of your peers is hard to work with. Or one engineer misses commitments. How do you handle it?"

What this tests He tests empathy, directness and a fair process.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

I would talk to the person early and in private, with facts and curiosity. I would use SBI: what I saw, and the impact. I would ask for their view first, because there may be a cause I do not know. Then we agree on clear next steps and a date to check. If it does not improve, I would involve the manager with the facts, not with opinions.

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. Check your facts

    Write down specific examples and the impact. Remove adjectives.

  2. 2. Talk early and privately

    Open with the shared goal. Describe the situation and the impact with SBI. Ask: "What is your view?"

  3. 3. Listen

    There may be a cause: overload, unclear goals, a personal issue or a process problem. Do not guess. Ask.

  4. 4. Agree specific steps

    What changes, by when, and how you will check. Offer help that you can really give.

  5. 5. Follow up

    Check in on the date. Praise the progress.

  6. 6. Escalate fairly

    If nothing changes, bring the facts to the manager. Say what you tried. Ask what support you can give.

Follow-up questions

  • What if the stakeholder is senior to you?

    Use the same facts-first approach. Find their goal. Show how your request supports it. Ask a trusted peer or manager for advice if it stays hard.

  • What if the person gets defensive?

    Pause. Restate the shared goal. Offer to continue later. Keep your tone calm and your facts clear.

Caution
  • Gossip to others before talking to the person.
  • Judging character, not behaviour.
  • Waiting until it is big.
  • No follow-up.
Staff signal

A Staff answer is early, private, specific and kind, and it escalates with facts and a record of support.

UKG-LD9

Interviewer

Hiring manager: "You join us next month. What do you do in the first 90 days?"

What this tests He tests if you will learn before you act, build trust and deliver a visible result without breaking things.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

First 30 days: listen and learn. I meet the people, read the code and the incidents and ship a small fix. Days 31 to 60: I write down what I learned and propose two or three priorities with the team. Days 61 to 90: I deliver one visible improvement with a measure, and I share the plan for the next six months.

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. Days 0 to 30: learn

    Meet the team, the key partners and your manager. Read the architecture, the pipelines and the last five incidents. Ship one small fix to learn the delivery path.

  2. 2. Days 31 to 60: propose

    Write a short document: what you saw, what hurts most and two or three options. Agree on priorities with your manager and the team.

  3. 3. Days 61 to 90: deliver

    Deliver one visible improvement with a measure, such as faster builds or fewer flaky tests. Share the result.

  4. 4. Build trust all through

    Ask questions. Give credit. Do not announce a big plan in week one.

30-60-90 day rollout

Days 0–30
  • Meet the team, the partners and the manager.
  • Read the architecture, pipelines and the last five incidents.
  • Ship one small fix to learn the delivery path.
  • Ask what success looks like in six months.
Days 31–60
  • Write a short document with the top problems and options.
  • Agree two or three priorities with the manager and the team.
  • Start one pilot with a willing team.
  • Set up a measure for the baseline.
Days 61–90
  • Deliver one visible improvement with a number.
  • Share the result and the next six-month plan.
  • Start mentoring or a review habit.
  • Ask for feedback and adjust.

Follow-up questions

  • What do you ask in the first week?

    What hurts most? What did we try that failed? Who should I meet? How do we decide here? What does success look like?

  • What if you find a big problem early?

    Check the facts and the history first. Share it with your manager as a question, not an attack. Propose a small first step.

Caution
  • A big plan in the first week.
  • No visible result by day 90.
  • Ignoring the history and the people.
  • No measure.
Staff signal

A Staff answer learns first, builds trust, picks a visible result and measures it.

UKG-LD10

Interviewer

Hiring manager: "Give me an example of..." You will hear this ten times. Prepare six real stories now. Each story can answer many questions.

What this tests He tests if your examples are specific, real and show Staff-level scope. Vague stories lose the round.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

Choose six stories: a cross-team change, a hard technical decision, a failure, a conflict, helping another engineer and a result with numbers. Write each in STAR+ form with one number. Practise each in under two minutes. Map each story to the questions it can answer.

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. Pick six real moments

    Use the starters below. They come from the work you described: the end-to-end test framework, the pipelines, the shared component library and the migration of dashboard pages. Confirm every fact is true before you use it.

  2. 2. Write each in STAR+

    Situation, Task, Action, Result, then the lesson. Add one number: [your number].

  3. 3. Add the Staff framing

    One sentence on why this was Staff-level: scope, a decision, influence or multiplying people.

  4. 4. Map the stories to questions

    Use the "Use for" line. One story can answer three or four questions.

  5. 5. Practise out loud

    Two minutes each. Record yourself once. Fix the long parts.

Your stories (fill every placeholder first)

Own the test framework used by many teams

Use for LD1, LD3, LD5, LD7

Situation

[fill: the team and the time] needed a reliable end-to-end test suite. Tests ran on hosted runners across several environments and regions. [fill: the pain, with a number]

Task

I owned the framework and the pipeline setup: how tests were built, run and reported.

Action

[fill: 3 actions. For example: the shared pipeline with a matrix of suites and environments. Scheduled uptime runs. Failure alerts to chat. Guides for other engineers]

Result

[your number]. [fill: faster feedback, fewer escalations, more teams using it]

Staff framing

Owned a platform that other teams relied on. Decided how tests were built and reported, and set the standard.

Do differently

[fill: one real thing, for example measure flake rate from day one]

Move pages to a shared component library

Use for LD3, LD7

Situation

Service dashboard pages used many one-off components. They looked and behaved in different ways. [fill: the cost, with a number]

Task

Move the pages to the shared component library and keep the user experience steady.

Action

[fill: 3 actions. For example: an inventory of components. A migration order. Tests that proved the pages still worked. Talks with design and product]

Result

[your number]. [fill: fewer bugs, faster pages, less code]

Staff framing

Changed a shared foundation across many pages and coordinated with several teams.

Do differently

[fill: one real thing]

Investigate failing tests across many specs

Use for LD6, LD4

Situation

Many end-to-end specs failed in one environment. Some failures came from shared fixtures and test data. [fill: the details and the impact]

Task

Find the cause and stop the repeat failures.

Action

[fill: how you grouped failures, found the shared cause, fixed the fixtures, and told the teams]

Result

[your number]. [fill: pass rate before and after]

Staff framing

Fixed a systemic cause, not a single test, and shared the learning.

Do differently

[fill: for example isolate test data per run from the start]

A disagreement you lost, and how you committed

Use for LD4

Situation

[fill: the decision, who decided, and what you wanted]

Task

State my case clearly and then support the decision.

Action

[fill: data you used, what you offered, how you helped the other path succeed]

Result

[fill: the outcome and the lesson]

Staff framing

Strong opinion, held loosely. Full commitment after the decision.

Do differently

[fill: one real thing]

Helping another engineer grow

Use for LD5

Situation

[fill: the person, their goal and where they were stuck]

Task

Help the person reach the goal in [fill: time].

Action

[fill: pairing, stretch work, reviews, feedback with SBI]

Result

[fill: what the person did alone afterwards]

Staff framing

Multiplied the team, not only my own output.

Do differently

[fill: one real thing]

Working across backend, product, QA and design

Use for LD7, LD8

Situation

[fill: a feature or release that needed several teams, and a conflict or delay]

Task

Align the teams and keep delivery on track.

Action
