[fill: how you clarified the goal, set the agreement on scope, handled one hard conversation]

Result

[fill: the result with a date or number]

Staff framing

Led without authority across functions.

Do differently

[fill: one real thing]

Follow-up questions

  • What if I have no number?

    Use an honest estimate and say it is an estimate. For example: "about half". Or use a count: teams, people, runs. Do not invent a number.

  • What if the interviewer asks for more detail than I remember?

    Say what you remember well. Say what you are less sure of. Offer to share what you can. Do not fill gaps with guesses.

Caution
  • Using a story that is not yours.
  • Making up numbers.
  • Telling all six stories with the same shape and the same hero.
  • Not practising out loud.
Staff signal

A Staff candidate has a small set of true, rehearsed stories that cover scope, conflict, failure, growth and results.

UKG-LD11

Interviewer

Hiring manager: "Tell me about a time you gave technical leadership during a critical production incident."

What this tests He tests calm under pressure, clear roles, communication and what changed afterwards.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

I would use a real case. First I stabilised: roll back or mitigate. I named an incident lead, a communicator and people to investigate. I gave short updates on a fixed schedule. Afterwards we ran a blameless review with actions, owners and dates. [fill: the incident, the time to recover and one change that stuck].

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. Situation

    What broke, who was affected and how you knew. One number: [your number].

  2. 2. Stabilise first

    Roll back, disable a flag or fail over. Find the cause later. Say what you chose and why.

  3. 3. Set roles

    One person leads, one communicates, others investigate. This keeps the room calm.

  4. 4. Communicate

    Short updates on a fixed schedule to the people who need them. State what you know, what you do not know and when the next update comes.

  5. 5. Review without blame

    Write the timeline. Ask what made the mistake easy. List actions with owners and dates.

  6. 6. Show the change

    The result: a new alert, a safer deploy step or a runbook. Say how you checked it worked.

Follow-up questions

  • What if you were the cause?

    Say it plainly. Focus on the fix and on the system gap that let it happen.

  • How do you stop a repeat?

    Add detection, a guardrail and a test. Track the actions until they are done.

Caution
  • A hero story with no team.
  • Hunting for the cause before the user impact is stopped.
  • No follow-up actions.
Staff signal

A Staff answer shows calm, roles, clear updates and a lasting system change.

UKG-LD12

Interviewer

Hiring manager: "Tell me about a time you got several teams to adopt a new tool or practice."

What this tests He tests influence without authority, empathy for other teams and how you measure adoption.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

I would start with the problem the teams already feel. I would run a pilot with one willing team, fix the rough edges and share the result in numbers. Then I would make adoption easy: templates, guides and office hours. I would not force it. [fill: your tool, the teams, the adoption number].

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. Find the pain

    Talk to the teams. Write down their top problems in their words.

  2. 2. Pilot

    Pick one team that wants to try. Agree on success measures first.

  3. 3. Show proof

    Share the before and after in numbers. Let the pilot team tell the story.

  4. 4. Make it easy

    Templates, a migration guide, a short demo and open office hours. Remove the first-day pain.

  5. 5. Handle resistance

    Ask what blocks them. Fix real blockers. Do not force a team before it is ready.

  6. 6. Measure and adjust

    Track adoption and the benefit. Retire the old way only when most teams have moved.

Follow-up questions

  • What if a team says no?

    Ask why. Offer a smaller step. Return later with new data. Keep the door open.

  • How do you know it worked?

    Adoption count, the benefit metric and feedback from teams.

Caution
  • Announcing a mandate.
  • No pilot.
  • No measure of adoption.
Staff signal

A Staff answer starts from the teams' pain, proves value and makes the new way the easy way.

UKG-LD13

Interviewer

Hiring manager: "Tell me about a time you argued for a significant refactor, and people did not want it."

What this tests He tests how you build a business case, manage risk and avoid a risky big-bang rewrite.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

I would turn the technical pain into a business cost: incidents, slow delivery or risk. I would propose small steps with a visible win in each, not a full rewrite. I would agree on a measure, and a stop point. [fill: your case, the cost you showed and the result].

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. Name the cost

    Link the debt to impact: incidents, lead time, onboarding time or security risk. Use numbers.

  2. 2. Hear the objections

    Delivery pressure, risk and doubt are real. Write them down and answer each one.

  3. 3. Propose small steps

    Use the strangler-fig approach. Each step ships value and can stop.

  4. 4. Agree on a measure

    For example: fewer incidents or faster builds. Report it every month.

  5. 5. Protect the roadmap

    Ask for a fixed share of capacity, not a freeze. Show the plan to product.

  6. 6. Review honestly

    If the measure does not move, say so and change the plan.

Follow-up questions

  • When is a full rewrite right?

    Rarely. Only when the old system blocks the business and cannot be changed in steps. Even then, run both for a time.

  • How do you convince a sceptical product owner?

    Show the cost of delay in their terms: features slowed, incidents and customer impact.

Caution
  • A technical argument with no business link.
  • A big-bang rewrite plan.
  • No stop point.
Staff signal

A Staff answer converts debt into business cost and delivers it in small, measured steps.

UKG-LD14

Interviewer

Hiring manager: "Tell me about a difficult trade-off you made between performance, scalability, reliability and delivery speed."

What this tests He tests whether you can name both sides, decide with data and own the consequence.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

I would name the options, the constraint and the decision. For example, we chose a simpler design that shipped in six weeks, and we accepted lower peak throughput. We set a trigger to revisit it at a clear load level. [fill: your real case and the result].

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. State the constraint

    Deadline, load, team size or risk. One number: [your number].

  2. 2. Give the options

    Two or three real options, each with its benefit and cost.

  3. 3. Decide with data

    What you measured or tested. Who you asked.

  4. 4. Name the cost you accepted

    Say it plainly. This is what separates Staff answers.

  5. 5. Set a trigger

    The signal that would make you revisit the choice.

  6. 6. Report what happened

    Was the trade-off right? What did you learn?

Follow-up questions

  • What if you were wrong?

    Say it, show how you found out and what you changed.

  • How do you decide when data is missing?

    Run a small experiment, choose the reversible option and set a review date.

Caution
  • Pretending there was no downside.
  • No trigger to revisit.
  • A choice with no data.
Staff signal

A Staff answer states the cost of the decision and the trigger to change it.

UKG-LD15

Interviewer

Hiring manager: "How do you balance developer productivity work with business deadlines?"

What this tests He tests if you can justify platform work in business terms and avoid gold-plating.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

I treat developer experience as a lever for delivery speed. I measure the pain: build time, flaky tests, wait time. I fix the biggest bottleneck first, and I show the time saved in business terms. I keep the work small and tied to a delivery goal. [fill: your example and number].

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. Measure

    Build time, test time, flake rate and time to first deploy for a new engineer.

  2. 2. Convert to cost

    Minutes lost per engineer per day, times the number of engineers.

  3. 3. Pick the top bottleneck

    Fix one thing at a time. Show the result.

  4. 4. Tie to delivery

    Link each improvement to a release or a goal that the business cares about.

  5. 5. Avoid gold-plating

    Stop when the metric is good enough. Do not build tools nobody uses.

  6. 6. Ask the users

    Survey engineers every quarter. Fix what they say, not what you guess.

Follow-up questions

  • How do you justify a platform team?

    Show lead time, failure rate and engineer survey results, and compare them with the cost of the team.

  • What if the business says no?

    Offer a smaller version with a clear gain. Ask what evidence would change the answer.

Caution
  • Tools nobody asked for.
  • No measures.
  • Pure engineer comfort as the reason.
Staff signal

A Staff answer ties developer experience to speed, cost and safety, with numbers.

UKG-LD16

Interviewer

Hiring manager: "Tell me about an ambiguous technical problem with no known answer. How did you approach it?"

What this tests He tests structured thinking under ambiguity and how you reduce risk step by step.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

I would break the problem into questions, find the riskiest unknown and test it first with a small spike. I would write down what I learned, involve people with relevant experience and decide with the evidence. [fill: your real problem and what you did].

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. Frame

    State what is known, what is unknown and what success means.

  2. 2. Find the riskiest unknown

    Test it first with a short, time-boxed spike.

  3. 3. Ask for help early

    Talk to people who have seen similar problems. Read how others solved close cases.

  4. 4. Decide with evidence

    Compare options with the results of the spike.

  5. 5. Share the learning

    Write a short note: what you tried, what worked and what did not.

  6. 6. Review

    Check the result after release. Adjust.

Follow-up questions

  • How do you know when to stop exploring?

    Set a time box and a decision date before you begin.

  • What if the spike fails?

    That is a result. Record it, change the approach and tell stakeholders early.

Caution
  • Starting to build before testing the risk.
  • Working alone for weeks.
  • No written learning.
Staff signal

A Staff answer turns ambiguity into small tests and shares what it learns.

UKG-LD17

Interviewer

Hiring manager: "Tell me about a decision you made with incomplete information and little time."

What this tests He tests judgement, reversibility thinking and how you communicate uncertainty.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

I ask if the decision is reversible. If it is, I decide quickly with the best data I have, and I set a check point. If it is not, I buy time to learn more. I say clearly what I know, what I assume and what would change my mind. [fill: your case].

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. Classify

    Is it a two-way door or a one-way door?

  2. 2. Gather the fast facts

    Spend a short, fixed time on the three most useful facts.

  3. 3. State assumptions

    Write them down. Share them with the people affected.

  4. 4. Decide and set a check point

    Pick the option. Name the signal and the date that will test it.

  5. 5. Communicate

    Say it is a decision with uncertainty, and why you chose it.

  6. 6. Review

    Check the assumptions later. Adjust.

Follow-up questions

  • What if the decision was wrong?

    Own it. Reverse it if you can. Share the learning.

  • How do you avoid analysis paralysis?

    Set a deadline for the decision and a short list of facts that you need.

Caution
  • Waiting for perfect data.
  • Hiding the uncertainty.
  • No check point.
Staff signal

A Staff answer matches the speed of the decision to its reversibility.

UKG-LD18

Interviewer

Hiring manager: "How do you explain a complex technical topic to a non-technical stakeholder, and to a senior engineer?"

What this tests He tests clarity, audience awareness and the ability to link to business impact.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

I start with the audience's question. For a business leader: the outcome, the risk and the cost, in plain words, with one analogy. For an engineer: the design, the trade-offs and the data. I check understanding by asking them to say it back. [fill: a real example].

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. Know the audience

    What do they care about? What do they already know?

  2. 2. Lead with the answer

    Say the conclusion first. Then the reason.

  3. 3. Use one analogy

    Pick one that fits their world. Do not stack them.

  4. 4. Show the numbers that matter

    For leaders: cost, risk and time. For engineers: load, latency and failure modes.

  5. 5. Check understanding

    Ask: "What would you do with this?" Fix the gaps.

  6. 6. Follow up in writing

    A short summary with the decision and the next step.

Follow-up questions

  • How do you handle a stakeholder who gets lost in detail?

    Go up a level. Return to the decision and the effect on their goal.

  • How do you explain a risk without scaring people?

    State the likelihood, the impact and what you will do about it.

Caution
  • Jargon.
  • Starting with the history.
  • No link to impact.
Staff signal

A Staff answer changes the message for each audience and checks that it landed.

UKG-LD19

Interviewer

Hiring manager: "Give me an example where a technical decision of yours supported a business goal."

What this tests He tests if you think beyond the code and know what the business wants.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

I would start with the business goal, for example faster releases or fewer customer-facing bugs. Then I link the technical choice to it, with a measure. For example, a shared test framework that cut release risk and time. [fill: your goal, your choice and the number].

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. Name the goal

    Revenue, cost, risk, speed or customer trust. In the business's words.

  2. 2. Link the decision

    How the technical choice moves that goal.

  3. 3. Show the measure

    A number before and after.

  4. 4. Show the trade-off

    What you did not do, and why.

  5. 5. Share the credit

    Name the partners in product, QA and design.

Follow-up questions

  • How do you learn the business goals?

    Ask your manager and product partners. Read the roadmap and the customer feedback.

  • What if the goals change?

    Re-check the plan. Stop work that no longer helps and say so openly.

Caution
  • A purely technical story.
  • No measure.
  • Claiming credit for the whole result.
Staff signal

A Staff answer starts from the business goal and ends with a measured result.

UKG-LD20

Interviewer

Hiring manager: "What have you done to build a good engineering culture on your team?"

What this tests He tests if you take responsibility for how the team works, not only what it builds.

Say this (30 seconds), then stop

I make good habits easy: clear standards, fast tests and kind, specific reviews. I make sure that quieter voices are heard, for example by writing design documents and asking for comments in advance. I praise good practice in public. [fill: two real habits you started].

Full Staff-level answer

  1. 1. Set clear standards

    A short guide for code, reviews and tests. Keep it in the repo.

  2. 2. Make quality easy

    Fast feedback, good tooling and templates.

  3. 3. Make reviews kind and useful

    Ask questions. Explain the why. Separate must-fix from nice-to-have.

  4. 4. Include everyone

    Written proposals, rotating facilitators and time for questions. Invite quiet people by name.

  5. 5. Learn from mistakes

    Blameless reviews. Share what you learned.

  6. 6. Notice and praise

    Call out good work. Culture grows from what you reward.

Follow-up questions

  • How do you handle a strong but dominant voice?

    Talk in private. Set meeting rules such as written input first. Praise listening behaviour.

  • How do you measure culture?

    Engineer surveys, retention, onboarding time and incident learning.

Caution
  • Slogans with no habits.
  • Only senior voices heard.
  • Blaming people after incidents.
Staff signal

A Staff answer builds habits and systems that make good behaviour the default.

Chapter 09

Quick-fire answers

Short answers for fast questions. Say each one in 20 seconds. Tick Studied when you can say it without notes.

Architecture: core ideas

What is a quality attribute, and why does it matter?

A quality attribute is a property like latency, availability, security or cost. You cannot maximise all of them. Architecture is the choice of which ones matter most for this product. Ask for the top two or three before you design.

What is an ADR?

An Architecture Decision Record is a short document for one decision. It states the context, the options, the choice and the trade-offs. It helps new people understand why the system looks as it does.

What is the C4 model?

C4 shows a system at four zoom levels: context, containers, components and code. Use level 1 and 2 in most talks. It gives a shared picture without too much detail.

When do you choose a monolith over microservices?

Choose a modular monolith when the team is small, the domain is unclear, or you lack the platform to run many services. Choose microservices when teams need to deploy alone and scale parts differently. Microservices add network failure, tracing and data-consistency work.

What is a bounded context?

A bounded context is an area of the domain where each word has one clear meaning. Service boundaries should follow these contexts. A boundary that cuts through a context creates heavy coupling.

What is the strangler-fig pattern?

You put a router in front of the old system. You move one capability at a time to the new system. The old system shrinks until you remove it. You can stop or go back at any step.

What does idempotent mean, and why do you need it?

An operation is idempotent if doing it twice gives the same result as once. Networks retry. Queues deliver twice. An idempotency key lets the consumer ignore a duplicate.

What is the outbox pattern?

You write the business change and the event to the same database transaction. A separate process reads the outbox table and publishes the event. This avoids the case where the data saves but the event is lost.

What is a saga?

A saga is a series of local transactions across services. Each step has a compensating step that undoes it. If a step fails, you run the compensations. It replaces a distributed transaction.

Explain CAP in simple words.

When the network splits, a system must choose: stay consistent and refuse some requests, or stay available and risk stale data. PACELC adds that, even with no split, you trade latency for consistency.

What is eventual consistency, and when is it acceptable?

Replicas may differ for a short time but converge. It is fine for feeds, counters and search. It is not fine for balances or inventory without extra checks.

What is a circuit breaker?

It stops calls to a failing dependency after a threshold. After a wait it lets a few calls through to test. It protects your threads and gives the dependency time to recover.

Why do retries need backoff and jitter?

Retries without delay make an overload worse. Exponential backoff spreads retries over time. Jitter adds randomness so clients do not retry at the same moment.

What is a bulkhead?

A bulkhead isolates resources, such as thread pools, per dependency. If one dependency is slow, it uses up only its own pool. The rest of the service keeps working.

What is backpressure?

It is a way for a slow consumer to tell the producer to slow down. Without it, queues grow and memory fills. Use bounded queues, rate limits or load shedding.

Architecture: data, scale and operations

Queue or log: how do you choose?

A queue, like SQS, removes a message after it is handled. It suits work distribution. A log, like Kafka, keeps events for a set time. Many consumers can read and replay it. Choose a log when you need replay or many independent readers.

How do you scale a stateless service?

Run more copies behind a load balancer. Keep sessions in a shared store or in a signed token. Scale on a real signal such as queue depth or requests per pod.

How do you scale a database?

First fix queries and indexes. Then add read replicas and caching. Then partition by a key such as tenant. Each step adds complexity, so measure before you go to the next.

What is sharding, and what is the risk?

Sharding splits data across databases by a key. The risks are hot shards, cross-shard queries and hard resharding. Choose a key with even load.

Cache-aside: how does it work?

The app checks the cache. On a miss, it reads the database and fills the cache. On a write, it updates the database and removes the cache entry. Set a time-to-live as a safety net.

How do you avoid a cache stampede?

Use request coalescing so only one caller refills a key. Add jitter to expiry times. Serve slightly stale data while one caller refreshes.

What is an SLI, an SLO and an error budget?

An SLI is a measure, such as the share of successful requests. An SLO is the target, such as 99.9 per cent. The error budget is the allowed failure. At 99.9 per cent, you have about 43 minutes per 30 days.

What are RTO and RPO?

RTO is how long you can be down. RPO is how much data you can lose. They set the disaster recovery design and its cost.

Name the AWS disaster recovery strategies.

From cheap and slow to costly and fast: backup and restore, pilot light, warm standby and multi-site active-active.

How do you design for multi-tenancy?

Choose an isolation level: shared everything with a tenant id, a schema per tenant, or a database or account per tenant. More isolation gives better security and noise control, and costs more. Add per-tenant limits.

What is the noisy-neighbour problem?

One tenant uses too many shared resources and hurts others. Use quotas, rate limits, fair queues and, for large tenants, separate capacity.

What is STRIDE?

A threat model checklist: spoofing, tampering, repudiation, information disclosure, denial of service and elevation of privilege. Walk each data flow and ask which threat applies.

What is zero trust in practice?

Do not trust a request because of its network. Authenticate and authorise every call. Use short-lived credentials, least privilege and encryption in transit.

How do you handle secrets?

Keep them in a secrets manager. Give workloads short-lived identities, such as OIDC or IAM roles. Rotate secrets. Never put them in code or images.

How do you roll out a risky change safely?

Use a feature flag, a canary release and automatic rollback on SLO breach. Make database changes backward compatible, in expand and contract steps.

What is observability, compared with monitoring?

Monitoring checks known failures. Observability lets you ask new questions about a system from its logs, metrics and traces. Use a correlation id across services.

How do you reduce cloud cost without hurting reliability?

Measure first and tag resources. Right-size, use autoscaling, use Spot for fault-tolerant work and remove idle resources. Protect the SLO and track the cost per unit of work.

How do you keep a platform from becoming a bottleneck?

Offer a self-service golden path with guardrails. Measure adoption and lead time. Keep an escape hatch. Treat the platform as a product with users.

What are the DORA metrics?

Deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate and time to restore service. Use them to see trends. Do not use them to rank people.

How do you choose between build, buy and adopt?

Build what gives you an edge. Buy or adopt what is a commodity. Count the total cost: run, upgrade, security and the people who know it. Plan an exit.

What do interviewers score in a design answer?

Problem framing, justified choices, depth on the riskiest part, simplicity, technical depth and decisiveness. State the main downside of your choice. For each decision, say the constraint, the choice, the benefit, the cost and the trigger to revisit.

How do you start every design question?

Ask about users, scale, latency, availability, consistency and what is out of scope. State your priority. Then draw the smallest design that works and add parts only where needed.

What are the common red flags in a design interview?

Jumping to a solution, listing tools with no reasons, overengineering, ignoring failure cases, waiting for prompts, memorised diagrams and not checking alignment with the interviewer.

A dependency becomes slow. What do you add?

Timeouts, a circuit breaker, a bulkhead and a fallback. Serve cached or degraded data. Alert on the dependency latency.

A region goes offline. What happens?

Health checks trigger a failover through DNS or a global load balancer. State the RTO and RPO. With async replication, some recent writes may be lost.

Traffic rises ten times. What do you do?

Find the first bottleneck. Scale stateless layers, add caching, queue heavy work and shed low-priority load. Fix the database last and carefully.

The budget is cut in half. What do you do?

Rank parts by value. Remove extras, right-size, use Spot for fault-tolerant work and agree a lower target where the business accepts it.

A stronger consistency requirement appears. What do you give up?

Latency or availability. Limit the strong guarantee to the data that needs it, for example with a single writer or a consensus store.

Feature flags: why evaluate locally?

A remote call per check adds latency and a failure point. The SDK keeps rules in memory, updates them by stream or poll and uses safe defaults if the service is down.

Token bucket or sliding window?

A token bucket allows bursts at a steady average rate and is cheap. A sliding window is smoother but needs more memory. Choose by whether bursts are acceptable.

API gateway: what belongs there?

Authentication, rate limits, routing, TLS and access logs. Business logic does not belong there. Keep it thin and stateless.

What is a burn-rate alert?

An alert on how fast you spend the error budget. A fast burn pages a person. A slow burn opens a ticket. It beats alerting on every spike.

Leadership: short answers

What does a Staff engineer do that a Senior does not?

A Staff engineer sets technical direction across teams, picks the problems worth solving, and multiplies others through design, review and mentoring. The scope is larger and the ambiguity is higher.

Name the four Staff archetypes.

From Will Larson: tech lead, architect, solver and right hand. Say which one you fit best and give one example.

How do you influence without authority?

Build trust with small wins. Write a clear proposal with data. Listen to concerns. Find a sponsor. Run a pilot. Give credit.

How do you write a good design document?

State the problem, the goals and non-goals, the options with trade-offs, the choice and the risks. Keep it short. Ask reviewers for the hardest questions early.

What is DACI?

A decision role model: Driver, Approver, Contributors and Informed. It makes clear who decides, so a decision does not stall.

Two-way door or one-way door: what do you mean?

A two-way door is easy to reverse, so decide fast. A one-way door is hard to reverse, so decide slowly with more review.

How do you give hard feedback?

Use SBI: situation, behaviour, impact. Do it soon and in private. Focus on the behaviour. Ask for their view. Agree on a next step.

How do you receive hard feedback?

Listen without defending. Ask for examples. Say thank you. Take time to think. Then act and report back.

How do you handle a conflict between two teams?

Find the shared goal. Separate positions from needs. Bring data. Agree on a trial. Escalate only with facts, and after you try to solve it.

How do you run a blameless post-incident review?

Focus on the system and the timeline. Ask what made the mistake easy. List actions with owners and dates. Share the learning widely.

How do you manage technical debt?

Make it visible and link it to business cost. Agree a fixed share of capacity. Fix debt near the code you change. Do not stop feature work for a big rewrite.

How do you estimate and handle uncertainty?

Give a range, not one date. List the risks and test the riskiest part first. Re-estimate as you learn. Tell stakeholders early when it changes.

How do you say no?

Say what you understand about the need. Give the reason and the trade-off. Offer an alternative or a later date. Keep the relationship.

How do you onboard a new engineer?

Give a clear first-week plan, a buddy, a small first task that ships and a map of the system. Check in often.

How do you keep your technical skills sharp as a leader?

Stay in code reviews and design reviews. Write some code on the hard parts. Read incidents. Build small prototypes. Teach, because teaching exposes gaps.

How do you measure your own impact?

Use outcomes, not activity: lead time, failure rate, adoption, engineer growth and incidents avoided. Add what others say.

What would you do if you disagree with your manager?

Say it in private with data and a proposal. Listen to their context. If the decision stays, commit and help it succeed. Escalate only for safety or ethics.

How do you build a culture of quality?

Make the right way the easy way: fast tests, clear standards, good tooling and quick feedback. Praise good practice. Fix the cause when something fails.

How do you lead in an incident?

Stabilise first. Name an incident lead and a communicator. Give updates on a fixed schedule. Review without blame and track actions.

How do you drive adoption of a tool across teams?

Start from their pain. Pilot with a willing team. Show numbers. Make adoption easy with templates and guides. Do not force it.

How do you argue for a refactor?

Convert the debt into business cost. Propose small steps that each ship value. Agree on a measure and a stop point.

How do you justify developer-experience work?

Measure the pain, convert it to cost, fix the top bottleneck and tie it to a delivery goal.

How do you decide with incomplete information?

Ask if the choice is reversible. Decide fast if it is. State assumptions. Set a check point.

How do you explain a complex idea to a non-technical person?

Lead with the answer. Use one analogy. Show cost, risk and time. Ask them to say it back.

Hiring manager: common questions

Why do you want to join UKG?

Give a real, specific reason: the product area, the scale, or the platform problems. Add what you can offer. Prepare one true fact about UKG before the call.

Why this role and not a management role?

Say that you like technical depth and leading through design and mentoring. Say that you respect management. Be honest and positive.

What are your strengths?

Pick two that fit the role. Give a proof for each. Example: building shared test and delivery platforms that many teams use.

What is a weakness?

Choose a real one that you work on. Say what you do about it. Example: you used to take on too much alone, and now you delegate and write guides.

Where do you see yourself in three years?

Say that you want to grow in scope: owning a larger platform area and growing other leads. Link it to what the team needs.

Tell me about a time you received critical feedback.

Use SBI. Say what the feedback was, what you felt, what you changed and the result. Show that you act on feedback.

How do you handle pressure and deadlines?

Clarify the real deadline. Cut scope, not quality. Communicate early. Protect the team from panic. Review after.

Do you have any questions for us?

Always ask. Use the list in the last chapter. Good questions show how you think.

AI, MCP and Claude Code

What is MCP?

The Model Context Protocol is an open standard that connects AI apps to tools and data. A server exposes tools, resources and prompts. A client in the AI app discovers and calls them.

MCP versus REST API in one sentence?

An API is a contract for developer-written code. MCP is a standard that lets an AI agent discover and use tools at run time. An MCP server usually wraps an API.

When would you not use MCP?

For a fixed, deterministic pipeline step, a high-volume call or a strict latency path. Call the API directly.

What are tools, resources and prompts in MCP?

Tools are actions the model can call. Resources are read-only data. Prompts are reusable templates that a user can start.

Which transports does MCP use?

stdio for local servers and streamable HTTP for remote, shared servers. Check the current spec for details.

How many tools should a server expose?

Few, shaped around user tasks. Many tiny tools confuse the model and use up context.

What is prompt injection?

Untrusted text that tries to give the model new instructions. Limit damage with least privilege, approval for risky actions and treating tool output as data.

What makes a model call safe in a pipeline?

Schema validation, retries with a fallback, human approval for risky actions, logging, cost limits and a kill switch.

What is an evaluation set?

A fixed set of examples with known good answers. It runs in CI on every prompt or model change and blocks a release when the score drops.

Can a model judge grade a model?

Yes for fuzzy quality, but it has bias. Calibrate it with human labels and spot-check it. Use exact checks first.

What is CLAUDE.md?

A file in the repository with project instructions that Claude Code loads each session: commands, standards and conventions.

What are hooks in Claude Code?

Scripts that run at set points, such as after an edit. They make rules deterministic, for example run lint, or block edits to a protected file.

What are subagents and skills?

A subagent is a helper with its own context and tools, such as a security reviewer. A skill is packaged instructions and scripts that load when needed.

How do you run Claude Code in CI?

Use headless mode with claude -p and a clear prompt, or the official GitHub Action. Limit permissions. Send the output to a person.

What can Claude Code do besides writing code?

Explore a codebase, turn bugs into failing tests, migrate many files, read Terraform plans for risk, draft runbooks, generate test data and summarise pull requests.

Who owns AI-written code?

The author who submits it. It gets the same review, tests and security checks as other code.

What should never go into a prompt?

Secrets, credentials and customer or personal data, unless the tool and policy approve it.

What is A2A?

Agent2Agent is a protocol for agents from different vendors to talk to each other. MCP connects an agent to tools. A2A connects agents to agents.

What does UKG say about its AI agents?

UKG says its Bryte AI agents have human review and approval checkpoints, and customers choose which tasks agents can complete alone. Cite the press release, not a guess.

Chapter 10

Questions to ask them

Always ask two or three. Pick the ones that match who is in the room. Good questions show how you think.

For the hiring manager

  1. What does success look like for this role in the first six months and the first year?
  2. What is the biggest technical or delivery problem the team has right now?
  3. How do Staff engineers work with product and with architects here?
  4. How are technical decisions made and recorded?
  5. What does the on-call and incident process look like?
  6. How does the team handle technical debt and quality?
  7. How do you measure the health of the team and the platform?
  8. What did the last Staff engineer here do well?
  9. What would make you say, in a year, that this hire was a great one?
  10. How does the team grow its engineers, and what support exists for mentoring?
  11. How do your teams use Claude and Claude Code today beyond writing and reviewing code?
  12. How do you decide which AI-generated changes need extra review?

For the architect

  1. Which architecture decisions are you most proud of, and which would you change?
  2. How do you keep architecture consistent across teams without slowing them?
  3. What are the biggest scaling or reliability risks in the system today?
  4. How do you handle data consistency across services?
  5. What is your approach to observability and SLOs?
  6. How do you decide what to build and what to buy?
  7. How do teams share platform and testing tooling?
  8. What is the plan for legacy parts of the system?
  9. How do you review and approve design documents?
  10. What technology bets are you considering in the next two years?
  11. How do you test and evaluate AI features before release?
  12. Do you plan to expose internal APIs through MCP servers, and how do you control access?
  13. How do agent actions get approval and audit in your products?
